The enemy-level event also has no producer in the shown code. There is now no code path from lethal health to the entity-destruction method. This strengthens the death-lifecycle finding: even a consumer subscribing to the derived `EnemyHealth.OnKilled` property would not hear the base event used by `Health.Kill`. |
| Arc targeting factory metadata is mislabeled | `ArcTargetingData` is the type used by `ArcTargeting`, but its `[CreateAssetMenu]` declares `fileName = "ProjectileTargetingData"` and menu path `Data/Targeting/ProjectileTargetingData`. | The authoring surface produces an Arc data type under Projectile naming. | Data migration adds valid-looking but zero runtime wrappers | New `EnemyMovementData` and child scalar assets are created with zero values and null variable references; new Player targeting runtime data starts with empty tag and ignored-target lists. | Arc code specialization is nominal, not shared composition | `ArcTargeting` is added as a third full targeting implementation with its own `Data`, config copying, random source, caches and physics scans; Arc’s own code switches from generic `Targeting` to `ArcTargeting`. | Arc has a type suitable for Arc-specific configuration, but common mechanics remain copied. The patch therefore turns the earlier broken one-type split into role-specific classes without delivering a common implementation boundary. |

**Cross-file conclusion:** `4fe419cb` repairs the removed-Targeting symbol at the Player source level and introduces meaningful specializations, but it is not a clean recovery of the preceding patch. It copies the targeting algorithm three times with identical defects, leaves the EnemyHealth `Stats` member unresolved, removes the Health→Enemy destruction subscription, and drops the base movement component requirement for EnemyMovement. The prefab/data churn is large enough to obscure these lost connections; review of serialized references is essential here. No compile or Unity run was performed, so the compile issue is source-proven and the death/movement findings are traced code-contract failures, not play-mode observations.

#### Hunk-level semantic supplement: `74384e20` — Health becomes four copied implementations, with authored data only partly wired

The patch removes both shared `Health` and `StationHealth`, replaces them with an `IHealth` interface, and rewrites Player, Enemy, PlayerStation and EnemyStation health as direct `ExtendedMonoBehaviour` implementations. It also updates projectile lookups to query `IHealth`, and adds a damage-indicator reference to each static health-data type. This is a broad ownership change across runtime behavior, configuration and serialized component fields.

| Area | Patch evidence | Semantic result |
|---|---|---|
| Shared health behavior is copied four times | The deleted `Health` base previously owned damage calculation, defense/armor penetration, critical-strike handling, regeneration, damage indicators, healing, kill event, and knockback. The repeated implementations already diverge: only PlayerHealth retains the old critical-strike path; EnemyStationHealth adds a separate five-times-damage roll; PlayerStationHealth and EnemyHealth omit critical strikes. Future fixes to defense, regeneration, death idempotence or damage presentation now need four coordinated edits. |
| EnemyHealth Stats null after serialized-field rename | `EnemyHealth` now declares `[SerializeField] private Stats stats` and dereferences `stats.RandomChanceMultiplier` during `Start`. The `SmolEnemy.prefab` still serializes the old field name `Stats: {fileID: 0}` under the same EnemyHealth MonoScript GUID; this commit does not change that prefab. | Unity serializes by field name; `Stats` does not populate lowercase `stats`, and the serialized old value is explicitly null. On this prefab the first `Start` access is therefore a source/asset-provable null dereference unless some unshown runtime injection occurs; the inspected code contains no such injection. This is the concrete follow-up to the missing `Stats` member recorded in `4fe419cb`: the compile-time symbol was added, but the serialized dependency was not migrated or initialized. |
| New damage-indicator data is dead configuration | All four health data classes add `DamageIndicatorPrefab`; `PlayerHealthRuntimeData.Initialize` copies it and EnemyHealth/EnemyStationHealth copy it into a property. `PlayerStationHealth.Start` never assigns its property. All four `IndicateDamage` methods still call `Resources.Load<GameObject>("Prefabs/DamageIndicator")` and instantiate that fixed resource. The commit changes no health-data assets to assign the new field. | The advertised authored customization does not control the indicator. For most types the property is unused; for PlayerStationHealth it is also left null. This patch adds configuration surface without routing the effect through it. The fixed Resources lookup remains the real owner and can silently return null if the path is absent. |
| Player-health Stats has competing unused ownership | `PlayerHealth` adds a serialized private `Stats stats` field, but its runtime values are initialized through `PlayerHealthRuntimeData.Initialize(Data)`, which reads the separate `Stats` field on the runtime-data ScriptableObject. The new private field is not read in the class. | The serialized component now presents a second Stats slot that does not affect health. The runtime-data asset is the actual multiplier source. This invites authors to edit the wrong field and leaves component/data ownership unclear. |
| Kill event assignment discards authored listeners | Every rewritten class assigns `OnKilled = new UnityEvent()` in `Start`; the properties set the serialized backing fields. `PlayerHealthRuntimeData.Initialize` separately constructs state, but does not create/restore the event listeners. Existing serialized health event data/prefab values are not migrated by this 26-file patch. | Any UnityEvent instance serialized on the component is replaced at startup, so its persistent callbacks are lost. The new interface surfaces `OnKilled`, but initialization clears the very listeners that the serialized event is meant to carry. | Enemy death no longer clears EnemyRuntimeSet | `EnemyHealth.Kill` now directly sets its local IsAlive false, raises its own OnKilled, emits a sound, calls `Destroy(gameObject)`, and then creates drops. The previous `Enemy.Kill` removed the enemy from `EnemyRuntimeSet`; `Enemy.Start`’s Health.OnKilled subscription was already removed by `4fe419cb`. `Enemy` is not changed here. | The direct-destroy rewrite restores destruction after the previous commit severed the Health→Enemy.Kill route, but bypasses `Enemy.Kill` and its runtime-set removal. The `EnemyRuntimeSet` retains a destroyed Unity object unless another cleanup hook removes it; the inspected Enemy implementation has no `OnDestroy`/disable removal path. This is a source-level lifecycle leak risk, not a play-mode observation. |
| Player-station data property is never initialized | `PlayerStationHealth` implements `IHealth.DamageIndicatorPrefab` with an auto-property but its `Start` initializes Health/MaxHealth/Regeneration/Defense/IsAlive and never copies `Data.DamageIndicatorPrefab`; unlike the Enemy variants, it has no assignment. | The interface contract is non-null-capable but the implementation does not fulfill it. Current `IndicateDamage` ignores the property, hiding the defect; any consumer that starts relying on the new interface field receives null for player stations. |
| Health interface is broad and Unity-bound | `IHealth` exposes mutable-wrapper domain types, a GameObject prefab, UnityEvent and all operations including `IndicateDamage` and `Knockback`. Projectile call sites switch to `GetComponentInParent<IHealth>()` and immediately invoke `Damage` with no null guard. | The decoupling is from a shared base class, not from Unity/runtime concerns. The interface groups state, presentation, and effects, and its methods still depend on Unity objects. A target that has no IHealth still produces a null lookup followed by a dereference, as before; the new interface has not added validation or damage-routing diagnostics. |
| Regeneration interval remains dead data | The new types all expose and initialize `RegenerationTime` and `RegenerationTimer`, but their pauseable update calls `Heal(RegenerationAmount.Value * Time.deltaTime)` every frame. **Cross-file conclusion:** `74384e20` repairs the previous EnemyHealth unresolved-`Stats` source reference by adding a component field, but the prefab still contains a null, differently named serialized slot; the code change trades a compile-time defect for a likely startup null failure on the reviewed enemy prefab. The larger semantic move removes shared health behavior without supplying a shared service/policy, then diverges in combat rules across four copies. The new damage-indicator data is not used and no corresponding data assets are migrated. Direct enemy destruction also bypasses the runtime-set cleanup formerly owned by `Enemy.Kill`. These are conclusions from the exact source and Unity YAML revisions, not from a compile or play-mode run.

| Interface extraction is only partly generic | `ExperienceRuntimeSet<T>` derives from `RuntimeSet<IExperience>` but never uses `T`; its CreateAssetMenu still says `ExampleComponentRuntimeSet`. `IExperience` contains only `AddExperience(float)`, and `ExperienceOrb` now calls `GetComponent<IExperience>()` then invokes it without a null check. The old abstract `Experience` source is deleted. | The interface narrows the caller’s required capability, but the generic parameter is vestigial and the asset-creation label is stale. The orb’s component lookup is still a hard runtime prerequisite with no diagnostic path; this is not resilience gained by interface dispatch. |
| Runtime-set abstraction remains a list wrapper | `RuntimeSet<T>` stores a `List<T>`, appends unique values, removes values, and clears them in `Initialize`; it does not remove destroyed Unity objects automatically. | This is generic storage, not a lifecycle-aware entity set. **Cross-file conclusion:** `a90c72c1` repairs PlayerStation’s serialized targeting reference, but introduces more copied query code and adds an EnemyStation targeter without attaching it to the prefab. The interface-based experience call narrows coupling, while its runtime-set specialization contains an unused type parameter and misleading editor label. Experience state is split between a runtime-data asset and a component Stats field, with the shipped prefab synchronizing them manually. The commit increases authored structure but does not converge the repeated behaviors or make their initialization contracts self-validating.

The checked default asset supplies these references, but no validation protects alternate or incomplete Stats assets. |

The aggregate getters are live; the derived movement/health/experience calculations are not. This is a confirmed propagation gap in the shown data flow unless some omitted system reinitializes these runtime records (none appears in the inspected initializer/call path). |

The runtime-data classes expose public mutable wrapper fields and `Initialize` replaces those fields during component `Start`. | These objects are asset-backed mutable state, not inherently per-entity runtime instances. If multiple spawned components reference one runtime-data asset, each initialization overwrites the same state and their health/energy/experience are shared. The default Player prefab points at one set; no clone/allocation step is shown in these paths. This is a reuse/lifecycle hazard established by the type and reference shape, though the default scene’s exact number of Player instances is not being inferred here. |
| Stat asset formulas move from data to code, but the editor layer remains bespoke | The concrete stat classes hard-code coefficients in property getters (e.g. most multipliers are `1 + Level * 0.1`, Fortitude and Endurance use `0.05`, Knowledge and Quickness decrease values, several integer increases scale directly with Level). The commit rewrites a large family of stat-specific Editor classes to fit the new property-based representation and keeps a custom `StatEditor`. | The data assets no longer author those formulas; changing balance now requires code edits and code review, while the Level/max-level state remains authored. Custom inspector maintenance is replicated across many near-identical stat classes rather than derived from a shared data/formula descriptor. This is a shift of balance ownership from assets to C#, not simply cleanup. |
| Movement effects remain a component lookup convention | `MovementEffect` declares `[RequireComponent(typeof(IMovement))]`, stores an `IMovement`, and resolves it with `GetComponent<IMovement>()`. `FreezeMovementEffect.Initialize` installs a timed multiplier and destroys itself when its timer event fires. | The effect is now written against an interface, but Unity’s `RequireComponent` is type-based and the attribute names an interface rather than the concrete component Unity can add. The method also assumes the host has a suitable movement component and an initialized `Speed`; it does not validate either. This is not a self-contained effect attachment contract. |
| Energy and movement behavior still use frame/fixed-step assumptions | `PlayerMovement` applies force in `OnPauseableFixedUpdate` but energy generation/consumption in `OnPauseableUpdate`; those per-frame adjustments add/subtract configured values without multiplying by `Time.deltaTime`. Acceleration normalizes the input vector and applies `Speed` as a force each fixed tick. | Energy drain and recharge depend on render/update frame rate while force depends on physics tick rate. This is present in the code at this revision; the balance parameters may have been tuned around it, but the patch supplies no rate-normalization policy. |
| Player callbacks are promoted from the scene to the prefab | The preceding commit added scene-instance overrides for the four movement events. This patch removes those overrides and serializes the same particle-spawning callbacks on the `PlayerMovement` component in `Player.prefab`. The component invokes only the accelerating pair in its own code. | The event wiring is now reusable with the prefab rather than attached only to one scene instance. `OnMovementEnabled` and `OnMovementDisabled` remain unraised in `PlayerMovement`’s own methods; whether an external caller invokes them is not demonstrated by this hunk review. |
| Player attribute wiring is added alongside the Stats aggregate | The Player prefab gains an `Attributes` asset reference while retaining `Stats`, plus the separate runtime data references. Attribute is an aggregate of Stat references and `Refresh` propagates Attribute.Level to each Stat.MaxLevel. | The intended graph now includes both direct stat access and attribute-group access. They are related but distinct assets, and both are wired at Player level; there is no single explicit startup routine in this patch proving their cross-reference graph and lifecycle are valid. The ExperienceOrb caller regresses from the just-added `IExperience` seam to a concrete PlayerExperience dependency, so the interface experiment is not retained as the interaction boundary in this commit. |

**Cross-file conclusion:** `d07cc279` is a meaningful recovery and integration step: gameplay values return, the Player’s movement event connections move into the reusable prefab, and stat access gets a coherent facade. At the same time, balance formulas become hard-coded, runtime multipliers snapshot stat levels at initialization, and mutable runtime wrappers remain stored in asset-backed ScriptableObjects. The movement schema also leaves a serialized reference to a deleted BaseEnergy asset, and EnergyBar/UI state continues to point directly at runtime-data assets. The source strongly supports “the scene mostly works again” as the owner’s contemporaneous assessment, but does not prove a clean compile, complete recovery, or correct progression updates.

#### Hunk-level semantic supplement: `fd5ceda3` — global pause registry and scene-lifecycle rewrite

The commit is titled “Mostly finished work on Data Modularization / Issue: Pausing is broken.” It deletes the old application/game/initialization/main-menu manager classes, adds a new `MenuManager`, and rewrites `GameManager` as the owner of pause state, scene loading, audio and runtime-set reset. It also changes screen setup from a canvas-driven initialization pass to individual component `Start` methods, changes generator setup from discovery to an authored list, and removes the Initialization scene contents.

| Area | Patch evidence | Semantic result |
|---|---|---|
| Manager ownership and lifecycle | `ApplicationManager`, `GameSceneManager`, `InitializationSceneManager`, `MainMenuSceneManager`, and the empty `Manager`/`SceneManager` base classes are deleted. `MenuManager` becomes a scene singleton responsible for quit/load, while `GameManager` owns pause/resume and game-scene loading. | This is a substantial simplification of the previous inheritance shell, but lifecycle authority is still split by scene and static singleton. Duplicate managers call `Destroy(gameObject)` but continue through `Awake`, so a duplicate `GameManager` still initializes shared `RuntimeSets` and resets its local pause flag in that frame. No persistent cross-scene manager remains. |
| Pause membership | A new `ExtendedMonoBehaviourRuntimeSet` is added, `RuntimeSets` includes it, and `ExtendedMonoBehaviour.Start` registers each component; `GameManager.Pause/Resume` enumerates that list. `OnDestroy` removes the instance. | This is the first explicit shared pause registry and addresses the prior ad-hoc manager scan. It is only reliable if every subclass reaches the base `Start` and every destroy occurs while `GameManager.Instance.RuntimeSets` remains valid. Several descendants define their own private `Start` (including `PlayerMovement`), so base lifecycle dispatch is a critical Unity-version/runtime integration point that cannot be proven from source alone. `OnDestroy` has no null/lifecycle guard. The registry list is mutated during callbacks if a callback destroys a member, while the caller is enumerating it. |
| Pause state and callback ordering | `GameManager.Pause` sets manager pause true before iterating; each component’s `Pause` invokes `OnPause` then sets its own `IsPaused`. Resume sets manager pause false before callbacks; each component invokes `OnResume` then clears its own pause flag. `PlayerMovement` saves and zeroes velocity on pause, then restores it on resume. | The pause callbacks execute while the component still reports its previous state: `OnPause` sees component `IsPaused == false`; `OnResume` sees `IsPaused == true`. This may be intentional for callback semantics, but no contract states it. If the registry misses a component, its own `Update`/`FixedUpdate` continues because this mechanism does not change Unity time scale. Non-`ExtendedMonoBehaviour` systems are unaffected by this pause path. |
| New global instance tracking in following fix | This commit’s runtime-set registry is temporary; the next `7e6d2335` deletes the set and replaces it with a process-static `ExtendedMonoBehaviour.Instances` list populated in `Awake`. | The boundary changes almost immediately, before there is evidence of a stable lifecycle abstraction. The change improves availability before `Start`, but moves ownership from an authored registry resource to mutable static state with domain-reload/scene-lifetime implications. |
| Screen and canvas initialization | `Canvas.Initialize` and `InterfaceCanvas`’s screen-discovery array/loop are removed. Individual screens call their protected `Initialize()` from `Start`; Canvas still owns a stack. Screen visibility now reads serialized `Canvas` references. | This removes reflective/scene-wide discovery, but changes setup into distributed component lifecycle logic. Every screen must now have correct authored references and initialization order. `SetVisibility(false)` calls `Stack.Peek()` without checking emptiness; visibility and stack state can diverge if called out of order. `SetVisibility(true)` can push the same screen again because it does not reject an already-visible screen. These are source-level edge cases. |
| Pause menu integration | `GameCanvas` handles Escape by showing the PauseScreen and calling `GameManager.Pause`; when a screen is already open, Escape hides the top screen. The Game scene deletes its `GameSceneManager` object. | Pause is now a UI-owned action routed to the new singleton. The stack is therefore a gameplay-pause authority: the last screen closing resumes the game. The shown code does not establish how other modal screens, focus changes, or scene teardown interact with this rule. |
| Generated-object initialization | `Generators.Initialize` becomes `Start` and no longer discovers child `Generator` components; the Game scene supplies a serialized generator list. `Background.Initialize` also becomes `Start`. | This trades runtime discovery for explicit authored composition, which is clearer if all scene/prefab instances have complete lists. It introduces a setup-order dependency: consumers that expect generation before their own `Start` have no explicit ordering contract, and an incomplete list silently omits generators. |
| Audio initialization | `GameSoundHandler` and `MenuSoundHandler` call the now non-virtual `SoundHandler.Initialize()` from their own `Start`; manager-driven explicit initialization is removed. | Audio configuration is moved closer to the components that own it, but scene-specific setup ordering is now implicit. `GameManager` still exposes a `GameSoundHandler` reference for energy depletion, so initialization and use remain coupled through a manager field. |
| Serialized scene/build graph | `Initialization.unity` is deleted in this commit, while `EditorBuildSettings.asset` at the same revision still lists that exact path enabled. The `MainMenu.unity` patch is empty, and GitHub’s file endpoint does not provide content at either checked revision, so no conclusion is drawn about its scene payload. | The enabled build-scene entry pointing at a deleted scene is a concrete repository-level inconsistency. It likely makes the startup/build configuration invalid until the scene entry is removed or the scene restored; no Unity build was run to observe the exact failure. This directly qualifies the “mostly finished” title. |
| Player energy and menu reset | Energy drain/recharge remains in `Update` with no `Time.deltaTime`, while force is applied in `FixedUpdate`; Hardreset now also invokes `Stats.Uncheat` and `Attributes.Uncheat`. | Frame-rate dependence remains in the energy model. The reset path mutates referenced ScriptableObject data graphs, so whether it resets only a local run or shared authored state depends on how those assets are instantiated; the patch does not define that persistence boundary. |

**Cross-file conclusion:** the patch replaces scene-manager inheritance with explicit scene components, adds a centralized pause registry, and changes UI/generator setup to authored references. These are coherent directions, but the registry lifecycle and screen stack remain fragile, and an enabled build-settings entry still names the deleted Initialization scene. The following commit immediately replaces the runtime-set registry with a static instance list, showing that the pause ownership model was still being revised. Findings here are source-level; no Unity compile, scene load, or play-mode run was performed.

#### Hunk-level semantic supplement: `3f654f42` and `0bf0ba93` — persistence shifts from JSON asset snapshots to runtime save APIs

`3f654f42` has no C# changes. It adds default JSON representations for Attribute/Stat state and broadly regenerates metadata/GUIDs for corresponding assets; its title says persistence has started, but this patch only introduces serialized shapes. `0bf0ba93` is explicitly “WIP Data Persistency” and adds the first code path. The earlier review shorthand that this patch “adds the `ISaveable` contract” was wrong: it deletes `ISaveable.cs`, removes that interface from `Attribute` and `Stat`, and replaces those per-object methods with explicit aggregate orchestration. `Coins` and `Tokens` still contain `Save`/`Load`, but no longer share a common interface.

| Area | Patch evidence | Semantic result |
|---|---|---|
| Data model and file-format direction | `3f654f42` adds default JSON snapshots for Attribute and Stat state. `0bf0ba93` adds public nested `DataContainer` shapes and puts explicit load/save loops on aggregate `Attributes`/`Stats` ScriptableObjects. It deletes `ISaveable.cs` and removes the interface from `Attribute`/`Stat`; `Coins`/`Tokens` retain their methods but are not interface implementations. The new non-default JSON files set all Attribute and Stat `maxLevel` fields to 0; `JSONUtil.LoadData` prefers these files over `Default/`. | The persisted zeroes shadow the authored defaults instead of falling back to them. The follow-up `cf2b6964` changes only the ten Attribute `maxLevel` values to 10; it leaves the 34 Stat JSON `maxLevel` values at zero. This is a JSON-backed load/save path, but not a generic saveable-object facility. Persistence ownership becomes split: aggregate loops own Attributes/Stats, while currency assets retain independent `OnEnable`/`OnDisable` behavior. Serialized ScriptableObject fields and JSON become competing representations; load-on-enable and save-on-disable determine which wins at each lifecycle boundary. |
| Save/load entry point | `Attributes.OnEnable` loads ten named Attribute JSON files; `OnDisable` saves them. `Stats` similarly loads/saves its 34 member stats. Each container resolves related objects by names through aggregate lookup functions. The later `59ed56a6` patch adds an Attribute-level listener that copies the Attribute level into every member Stat’s maximum. | The orchestration is centralized but hard-coded across every member, and persisted identity is a display/domain name rather than a stable ID. Renames or duplicate names can misassociate or fail to resolve data. Missing-file fallback to `Default/` exists in `JSONUtil`, but errors are thrown if both locations are absent; no schema version or migration is shown. The later listener encodes a rule at load time and has no demonstrated duplicate-subscription guard. |
| Runtime value wrappers | `Variable<T>` and `ComputedVariable<T>` now expose `IsInitialized`, initialize their UnityEvent before assigning the initial value, suppress change notification until initialization, and return default values before initialization. | This specifically fixes premature event use during construction; the previously suspected generic event mismatch was incorrect and is removed from this review. The wrapper still reports default(T) for uninitialized state, which can conceal missing initialization as a plausible zero/false value. |
| Save destination and write behavior | `JSONUtil.dataPath` is `Application.dataPath + "/Data/"`; writes create directories and overwrite files with `StreamWriter`, while reads prefer the writable path and fall back to `Default/`. | For desktop installs, `Application.dataPath` normally points inside the installed application directory, not the platform’s per-user writable save-data directory. This makes writes vulnerable to permission failure and couples mutable progress to installation layout. Writes are not atomic, exceptions are not handled, and there is no backup or recovery path. This is a strong portability/deployment risk inferred from the source path, not a demonstrated failed save on a built player. |
| Aggregate asset mutability and lifecycle | `Attributes.OnEnable`/`Stats.OnEnable` load by iterating serialized asset references and immediately dereference those references; their `OnDisable` methods synchronously save every item. Currency `Coins`/`Tokens` independently load/save themselves on enable/disable. | Persistence is spread across aggregate and leaf assets without a common contract, explicit flush point, or coordinated transaction. A missing reference/file or failed write can abort a lifecycle callback; there is no local recovery path. Runtime variables are assigned into referenced ScriptableObjects, so shared asset references can share mutable state. No distinct profile object or save-service boundary is shown. Unity callback ordering and failure behavior were not runtime-tested. |
| Inspector/editor UI | The patch removes “Create default data!” buttons from Attribute and Stat inspectors while moving default fallback into `JSONUtil.LoadData`. | Default provisioning becomes an implicit file convention rather than an editor action. The fallback supports runtime startup only if every corresponding file exists under `Assets/Data/Default`; the commit’s new user-data snapshots are not themselves a complete default tree. |

**Cross-file conclusion:** persistence has a source-level JSON read/write path, but the commit’s actual ownership is inconsistent: Attributes/Stats are saved by aggregate lifecycle loops, currency objects save themselves, and the shared `ISaveable` abstraction is removed. Names act as identities, members are enumerated manually, app-install paths are used as writable storage, writes overwrite in place, and save/load is coupled to Unity asset lifecycle. This is not a durable or portable save contract demonstrated by the source. The work is explicitly WIP; no player build or runtime save was executed.

#### Hunk-level semantic supplement: `92302b11` and `59ed56a6` — UI wrapper correction and attribute-to-stat propagation

`92302b11` changes the Attribute/Stat level UI to render `.Value` from wrapped variables, correcting a consumer/schema mismatch introduced by the data-reference migration. `59ed56a6` adds an `OnValueChanged` listener in `Attributes.LoadAttribute`, iterating every `attribute.Stats` entry and assigning `stat.MaxLevel.Value = attribute.Level.Value`.

This creates one explicit progression rule: an Attribute’s current level is also the cap for every contained Stat. It is installed during data loading rather than declared as an invariant in the Attribute/Stat model, and repeated `LoadAttribute` calls add repeated listeners because there is no unsubscribe/duplicate guard. Listener lifecycle is therefore coupled to reload count. The UI correction only fixes representation; it does not validate range constraints, persistence, or refresh behavior across every editor/runtime path.

Generator chooses asteroid prefabs from a simple array. | The first shape combines behavior, random sampling, physics, and lifecycle registration on one MonoBehaviour, with authored curves and runtime set as its data contract. `Start` and `OnDestroy` dereference the authored RuntimeSet without validation. The Z clamp contradicts the introduction of 3D rigidbody/model assets unless the gameplay plane is intentionally constrained; that intent is not stated. |
| `5f81cffc` — weighted prefab and mesh physics | Adds cached MeshFilter/MeshCollider/Rigidbody references, random mesh choice, size-scaled velocity/mass, weighted asteroid prefab selection, matching-length validation and an `enabled` check before generation. | This introduces two layers of content selection (generator chooses a prefab; asteroid chooses a mesh) and parallel prefab/weight arrays. Their equal-length check is useful, but empty arrays and nonpositive weights are not guarded in the shown path. The mass formula uses the curve scale cubed while transform scale is the same sampled scale; it assumes a fixed density and a curve with strictly positive values. |
| `4de002ee` — rarity/size become array-indexed enums | Replaces random-mesh selection with `Size` and `Rarity` enums, `SizeWeights`/`RarityWeights`, arrays of meshes/materials, and per-rarity/size authored assets; removes the earlier weighted prefab chooser and `Rarity` type file. Random weighted indices are cast directly to enum values, which then index the mesh/material arrays. | The content model changes substantially again: rarity/size become separate dimensions and prefab diversity is collapsed into one prefab. Correctness now depends on weight-array length, enum ordinal order and asset-array ordering all matching; those invariants are not validated. It scales transforms by `100 * randomScale`, while mass still uses `randomScale³ * density`, so physical mass no longer follows the actual transform scale if those values are intended to share units. |
| `bfcef7d7` — basic resource-bearing asteroid | Adds `ResourceDeposit`, `AsteroidSizeData`, `AsteroidRarityData` and a `Resource` asset type. `AsteroidData` now references arrays of size/rarity data; rarity data contains Resources and parallel deposit curves plus material. The asteroid chooses rarity/size by weighted indices, samples deposits, then chooses a mesh and assigns visual/physics components. The generator returns to one authored prefab. | This is the most compositional model so far: physical size/mesh and rarity/material/resources are authored independently, and generated asteroids expose deposits. However, the enum-to-array positional contract remains implicit. Each rarity asset’s `Resources` and `Deposits` arrays must align, neither that constraint nor the expected set lengths are validated, and random mesh selection assumes the size has at least one mesh. Runtime deposit quantity is a sampled float but no collection interaction is added in this change. |

**Cross-commit conclusion:** asteroid development is exploratory, not a linear completion: the prefab-selection model is replaced, enum-indexed data arrays are introduced, then rarity/size get separate ScriptableObject shapes and resource deposits. This is a useful authored-data direction, but the emerging “content” contract relies on positional invariants spread across enum declarations and Unity assets rather than keyed validated records. The source proves the model changed rapidly; no runtime evidence establishes whether any of these snapshots spawned correctly.

The script-execution-order edits treat lifecycle ordering as a global numeric configuration rather than an explicit inventory readiness contract. |
| `4b90dfad` — changed-slot notification | Replaces an untyped content event with `UnityEvent<int[]>` and updates Hotbar to refresh only reported slots. | This is a focused and valuable UI invalidation contract: mutations can identify affected slots. | `155daef3` — asteroid deposits become world pickups | Adds `ResourceDeposit.DropAll`, which resolves a ResourceItemData and prefab by resource name, splits deposit quantity into `MaxAmount` chunks, instantiates resource objects with randomized offsets, and sets each stack amount. It adds `ItemObjectPrefabs` as a name-to-prefab map. | This connects asteroid destruction to the item pipeline, but performs two dictionary lookups whose backing maps are again built only in `OnValidate`; no runtime initialization is shown for either `ItemDatas` or `ItemObjectPrefabs`. Thus the editor path may work while the standalone player path can hit a null dictionary. The loop also emits one final chunk even if its amount is zero; item setters permit zero despite their exception wording claiming zero is invalid. |
| `57ea0542` — physical pickup scale/mass | Adds `Density` to amount/count data and refreshes resource pickup rigidbody mass and transform size from current amount, with a configured minimum/maximum object scale. | This gives resource quantity visible/physical consequences. It assumes nonzero `MaxAmount` and appropriate positive density. `Amount=0` maps to the minimum visible scale and zero mass, which may or may not be a desired resting pickup. No numerical/physics test is included. |
| `b7bd347f` — partial pickup | Changes `ItemContainer.AddItem` to return a remaining item and changed slot indices. `ItemObject` leaves the remaining stack in the world or destroys itself when no remainder remains; the resource object refreshes after amount change. | This is an actual semantic improvement over all-or-nothing pickup and carries UI invalidation through the same operation. However, the shown item-container algorithm can place a stack in the first empty slot before trying later compatible partial stacks, so it does not preferentially consolidate. It mutates the incoming item object while filling existing stacks and reports changed slots, but the API has no transaction/result object for invalid content or callbacks that fail midway. |

**Cross-file conclusion:** the item pipeline is built end-to-end in rapid steps—authored resource data, runtime item objects, inventory slots, hotbar rendering, asteroid drops, physical mass/size, and partial pickup. The central semantic failure is that the new item/prefab dictionaries are populated by editor-only validation callbacks while their consumers run at gameplay time. Other concrete weaknesses include invalid item equality semantics, a stack-overflowing hotbar getter, null-unsafe container scans and lifecycle-order dependence. The source shows real feature integration, but the player-build path is not established by the authored editor data or commit labels.

**Cross-file conclusion:** the inventory evolves from data storage to a full drag/drop/cursor/world-pickup loop. Ownership remains distributed among `InventoryHotbar`, `InventorySlot`, `InventoryItem`, `ItemContainer`, and `ItemObject`, with setters and UnityEvents acting as implicit synchronization. The code repeatedly responds to concrete lifecycle/UI defects with localized ordering or hierarchy adjustments. This is substantive UX work, but the implementation does not yet articulate one authoritative inventory mutation path or guarantee event initialization independently of frame order.

**Cross-commit conclusion:** “Weapon as inventory content” is a coherent direction, but its implementation changes across several ownership seams at once: data asset, runtime instance, station inventory, player component, target selection, cooldown, and UI interaction. Some failures are repaired quickly; other semantics are silently weakened (default weapons become capacity only, slot-level change events become generic invalidations). The recurring issue is not simply incomplete code: each subsystem boundary is being redesigned independently, so the compiler catches some type mismatches while serialized authoring and runtime ownership can still drift apart. No Unity build or play session was available to determine which intermediate snapshots shipped or how the timer behaved in practice.

**Cross-commit conclusion:** the mission feature grows rapidly from names and serialized data into a runtime factory, provider, manager, active slot, and reward pipeline. #### Hunk-level semantic supplement: `adb83aa9` — runtime-stat migration leaves constructors and startup disconnected

The patch adds regeneration-time data, introduces mutable `PlayerHealthRuntimeData` and `PlayerMovementRuntimeData` ScriptableObjects, and moves health/movement calculations toward `FloatStat`/`IntStat` modifiers. It also adds temporary movement effects and rewrites player/enemy movement around the new stats. The source shape is ambitious, but several new paths are not connected end to end:

| Changed area | Source evidence | Semantic finding |
|---|---|---|
| `Stat<T>.BaseValue` and constructor | The setter assigns `BaseValue = value` rather than `baseValue = value`; the constructor calls that setter before initializing `OnValueChanged`. | **Confirmed source defect:** constructing either `FloatStat` or `IntStat` recursively re-enters the setter indefinitely. The initial stat abstraction therefore cannot be instantiated as written; the new health and movement startup paths depend on this broken primitive. No runtime/compiler claim is made. |
| Timed stat modifiers | `AddTimedMultiplier`/`AddTimedIncrease` attach elapsed handlers, while both `Temporary*` constructors create a `System.Timers.Timer` without enabling or starting it. | The removal callback is present but the timer has no start path in these classes, so expiry is not established. The callback also runs on the timer event thread and mutates lists / raises UnityEvents there; Unity-facing consumers are not marshalled to the main thread by this code. This is a source-level lifecycle/thread-affinity concern, not measured runtime evidence. |
| `PlayerMovement.Start` versus `Movement.Initialize` | `Movement.Initialize` constructs `Speed`, movement events, `Rigidbody` and `Collider`. The new `PlayerMovement.Start` reads and modifies `Speed`, but never calls `Initialize(Data)`; `Movement` has no `Start`/`Awake` initializer. | **Confirmed disconnected initialization path:** `Speed.AddPermanentMultiplier` dereferences a value this class never creates, and the fixed-update path also depends on the uninitialized cached body/events. `EnemyMovement.Start` does call `Initialize(Data)`, so the two implementations of the base contract already diverge. |
| Player energy runtime state | `PlayerMovementRuntimeData` adds `MaxEnergy`, and authored `PlayerMovementData` adds `BaseMaxEnergy`; `PlayerMovement.Start` initializes current energy, consumption, generation and flags but never assigns `RuntimeData.MaxEnergy`. | The regeneration branch compares against the default/uninitialized maximum, so the newly declared cap is not wired into runtime state. Movement consumption/generation also omit `Time.deltaTime` in `OnPauseableUpdate`, making their effective rates frame-rate dependent. |
| `PlayerHealth` ownership and death state | `PlayerHealth.Start` initializes runtime fields and death dependencies instead of calling `Health.Initialize`. `Kill` tests `RuntimeData.IsAlive`, calls `base.Kill()`, but never sets `RuntimeData.IsAlive` false; `base.Kill()` only changes the separate inherited `isAlive` field. | The split leaves two alive flags with different owners. Repeated calls can pass the runtime guard and replay pause/audio/death-screen effects because the base mutation does not update the runtime-data flag. The `RegenerationTime`/`RegenerationTimer` fields are populated but the per-frame heal path does not consult them. |
| `FreezeMovementEffect` | `Initialize(float freezingSlowness)` ignores its argument and adds a hardcoded `0.75` multiplier for `10` seconds. `MovementEffect.Movement` is assigned only in `Start`, while initialization immediately dereferences it. | The call contract is misleading: callers cannot select the supplied strength, and initialization order must ensure `Start` has assigned `Movement` before `Initialize`. Adding and initializing the effect within one callback can violate that ordering. |

**Cross-cutting reading:** this is not simply a move from plain values to stat objects. It changes who owns runtime state (mutable ScriptableObject versus component fields), how initialization occurs (explicit `Initialize` versus Unity `Start`), and how time-limited effects execute (worker-thread timers). The new boundaries are declared together, but construction, startup, expiry and death transitions do not yet form one coherent lifecycle. These findings are based on the exact commit source; no build or runtime validation was performed.

| Commit | Patch evidence | Semantic result |
|---|---|---|

Task and mission identity again use global integer counters and GC finalizers; `Equals(object)` casts without type/null checks, while finalizers invoke UnityEvents. This fits the broader pattern of solving one local need with a library-like subsystem, then discarding it before its ownership/API is stabilized. UI rebuilding explicitly destroys and recreates children rather than updating by stable identity; acceptable for small lists, but object lifetime and listener cleanup need care. This is a source-level description only; no rendered UI inspection was available. |
| `797d7b41` — second item-drop design replaces prefab map | Removes `ItemObjectPrefabs`; asteroid deposits now request `ItemData.CreateItem()`, set quantity, and invoke `DropItem(position)`. | This removes a second name-keyed lookup table and delegates object creation to ItemData, simplifying one seam. It also makes the August item-factory path the new authoritative path after the prefab-map implementation had just been integrated. The available patch proves the call shape, not whether `CreateItem` initializes every concrete item correctly in the live scene. |
| `1e97739f` — mission task system shelved | Comments out task state, completion, unlocking and UI binding rather than removing the subsystem; creates `World` with only private `chunkSize=64` and `seed=0`, plus noise-map classes/editor. | This is an explicit scope pivot, but “shelved” leaves dead code and commented-out contracts in place. The new `World` is only a placeholder: no chunk collection, generation, seed flow, or scene integration exists yet. The actually implemented work is a Unity editor-facing noise-map generator. Its algorithm allocates a 2D float array, samples Unity Perlin per pixel/octave, normalizes values and maps heights to color. The path assumes a `MapDisplay` exists and that region thresholds cover all output; neither is validated. This should be described as procedural texture tooling, not as a generated playable world. |

**Cross-commit conclusion:** September’s mission implementation is not iterated to a stable feature; it is repeatedly reshaped, receives partial repairs, grows a task hierarchy, and is then disabled by commenting it out. At the pivot, world generation begins under that name while the `World` object itself remains empty. The real new capability is an editor-oriented noise visualization pipeline. The transition is important historically: it marks scope moving away from station/missions and toward procedural space/world concepts, but does not yet implement the later spatial simulation architecture.

#### Hunk-level semantic supplement: `142e9cf5` and `ddbab001` — save metadata is rediscovered, but the world is still not restored

The patch removes `SaveGameManager::default()` from plugin construction and inserts `init_save_game_manager` in Bevy `Startup`. That system scans `data/saves`, reads every directory entry as UTF-8 JSON, deserializes each into `SaveGameInfo { name }`, and inserts the collected list as a resource.

| Area | Patch evidence | Semantic result |
|---|---|---|
| Startup discovery | `read_dir("data/saves").unwrap()` is synchronous and relative to the process working directory. Directory iteration, file open/read and JSON parse all unwrap or panic. The loop does not filter by extension or require regular files. | This makes the save-list startup dependent on a pre-existing working-directory-relative folder and assumes every entry is a valid metadata JSON file. A missing folder, unrelated file, subdirectory or malformed record can abort startup. No source evidence here says the directory is provisioned before the plugin runs. |
| Persisted object | The only deserialized type is `SaveGameInfo`, which contains a single `name: String`. `handle_load_save_game` looks up that record and emits a confirmation containing a clone of it; it does not load a Universe or world payload. | The commit repairs discovery of save **names**, not restoration of a saved game world. The word “persistence” here is metadata persistence only. |
| Create/delete path (`142e9cf5`) | `handle_create_save_game` and `handle_delete_save_game` format `data/saves/{event.save_game_name}.json` directly from the supplied name and use `File::create`/`remove_file`; I found no path-component validation, parent-directory creation or non-panicking error result in these handlers. | The create/delete API lets UI input influence a filesystem path and treats ordinary I/O errors as process panics. If names can contain separators or traversal components, the operation can address paths outside the intended save directory; the UI validation and platform behavior were not established in this commit review. |
| Directory layout (`ddbab001`) | The next commit changes creation to `data/saves/{name}/info.json`, creates the directory recursively, and changes startup discovery to inspect only directory entries and open each `info.json`. Deletion removes that file and then calls `remove_dir_all` on the save directory. | This is a more extensible on-disk shape, but no additional save payload is written. The supplied name still participates directly in the directory path; absent validation in the reviewed handler, traversal or destructive-path consequences are possible, but actual reachability depends on caller-side validation not examined here. `remove_dir_all` also deletes any other files placed in that named directory. |
| Synchronization and durability (`142e9cf5`, `ddbab001`) | Create writes the JSON metadata synchronously, pushes the in-memory record, and emits confirmation. Delete removes the file/directory, then removes the first matching in-memory record and emits confirmation. Writes use `write_all` without a temporary file/rename or explicit flush-and-sync protocol. | The in-memory list follows the simple success path, but there is no transactional recovery if the filesystem mutation partially succeeds or the process exits during a write. This is not evidence of a durable, atomic save contract. |
| Adjacent shared-input change (`ddbab001`) | In the same commit, `ReceivedInput` is deleted, its event registration and writer are removed, and pressing Return no longer emits the input-field value or clears it. | Save-directory refactoring and text-entry submission semantics share one commit despite separate ownership. The patch proves the old Enter-submit path was removed; it does not show whether every consumer was removed or replaced, so downstream behavior needs a wider call-site check before claiming the text field remained usable. |

**Cross-commit conclusion:** the 2022 ScriptableObject/JSON approach was removed; the 2023 Rust reset introduced a different save-list format and then fixed when that list is loaded into Bevy. `142e9cf5` improves the list’s initialization timing; `ddbab001` gives each save a directory but still persists only its name. Neither restores Universe data. Startup depends on the expected metadata file being readable and valid for each save directory. The save-list label should therefore be read narrowly: metadata round-trip and enumeration are present, while full world persistence remains unimplemented in this path. No runtime execution or security test was performed.

#### Hunk-level semantic supplement: `7b388def` — the prototype removes Universe persistence before replacing it

About 52 minutes after the save-directory commit, `7b388def` introduces an empty `GameConfigurationPlugin` and a `LooCastBasePlugins` group, then removes the Universe persistence path. The diff is a compact but consequential reversal: the Universe resource loses `Serialize`/`Deserialize`; the complete `universe/systems.rs` implementation is deleted, including `create_universe`, `save_universe`, `load_universe` and `print_universe`; the Universe plugin module and resource references are removed or reduced. The `SaveGamePlugin` remains registered, so save-name records and their UI lifecycle survive as a separate feature from Universe state.

| Area | Patch evidence | Semantic result |
|---|---|---|
| Universe persistence | Removes the file read/write systems and Serde derives from `Universe`; the deleted loader had required `data/saves/universe.json` and inserted the decoded resource. | This abandons even the prototype’s single fixed-file Universe snapshot. No replacement payload path is introduced in this commit. The later save-slot metadata must not be read as world persistence. |
| Configuration boundary | Adds `GameConfigurationPlugin`, whose `build` method is empty. | The name establishes an architectural intention, but the diff provides no configuration schema, storage, defaults, or behavior. |
| Plugin composition | Adds `LooCastBasePlugins`, moving the application’s plugin list into a `PluginGroup`; also relocates `AppState` in `main.rs`. | This gives the application a named grouping seam, but does not yet prove independently configurable game/engine compositions or removable plugin ownership. The group still hardcodes the same first-party plugins. |
| Save metadata | Keeps `SaveGamePlugin` in the group while deleting Universe’s serializer and systems. | Save slots continue to describe metadata without an attached/restorable world in this snapshot. The structural split makes that semantic gap clearer rather than closing it. |

**Cross-commit consequence:** within roughly an hour, the sequence goes from fixed-file Universe loading, to a separate save-name manager, to per-save metadata directories, and then to deleting Universe persistence entirely. This is not an incremental implementation of one durable save design; it is adjacent experiments with different ownership and payload assumptions. The plugin group and configuration plugin foreshadow composability, but remain scaffolds. No historical build or runtime was performed.

#### Hunk-level semantic supplement: `40850c07` and `7d98cf2a` — staged “loading” is marker creation, then a synchronous foldback

`40850c07` creates a nominal pipeline: a confirmed save selection requests configuration; config confirmation requests state; state confirmation requests Universe; Universe confirmation is only printed. The concrete handlers do not deserialize those layers. Config and state each create `data/saves/<save>/config|state` only if the directory does not exist, create an empty `info.json` in that new directory, insert an empty `GameConfigManager`/`GameStateManager`, and immediately emit confirmation. If the directory already exists, no file is checked or read. The Universe handler at this point only inserts a zeroed `UniverseManager`; the saved Universe data deleted in `7b388def` is not reintroduced.

`7d98cf2a`, about 14 minutes later, removes the external `game_config` and `game_state` modules and folds directory creation/resource insertion directly into `GamePlugin::handle_load_game`. It introduces `LoadState` variants named for the stages and `FullyLoaded`, but the handler does not set a `NextState<LoadState>` or otherwise transition that state. `ConfigPlugin::build` and `StatePlugin::build` are empty. The same patch simplifies load/unload events and emits `LoadedGame`; a receiver is not established by this diff. This is a real simplification of the event cascade, but its result is an opaque synchronous routine with no payload validation or restoration, not a completed staged loader.

| Ownership seam | Source evidence | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Save identity to filesystem | Both handlers interpolate the save name into `data/saves/<name>/...`; earlier code has no path validation in the reviewed handler. | Save selection remains coupled to process CWD and mutable user-facing names. Directory creation failures panic. Whether callers constrain names remains unverified. |
| Config/state “loading” | Empty managers are inserted; `info.json` is created empty only on first directory creation; there is no read/deserialize path in these handlers. | The lifecycle reports successful config/state load without any persisted values being acquired. Existing directories can lack the marker file and still produce an empty in-memory manager. |
| Universe stage | The event chain requests Universe after state, but the current Universe handler inserts scale and offsets all set to zero; the later foldback no longer issues the Universe request. | The staged model briefly implies an ordered world-load contract, but neither version restores world contents. The refactor removes the event chain before implementing that contract. |
| Load-state machine | `LoadState` is registered with states for each stage and `FullyLoaded`, but there is no state transition in the handler. | A type-level list of stages is not operational phase tracking; UI/other systems cannot rely on its state to know actual progress. |
| Parallel domain scaffolds | Config/state plugins have empty `build` methods; the initial plugin group still owns the concrete game plugin list. | Module names suggest separable systems, but no independent scheduling/ownership or replaceable composition is established. |

**Cross-commit conclusion:** this 2023 save path repeatedly models “load” as a lifecycle event while separating metadata, configuration, state and Universe in names only. Its persisted content is a save name plus empty marker files; each manager is empty; world restoration is deleted, briefly represented by a zeroed manager and confirmation chain, then omitted from the folded routine. No schema, payload, migration, or error-recovery contract is shown.

### August findings

1. **The data architecture is churn, not a completed migration.** The July generic Core/Data taxonomy is extended on Aug 3, its shared bases and examples are deleted on Aug 5, and Aug 6 begins a new authored-data/runtime-variable split. The intermediate patches leave constructors, component startup and event ownership unusable or incomplete; one base movement initializer is restored, but runtime max-energy and Awake/Start ordering still fail source inspection. Later backup restoration and still more direct system expansion proceed against this moving model.
2. **Serialized authoring data is part of the product contract, and it regresses during schema work.** The capped 300-entry view of the Aug 7 `355c1519` change shows 71 previously nonzero scalar values changed to zero. The full commit is 1,559 file blobs and includes 69 C# path changes; the 71-value count is evidence from the reviewed subset, not a full-commit total. A later `afa5efd3` subset adds persistent event calls, while its full diff also contains C# changes. Neither batch proves runtime behavior or complete restoration.
3. **Editor support is substantive, but its editing boundary is fragile.** Custom drawers and inspectors make wrappers/data assets editable, yet reflection-based drawers mutate object values outside Unity’s serialized-property/Undo path and write on every repaint. The interface looks convenient while persistence, undo and event timing remain unresolved.
4. **Gameplay expands while foundations keep moving:** Steam achievements, asteroids, inventory/resource collection, itemized weapons, station UI and missions. Many designs are replaced within days; “implemented” subjects describe a snapshot, not a durable architecture.
5. **Platform coupling appears early:** Steamworks is called directly by currency/achievement code. This is a confirmed ownership coupling, though its later fate is not established by this period.

#### Hunk-level semantic supplement: `5f5002e1`–`816884a1` — hierarchical universe model and generator experiment

| Commit | Patch evidence | Semantic result |
|---|---|---|
| `5f5002e1` — Chunk/World becomes Universe/Region | Replaces the earlier `World`/`Chunk` vocabulary and code with `Universe`/`Region`, adds generation settings, authored coordinates, a loaded-region dictionary and DEV generate/load/spawn/unload entry points. Removes the prior custom World inspector and adds an almost-default Universe inspector. | This is a real model change, not a rename: the flat chunk surface is now a hierarchy with universe-level data and authored development coordinates. But most lifecycle calls are still manual developer controls, and region naming continues to spawn objects named “Chunk”. `universeSize`, the `voids` representation and portions of filament/sector hierarchy are declared before they have an operational owner. The project is not yet performing player-centered streaming. |
| `d109e091` — separate Filament/Sector/Region classes plus JSON lifecycle | Creates three level types and three parallel dictionary/lifecycle APIs. Each level has `Generate`, `Save`, `Load`, `Unload`, `Spawn`, and `Despawn` logic; generated JSON paths are based on that type’s local `x.y` coordinate. | The repetition gives each level an apparent independent lifecycle, but the key omits parent identity: Region `(x,y)` is the same file regardless of Sector, just as Sector coordinates are not qualified by Filament. The classes also omit parent-coordinate fields, so containment is not represented in persisted identity. `voids`, `universeSize`, the serialized development coordinate list, and the empty `Start` do not drive generation. Files are written beneath `Application.dataPath`, which is a likely unwritable install-data location in a shipped desktop player; this is a platform/runtime concern inferred from Unity path semantics, not verified by running a build. `Despawn` uses `DestroyImmediate`, which is an editor-oriented destruction API being used in runtime object lifecycle code. |
| `d109e091` — generation vs. loading vs. spawning | `Get*` requires a key to be loaded and also checks whether a corresponding generated file exists; generation creates and saves an object but does not add it to the loaded dictionary; spawning requires `Get*`. | The lifecycle is intentionally split, but there is no composed operation or scheduler that advances through those states. A caller must know the exact three-step order and private methods prevent external callers from doing so in this version. The API is not an actual usable streaming boundary yet. The parallel per-level methods substantially duplicate the same transition logic. |
| `383e2df2` — serializable map wrapper | Introduces `FloatMap2D`, packing a rectangular float array into a serialized flat array and reconstructing a new 2D array in its getter. Noise generation switches from returning `float[,]` to this wrapper; Universe loses `MonoBehaviour` ownership and adds a static `Instance`. | The wrapper solves a concrete Unity serialization constraint, but the getter copies every element on every access, so consumers cannot read a row/value without allocating a full copy. Array dimensions and backing-array length are not checked against one another. Removing `MonoBehaviour` while adding serialized fields/static instance creates a hybrid object that Unity cannot own as a scene component; construction and singleton initialization must therefore be custom, but the patch does not show a complete owner. |
| `383e2df2` — hierarchy and generator access | Adds a Void type and generator/editor classes while making Filament/Sector/Region nested namespaces and wiring generation settings. | The change increases the number of layers before defining how parent coordinates, extents, or demand connect them. `Universe` is a regular class with private constructor and static `Instance`, while its fields still carry Unity `[SerializeField]`; this relies on serialized object behavior that belongs to MonoBehaviour/ScriptableObject and is not demonstrated. The initial hierarchy remains primarily a manually driven test harness. |
| `30be83c4` — GPU Voronoi implementation | Adds a compute-shader route that allocates full CPU arrays for every pixel and cell, uploads both to GPU buffers, dispatches, then synchronously reads every pixel back before producing a CPU texture. Its dispatch dimensions are integer-divided by 32; `OnValidate` forces dimensions to multiples of 64. | The title’s “500,000%” speed claim is not supported by a benchmark in the patch. GPU compute may accelerate the nearest-cell search, but it still incurs full-buffer allocation/upload/readback and a synchronization stall, followed by CPU color conversion and texture construction. The implementation is an editor/test generator, not integrated universe generation. The claimed speedup is therefore author-reported, not independently established. |
| `42de9340` / `53c7fd52` — vendored FastNoiseLite | Vendors the third-party implementation, then edits its wrapper/integration to apply FNL to Filament. | This is the first clear third-party algorithm dependency for procedural noise, but the source becomes locally modified, so upstream updates are no longer straightforward. The vendor’s license/provenance should be retained and the local delta isolated; commit history later shows implementation rewrites, not evidence that the vendor was benchmarked against the custom path. |
| `464bb688` — hierarchy classes nested back under Universe | Deletes the separate Void, Filament, Sector and Region files and moves their bodies into nested classes in `Universe`. | This reverses the prior decomposition within a week. It may satisfy Unity serialization or simplify ownership, but nests four domain entities and their rendering/lifecycle behavior into one large owner type. It does not solve the underlying identity issue by itself; nested types still require parent-qualified stable coordinates and deliberate persistence contracts. This is evidence of unresolved module boundaries, not proof that nesting is inherently wrong. |
| `816884a1` — hierarchical noise combination | Remaps parent noise from `[0,1]` to `[-1,1]`, multiplies child noise by `1 + influence * parentNoise`, and adds explicit TODOs that each parent map is sampled again in the child layer. | This is a more expressive multiscale combination than the prior subtractive formula, but multiplication can create negative values or values above one depending on influence and noise normalization. The source does not clamp or state a valid range. The author explicitly observes duplicate map evaluation across Universe/Filament/Sector, confirming avoidable repeated work at the hierarchy seam. No artifact image or benchmark establishes output quality/performance. |

**Cross-commit conclusion:** by late September, “world generation” has become a hand-authored, multi-resolution noise and object-persistence experiment. It is not yet a general world runtime: the coordinate hierarchy is not encoded into durable identity, load/generate/spawn steps are not composed, authoring/dev hooks dominate, and the GPU route synchronizes full results back to CPU. The module hierarchy itself oscillates between separate files and deeply nested classes in days, while the data ownership/path semantics remain unresolved. This is an important precursor to later spatial/USF work, but should not be retroactively described as an implemented universe model.

### September findings

1. **The project oscillates between modularity and consolidation.** Separate hierarchy types are introduced and then nested into Universe; item-prefab/drop APIs are replaced; the mission task system is explicitly shelved.
2. **Editor tooling is often the only integration surface.** Many “generator” commits create test harnesses and editor controls rather than a reusable runtime content contract.
3. **World generation is an experimental lineage, not yet a stable algorithm.** CPU/GPU implementations, naming, hierarchy levels and settings move rapidly; no profiling/visual validation can be inferred from code changes alone.
4. **A latent performance/ownership issue is acknowledged in-code:** Universe map sampling happens twice. That is confirmed intent/known debt, not a measured bottleneck.
