The protocol has reusable semantic-object identities, kinds, ranges and attributes, but each adapter decides what it recognizes and what context labels it attaches.

Their object shapes differ materially despite sharing `SemanticObject`. TOML projects tables, arrays-of-tables, arrays, and scalar *types/counts* with source key/value spans; it intentionally does not put literal values into the object detail. XML projects nested element names and attribute names but omits attribute values and text nodes. Rhai projects function declarations, parameters, and `let`/`const` bindings; bindings found in nested blocks are flattened into the containing function’s child list, and the projection neither executes nor type-checks scripts. These are sensible lightweight editor choices, but a generalized inspector or future refactoring API cannot assume that an object tree encodes the source language’s full scope, data, or execution semantics. The shared model standardizes identity and navigation shape; domain adapters still define different semantic granularity and privacy/exposure policy. [TOML projection](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/toml_semantics.rs#L311-L414), [XML element/attribute projection](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/xml_semantics.rs#L44-L138), [Rhai outline](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/rhai_semantics.rs#L29-L165), [Rhai binding projection](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/rhai_semantics.rs#L360-L430).

The new `docs/ide.md` is useful because it states that projected objects are not duplicate editable documents and that broader LSP features/external dependency source editing remain incomplete. Its neighboring implementation plan is upstream project material; it describes intent and invariants, not proof that every planned integration shipped. The diff and tests establish selected parsing, stale-anchor, hierarchy, filter and navigation behavior as test cases, but this audit did not execute them and does not claim runtime verification.

**Boundary trade-off:** the semantic projection implementation sits in `Vapor-GUI` (`vapor_gui_core`/`vapor_ide_ui`) and consumes shared console/protocol contracts from `Vapor`. This keeps GUI/domain parsing away from the service process, while workspace file access and managed tools remain service-owned. It also creates a new likely pressure point: Rust/TOML/XML/Rhai interpretation and source editing logic now live in GUI-side crates, so future CLI/editor/LSP reuse is not established by this commit. The owner’s broader plan for generalized semantic authoring is directionally reflected, but semantic IDs alone do not provide shared parser ownership or authoritative schema/type behavior.

One useful partial integration does exist: `Vapor-Studio` depends on `vapor_gui_core` and calls its code editor, workspace tree, and console components. However, its current UI source does not consume `SemanticWorkspaceIndex`/`SemanticObject`; the semantic Inspector, Rust/TOML/XML/Rhai projections, and managed Rust Analyzer path remain IDE-owned. So the UI primitives are shared across products, but the richer semantic authoring model is not yet a cross-product capability. [Studio dependency](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/blob/b02ecb40d038f1123d4a8313979ba0d69f0adec3/crates/vapor_studio_ui/Cargo.toml#L6-L17), [Studio shared editor use](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/blob/b02ecb40d038f1123d4a8313979ba0d69f0adec3/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workspace_files_panel.rs#L380-L390). This is a current-tree cross-check; absence of a symbol in that UI tree is a source search result, not a runtime limitation test.

### `Vapor` `868bbc1d` and `57430651`: canonical module creation crosses the service boundary

[`868bbc1d`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/868bbc1d28d89beb46a6e2ae7299c8ba533e5f76) adds `syn` to `vapor_client_application` and implements `create_canonical_rust_module`. It accepts an existing parent file plus its expected fingerprint and one of nine allowed module names (`components`, `constants`, `events`, `functions`, `resources`, `run_conditions`, `statics`, `systems`, `types`); validates Cargo `src` placement and Rust syntax; rejects an existing declaration; creates the child file with a starter module doc comment; and updates the parent only if its fingerprint remains unchanged. The new client action/result travels through domain action, protocol, service session and workspace operation layers, so this is a real service-owned filesystem mutation rather than direct IDE file writing. Focused tests are added for ordinary/nested paths, duplicate declarations, stale parent content and bad source files; they are evidence of intended cases, not executed results in this history review.

The first revision transports an arbitrary string and repeats the allowed-name/documentation table inside the application function. [`57430651`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/574306517d60d6be7f165481881fa85c373d1d51), roughly ten minutes later, moves the vocabulary into `vapor_client_domain::CanonicalRustModuleKind`, a serialized nine-variant enum with stable snake-case names and starter documentation. The GUI/service protocol now rejects unknown kind strings through typed deserialization rather than accepting a string and validating late. This is a small but meaningful domain correction: “canonical module kind” becomes a shared value, not a caller-provided filename convention.

The operation is intentionally narrow. It creates one module, always appends `pub mod <name>;`, and seeds only a one-line module doc comment. It does not move existing code, classify existing declarations into modules, decide whether a module should be public/private, render type-specific templates, validate all `syn` syntax constraints beyond parse/duplicate checks, or enforce an organization rule across the workspace. The accepted set is hard-coded as nine kinds; no `mod.rs`/`module.rs` display semantics are created here. The filesystem helper cleans up a newly created file if writing its contents fails, and removes it if the parent fingerprint-guarded write fails; the latter error path does not visibly clean any newly created containing directories. Treat this as a first safe, typed authoring action—not implementation of the owner’s full source organization dogma.

The layer placement is also notable: Rust syntax validation and file mutation live in `vapor_client_application`; the shared vocabulary lives in `vapor_client_domain`; the service dispatches; protocol carries the request/result; the IDE later renders the chooser and handles the result. That is a coherent vertical slice of one operation. The reviewed hunks do not establish the same separation for the GUI’s Rust item template insertion or its Rust/TOML/XML/Rhai semantic parsers.

The result is consumed by two authoring surfaces in this same workspace family. `Vapor-GUI/3f43819f` extracts a helper that replaces the IDE's opened-file document, indexes it locally, notifies Rust Analyzer, and requests document symbols; the module-creation response now directly opens the returned child contents/fingerprint instead of issuing a second read. `Vapor-Studio/f5155004` handles the same protocol result in a separate editor model: it merges the server-returned parent baseline/fingerprint with the current editor buffer, ensures the `pub mod` declaration is present, inserts/opens the returned child, and completes the operation. This confirms shared service ownership and shared wire data, but also two separately maintained front-end document reconciliation paths. That duplication is small in this feature and justified by separate product crates today; whether both should use a shared editor-document abstraction is a broader toolkit/product-boundary question, not settled by the commit.

### `Vapor-GUI/320541c3`: the first authoring UI, and its limits

[`320541c3`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/commit/320541c3de8589218b24d75181a59f4fa02a33cc) adds the IDE command and dialog for canonical Rust modules, sends the typed request through the service session, and updates the open documents from the service’s returned child/parent contents and fingerprints. A separate earlier semantic Rust item workflow also appears in the same IDE workbench: it renders selected declarations into open canonical files and applies them through the editor’s source model. This makes a meaningful division for module creation (service owns disk mutation) but leaves declaration templates/editor mutations in the GUI. The file tree labels `mod.rs`/Rust modules specially and chooses an ordering policy, but this commit does not implement a generalized tree of semantic objects replacing filesystem structure.

The generated item templates also reveal a framework ownership leak: the IDE offers its Component/Resource/Event creators for any recognized canonical Rust file under a Cargo `src` tree, but emits `bevy::prelude::{Component,Resource,Event}` derives. It neither checks the selected crate’s dependencies nor lets the crate/framework define those templates. Thus the generator is currently a Bevy-oriented convenience exposed as if it were generic Rust/Vapor authoring. It may be correct in the current Bevy game, but a plain Vapor-managed crate or a non-Bevy engine can receive code that cannot resolve its derive path. This is an architectural limit in template placement and applicability, not a compiler failure reproduced here. [Eligibility is based on path/module name](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/rust_semantics.rs#L30-L47), [hard-coded Bevy templates](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/rust_semantics.rs#L196-L225).

The subsequent `Vapor-Client` synchronization commits (`82b26a5b`, `4386710f`, `d8afd842`) update the linked Vapor, GUI and Studio workspaces and correct typed request/result handling. Their names and file lists confirm cross-repository propagation; the central Vapor changes above provide the semantic evidence, while the GUI commit supplies the concrete user-facing operation. They should not be mistaken for a separate new architecture at each mirror update.

**Sequence assessment:** October 23 advances from a file-only IDE toward a semantic workbench through three separate layers: indexed interpretations, typed/service-owned structural authoring, and GUI navigation/inspection. This is substantially more integrated than a file tree plus raw editor, but remains partly bespoke: four domain adapters have different parser maturity; canonical module creation is a narrow one-file operation; structural conventions are opt-in via the IDE command rather than enforced on arbitrary source; and common authoring semantics are not demonstrated as reusable by CLI or other frontends. These are confirmed limits of this sequence, not evidence that the direction itself is wrong.

### Same-day refinement commits: LSP ownership, Rhai parsing, and content authoring

The surrounding Oct 23 changes refine the workbench rather than add one uniform feature:

- `220cc867` moves roughly 1,100 lines of language-server request state and methods out of the main IDE module into `language_server.rs`. The request cancellation and stale workspace-version helpers move with it. This makes an existing responsibility visible as a module boundary; the diff is predominantly extraction, not proof of a new transport or Rust Analyzer capability.
- The earlier [`92ab2b9b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/92ab2b9b075a3d52976b9ce5e2ec99ea4d0278a2) service change gives Rust Analyzer a real process boundary: the Client service owns a process per frontend client, checks that the requested canonical workspace matches the selected Client workspace, speaks bounded Content-Length JSON-RPC over pipes, and stops/reaps the child on explicit stop or client disconnect. `ChildGuard` also kills and waits if startup fails partway through. [`60ff4eee`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/60ff4eee92a02f768d14625a51b77e3eee385027e) corrects toolchain discovery to use that selected source workspace rather than the service's working directory—important because the service may itself run from an installed app root. The GUI then rejects diagnostic batches outside the active workspace and discards versioned batches that do not match the open document. The protocol accepts an absent LSP document version, however, and the GUI applies such a batch without a freshness comparison; the source therefore establishes a strong versioned-result guard, not unconditional stale-diagnostic rejection. Process lifecycle is source-verified only; no live Rust Analyzer startup/shutdown was exercised here.
- `16df77ea`, `4a965ecc`, and `e38aad96` build local Rust semantic outlines and then refine nested-outline/projection bounds. These projections give immediate open-file structure; Rust Analyzer still supplies workspace-wide language features. The workbench therefore has two Rust sources of information with different jobs and freshness constraints. Later `bb31c903` centralizes result publication so stale local parse results cannot overwrite newer diagnostics/index state; its regression test is source evidence for the race being guarded, not proof from an executed test.
- `30e8c7d9` adds the pinned Rhai parser crate and calls `Engine::compile` only after its bounded delimiter scan finds no earlier structural error. It reports parse errors without evaluating the AST. This corrects the earlier delimiter-only checker, while still not type-checking injected capabilities or proving a script can execute in its eventual host context. The path is deliberately bounded: documents over the shared 2 MiB limit produce no local result; a token-limit hit produces an informational diagnostic and skips parsing; delimiter findings take precedence over a parser follow-on error. `rhai_position_span` maps Rhai's line/column to a source byte span, and the shared range converter then emits UTF-16 columns for LSP. `972a3f60` adds a same-line astral-Unicode regression case to the existing post-Unicode-line test, specifying that mapping. Tests exist for these cases but were not executed in this audit. `a5c302a` only advances the Vapor-Client submodule pin to that GUI revision; it adds no parser behavior itself.
- `3f1668d4` adds an IDE dialog titled “New Vapor content.” It offers `ContentKind::ALL`, one Vapor ID, one version, and a line-based required-dependency field; optional dependencies are sent empty and Workshop metadata is defaulted. The request is one `AuthoringAction::CreateContent` carrying a string kind and the workspace root. Its UI text explicitly says it creates/registers source and runs no build. This is concrete authoring functionality, but it puts all listed kinds through one UI/action shape. The service/provider path is kind-aware: `create_source_project_with_dependency_policies` receives the parsed kind; `content_project_output` returns no Cargo target for Packagepack/Enginepack/Gamepack/Modpack, and `scaffold_content_project` returns `MetadataOnly`; code-bearing kinds get Rust/Cargo output. Thus the backend does preserve the pack-vs-code scaffold distinction. The user-facing form still does not visibly distinguish “create a pack manifest” from “create implementation content,” nor offer pack-specific composition semantics, optional dependencies, conflicts, or Workshop metadata controls. Do not infer that all those fields are impossible elsewhere.

This same-day sequence reveals both the strength and the stress in the emerging design. One semantic object vocabulary supports multiple readers and navigators; service actions make file mutations explicit; source versions bound stale edits. But a shared object schema can make unlike workflows look deceptively uniform. The `CreateContent` dialog is a specific example where shared IDs/types do not remove the need for separate content-vs-pack creation semantics.

The immediate follow-ups make the IDE’s relationship to the workspace catalog more concrete:

- `f5af8fc0` adds an Inspector action for a semantic TOML object labeled `Vapor content reference`. It reads the referenced ID from the open manifest, looks it up among the service snapshot’s registered source projects, validates that the referenced project/manifest resolve inside the active workspace, then opens that source manifest. This is not Workshop/installed-library browsing; it is navigation between authored source projects in the same workspace. That is the right distinction for this IDE context, but the action is constrained to registered local sources and does not promise resolution for remote/acquired references.
- `0cdb045c` changes required-dependency entry from only free-form selectors to a checked list of compatible *registered local source projects* plus a collapsed “Advanced selectors” text area. The list calls the shared `dependency_kind_allowed` predicate and pins a project’s current version when the snapshot supplies one; changing the selected content kind clears previous checked dependencies. The action still accepts arbitrary advanced selector text, sends no optional dependencies, and uses the helper’s current compatibility semantics. Because the domain review elsewhere shows that this predicate is broader than the owner’s eventual required/optional/cardinality/pack rules, this UI list is a convenience filter, not a complete graph validator. It also chooses a specific source project version rather than presenting a version-range solver.
- `760b094a` resolves a Rust Analyzer workspace-symbol result back to a unique current local semantic object by URI, name, kind, path suffix and overlapping source range; if local structure is not yet indexed, it keeps a pending selection and requests document symbols. [`957bf971`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/commit/957bf9716177e4729e2edc8d76978f3904b0f47f) tightens range overlap from inclusive to strict endpoints and adds a regression case for a moved symbol. This is a deliberate defense against selecting a different declaration at an old location; the fallback still depends on fresh document symbols.
- `f049c642` merges duplicate source/build diagnostic rows while retaining their origins, rather than showing two unrelated errors for the same issue. `c5414280` clears search, selection, edit previews, workspace symbols and diagnostic filters when changing workspaces. A current-tree cross-check finds an incomplete reset: neither `open_workspace` nor the `OpenWorkspace` response clears `language_server.hover`, `references`, or `references_omitted`; `start_language_server` clears pending requests and completion items but leaves those three values intact. The Inspector renders stored hover text and reference locations whenever present, so after a project switch it can display data originating in the previous workspace until a later interaction replaces or clears it. This is a confirmed state-flow defect from source, not a reproduced UI report. These changes target stale/duplicate state but do not make the IDE's separate diagnostic sources share one parser or authority.

This follow-up is an example of composition gradually taking shape: project registration feeds authored-content navigation; declared types feed dependency-choice filtering; Rust Analyzer feeds the same semantic Inspector. Its limit is equally concrete: UI filtering relies on the present domain predicate and makes manually entered selectors available. Typed transport and an IDE checkbox list do not by themselves enforce the user’s intended dependency graph.

### Cross-check against the canonical ten-kind model

The source definition at [`vapor_content/src/content.rs`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/blob/868bbc1d28d89beb46a6e2ae7299c8ba533e5f76/crates/vapor_content/src/content.rs) confirms `ContentKind::ALL` is exactly the ten owner-listed names, with per-kind manifest filenames. The Rust enum is a single sum type for all ten and its module documentation calls it a content-artifact kind. That is useful as a closed catalog of allowed roles, but it does not itself encode the higher-order distinction that Packs are manifests and non-Pack Content is reusable implementation/artifact material. The authoring backend does encode one important consequence: all four Pack kinds become metadata-only projects with no Cargo member, while the six implementation kinds receive code-bearing Cargo scaffolds. The specific output choices in [`source.rs`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/blob/868bbc1d28d89beb46a6e2ae7299c8ba533e5f76/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/source.rs) vary by helper: generic `scaffold_content_project` makes Engine a binary; Game/EngineMod/GameMod/ExtensionMod `rlib`+`cdylib`; Crate `rlib`+`staticlib`. Separately, `init_basic_content` writes both `src/lib.rs` and `src/main.rs` for its Engine (plus a Game library and Packagepack metadata). Therefore Engine has two scaffold shapes in this source revision. Neither path realizes the full owner-stated target of reusable compiled Engine/Game/mod libraries composed into a Packagepack-owned executable: the basic template has no Packagepack Cargo target, while generic Pack scaffolds are metadata-only. These are skeletal authoring outputs, not proof of the ultimate build contract, but the mismatch is architectural, not cosmetic. The UI’s `CreateContent` verb still uses the broad catalog without exposing Packs versus implementation Content as distinct tasks; further workflow design must not assume the enum alone provides that separation.

The dependency helpers make some current rules explicit: Packagepack requires one `engine-choice` and one `game-choice`; Game and Enginepack require `engine`; Gamepack requires `game`; Crate-to-Crate is the only direct Crate relationship; and `Game` is limited to Engine/Crate children. The graph validator does more than the helper: `validate_member_kinds` checks pack-child allowlists, `validate_target_relationships` requires exactly one Engine for each Game/EngineMod, one Game for each GameMod, and one mod of any supported mod kind for each ExtensionMod; root pack-shape validation requires the relevant Engine/Game counts and at least one mod in a Modpack. This is real enforcement, not merely vocabulary.

There are still concrete limits. `dependency_kind_allowed` returns `true` for most non-Pack, non-Game, non-Crate parents, so that function alone is not a full edge policy; `validate_target_relationships` does not constrain all other edges those nodes may declare. ExtensionMod’s one-target rule treats EngineMod, GameMod and ExtensionMod as the same target category, consistent with a generic “mod of a mod” goal but not a richer compatibility proof. Optional edges are skipped by automatic required-graph resolution, conflicts have no mention in the reviewed resolver, and exact root-kind cardinality is not a global version-unification algorithm. The GUI’s `compatible_source_projects` presents the broad helper as a picker filter and still allows advanced free-form selectors, so the chooser is not the authority that closes the graph. Executable/build realization remains a separate gap.

### October 23 follow-up: typed diagnostics and module creation reach the service boundary

[`1a5796a1`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/1a5796a19b13fc82e13c3b60d134758626139626) adds a shared `DiagnosticContext` (`domain`, `scope`, workspace, document version, semantic path, operation ID) to `StructuredDiagnostic`, with serde defaults so older serialized diagnostics still deserialize. Cargo JSON diagnostics infer `Document` scope when a primary span exists and `Operation` otherwise; Rust Analyzer diagnostics carry the `rust` domain, `Document` scope and the LSP document version. This is a compatibility-preserving data-model step, and the patch adds a round-trip/legacy-record test. It does not itself populate all context fields: the shown Cargo/LSP producers leave workspace, semantic path and operation ID unset. The following `Vapor-GUI/96314884` patch bridges every populated context field into console-record fields and adds domain/scope filters, so the model-to-console path is present for those fields. It does not manufacture the context the producers omitted; a Rust diagnostic without a populated workspace or operation ID remains uncorrelated on those dimensions.

[`4fe3ab21`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/4fe3ab2121b81c4eaeb62effaf16ac298607d6da) connects more of the data path: operation output now carries Cargo diagnostics and bounded raw payloads; release builds receive a structured-output callback; installed/source composition launch can forward child stdout/stderr as operation output marked `launched-composition`. The Client stamps requests with an origin inferred from the executable filename. Its fallback maps `vapor-gui` to `Launcher`; this is a heuristic and is only as accurate as the executable naming/mode split. Tests cover common names, but neither those tests nor the patch establish correct attribution for every Steam entrypoint or child process. The transport error classifier reports byte count and first-byte category rather than echoing rejected protocol data, avoiding accidental disclosure of arbitrary child output. These are concrete observability/privacy improvements, not proof of a retained log console or correct per-product attribution in a running installation.

[`868bbc1d`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/868bbc1d28d89beb46a6e2ae7299c8ba533e5f76) adds `CreateCanonicalRustModule` as a typed workspace action carried through domain, protocol, service, application and result state. The application validates a Cargo `src` parent, its file fingerprint and Rust syntax, creates a documented module stub, then registers it in the parent with optimistic-concurrency protection and rollback on a failed parent write. The GUI consumes both returned file contents and fingerprints. [`57430651`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/574306517d60d6be7f165481881fa85c373d1d51) centralizes the nine supported categories in `CanonicalRustModuleKind`, including their names and starter documentation, replacing duplicated string allowlists. This is a meaningful end-to-end authoring slice and a move toward machine-enforced conventions. Its scope remains narrow: it creates an empty documented module and `pub mod` line, rather than classifying or reorganizing existing Rust items; it does not enforce a complete crate/module taxonomy. The service classifies this file-authoring operation as `OperationPhase::Building`, as it already does for SaveFile/CreateFile, so the phase vocabulary is not yet a clean semantic description of work. Tests are included in these patches but were not run for this review.

#### October 23: IDE workspace actions remain serialized at the frontend

At the current GUI source snapshot, `vapor_ide_ui::ServiceSession` stores a single `workspace.pending: Option<PendingRequest>`. Its `send` method records an accepted request there; it does not reject a second request itself, so transport-level correlation and backend scheduling remain separate questions. The UI and action handlers nevertheless serialize the ordinary user path: Run and Save are disabled while pending; Save All returns early; `save_next` waits for the active request before advancing its local queue; canonical-module and Vapor-content dialogs close after one accepted request; other authoring paths check for a pending action. The save queue is sequential, not a general queue of user actions.

This is narrower than saying “Vapor blocks everything.” Studio has its own bounded 64-entry FIFO, introduced when it queued every request behind any running operation. The same-day service registry then allowed unrelated operations concurrently and rejected only conflicting resource reservations; Studio evolved to submit requests directly and queue only when it received the service’s conflict response. A later guard clears queued work if dispatching the next operation fails, while disconnect clears active/pending tracking and the queue because the server-side outcome may be unknown. This is useful progress, but the queue remains Studio-owned; the service itself rejects conflicts rather than preserving the user’s request. The IDE does not use that Studio queue. The visible “wait for the current operation” behavior is therefore a product-level limitation of the IDE surface, not evidence that every Vapor frontend or service operation is globally serialized. Whether this caused a reported long composition check or refresh hang is unverified; no runtime reproduction was performed in this history review. The architectural gap is that queueability, conflict feedback and uncertain-outcome recovery are not represented by one shared service-owned operation contract.

The sequence is visible in [`Vapor-Studio/b7d457d`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/b7d457d3832bfea0e070a6713a7b3c49880f7e3c) (“Queue independent Studio operations”), [`Vapor/3b692e7d`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/3b692e7d8f89d6b07f51dcb2befd8698e8ed9b16) (multi-operation resource reservations), and Studio’s current response path in [`catalog.rs`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/blob/b02ecb40d038f1123d4a8313979ba0d69f0adec3/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/catalog.rs#L235-L268). The queue cap and clear-on-disconnect behavior are visible in [`operations.rs`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/blob/b02ecb40d038f1123d4a8313979ba0d69f0adec3/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/operations.rs#L20-L80). The queue stores no conflicting-operation identity or resource key. Studio retries its FIFO head after any operation finishes; if still blocked, the service returns the conflict and the UI appends it again at the tail. Thus the storage queue is FIFO, but the dispatcher does not establish blocker-aware wakeup or fairness under a mix of concurrent operations. The focused unit test checks the 64-item bound and storage order only, not this dispatch loop. This is a source-derived scheduling risk, not evidence of a reproduced starvation or excessive retry case.

#### October 18–23: shared service workspace identity conflicts with per-IDE roots

The service extraction in [`f9e8b13`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/f9e8b13a8eeb71dbe04a89d7aa4a93bead303d55) establishes one mutable `ClientSession` in the local service loop ([`server.rs:108–115`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L108)). The service may have multiple authenticated clients, but all requests dispatch through that same session. Opening a workspace canonicalizes the supplied root, replaces `bootstrap.workspace_root`, persists it as `authoring_workspace_root`, and resets/refills the shared catalog and workspace snapshot ([`session.rs:953–983`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L953)). Snapshot events are broadcast to connected clients ([`server.rs:800–815`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L800)).

Workspace file actions (`ListFiles`, `OpenFile`, `SaveFile`, and related operations) carry relative paths without a workspace identifier ([`actions.rs:125–140`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/actions.rs#L125)). `start_workspace_operation` resolves those paths against the one service-level `bootstrap.workspace_root` ([`workspace.rs:52–55`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L52)); the executor then reads/writes under the resolved root ([`workspace.rs:721–746`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L721)).

The IDE maintains a local `workspace.root`. It changes that root on its own successful `OpenWorkspace` response and clears the corresponding tree, documents and semantic index ([`service_session.rs:383–403`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs#L383)). Studio, by contrast, reads `authoring_workspace_root` from any service snapshot and updates its displayed root when it has no dirty editor documents ([`catalog.rs:434–443`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/catalog.rs#L434)). Therefore a second frontend can change the service's active file-operation root while the IDE still displays and indexes its previous root. A later IDE request such as `OpenFile { path: "src/lib.rs" }` is then interpreted by the service against the other workspace. This is a source-confirmed ownership mismatch and a plausible cross-client wrong-file/read-or-write hazard; no two-client runtime reproduction was performed.

The service already scopes some neighboring state per client: Language Server processes are stored by `client_id` ([`server.rs:108–112`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L108)). That makes the mixed boundary more visible: language-server lifetime is per connection, but workspace identity for file operations is shared. Even LSP startup compares the IDE's requested root to the one global active root and rejects the request when they differ ([`server.rs:550–585`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L550)). A client can therefore retain its own analyzer process for one root while the shared service has selected another root for file operations and future analyzer startup. The protocol also broadcasts operation events to all connected clients ([`server.rs:345–350`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L345), [`server.rs:474–500`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L474)). There is a useful correlation guard: each `WorkspaceFileResult` includes its operation ID, and IDE applies list/open/save/create results only when they match its pending operation ([`state.rs:592–630`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/state.rs#L592), [`service_session.rs:541–620`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs#L541), [`service_session.rs:774–780`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs#L774)). That protects the frontend from applying an unrelated client's result payload; it does not protect the requested operation from being resolved against the service's wrong active root in the first place. Rust Analyzer messages and normalized diagnostics are sent back only to the client that owns that analyzer process ([`server.rs:424–439`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L424)); the IDE also rejects diagnostic URIs outside its displayed root ([`language_server.rs:1319–1347`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/language_server.rs#L1319)). The concrete cross-client context gap instead affects shared operation output: `OperationOutputEvent` carries origin and optional composition identity but no workspace identity ([`state.rs:559–583`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/state.rs#L559)); IDE consumes all output and, for diagnostics, assigns its current local root as the workspace ([`service_session.rs:411–436`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs#L411)). A relative diagnostic path from another frontend's operation can consequently be resolved against the IDE's currently selected workspace if it matches a known suffix; an absolute path outside that root fails navigation, but the diagnostic is still presented with that IDE workspace context. This is a source-visible routing/context weakness, not a reproduced multi-client incident.

This may be acceptable only if exactly one active authoring workspace per service is an explicit enforced invariant. The protocol does not encode that invariant, bind a request to the caller's workspace revision, or identify the workspace in file operations or operation diagnostics. It also does not match the owner’s expressed direction of opening multiple workspaces as separate IDE tabs and operating on them independently or in batches. Workspace tabs therefore need stable workspace identity carried through operation requests and the corresponding client/editor context, or the product must deliberately enforce one exclusive global workspace and make the IDE follow snapshots before sending file requests. This is a source-level integration risk, not a reproduced multi-client incident.

**Workspace switching is also outside the operation reservation path.** `WorkspaceAction::Open` directly replaces the active root and refreshes shared state in request dispatch ([`session.rs:953–1015`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L953)); it does not acquire a workspace operation key. Other workspace operations capture the then-current root before being spawned ([`workspace.rs:52–60`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L52), [`workspace.rs:258–288`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L258)) and write through that captured root for Save/Create/module creation ([`workspace.rs:736–760`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L736)). When they finish, the service compares the captured root with the *currently selected* root and replaces a successful result with a failure if they differ ([`workspace.rs:290–314`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L290)). Therefore a save or file creation can complete on disk under workspace A, while its operation is reported as failed and the frontend receives no file-result event because that result is produced only after the root check. This is source-confirmed ordering; it was not reproduced at runtime. It does not mean the filesystem write is necessarily lost—the risk is that the user sees failure and no editor reconciliation despite the write having happened. `Open` either needs to serialize against in-flight work, or operations need immutable workspace identities and completion should be routed back to the owning workspace without invalidating completed side effects merely because the selected tab changed.

**One action already carries an explicit workspace root but its reservation does not use it.** `WorkspaceAction::RunConfiguration` includes `workspace_root` ([domain action](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/actions.rs#L93)); the service canonicalizes and runs that requested root ([`workspace.rs:15–60`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L15)), and the CLI's `launch --current-workspace` supplies its current directory ([`client_commands.rs:73–87`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/client_commands.rs#L73)). However, `operation_resources` always derives the workspace key from `self.bootstrap.workspace_root` ([`session.rs:711–752`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L711)); the `BackgroundOperationSpec` does not carry the explicit Run Configuration root. If the requested root differs from the service's selected root, two runs targeting distinct roots can unnecessarily conflict under the same key, or a run can reserve a key for a different workspace than the one it acts on. This is a narrow source-confirmed reservation mismatch; the GUI normally passes its selected root, so its common path masks it. No concurrency reproduction was performed.

#### October 22–23: Studio console moves from local rendering to shared indexed views

`Vapor-Studio/13b829df` docks the operation console and `3ed230a9` separates Problems from Console. The first Problems implementation rescans all retained records during each draw and renders the rows in a plain vertical `ScrollArea`. `442f8d6b` replaces that local row construction with `vapor_gui_core::console::show_records`, caches warning/error row indices by history revision, and gives the bottom panel a user-resizable range (140–520 px expanded, 40–80 px collapsed). The shared renderer uses egui `show_rows` with a fixed estimated row height, so it does virtualize visible rows. Each row is single-line and truncated; full text and fields are available on hover. Operation text is converted to plain terminal text and split into nonempty lines before record creation, so this is a searchable structured log view rather than a live Cargo TUI passthrough. Studio routes operation output through the shared `records_from_operation_output` adapter; its test asserts origin and composition fields survive the projection. This is a substantive response to duplicated rendering and repeated filtering. The source does not prove cross-OS sizing quality or behavior at real log volume, and a fixed-height row model could need revision if rows become multiline. Nor does shared record rendering make the CLI/Studio/IDE visual experiences identical; they remain separate renderers over shared data/components.

`Vapor-CLI/a09c49c5` adds the service event's `origin` and optional `composition_id` to each printed console record. This closes a small but important presentation seam for the terminal facade. It remains downstream of the Client's executable-name origin inference; it does not independently identify the actual command/app mode or prove that all operations set `composition_id`.

#### October 23 — `Vapor-GUI/972a3f60`: Unicode Rhai diagnostic-column regression

This one-test commit adds a malformed Rhai statement after an astral-plane rocket emoji on the same line and expects the parser diagnostic to map to column 32. It exercises the full helper path: Rhai's parser position is converted to a byte span by counting Unicode scalar values within the source line, then the shared byte-span mapper produces the IDE's UTF-16 semantic range. The added case guards against treating the parser's character position as a UTF-8 byte offset or as an LSP UTF-16 code-unit offset. The implementation remains unchanged; this is regression coverage for the coordinate conversion. The test was not run during this history review, so the record establishes test intent and source structure, not a passing execution result. Existing adjacent tests separately cover ASCII and multiline locations.

## Cross-repository hunk supplement — Loo-Cast's first shared console and authored-code surface (October 17–22, 2026)

The local Loo-Cast checkout advanced from `b77a397` (Oct 8) through nine commits to `c070bf3` (Oct 22). The working tree at this audit has only a modified `Cargo.lock`; its contents are excluded from committed-history claims. The range is summarized in the chronology. Selected ownership-defining patches are reviewed below, including representative schedule, canonical sweep, voxel resolution, transition, safety, and editor-group paths. This is not every hunk in the Oct 9 64-file patch.

### October 17 — `4551c534`: the executable moves to Packagepack

The workspace registers the Packagepack, Game and Engine as Vapor projects. The Packagepack changes from a library shell to the named binary `loo-cast-packagepack`, depends directly on the Engine and Game crates, and declares that binary in its manifest. Its `main` calls `spacetime_engine::run(loo_cast_game::install)`. The Engine's standalone binary and the Game's `cdylib` output are removed; Game installation now registers `LooCastGamePlugin` and `LooCastDeveloperAdaptersPlugin`, while the Game manifest declares its Engine dependency and no longer claims a separately delivered library at this intermediate commit.

This is a significant movement toward owner intent: a Packagepack is the launchable executable composition, with code linked together by Cargo rather than an Engine executable dynamically loading the Game library. It remains a hand-authored composition, not evidence of the Vapor resolver generating arbitrary Cargo dependencies from a content graph. The Packagepack root is still one known workspace member; the project-registration list is explicit. No build/run result is inferred from the patch.

### October 25 — the Game artifact boundary is real; the source-ownership boundary is not

The current three-crate graph is concrete: `loo-cast-packagepack` is a binary whose `main` calls `spacetime_engine::run(loo_cast_game::install)` ([Packagepack entry](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-packagepack/src/main.rs#L1-L5>)); `loo-cast-game` is a library adapter that registers two plugins exported from `spacetime_engine::game` ([Game adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-game/src/lib.rs#L1-L17>)); and `spacetime-engine` itself publicly exports the `game` module ([Engine public surface](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/lib.rs#L45-L49>)). That module contains 158 Rust files / 20,226 lines and defines `LooCastGamePlugin`, which owns cross-domain game scheduling and composition ([Game module root](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/mod.rs#L1-L105>)). The separate `loo-cast-game` crate is 17 lines and delegates to that implementation. The Packagepack Cargo manifest directly names both path dependencies ([Cargo composition graph](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-packagepack/Cargo.toml>)), so this is a working shape for one statically linked composition, but not yet a Vapor-generated composition whose resolved content graph determines those link edges.

The history matters because the text changed along with the executable shape. Immediately before Oct 17, `loo-cast-game/src/lib.rs` explicitly said the implementation was “temporarily housed” in `spacetime_engine::game` and that physical relocation could follow. Commit `4551c53` removed that caveat while it moved the entrypoint into Packagepack, removed the Engine binary, and removed the Game's `cdylib` declaration. It did not move the game modules. The current Game manifest again advertises `loo_cast_game` as a library, and Cargo's default library output is an `rlib`; this declaration plus the local Cargo edge does not prove that a standalone published Game artifact is consumed by a different composer. This is evidence of semantic closure at the executable boundary alongside unresolved implementation ownership—not proof that the adapter or Engine package is unusable. The module-classification work remains necessary: `game/mod.rs` itself calls health, inventory, item, locomotion and navigation generic, while player/world/console adapters and scenario orchestration are Loo-Cast-specific, with other modules straddling the line. A file move would therefore be a consequence of classification and dependency/schedule redesign, not a mechanical remedy. See the [current ownership map](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#6-loo-cast-enginegamepackagepack-ownership), [timeline synthesis](loo-cast-vapor-history-timeline.md#october-25--the-game-artifact-is-distinct-but-game-implementation-remains-in-engine), and the [owner's content model](loo-cast-vapor-origin-and-intent.md#the-intended-content-model-emerges).

### October 18 — `7709f31b`: broad-overhaul review method enters the repo prompt

The two added lines in `.ai_stuff/loo_cast_dev_startup_prompt.md` turn the owner's review instruction into a durable project convention: diagnose demonstrated problems across relevant domains, ground each negative dimension in evidence and ownership impact, connect shared causes, distinguish confirmed findings from hypotheses, and keep an implementation request from ending at a plan. The adjacent paragraph favors coherent architectural tranches and an explicit contract → proof → runtime evidence → authority handoff → productionization sequence. This records how the owner wants AI-assisted work to be evaluated; it does not prove that later assistants followed the process or that the review map was complete.

### October 20–21 — target, profiles, and reusable-library declarations

[`1007e2a5`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/1007e2a5ba000b664fe254be7c8e71d19863b006) declares the workspace runtime target set as Linux GNU and Windows GNU-LLVM. This makes the target promise explicit in workspace metadata; it does not establish that every content dependency has a compatible artifact. [`4273a1f`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/4273a1fb954dbcff062aa27f504078d6c419b5eb) changes ordinary dev dependencies to line-table debug information, adds a separate `full-debug` profile, and declares its Vapor run configuration. This assigns a clear disk/performance trade-off: normal development retains line-level backtraces; full variable/type data is opt-in. It does not demonstrate that all Vapor commands honor that profile or that caches are actually reclaimed.

[`df346baf`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/df346baf9646836170456e55b03c931e51e6a2ca) later adds `libraries = ["loo_cast_game"]` and `libraries = ["spacetime_engine"]` to the Game and Engine manifests. That is authored metadata declaring reusable crate artifacts, complementary to the Packagepack's direct Cargo dependencies. The two facts belong to different stages: the manifest advertises content libraries; this Loo-Cast executable still links local path dependencies. The change alone does not prove those libraries were published, acquired, or used to generate the executable.

The Oct 21 commit titled “formatting” is not formatting-only. Besides formatting, it changes config discovery to prefer an explicit `SPACETIME_ENGINE_CONFIG`, then `VAPOR_ENGINE_ROOT/assets/config/engine.ron`, then source/current-directory candidates; the Engine's Bevy AssetPlugin root follows `VAPOR_ENGINE_ROOT/assets`. This is a necessary installed-content seam because the process CWD may be the Packagepack, not the Engine root. It also rewrites the fixed 71-value scale conversion tables over multiple lines, plus worldgen/view formatting and imports. The values appear textually preserved in the inspected diff; no numeric behavior change is claimed. Tests were added for path selection and assets, but were not run in this history audit.

### October 22 — one narrow shared console core, plus a typed Workshop filter

[`Vapor/7ab704bf`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/7ab704bf7978a9e387e29236b750f9002135b64a) adds `vapor_console_core`, with host-neutral structured records, levels/style roles, source/target/fields, bounded `ConsoleHistory`, a `ConsoleFilter`, `PromptHistory`, and a small Rhai lexical surface. `vapor_telemetry` re-exports those types; Vapor Devtools stores bounded records and renders a searchable colored log list. The same change adds optional typed `ContentKind` to Workshop search across domain action, protocol snapshot, service operation and Steam provider. The provider combines kind and user tags, canonicalizes/deduplicates them, asks Steamworks for required tags, and post-filters returned tags; fixture search mirrors the kind filter. Backward-compatible serde defaults are added. This is the first directly inspected shared implementation in both user-requested areas: Workshop type filtering and common console data.

The console-sharing claim needs exact bounds. Loo-Cast's [`c070bf3c`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/c070bf3cadfeceb011742acce00381803e8561e6) embeds a `vapor_telemetry::ConsoleRecord` payload in its local wrapper, and the script workbench builds an `egui_code_editor::Syntax` from shared Rhai keyword/type/literal lists. Loo-Cast still owns command/tracing origin and record-kind wrappers, command execution, rendering and terminal adapters. It reuses shared `PromptHistory`, but transcript storage remains a local 512-record `VecDeque`; it does not use the shared `ConsoleHistory` revision/filter model. The Engine's `TelemetryEmitter` is wired to publish runtime/world metric maps, while Bevy console tracing feeds the in-process `ConsoleTransport`; this commit does not bridge console records to Vapor's telemetry Log events. The in-game editor does not call the shared `RhaiLanguage::tokenize`; the egui crate performs its own tokenization from the shared vocabularies. Both GUI and game pin `egui_code_editor` at 0.2.24, but the game uses its `CodeEditor` widget while Vapor-GUI wraps `egui::TextEdit` with its own `LayoutJob` highlighting and cursor selection. Thus the change shares a record payload, prompt-history behavior, a low-level editor dependency and lexical names, not a unified command system, renderer, editor widget/state, parser, diagnostics pipeline, cross-process console stream or transcript-history implementation. The core tokenizer is a compact lexical pass, not Rhai evaluation or a complete language-service contract. The included tests specify boundary cases but were not run here.

**Cross-repository pin:** the Loo-Cast manifest declares `vapor_telemetry` as a Git dependency without a `rev` or tag, while the `c070bf3c` committed `Cargo.lock` records both `vapor_telemetry` and `vapor_console_core` at Vapor commit `7ab704bf`. Vapor-GUI instead depends on `vapor_console_core` through the Vapor submodule path, currently at `5743065`. The checked-in Loo-Cast lock therefore fixes a different source revision from the GUI's current submodule; this is a real coordination boundary, but not proof of an API failure or intentional compatibility break. The lockfile fixes the Loo-Cast source revision for locked builds, while its manifest alone does not. The current local Loo-Cast checkout has a dirty `Cargo.lock` whose only change reorders the `vapor_console_core` and `vapor_telemetry` package blocks alphabetically. Both package source revisions and dependency lists remain unchanged, including the telemetry-to-console-core dependency; the local diff is preserved and excluded from claims about the committed revision.

The Workshop change similarly establishes a typed path, but its matching policy is currently a tag convention: a selected `ContentKind` must be present as a Workshop tag with the canonical `ContentKind::as_str()` value. Steam search semantics and client-side filtering both depend on publishers applying that exact tag taxonomy. The patch tests tag normalization/matching and fixture propagation, but does not prove that existing public items are consistently tagged. A later read-only check confirmed both current frontends send the typed field; see the Oct 21–23 cross-frontend review below. The service also contains a narrowly scoped `seed_legacy_empty_selection` migration for an empty persisted `default` composition; this preserves a legacy slot and fills it from the default Packagepack selector rather than replacing the identity with a generalized persistent selection model. That migration should not be mistaken for completion of the user's “default is the same selected composition twice” concern.

### October 9 spatial tranche: broad integration review still open

[`46e1eac`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/46e1eac) changes 64 files (+2,476/−547) and adds the dated spatial-authority plan. The touched ownership surfaces span flight/locomotion/navigation, collision-query contracts and runtime, voxel collision resolution, input/HUD/camera, editor hierarchy, travel console commands and world fixtures. The later current tree now also separates the Packagepack executable and target metadata described above. A focused collision/flight/cross-scale review now examines the fixed-step transaction, voxel broad/narrow phase, readiness predicates, writer domains, moving-target safety and selected HUD/control wiring; see [the detailed Oct 9 pass](#october-9-controls-travel-handoff-camera-and-telemetry--focused-source-pass) and [the collision-query audit](#additional-collision-query-audit--spatial-global-failure-and-edit-count-scaling). The pass is not a semantic review of every hunk or unaffected consumer in the 64-file patch. The plan document is intent and ordering evidence, not proof that each listed invariant was achieved or runtime-verified.

The patch replaces the old `PostUpdate` observation-only sweep collector with a fixed-step sequence. `LocomotionSet::Prepare` computes a proposed canonical displacement and submits it to `UsfProposedSweeps`; `UsfCollisionQuerySet` resets, collects, runs providers, and finalizes in `FixedUpdate`; `flight_movement` is ordered after finalization. `VoxelPlugin` registers the semantic voxel provider in the provider set. For canonical flight, a missing request/result becomes `Unknown { safe_fraction: 0 }`, and the commit clips displacement and either projects velocity along a valid contact normal or stops for invalid/unknown contact. This is a real safety-ownership change in source, not merely a diagnostic journal.

The voxel provider builds conservative candidates from each semantic celestial field's outer bound and separately from edited bounds. It then traces signed distance in body-local metres, including Add/Remove edits, with a 256-step limit. Missing/unrepresentable input, incomplete broad phase, or exhausted refinement returns Unknown; no candidates after a complete query returns Clear. Candidate intervals are evidence only; response is owned by the flight commit. The fixed-step frame is shaped to accept provider observations, but the patch wires only the voxel provider; the intended provider-neutral architecture is therefore an interface seam, not yet a multi-provider implementation. This establishes a conservative provider contract for this voxel field and this one controlled flight path. It does not establish all-world collision coverage, collision for other motion owners, a general provider registry, terrain/contact testing, or high-speed behavior in runtime.

The new transition admission layer checks destination capability roles and optional authority over a radius before switching the chart. One-shot relocation is requeued when coverage is insufficient; a motion reanchor bypasses interaction readiness as a representation-only operation. `UsfCanonicalMotion` keeps SI velocity distinct from native chart velocity, and `runtime_step_is_representable` promotes flight to canonical integration when an f32 chart cannot represent the proposed displacement within the relative-error budget. However, `motion_contract` still maps `layer == detailed` to `DetailedBody` and coarse layers to `ScaleProxy`; the new decision selects canonical authority when that policy is not detailed or the local collider is absent. Thus chart scale is no longer the only authority input, but it remains directly coupled to collision-backend choice. The [surface-readiness computation](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/surface.rs#L234-L247) and [motion-policy selection](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/state/policy.rs#L167-L203) use two different readiness signals with similar names: `SurfaceContext.collision_ready` is a coverage-snapshot test for the body’s `COLLISION` role within a support-radius probe; `MotionPolicyInputs.runtime_collision_ready` is only `runtime_collider.is_some()` on the controlled subject. Neither alone proves a valid Avian contact result against the destination body. Coarse-scale flight selects the canonical sweep path regardless of local collider presence; detailed-scale flight can select runtime physics based on the local component. These predicates govern different layers and should not be read as one end-to-end collision-readiness guarantee. The handoff/resolve systems still run in multiple schedules, so the intended “one owner per subject-step” is established for the fixed-step flight commit, not proven as a universal writer audit across every subsystem.

The public collision contract describes a `Contact` normal as unit length, but `publish_resolution` accepts arbitrary provider output and the flight commit checks only finiteness and a squared length greater than `0.5` before using `v - n(v·n)` as a projection. That formula assumes a normalized normal. The in-tree voxel resolver normalizes its finite-difference normal, so this is not demonstrated as a defect in that provider's current path; it is an unenforced contract for future or external providers, where a non-unit vector can over-remove or inject normal velocity. Normalize or validate at the provider boundary before claiming the shared contract is robust.

`FlightSafetyState` computes radial closing speed, TTC, required deceleration and an Advisory/Emergency level. Its inputs come from `SurfaceContext` or primary-body radial clearance, plus a rough available-deceleration estimate. A further source-level gap is body-relative velocity: [`evaluate_flight_safety`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/flight/runtime.rs#L25-L97) passes the controlled subject's absolute canonical velocity and the radial direction from the body center, while [`PrimaryBodyContext`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/navigation/travel/body.rs) and [`SurfaceContext`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/surface.rs) retain no body velocity. The [`KeplerianOrbitPropagation` system](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/orbit/mod.rs#L194-L239) does maintain canonical velocity for orbiting bodies, but this safety system never reads it. The code currently uses `max(0, -v_ship · r̂)`; body-relative closure requires `max(0, -(v_ship - v_body) · r̂)`. TTC and required braking can therefore be wrong for a moving target when its radial velocity is material. This establishes a missing relative-motion term in the model; it does not establish that it caused the reported Moon braking failure. The supervisor is also observational: it does not consume `UsfSweepResolution`, apply braking, or guarantee an admitted path. Main-thruster acceleration is treated as available braking whenever propulsion is enabled, without checking whether attitude/actuation can direct it against closing velocity; this can overstate capability. The patch tests arithmetic examples only and those tests were not executed in this historical review.

**Plan/code inconsistency:** the plan committed in this same change explicitly says “Do not run or add tests,” while the patch adds test modules for editor grouping, flight safety, navigation context, travel assistance, and flight policy. This audit observes both facts and does not resolve the contradictory policy; none of those tests were executed here.

**Plan-to-source completion cross-check:** the plan's five numbered work areas are stronger than the concrete path at this commit. At the current local `c070bf3` snapshot, the relevant edited paths remain unchanged from `46e1eac`.

| Plan objective | Source evidence at this checkpoint | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| One semantic motion owner per subject-step | Canonical controlled flight has a prepare/query/commit owner, but orbit propagation, transform-to-semantic sync, landing, disembark and fixture placement remain separate writers; no universal disjoint-owner invariant is enforced. | Partial; local transaction is explicit, system-wide ownership is not. |
| Collision decision follows the proposed path | Canonical controlled flight consumes a swept result; local Avian motion remains a separate backend, only the voxel provider is registered, and provider/edit work is not globally bounded. | Partial; no universal provider-neutral path or completeness proof. |
| Demand and admission follow motion/readiness | Refresh uses canonical speed and relocation can wait on explicitly requested roles; coverage defaults to none and backend overlap guards cover only continuous coarsening requirements. | Partial; coverage and physical readiness are not mandatory across transition callers. |
| Separate local focus from semantic capability | Authored scale affinity and a representation-only motion reanchor exist, but game flight/navigation still select one `LocalControlSubject`; this tranche does not establish the plan's broader per-subject capability model. | Partial; intended distinction is present in APIs but not generalized through consumers. |
| Make navigation, HUD and diagnosis truthful about accepted safety | Telemetry reports canonical velocity, cooldown, safety and sweep observations, while safety remains predictive/observational and emergency capture changes speed by direct magnitude clamp. | Partial; rich observability exists, but it does not prove collision-safe braking. |

This is a source-to-plan comparison, not a claim that later runtime observations were impossible or that every intended behavior failed. The plan itself requires owner-side scenarios and says code size or compilation is not completion evidence; this historical review contains no run of those scenarios. The detailed admission and readiness conditions are in the [second focused source pass](#second-focused-source-pass--travel-readiness-and-transition-admission).

The added editor relationship `EditorGroupOf`/`EditorGroupMembers` uses Bevy's semantic relationship API and does not set `ChildOf`, so the intended editor-only grouping is explicit in the data model. Its UI creates, nests and selects groups and selected entities. The inspected `can_group` bounds ancestry traversal and rejects a detected cycle; grouping is UI-local, with no persistence, bulk move, drag/drop, rename or cleanup behavior shown in this patch. It is an initial facility, not evidence of a complete reusable hierarchy workflow.

The flight-input slice adds a ship-owned signed throttle value in [−1, 1], integrates key axis over time, preserves it after input release, and lets the wheel nudge it; the inherited W/S actions set the axis. It adds an independent angular-assist toggle, changes ship attitude input from “follow view” to manual angular rate, and adds FirstPerson/ThirdPerson/Orbit camera modes with target-specific orientation policy, independent orbit rotation and persistent boom zoom. This is closer to the requested separation of pilot attitude from observer camera; the mode still uses one toggle cycle and only one authored spacecraft profile in the inspected slice. The camera and control changes are concrete source behavior, not proof of a polished binding UX or runtime feel. The travel-neighborhood cache now receives canonical position and velocity and refreshes ahead of a fast subject crossing half its measured margin, addressing the stale-neighborhood risk in source; no latency/load test proves that this demand is early enough for generation.

Console integration adds typed `camera [cockpit|chase|orbit]` and `debugfly [on|off]` commands; `debugfly` directly selects collision-free characteristic-speed traversal, routes wheel input to pace, and requests Manual travel assistance on enable. The `attitude` vocabulary changes from `view` to `manual` while preserving `view`/`follow` as aliases. The spatial dev panel now distinguishes native projected velocity from canonical SI velocity and prints the last sweep outcome, making the new authority path inspectable in source. The contextual HUD also changes its action list for flight versus on-foot and exposes throttle, wheel, rotation and camera behavior. These are more integrated owner-facing surfaces than the previous structure-only work, but they still consume the game's own console/widget path; they are not evidence of a common Vapor/game console or a generic typed command ecosystem.

The new command set still has several target identities, rather than one command-context contract:

| Command | Selected entity/context | Concrete effect and boundary |
|---|---|---|
| `zoom` | First `UsfViewRenderAnchor`; reports the global `UsfPrimaryInteractionSlice` | Changes observer exponent only. The user-facing “interaction remains S…” status is a single global focus adapter, not a per-subject capability query. |
| `speed` | First entity with `Player` and `TravelPace` | Changes player-owned pace. Input adapters copy that multiplier into the current `LocalControlSubject` intent, so the current human-player path composes correctly, but this command is not suitable for selecting arbitrary controlled subjects without that adapter. |
| `camera` | Checks first `LocalViewTarget` profile, then mutates first `PlayerCamera` + `Transform` pair | Orbit eligibility and the camera being changed are not joined by entity identity. A single-camera fixture masks the mismatch; additional cameras/view targets make the result query-order-dependent. |
| `cruise`, `attitude`, `autopilot`, `debugfly`, `motionstack` | First `LocalControlSubject` matching each command's component query | Each has a different required component tuple and its own unavailable-state error, so the apparent shared “current subject” is not one validated command context. |

This is a source-visible scope of the one-subject product fixture, not a demonstrated failure in that fixture. It is relevant to the commit's reusable-domain claim: the player input bridge intentionally owns Player pace, while the camera command resolves view eligibility and camera mutation independently. No test checks multiple cameras, missing command-context components, or query identity. `debugfly` itself is explicit and useful for the requested free traversal: `characteristic_traversal` also implies collision/gravity ignore, and the flight policy derives its speed from the controlled subject's manual envelope times player pace. Its emergency-capture branch deliberately clears the pending capture without clamping while this override is active. That behavior is an intentional god-mode escape, not evidence of safe ordinary flight.

The same 64-file diff also changes travel commands, camera/input routing and HUD telemetry/text. Selected input/camera/navigation contracts are reviewed here, but there is no exhaustive command-by-command or telemetry-field review. A targeted writer search finds separate `UsfPosition` writes via projection sync, orbital propagation, transition application, landing settlement, ship exit, fixture bootstrap, and fixed-step flight; these are distinct domain paths, but they do not all route through the same transition queue or flight commit. The plan's claims about one writer, readiness corridor, stopping-distance demand, full handoff atomicity and truthful diagnostics must not be read as proven universal properties. The control systems use `Single<... With<LocalControlSubject>>`, so the visible flight path is one locally controlled subject even though module docs describe reusable generic locomotion. The focused collision-query supplement below adds source-confirmed non-local failure behavior and edit-count scaling risk. The focused `UsfPosition` writer-domain pass below audits those callsites; a complete repository-wide ownership audit, including non-position motion writes, and runtime confirmation remain open. This historical review did not compile Loo-Cast or run its tests.

#### October 9 controls, travel handoff, camera and telemetry — focused source pass

The cross-domain schedule in `game/mod.rs` orders one `RunFixedMainLoop` chain as control sample → flight control → orbit propagation → gravity sample → navigation observation → flight safety → control requests → navigation planning → locomotion resolution/realization → character reference frame → character intent → navigation publish. This proves that the safety state computed from the observed semantic state is available before the Cruise transition resolver in the same outer fixed-main-loop pass. `resolve_travel_assistance` decrements cooldown, automatically drops out when the safety state is Emergency, entry capability is lost, or travel reports critical dropout, and zeros Cruise's own throttle/speed fields. A spool is canceled if cruise capability, entry readiness or safety fails; a valid completed spool engages Cruise. This is a connected state path in source, though no scheduler/runtime test was run here.

Dropout does not merely flip `TravelAssistanceState` to Manual. Disengaging an active Cruise sets `capture_pending`; the fixed-step flight resolver reads the next velocity policy, clamps it to the emergency-contact-speed limit for `CriticalApproach` or the manual maximum for pilot disengagement, logs prior/captured speed, then clears the pending flag before constructing the proposed displacement. Thus the emergency/manual capture distinction is encoded by `last_transition`, not by separate booleans. The travel-assistance tests assert the state lifecycle, but not the complete scheduled velocity/collision handoff. The emergency check uses a radial TTC and rough braking estimate, not the actual sweep outcome; this remains a supervisor, not guaranteed collision avoidance.

The control surface is more coherent than the earlier “follow view” prototype but its semantics change materially. A signed persistent throttle is integrated from W/S through a separate throttle axis; horizontal/vertical translation remain on the movement vector. Ordinary wheel input nudges throttle, Shift+wheel changes characteristic pace by powers of two, Alt+wheel changes view scale, and holding Descend while scrolling routes to camera zoom. In developer traversal, ordinary wheel changes pace. Manual angular-rate input uses the arrow-key pitch/yaw axes and Q/E roll; mouse delta contributes pitch/yaw rate except in Orbit mode. The render input frame is sampled in `PreUpdate`, while `ControlSet::Sample` is ordered before the fixed main loop; this is deliberately a once-per-frame adapter, not a Bevy system repeated inside each fixed tick. It converts accumulated mouse delta to rate using the render-frame `Time` delta, then the fixed flight policy consumes the sampled intent. This design is source-visible; sensitivity, frame-pacing and actual flight feel were not measured.

The added velocity-aware neighborhood refresh prevents a fast observer from consuming its measured spatial margin before the next refresh, but the empty-neighborhood case is intentionally special: `needs_refresh` returns true whenever no influence was found. `sync_navigation_context` then iterates the full ECS influence query to build candidates again on every invocation. Since this system is registered in the fixed-main-loop context chain, an empty-space observer can repeatedly rescan all authored influence entities at fixed cadence until one enters view. This improves discovery after world streaming, but lacks a retry interval, dirty-generation signal or spatial-index lookup. It is a source-confirmed scaling trade-off; actual entity counts and frame cost were not measured.

Default bindings change `E` from `+use` to roll-right and move interaction to `F`; `Q` is roll-left, arrows steer, `B` toggles angular flight assist, and F5 cycles camera modes. The cycle is cockpit → chase → orbit → cockpit for a spacecraft profile that supports Orbit; other profiles skip Orbit. Per-mode orientation policy is explicit: cockpit follows subject attitude, chase horizon-stabilizes subject heading, orbit uses camera-owned rotation. Zoom remains stored as boom intent and is collision-resolved separately. This is a genuine three-mode camera model, but it is still a single toggle cycle rather than a discoverable chooser or multiple named camera rigs. Key conflicts, accessibility/remapping UX and runtime camera collision were not verified here.

The contextual action projection does not fully inherit these bindings. In flight it prints literal `WHEEL`, `SHIFT+WHEEL` and `CTRL+WHEEL` strings; the actual routing is keyed to `FastModifier` and `Descend`, both user-rebindable through the same binding resource. After rebinding either action, those help lines remain stale. It also omits the Alt+wheel view-scale action. On foot, `append_view_actions` lists camera-mode and creative-menu actions but no camera-zoom or view-scale wheel help, even though the camera input systems support those operations. Separately, `PlayerInputBindings::label` reports only the first bound button for an action, so extra bindings are not represented in the contextual text. These are source-confirmed gaps in the advertised “available inputs” panel; no screenshot/runtime check was performed.

The new console handlers also do not share one target-selection contract. `camera_command` derives Orbit availability from the first `LocalViewTarget` profile, then mutates the first entity with `PlayerCamera` and `Transform` without requiring it to be the primary/local camera or associating it with that target. `speed_command` now looks for the first `TravelPace` on any `Player`; Cruise and attitude commands query the `LocalControlSubject`. This may be correct for the current one-player fixture, but the command boundary no longer guarantees it acts on the same controlled subject/view when those concepts separate or multiply. The source has no explicit uniqueness/error path for either query. This is a current single-player assumption exposed by the patch, not a reproduced multi-player failure.

The HUD gains an explicit telemetry component as the source for left/right text. `sync_flight_telemetry` derives total/forward/lateral velocity from canonical SI velocity and body forward, reports the actual `FlightThrottle`, assist/propulsion/RCS state, cooldown/spool, surface clearance/readiness, gravity, handoff and safety fields. The HUD formatter presents those values, mode/camera labels, TTC, cooldown/charge messages and context-dependent action hints. A center marker projects canonical velocity into the camera orientation after f64 normalization, then clamps the displayed offset to a fixed ±110 px extent; it does not use a camera projection/FOV or viewport geometry in this formatter. That is a concrete potential limitation to inspect visually, not proof the marker is wrong on screen. The presentation still uses a Unicode diamond glyph, so font coverage is also not established by source. Telemetry is structurally centralized within the game, but its producer remains coupled to a single locally controlled subject. The producer is ordered before `PresentationSet::PrimaryView`, which contains the HUD projection, so same-frame producer-to-widget ordering is explicit in source; screen appearance and underlying fixed-step freshness still lack runtime validation.

This focused pass covers the navigation handoff and the touched camera/control/HUD files, not all 64-file hunks. It improves confidence that several advertised pieces are integrated in one schedule, while leaving the actual flight feel, full collision safety, multi-controller reuse, input discoverability and HUD geometry as open runtime/design questions.

A follow-up path history check from `46e1eac` to local head `c070bf3` finds no later commit touching these collision-query, voxel-query, flight safety, locomotion-flight, transition or camera paths.
