The Oct 9 implementation therefore remains the committed spatial baseline at this checkout; this is not evidence it was deployed or exercised.

#### Additional collision-query audit — spatial global failure and edit-count scaling

The committed source review exposes two further risks in the provider path:

| Source behavior | Evidence | Consequence and confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate collection visits every entity with `UsfPosition`, `UsfSemanticFrame`, and `CelestialVoxelField`. A failed relative-position conversion for any one authority or a failed `world_bounds` conversion for any one edit sets the shared `complete` flag false; `resolve` then returns `Unknown { safe_fraction: 0 }` before considering otherwise usable candidates. During refinement, `local_edits` also converts the full edit list and fails the whole provider if any edit cannot be represented, even when that edit's own bounds did not intersect the sweep. | [`voxel/collision_query/mod.rs`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/collision_query/mod.rs#L48-L101), [`resolve.rs`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/collision_query/resolve.rs#L129-L147) | **Confirmed control flow; impact inferred:** one distant/unrepresentable authority or one unrelated malformed edit can turn a local path into a zero-safe-fraction result, even if its bound cannot intersect the sweep. This is conservative but non-local: unrelated world state can stop the subject. The future contract needs to distinguish “could not test an intersecting candidate” from “could not encode irrelevant authority/edit data.” No runtime repro was performed. |
| Every body candidate and every intersecting edit-bounds candidate is refined using the full ordered Add/Remove edit list for that body. `field_distance` replays every edit on each sphere-trace sample; each candidate may consume 256 samples, and contact-normal estimation makes six more distance samples. The publish system also calls `candidates()` and then `resolve()`, which independently reruns broad-phase collection. | [`mod.rs`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/collision_query/mod.rs#L48-L101), [`resolve.rs`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/collision_query/resolve.rs#L16-L72), [`publish`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/collision_query/mod.rs#L258-L271) | **Confirmed structural cost; runtime cost unmeasured:** with `K` candidates and `M` edits on an authority, refinement can scale on the order of `K × 256 × M` field/edit evaluations, plus normal probes and repeated candidate collection. Since multiple intersecting edit bounds can each create candidates, this can approach quadratic edit-count growth before fixed-step budget is considered. The provider currently has no per-candidate edit subset or cached prepared field in this path. This is a concrete performance risk, not a benchmark result. |

These findings sharpen the earlier limitation: “Unknown is safe” is only a local safety rule if query completeness and work are scoped to the swept neighborhood. As written, completeness is global to the entire authority query, while narrow-phase work can be global to each candidate’s full edit set. The implementation has the right failure value but not yet a demonstrated sparse, bounded query contract at scale.

#### Motion-authority routing — canonical sweeps are not the universal fast-motion path

The same patch selects the canonical integrator for three distinct reasons: travel Cruise, an explicit developer override, or a fixed-step displacement that cannot be represented in the local `f32` chart within a `1e-3` relative-error threshold. Independently, a non-detailed collision policy or absence of the subject's runtime `Collider` selects canonical kinematics in `resolve_locomotion_state`. These are authority/representation decisions; none asks whether a local runtime sweep is likely to tunnel, whether the canonical voxel provider covers the destination, or whether the two collision backends share equivalent geometry.

The collision route follows that authority choice. `prepare_flight_movement` submits `UsfCanonicalSweep` only when motion is canonical-kinematic and collision is not explicitly ignored. After provider resolution, canonical flight clips the semantic displacement and commits it. Runtime-authoritative flight instead calls Avian `MoveAndSlide` when a `Collider` exists; the helper directly advances the transform when it does not. In the ordinary state-policy path, missing collider presence should already have selected canonical authority, but the movement helper itself has a collision-free fallback and does not enforce that precondition.

This leaves two materially different collision contracts behind one controlled-flight feature: local physics-query response for detailed runtime motion, and the voxel provider's conservative semantic sweep for canonical motion. A large step can be perfectly representable in `f32` yet still cross thin geometry; the precision predicate does not route it to the canonical sweep. Whether Avian's `MoveAndSlide` catches any particular high-speed case depends on collider/query behavior and the available realized shapes, which this source review did not execute. The specific evidence therefore establishes a **coverage gap in the authority-selection rule**, not that every high-speed runtime step tunnels. It also means that adding the canonical sweep did not, by itself, close the reported high-speed terrain-collision problem: the request's demanded semantic coverage, body/collider readiness, and motion authority are not one decision.

The follow-up architecture test should vary speed, local chart magnitude, collider presence, demanded collision coverage, and a thin obstacle independently. It should show which backend owns each step and prove the accepted semantic displacement is bounded by the relevant collision result. Those experiments are still open; no compilation, automated test run, or runtime repro was performed in this historical review.

**Coverage gap:** this commit adds tests for grouping, flight-safety arithmetic, navigation context, travel assistance and flight policy, but not for the voxel candidate or narrow-phase resolver. The current source search finds no test invoking `VoxelCollisionQuery`, `trace_candidate`, or either segment-bound helper anywhere in Loo-Cast; those files contain no test module. Consequently the central claims “a complete query can clear,” “contact has a conservative safe fraction,” “unknown remains non-clear,” and “edited fields are resolved correctly” have no direct automated test evidence in this tree. This is an inspected coverage gap, not a test failure, and no tests were run as part of this historical review.

#### Follow-up audit — semantic-position writer domains

A targeted writer search distinguishes several intentional write paths that the broad “multiple writers” warning otherwise conflates. These are **separate source domains**, not one generic mutation pipeline:

| Writer | Scope and source of the new position | What this establishes / leaves open |
|---|---|---|
| `sync_semantic_positions` (`spatial/systems.rs`) | Mirrors a changed runtime `Transform` from the one active `UsfSpatialAnchor` to its canonical semantic owner. It skips anchors whose `UsfCanonicalMotion` is canonical-kinematic. `reconcile_local_control_adapters` removes the old anchor marker when local control transfers. | A clear projection-to-semantic fallback for native/runtime-authoritative motion, with explicit suppression for canonical motion. The anchor tag is moved by the control-transfer adapter rather than imposed by the `UsfPosition` type. |
| `propagate_keplerian_orbits` (`game/orbit/mod.rs`) | Each `RunFixedMainLoop` tick computes body position and velocity from the primary's canonical state plus Keplerian elements and elapsed virtual time; it writes `UsfPosition` and sets canonical-kinematic authority. | Celestial ephemeris is an independent periodic owner, not a flight commit. Its query does not exclude a Keplerian authority that is also the semantic owner of a `LocalControlSubject`. Current fixture construction attaches it to authored orbital scenery, but neither the query nor an inspected validator enforces disjoint ownership. If the semantic authority for a controlled subject also receives `KeplerianOrbitPropagation`, orbit propagation precedes locomotion in the ordered fixed loop and can reset its controlled path each tick. This is a **confirmed missing guard, conditional conflict**, not a reproduced live entity. |
| `commit_canonical_motion` / `commit_runtime_position_to_canonical` (`game/locomotion/runtime/flight/commit.rs`) | The controlled-flight commit writes the collision-accepted canonical displacement, or converts the collision-resolved runtime `Transform` back through the chart origin. An out-of-bound f32 projection preserves canonical position and queues a motion reanchor. | Both canonical and detailed/local flight converge on semantic position; collision response is consumed before the write. The source shows these functions, but not runtime collision correctness. |
| `apply_spatial_transitions` (`spatial/transition/apply.rs`) | Writes only after a queued transition is admitted; then re-charts all runtime projections mapped to that semantic subject. It is ordered after `sync_semantic_positions` in the PostUpdate synchronization chain. | Transition is a distinct, admitted discontinuity/rechart transaction. The ordering prevents the ordinary transform mirror from overwriting the admitted destination in that same chain. |
| Fixture, landing and disembark actions (`game/world/fixture/player`, `game/spacecraft/landing.rs`, `boarding/exit.rs`) | Bootstrap writes a resolved safe spawn and queues a relocation; landing writes a resolved settled pose after an opportunity; disembark writes a separately resolved walkable player pose before control transfer. | These are event-scoped placement transactions with domain checks, not the per-tick motion integrator. Bootstrap's direct canonical write plus queued transition is intentional dual work: establish the semantic spawn and then request chart/readiness admission. No common typed transaction abstraction unifies these paths. |

This narrows—but does not erase—the earlier ownership concern: current code has distinct periodic, runtime-projection, controlled-flight, rechart and event-placement writers. The ordinary local-control anchor is explicitly reassigned, and the celestial fixture has a separate Keplerian component path; however, no component invariant or query filter prevents cross-domain ownership overlap. The review is source-level, the conditional dual-owner case was not runtime-reproduced, and no test or compile was run.

The latest locomotion source does enforce a meaningful, narrower invariant: one `MotionKernel` (`Character`, `InertialFlight`, or `Disabled`) is selected for the controlled subject per tick ([contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/execution.rs#L5-L17>)). `LocomotionPlugin` resolves and realizes that choice, schedules Avian character simulation before flight preparation, and schedules the flight resolver after collision-query finalization ([schedule](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/mod.rs#L89-L116>), [motor realization](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/state/systems.rs#L208-L213>)). Character/Disabled subjects leave the flight preparation path; inertial flight has one resolver that selects semantic sweep-and-commit or local `MoveAndSlide` ([dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/flight/mod.rs#L96-L160>), [resolver](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/flight/mod.rs#L295-L401>)). `MotionKernel` is not the same axis as `UsfMotionAuthority`: the former selects the controlled-subject integrator, while the latter selects whether canonical SI velocity or the Avian `LinearVelocity` projection is authoritative ([motion representation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/spatial/motion.rs#L1-L16>)). Policy resolution may zero or transfer velocity when that representation changes; that is handoff logic, not evidence of two concurrent flight integrators ([handoff](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/state/systems.rs#L84-L109>)). This validates the per-subject kernel boundary while leaving the separately documented ephemeris/transition/placement overlap question open. It is source inspection only; no schedule test or runtime trace was performed.

#### Second focused source pass — travel readiness and transition admission

The ordered fixed-step schedule is coherent for the normal spacecraft path: navigation observes semantic position and travel context, flight safety evaluates that observation, control requests are sampled, then navigation resolves Cruise requests before locomotion. The reference spacecraft spawn includes `NavigationCapabilities::spacecraft()`, `FlightSafetyState`, and `TravelAssistanceState`, so its ordinary composition satisfies the resolver's safety-state expectation.

That expectation is not enforced by the resolver contract. `resolve_travel_assistance` queries `Option<&FlightSafetyState>` and tests emergency only with `is_some_and`; an entity without the safety component is treated as non-emergency. `evaluate_flight_safety` requires the component, so that same subject receives no safety evaluation. The normal spacecraft spawn is safe from this omission, but a custom controlled subject can expose Cruise capability without installing safety state and still pass the Cruise-entry check. This is a **conditional fail-open component invariant**, not a reproduced default-game failure; no test asserts that Cruise-capable subjects must carry safety state.

One current Rustdoc statement is now stale even though the safety algorithm remains intentionally advisory. `FlightSafetyProfile` says available braking/thrust will be supplied “when the predictive supervisor is added,” but the supervisor already exists and `evaluate_flight_safety` receives `available_deceleration_metres_per_second2` as an input; the runtime derives that scalar from the selected Cruise/manual policy and enabled actuators ([stale profile docs and evaluator](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/flight/model/safety.rs#L5-L120>), [runtime estimate](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/flight/runtime.rs#L25-L138>)). The adjacent `FlightSafetyState` comment says it does not apply a physical contact response, which is still accurate, but can now be misread as “it has no effect”: Emergency is consumed by `resolve_travel_assistance`, which exits Lattice Cruise and marks a capture pending; the following controlled-flight step zeros its throttle and clamps the resulting velocity magnitude to the emergency-contact cap before collision resolution ([dropout resolver](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/navigation/runtime/travel.rs#L10-L53>), [capture and motion preparation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/flight/mod.rs#L177-L237>)). This is a connected safety-to-motion transition, not a force-integrated brake or contact response. The distinction corrects the older shorthand that the safety supervisor “remains observational”: its state changes the Cruise lifecycle and subsequent velocity policy, while it still does not steer against the trajectory or consume the later sweep/contact result. No build, test, or runtime replay was performed.

Travel-context absence has a similarly important ambiguity. If no hard-body influence is measured, `sync_travel_state` replaces the state with `TravelState::default()`, whose `cruise_entry_available` is `true` and `critical_dropout` is `false`. The neighborhood intentionally refreshes every fixed observe pass while empty, which allows a streamed influence to appear later, but the interface has no separate `known-empty` versus `coverage-unavailable` state. Bodyless space therefore permits Cruise as intended; a temporarily incomplete influence set is indistinguishable from that known-empty case. The source establishes the assumption and its consequence, not that an actual stream omitted a nearby body.

Transition safety is also composed from caller opt-ins and a narrowly scoped backend guard. `UsfSpatialTransition::new` starts with `TransitionCoverageRequirement::NONE`; callers add required destination roles explicitly. The standard spacecraft control-affinity and fixture paths add coverage when their affinities request it, while controlled relocation adds a gate only when its hard-body refinement helper finds a qualifying destination. A relocation with no such gate is admitted without destination-role evidence. This makes “transition is admitted” weaker than “all destination collision and interaction capabilities are ready.”

The physics overlap provider only iterates continuous `interaction_requirements`, and `ResolvedTransition::guard_allows` applies the guard only to `InteractionRequirement` causes. Requested relocations—including one-shot spawn, control-transfer, or relocation transactions—do not receive this coarsening-overlap veto, even when they separately request capability coverage. That narrow scope is consistent with the provider's own comment (“coarsening interaction handoff”) and the explicitly deferred finer/contact-manifold protocol; it is not a universal collision-safe transition mechanism. Motion reanchors separately bypass capability coverage by design because they preserve canonical position and rechart at the current scale.

Tests in this tranche cover travel's semantic-position observation and the `TravelAssistanceState` lifecycle, but there is no direct admission test module, no resolver integration test for missing safety state, no unknown-versus-empty neighborhood test, and no test showing which transition causes are vetoed by the backend guard. These are **coverage gaps**, not observed failures; the tests were not run in this review. The relevant paths are unchanged between `46e1eac` and the October 25 `c070bf3` checkout, so these findings describe the current local committed baseline. They do not establish remote branch state or runtime behavior.

#### Focused input-help pass — the HUD is only partly binding-aware

The new contextual help uses the binding model for most semantic actions, but hardcodes three wheel gestures as literal strings: plain wheel, Shift+wheel and Ctrl+wheel. The actual routing is action-based: Shift means `FastModifier`, Ctrl means `Descend`, and Alt means `ViewScaleModifier`; all three actions can be rebound. With defaults, Ctrl maps to Descend and the HUD's “CTRL+WHEEL Camera zoom” accurately describes vehicle zoom. After rebinding Descend, the HUD can still say Ctrl while the runtime requires the new key. Likewise Shift+wheel pace and the omitted Alt+wheel view-scale action can diverge from the actual customized binding. The help also has no wheel-zoom or view-scale row in the on-foot branch, despite those input paths remaining active in eligible camera/view states. This is a **confirmed discoverability mismatch conditional on rebinding or context**, not an input-routing failure. [`context_actions.rs`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/ui/hud/context_actions.rs#L164-L242), [default modifier bindings](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/input/bindings/registry.rs#L93-L117), [vehicle zoom gate](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/camera/input.rs#L36-L56), [view-scale and scroll routing](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/controls/movement/mod.rs#L8-L32).

The same builder appends variable-length contextual rows and then truncates the result to 16. A fully capable spacecraft can contribute two view rows, up to five travel/flight rows, nine flight-movement rows, and—when the attitude autopilot is active—one status row. That reaches 17, so the final appended Boost hint is silently removed. The precise combination was not exercised, but the cap and append order make the truncation consequence deterministic when those states coincide. This is a **source-proven conditional omission**; whether the UI's narrow area makes a hard cap necessary is a separate presentation choice. [`row assembly and cap`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/ui/hud/context_actions.rs#L120-L151), [flight movement rows](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/ui/hud/context_actions.rs#L164-L242), [conditional autopilot row](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/ui/hud/context_actions.rs#L120-L145).

#### Focused braking pass — cruise, throttle and emergency capture are three different policies

The new source has no standalone Brake input/action. Manual flight stores a signed throttle and changes it at `0.5` units per second; moving from full forward to neutral therefore takes two seconds before the current command reaches zero. While any nonzero thrust wish is active, the velocity integrator suppresses RCS damping; once thrust is absent, RCS applies bounded damping opposite the current velocity. This can be a coherent propulsion model, but it means “hold reverse” first ramps down forward thrust, and “use RCS to brake” does not take effect while persistent throttle still commands thrust. There is no source evidence of an immediate brake override or a one-button zero-throttle-plus-RCS action. Also, the `B`/Flight Assist toggle controls angular damping only; translational RCS damping has its own `Z` toggle. The source explicitly models these as independent policies, so “Flight Assist off” does not mean translational braking is off or on. This is a deliberate model with a potentially surprising ED-like control expectation, not a confirmed defect. These control semantics are **confirmed**; they make inadequate braking plausible but do not prove the user's Moon-approach report followed this exact input path. [`throttle ramp`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/flight.rs#L18-L24), [RCS suppression while thrusting](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/flight/policy.rs#L90-L128), [separate RCS/flight-assist actions](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/controls/modes/mod.rs#L65-L108), [player throttle input](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/controls/movement/mod.rs#L56-L115).

Cruise makes reverse input unavailable by policy: it clamps the persistent throttle to `[0, 1]`, squares that value for requested speed, and approaches the requested scalar speed through logarithmic smoothing. Turning the ship redirects velocity gradually while normalizing it back to the commanded speed; it does not generate a reverse-speed command. Thus S can lower Cruise's commanded speed, but this is response-filtered deceleration rather than an immediate brake or physical reverse thrust. [`Cruise speed policy`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/flight/cruise.rs#L39-L95).

The device-independent intent API also has a stale forward-axis contract. Its docs say `translation_axes` includes `+Z forward`, and `forward_axis()` returns that stored Z value; the actual solver overwrites Z with the separate throttle argument before computing its wish vector. The human adapter stores zero in vector Z and correctly writes forward/back input to `throttle_axis`, but a future AI/network/replay controller following the documented vector-only shape can observe a nonzero `forward_axis()` while the solver ignores it. `set_throttle_axis()` also does not mark the intent active, while the executor advances persistent throttle only for active intent; alternate controllers must call the general `set()` and then the separate throttle setter to make the axis take effect. No non-human controller is present in this patch to show how it would be authored. These are **confirmed API/documentation inconsistencies with conditional integration hazards**, not demonstrated controller failures. [`intent docs and accessors`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/flight.rs#L91-L172), [solver override](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/flight/policy.rs#L19-L27), [intent activation and throttle setter](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/flight.rs#L120-L152), [human adapter's separate axis](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/controls/movement/mod.rs#L108-L115).

Emergency dropout then uses a third policy: after resolving a velocity step, it clamps the **magnitude** directly to either the emergency-contact cap or manual maximum, logs the before/after speed, and only then forms the next displacement. That is a discontinuous velocity change (a speed capture), not force-integrated braking; it may be intentional as the drive's emergency transition rule, but its momentum/damage/energy semantics need an explicit design contract. The displacement is submitted to the canonical collision provider only when that authority is active, collision is not ignored, a demand exists, and the semantic position resolves. A unit test in the patch confirms a `1e10 m/s` input can become `100 m/s`, but that only verifies the clamp arithmetic. It does not prove the swept destination, energy accounting, or a safe outcome in the live world. [`capture helper`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/flight/policy.rs#L28-L33), [capture before conditional sweep submission](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/46e1eacb33c18f6ff274f4d6acf6c98f45fe87b6/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/flight/mod.rs#L214-L270).

The tests in this area do not characterize the control transition that a player experiences: the throttle component has no direct ramp test, the local integrator test checks positive half-throttle acceleration, and the capture test checks only the scalar cap. The Cruise smoothing path has no test module in its file, and no test combines active throttle, RCS, reverse input, Cruise speed reduction, emergency dropout and collision result. These are inspection-based test-coverage gaps; no tests were run for this review.

### October 19 — `d7e1f589`: local line-count helper

This four-line script runs `cloc` on `loo-cast-game`, `loo-cast-packagepack` and `spacetime-engine`. It is a local measurement convenience, not a build/cache manager or a codebase-wide size policy; it omits workspace manifests and other repository content by design.

### October 21–23: typed Workshop search and the shared console reach multiple frontends

This is a cross-repository integration check of two user-visible claims, not a new implementation pass. The source checkouts are the local read-only mirrors at Vapor `5743065`, Studio `b02ecb4`, GUI `972a3f6`, CLI `a09c49c`, and Examples `80a30d2`; the nested Vapor and Installer submodules are pre-existing dirty entries and were not modified.

**Workshop filtering is carried through the client stack, but discovery still depends on Steam tags.** The Launcher stores `Option<ContentKind>`, resets its result offset on a new first-page search, and emits `WorkshopAction::Search { query, page, content_kind, required_tags: [] }`. The Studio selector stores its kind as a string, parses it to the same protocol enum, includes it in `pending_search`, and sends the same action. Studio and Launcher both retain query/page/type identity with the result snapshot; Launcher suppresses displaying a snapshot when the controls no longer match it. The service carries the enum into the provider call and writes it back into the search snapshot. The typed field therefore does not appear to be dropped at either current frontend boundary.

The Steam provider turns the selected enum into a required tag equal to `ContentKind::as_str()`, merges user tags, and requires all canonicalized tags both in the Steam query and in a second local post-filter over each returned item. The publisher constructs VDF tags from the content kind plus authored Workshop tags. That is a coherent exact-tag contract when records have been published through this path. It is not an independent server-side content-type index: existing/manual Steam records without the exact canonical tag are excluded; a Steam query can return no record for the type even when its descriptive text or manifest would imply that type. There is also a conditional pagination mismatch: the provider takes `total_results` from Steam's page before the local post-filter removes records. If Steam returns any item missing one of the requested tags (for example from stale cached query data), the visible page can be sparse while total/page navigation still counts the removed item. The source does not show this occurring against the live catalog. The Launcher also hides `Crate` from its player-facing type choices, while Studio exposes `ContentKind::ALL`, including Crate. These are deliberate-looking role differences in current source, but no shared policy object or test proves the product rule.

The tests added alongside the typed path check normalization, matching, fixture propagation, action shape, and query-control identity. They do not query Steam, inspect the actual public Workshop catalog, or establish that every already-published Workshop item has the canonical tag. No runtime result was obtained in this research. Thus the source rules out a simple “frontend forgot to send the filter” explanation, but it cannot identify which live item metadata or Steam query behavior caused the reported filter failure. This is a confirmed integration dependency and an unresolved live defect, not a claim that the user's report is mistaken.

**The common console is a shared record/view layer, not yet one console product.** `vapor_console_core` defines structured records, levels/style roles, source/target/fields, bounded history, filtering, prompt history, and a limited Rhai lexical surface. `vapor_gui_core::console` adapts operation output to records and renders indexed rows; Launcher, Studio, and IDE use frontend panels, and CLI has a terminal renderer over the same record model. In Studio, the Oct 23 indexed-view change caches warning/error indices until history revision changes and reuses the shared renderer; it bounds the open dock to 140–520 px. CLI's Oct 23 provenance patch prints service-provided origin and composition fields. These changes reduce duplicate representation code and repeated full-history scans.

However, the new core is not shown as the in-game F2 console's implementation: game console commands and Vapor command actions remain separate interfaces. Rhai tokenization support in the record crate does not amount to a shared command registry, type system, completion source, or execution authority. A shared renderer also does not prove that every operation emits enough structured output; earlier Client changes carry selected Cargo diagnostics and launched-child stdout/stderr, while origin attribution partly relies on executable-name inference and several structured diagnostic context fields remain unset. Therefore “shared console” is true for records/indexed views across Vapor frontends, but not for command semantics or game/Vapor integration. No layout screenshot, large-history runtime profile, or Windows session was captured here.

#### Latest-state console trace — game command runtime versus Vapor operation console

The source shows two intentionally different authority systems that have converged only at the level of display vocabulary:

- **Game F2/terminal console:** `DeveloperConsolePlugin` owns Bevy resources, schedule hooks, command dispatch, tracing capture, stdin and the overlay ([plugin and schedule](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/mod.rs#L60>), [dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/mod.rs#L109>)). Game command modules register Rust function pointers against `&mut World`, and handlers can inspect/mutate ECS state synchronously. The game layer registers its own `where`, `zoom`, `speed`, `camera`, `cruise`, `autopilot`, `debugfly`, `teleport`, runtime-variable and input-binding commands ([game command catalog](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/mod.rs#L42>), [command contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/command/contract.rs#L1>)). This is a domain-capable developer shell, not a thin presentation adapter over Vapor Client.
- **Vapor GUI/IDE console:** `vapor_client_domain::ConsoleCommand` parses a small fixed vocabulary into typed `ClientAction`s. Its catalogue distinguishes Launcher read-only from workspace scope; service execution and permission remain with the Client ([command model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/console_command.rs#L1>)). Studio, IDE and Launcher render through `vapor_gui_core::ConsolePanelState`; Launcher calls the panel without a prompt while the authoring surfaces enable it ([shared panel contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/console.rs#L35>), [IDE surface](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/console_view.rs#L20>), [Studio surface](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/operation_center.rs#L35>)). CLI has yet another terminal renderer over the record model; it does not use the Bevy command registry.

The game has its own synchronous command queue and queue-drain boundary. It uses `Arc<Mutex<VecDeque<...>>>` for commands and records, limits pending records to 4,096, then drains all accepted submissions into one Bevy `Update` dispatch pass ([transport](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/transport/queue.rs#L11>), [drain and dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/mod.rs#L109>)). A handler that performs expensive world work therefore runs inside that pass unless its own adapter defers the work. This is a source-level scheduling property, not a measured frame hitch. The record cap only bounds the pending diagnostic queue; the command-submission queue shown here has no corresponding capacity or per-frame work budget. The native stdin path reads complete lines and submits them without a byte limit; parsing then allocates tokens from the entire line ([stdin ingress](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/transport/terminal.rs#L16-L35>), [parser](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/command/parse.rs#L5-L25>)). Record capacity is also count-based, not byte-based, and the dispatch loop publishes each output line independently. So 4,096 records or one queued command do not imply a fixed memory ceiling. These are concrete source-level capacity asymmetries; no flood, memory-pressure, or frame-time experiment was performed. Separately, the visible F2 scrollback keeps at most 512 records ([overlay history](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/overlay/mod.rs#L25>)).

The tracing adapter copies event fields into a shared-record payload, but its module contract explicitly says raw stdout/stderr are not intercepted; Bevy's own formatted layer owns terminal output while the extra tracing layer feeds only the in-process overlay ([transport contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/mod.rs#L7>), [tracing adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/transport/tracing.rs#L45>)). `ConsoleRecord` is also a game-local wrapper around `vapor_telemetry::ConsoleRecord`, with a separate `origin`, `kind`, and optional game command source. The GUI-side record/history is another owner of presentation state. These are useful adapters, but not a common event transport: the inspected source does not publish F2 records through the Client service or receive service operation output into the game's overlay.

The shared GUI view does improve an earlier weak point: a 4,000-record bounded history, revision-aware filter/index cache, fixed-height virtual rows via `show_rows`, and source navigation for structured diagnostics are present ([GUI state/cache](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/console.rs#L35>), [virtual rows](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/console.rs#L305>)). Yet that history capacity and the in-game 512-record capacity are separate frontend policies; clearing either view does not imply a shared retained log authority. The GUI renderer constructs filters from conventions like fields named `origin`, `composition`, `domain`, and `scope`, rather than a fully typed console provenance envelope. Those values are semantically structured only by convention at this boundary. The view's source menu derives distinct values by scanning every retained record whenever the history revision changes, and the filtered-index rebuild also scans the full bounded history when the filter changes; it then virtualizes widget construction, not history ingestion or filtering ([cache refresh](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/console.rs#L60>), [row virtualization](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/console.rs#L322>)). With a 4,000-record cap this is bounded, but it is not a streaming/indexed event store.

Structured process output has a further view conversion: ordinary output becomes one record per non-empty line; a structured diagnostic becomes one record from only its first message line, with rendered/raw producer payload and source locations retained as fields for hover/navigation ([conversion](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/console.rs#L444>)). Thus a detailed diagnostic can be preserved but is not fully shown inline. This distinction matters when comparing the user-visible “summarized line, expandable full log” intention: source supports a concise first-line row and hover details, but does not by itself prove a good expansion interaction, readable long-term log persistence, or that every producer supplies machine-readable diagnostics.

History gives this split a clear sequence. Loo-Cast's September 27 `7d9af82` substantially rewrites its console into a game-native command/overlay surface (+730/−133 across three files). October 1 `cffbab6` adds runtime variables, bindings and the larger game/debug command surface in a 14-file pass; the game console is increasingly a developer control plane, not generic terminal chrome. October 8 `d806e3d` restructures completion and adjacent engine modules but does not remove that ownership. October 22, Vapor `7ab704b` adds `vapor_console_core`; Vapor `8e3d1ba` adds a separate typed command parser and operation-output protocol; GUI `ba6fe8c` / `dab912c` adds the shared Launcher/authoring panel; and Loo-Cast `c070bf3` adapts its existing console record to the shared telemetry record and shares Rhai lexical vocabulary. October 23 IDE changes add diagnostic linking/navigation but preserve the separate Vapor command authority. The direction is convergence by adapters, not a unified console runtime.

**Interpretation:** the product ambition—one recognizable, performant console across game F2, Studio, IDE, Launcher and CLI—is larger than “reuse the same egui renderer.” The current useful foundations are distinct and should be named accurately: a game-owned live-world command runtime; a service-owned typed Vapor operation API; a cross-product structured record and GUI view; and terminal adapters. The missing connective design is how commands are declared, scoped/authorized, completed, scheduled and audited across these authorities, and whether a console session can observe both an app process and the long-lived Client service without merging their state or permissions. No source here proves the eventual answer should be one process or one command registry. This is a boundary question, not an instruction to make the game console execute arbitrary Client actions.

**F2 presentation and command metadata expose a second, separate integration seam.** The game overlay has a bounded 512-record deque, prompt history delegated to `vapor_telemetry::PromptHistory`, cursor-aware completion, and colored structured records ([overlay state](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/overlay/state.rs>), [history cap and toggle](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/overlay/mod.rs>), [record presentation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/overlay/record.rs>)). The prompt renders each retained record in a normal loop; it does not use the virtual row renderer found in Vapor GUI. Its `Area` has explicit percentage/clamped geometry and fixed positioning, without an exposed resize interaction in this implementation ([prompt rendering](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/overlay/prompt.rs>), [window geometry](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/overlay/render.rs>)). The cap bounds row count, so source alone does not establish current lag or bad runtime feel.

Completion is decomposed into scanning/cursor-site detection, candidate selection, and string replacement. The scanner respects quotes and escapes and works on UTF-8 character boundaries; candidates combine command paths, runtime-variable paths/values, static values and nested command tails; editing replaces only the current token fragment and inserts a separating space after unique matches ([scanner](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/completion/scan.rs>), [candidate lookup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/completion/candidate.rs>), [edit behavior](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/completion/edit.rs>), [completion module](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/completion/mod.rs>)). This is substantive shell behavior, not merely a text box. No shared descriptor path with Vapor CLI/GUI completion is evidenced here, and no test suite was run to establish edge-case correctness.

The registry is extensible through Bevy App registration, but command metadata is only usage/summary/aliases and completion descriptors; handler authority is `fn(&mut World, ..)`. Duplicate or empty paths panic during registration. `help` lists all commands, and the spec has no role/scope authorization, mutation-risk, scheduling or capability declaration ([registry](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/command/registry.rs>), [descriptor and invocation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/command/contract.rs>), [built-in help](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/command/builtin.rs>), [command facade](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/command/mod.rs>)). This does not prove every command is unsafe or reachable by every user: individual handlers and outer focus/state checks still matter. It establishes that the shared registration contract cannot express the Player/Composer/Developer boundaries now expected from the ecosystem.

The runtime-variable registry is typed by labels but value access remains callback/string-based. `RuntimeVariableSpec` names a value type, units, authority and domain, while getter/setter/resetter callbacks translate values to and from strings. A `Range` can be displayed but its numeric limits are not enforced centrally. `SemanticOperation` is barred from generic set/reset and points toward typed causal ingress (#17), while local debug controls and engine overrides can be changed directly. No role-aware authorization is encoded in this adapter ([value and authority contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/runtime_variables/contract.rs>), [registry](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/runtime_variables/registry.rs>), [commands](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/runtime_variables/commands.rs>), [module integration](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/runtime_variables/mod.rs>)). This is a useful guardrail but not a full shared command/action type system.

Together with the queue budget above, the actual state is more precise than either “F2 is great” or “console is missing”: the game console already has completion, history, structured colored logs and tracing capture, but it is a game-owned synchronous shell with broad handler capability and separate UI/transport policy. Vapor shares some record and widget vocabulary, not execution authority or an end-to-end event stream. No UI render, runtime interaction, queue-flood test or command-authorization test was performed.

### Game command groups: domain ownership is clearer than command authority

The catalog's module split is meaningful: input bindings, observation/diagnostics, runtime variables, teleport and travel each adapt an existing game subsystem into F2. Configuration also calls the developer lab directly. The same descriptor/handler contract still covers every class ([registration module](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/mod.rs>), [observation module](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/observation/mod.rs>)).

The observation commands mix effects: `where`/`locate` report state; `voxelstream` reports worker telemetry; `navtrace` reads or mutates recorder enable/clear state; `presentation` changes `UsfPresentationDomainProbe` while reporting view/coverage state. This is a naming/metadata ambiguity rather than a proven user-facing defect ([position/landmark inspection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/observation/position.rs>), [presentation probe](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/observation/presentation.rs>), [history/worker commands](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/observation/runtime.rs>)).

Relocation follows the right semantic route: parse a unique fixture destination or finite f64 coordinates into canonical position, emit `ControlledRelocationRequest`, and leave coverage gating to navigation. It does not directly assign Transform. The command's success record is explicitly “requested,” so it is not a completion signal. For landmark destinations it updates PlayerAim immediately before the transition request is applied; this makes one portion of the action eager and the relocation deferred ([teleport implementation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/teleport.rs>)). No transition was run to see whether that timing is perceptible or harmful.

Runtime bindings have useful action completion and matching `+`/`-` press/release behavior, and their source comment intentionally routes bound commands back through the same dispatcher. However, the suggestion list is not validation: unknown nonempty targets are stored as command strings and fail only when executed. Dispatch is tied to gameplay focus/cursor capture; the binding state model is an ordinary Resource initialized from compiled defaults, with no serialization shown in this source path. This makes persistence unproven and makes binding a command a reuse of the full registry authority, not a separate capability check ([binding commands](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/input_bindings.rs>), [binding model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/input/bindings/model.rs>), [button dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/input/bindings/dispatch.rs>), [available targets](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/input/bindings/registry.rs>)).

Typed variable groups do preserve domain owners rather than introducing a second settings store: character controls write `CharacterMovementConfig`, freecam controls its camera settings/preset, locomotion regime checks subject capabilities, and voxel budgets write `EngineConfigOverrides` whose reset removes the override ([character adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/runtime_variables/character.rs>), [freecam adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/runtime_variables/freecam.rs>), [lab override](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/runtime_variables/lab.rs>), [voxel budget adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/runtime_variables/voxel.rs>), [parsers and registration](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/runtime_variables/mod.rs>)). Yet numeric range metadata is not itself validation, most upper bounds are open, and no Player/Composer/Developer gate or per-command scheduling policy exists in this adapter. This confirms a mixed picture: useful domain boundaries inside game code, but command effects, access scope and execution cost are not first-class at the console contract. No tests, builds or runtime commands were executed in this review.

**Current travel-command pass: debug traversal exists, but pace and authority are unevenly expressed.** The in-game registry exposes `speed`, `cruise`, `attitude`, `autopilot`, `motionoverride`, `debugfly`, and `motionstack` as separate World-mutating handlers ([travel command registrations](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/mod.rs#L99-L181>)). `debugfly` toggles characteristic traversal and requests Manual assistance; that one flag implies both collision and gravity suppression, and the solver moves at `manual_speed_metres_per_second × pace × boost` ([debug traversal command](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/travel.rs#L325-L363>), [override semantics](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/execution.rs#L46-L76>), [flight solver](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/flight/policy.rs#L179-L187>)). This is a real noclip-like characteristic-speed path, not absent functionality. Yet its pace control is split: Shift+wheel changes logarithmic octaves in normal ship flight, plain wheel changes throttle, and plain wheel changes pace only while debug traversal is active; the same `TravelPace` is sampled from the Player and passed into flight intent ([wheel routing](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/controls/movement/mod.rs#L5-L33>), [flight intent](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/controls/movement/mod.rs#L108-L115>)). The `speed` command writes that same multiplier directly after only finite/nonnegative validation ([command](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/travel.rs#L89-L123>)); although `TravelPace` defines a log2 range of −16…24 and clamps wheel steps to that range, direct command assignment and `character_units_per_second` do not enforce it ([pace model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/navigation/travel/motion.rs#L10-L42>)). Therefore the advertised bounded logarithmic control can be bypassed with a very large finite typed multiplier; multiplication in the character path is `f32`, so sufficiently large accepted values can overflow. This is source-derived, not runtime-tested. Finally, `ConsoleCommandSpec` contains only name/aliases/usage/summary; no role/scope authorization field is present, and the inspected `debugfly` path checks for an inertial flight subject but not a Vapor role ([command metadata](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/console/command/contract.rs#L7-L13>), [flight capability check](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/travel.rs#L332-L339>)). This does not prove every player can open or invoke F2, but it does mean the command contract itself does not encode the Player→Composer→Developer separation the owner wants.

No build, tests, UI launch, runtime capture, or Windows verification was performed for this source audit. The bounded queues and view code establish implementation limits, not measured performance or visual quality.

#### Design promises against the October 25 implementation

The October 22 console designs are unusually explicit about what “shared” means, so they can be audited point by point instead of treated as general inspiration. The shared-core design wants a canonical record with first-class timestamp, level/kind, **origin**, source, target, message and fields, plus host-neutral filters/history/prompt state; it also directs Loo-Cast to adapt tracing, game output and telemetry, and calls for representative-record comparison across game, GUI and terminal ([core ownership and contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-shared-console-editor-core-design.md#L12>), [host adapters](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-shared-console-editor-core-design.md#L23>), [record flow and acceptance](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-shared-console-editor-core-design.md#L31>)). The current shared `ConsoleRecord` has `level`, `source`, optional `target`, message and fields, but no typed `kind` or `origin`; GUI adapters encode origin in a conventionally named field, while Loo-Cast keeps a local wrapper for origin and record kind. This is not a lost string payload, but it is a **contract narrowing** relative to the design's stated canonical shape.

The same design says the first implementation is deliberately not a common visual widget or full parity, and its implemented-slice status explicitly leaves live game/Vapor stream comparison and richer terminal progress as remaining work ([status](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-shared-console-editor-core-design.md#L50>)). That accurately bounds the Oct 22 tranche. However, later Oct 23 IDE and Studio changes expanded the shared view and diagnostic navigation without updating this status section. The design therefore describes the semantic foundation correctly but is no longer a complete “what's now implemented” ledger; current-state findings should govern, and the doc should be updated only after this audit establishes the final map.

The command-console design is a separate layer, not a direct extension of the record core. It says Vapor Client owns the canonical command catalog and typed invocation; frontends share it; launcher is read-only; and Studio/IDE commands route through the already-connected service ([command authority](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-vapor-command-console-design.md#L5>)). Actual parsing does yield typed actions and service validation remains authoritative. But the present command catalogue is a fixed compile-time slice of help/status/catalog refresh/composition select/launch/workspace tools, not the design's implied extensible typed command registration. The GUI panel itself only emits a string; IDE and Studio each parse it locally and separately implement help/status responses. CLI keeps its independent grammar and its docs explicitly leave descriptor-based help/completion as follow-up ([static command definitions](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/console_command.rs#L13>), [IDE parser/dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/console_view.rs#L312>), [Studio parser/dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/operation_center.rs#L172>), [CLI output adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/console.rs#L1>)). The current implementation is a deliberately small common command vocabulary with repeated frontend dispatch glue, not one generic cross-product command descriptor registry.

The main console plan says to replace Studio's independent renderer, separate Problems from Console, use the same command descriptors in terminal help/completion, then remove obsolete parallel state after integration ([plan](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-22-vapor-command-console.md#L1>)). Source shows reusable Studio rendering and Problems selection; whether every old console buffer was removed is not established by this slice. The plan's terminal command-catalog reuse remains explicitly open. The IDE's later semantic-workbench plan raises a broader target—typed Cargo events, retained raw output, diagnostics with workspace/document context, common Problems and Console navigation, incremental bounds ([semantic-workbench plan](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-23-semantic-workbench.md#L10>)). Current IDE documentation claims structured compiler diagnostics, raw detail, navigation and grouped Rust Analyzer/build reports, and source supports these paths. It does not follow that the game F2 console and IDE have one console event stream.

**Owner direction not represented as a completed plan:** in the discussion preceding this research pass, the owner asked to reuse the in-game F2 console and editor as much as possible for Vapor, to build a substantial shared egui abstraction layer for consoles/editors/panels/virtual scrolling, and to create a fast context-aware UI preview workflow. The accepted Oct 22 design intentionally avoids common concrete widgets and explicitly leaves a full UI toolkit to another tranche. That is a defensible decoupling boundary, but it means the shared-toolkit ambition has not yet been elaborated into an approved architecture in the inspected artifacts. This audit records that open seam rather than claiming the shared records work satisfies the UI-toolkit request.

The console/history reconciliation also tempers the GUI docs: a current virtualized row view does not make the underlying log stream globally persistent or fully incremental. Record retention is per frontend panel; the Client service protocol transports operation output, but there is no evidence here of a durable unified console history spanning the Launcher, Studio, IDE, spawned composition and game process. The earlier user request that source identity make Launcher/Studio/IDE/launched-composition logs filterable is therefore only partly satisfied by existing `origin`, `composition`, `source`, `process` fields and their current producer coverage. It remains unverified whether every launched composition emits tagged records through the same channel.

### October 24 local WIP: the content-graph model becomes an ordered implementation proposal

At Vapor commit `5743065` on Oct 23, the read-only local checkout has an untracked `docs/superpowers/` directory containing `2026-10-24-vapor-content-graph-design.md` and `2026-10-24-vapor-content-graph.md`. These are local uncommitted documents, not repository history and not implemented features. They were read without modification.

The spec preserves exactly the ten existing kinds and accurately distinguishes the four manifest Packs from six code-bearing Content kinds at the role level. It treats Packagepack source/editability and executable as two projections under one Packagepack identity/release; defines Engine/EngineMod as reusable capability, Game as usage/composition, GameMod as gameplay extension, ExtensionMod as a generic mod-of-mod, and Crate as stack-independent Rust. Its graph vocabulary separates target role, required/optional edge, alternative selection, compatibility, conflict, and build/link usage. It explicitly rejects the assumption that every pack member is jointly compatible or selected, and calls for an explicit selected graph with explanations for excluded paths. These choices align closely with the owner's clarifications recorded in this conversation.

The five-step plan orders work as: canonical edge classes; compatibility/conflict/cardinality/optional resolution; pack path selection; source versus target-specific executable projections for Packagepack; then representative graphs and publishable examples. It proposes focused tests and managed target-matrix validation, but neither was run in this historical review. The plan is unusually explicit about not editing Loo-Cast in this content tranche and preserving dirty worktrees. It remains an implementation proposal only.

**Unresolved packaging boundary:** “Pack is a typed manifest and does not contain Content” must remain distinct from “Packagepack release provides editable source and a runnable executable.” The spec calls these source/runtime projections of one Packagepack identity/release, but it does not yet settle where source closure lives, whether it is carried alongside the manifest or resolved separately from source repositories/releases, and which exact files Steam Workshop versus another provider distributes. That needs a concrete artifact/provenance diagram before implementation; otherwise Task 4 could accidentally place Content inside a Pack or force player-side source/Cargo acquisition. A second unresolved policy is the user-facing difference between pack membership, a required relationship, optional feature dependency, and explicit selected alternative. The plan names these categories but defers their exact serialized shapes to the call-site audit, which is appropriate at this stage.

The spec also explicitly leaves the full UI toolkit, IDE, operation console, and Rhai-to-Rust/WASM lifecycle to separate workstreams. This is useful scope control, not evidence those domains are solved. It assumes the content graph will expose resolution diagnostics and lifecycle contracts to those products later. The draft is strong as an owner-aligned problem framing and sequencing proposal; its key next design proof is the manifest/source/build/distribution/runtime artifact boundary, followed by concrete edge examples for every kind before schema edits.

**Current implementation cross-check (read-only, October 25):** The proposal is directionally ahead of the committed domain model, but the existing layer already has some selection machinery. `DependencySpec` contains ID, version requirement, and optionality; the authored manifest carries free-form relationship labels and conflicts separately. Helpers derive exclusive Engine-vs-Enginepack and Game-vs-Gamepack slots for Packagepack, and require the Engine/Game slots for particular root kinds. The source authoring validator applies those fixed groups and target-count rules. This is a real, narrow precursor to the draft's graph model—not a generic alternatives mechanism.

The provider-neutral resolver selects the highest matching version independently for each required edge and recursively constructs a dependency closure. It deliberately has no global backtracking/version unification; every optional edge is skipped from the default graph. The content-graph validator checks exact nodes, allowed pack child kinds, fixed root-pack cardinalities and required mod targets. Conflict data is retained in authored/deployed records and checked by the launch verifier against enabled installed records, but is absent from the generic candidate/resolution graph. The current model therefore has version selection, closure traversal, role-derived fixed choice slots and runtime conflict checks. It still lacks generic selected alternatives/features, compatibility constraints, explicit cardinality policies, a unified conflict-aware candidate resolver, and diagnostics for branches deliberately omitted from a selected graph. Relationship strings are retained in authored records but the generic graph reduces their identity to binding keys; duplicate relationships can be represented only through generated keys such as `relationship#index`.

The content model exposes the difference between this gap and a missing kind: all ten kinds already exist, as do fixed role edges, optional flags, conflict declarations and some cardinality checks. The needed redesign is about completing and unifying relationship/selection semantics, not vocabulary expansion. The proposed task order recognizes that dependency: define edge meaning first, then constraints/selection, pack paths, artifacts, and examples. Its Task 1 file list names the domain model but not the existing authoring validator and candidate-provider interfaces; the plan says those will be discovered in a call-site audit, so that audit must happen before anyone claims the new semantics govern real catalog resolution. Task 4 names target staging tests but leaves the actual source distribution authority open. The spec’s completion criteria are stronger than the basic-workspace scaffold and package provider reviewed on October 21; tests alone will not close that authoring-to-executable path.

One exact asymmetry helps explain the proposal’s call to revisit edge policy. `dependency_kind_allowed` explicitly restricts Crate to Crate, restricts Game to Engine/Crate, and uses pack-specific allowlists for the four Packs; its fallback permits any child kind for Engine, EngineMod, GameMod and ExtensionMod. Separate validators then require exactly one direct Engine for EngineMod, one Game for GameMod, and one Mod for ExtensionMod. This may be a deliberate “ordinary capability dependencies stay open” policy, but the fallback and target-count rules are different layers and neither alone defines the full target/optional/conflict contract. It should be resolved through the planned typed-edge model rather than silently treated as a code defect or assumed intentional.

There is a sharper authoring-versus-resolution mismatch for those required mod targets. Resolution validation insists on the three exact target counts, but `required_dependency_choice_groups` returns no required group for EngineMod, GameMod or ExtensionMod. Their expected target pair is currently named `dependency`, not `engine`/`game`/`mod`, so the authoring cardinality helper cannot distinguish that target from an ordinary dependency. The inspected creation and save paths call the relationship-group checker; save also checks recursive local dependency integrity, but neither applies the resolver's target-count validator. As written, those paths can accept a mod project with no required target (or a target marked optional); later graph validation omits optional edges and rejects a missing/zero/multiple target. This is a source-level path mismatch inferred directly from the validators; no operation was executed, and it should be covered by the proposed target-cardinality and optionality design before refactoring.

The shared graph validator also does not call the existing `dependency_kind_allowed` predicate for each resolved edge. It checks allowlists for the four pack kinds and then validates selected mod-target counts; it does not apply non-pack restrictions encoded in the predicate, such as Crate→Crate-only or Game→Engine/Crate. Authoring uses that predicate, so source-authored paths are filtered earlier, but a candidate graph assembled from another provider can bypass those pair restrictions at this layer. The invariant is therefore provider-path-dependent rather than guaranteed by the canonical graph validator. This is source-confirmed; no malicious or malformed Workshop item was constructed.

Pack-shape validation is root-scoped. `validate_content_graph` validates edge existence/kinds across all nodes, then `validate_pack_shape` matches only `graph.root_node().kind`; it does not independently apply each nested Pack's own cardinality. The allowlists permit Enginepack→Enginepack, Gamepack→Gamepack, Modpack→Modpack and Packagepack→Packagepack, so nested pack nodes can occur in a resolved graph. Whether a nested Pack is itself a reusable valid manifest or only contributes its transitive closure is unresolved in the current contract. The October 24 plan’s “pack path” task should decide and verify this explicitly; outer root counts are not a substitute for validating a nested pack’s selected path.

This is a source comparison, not a live validation: the local proposal is untracked, source checkouts remain untouched, and no graph fixture, managed validation, target package or launch was run. It records a clear current design, but acceptance, schema shape, source hosting and cross-platform runtime proof remain future evidence.

## October 22 — accepted Workshop authority boundary, implementation still topology-only

Platform Server commit [`d02a0c6a`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Platform-Server/commit/d02a0c6acf083a00f06d62b35cff49852ed3cab1) adds an explicit accepted boundary: Registry is to own canonical Vapor content identity/type, Steam Workshop bindings, discovery metadata, and version/channel records; Steam is transport/distribution, with tags only hints; Identity supplies verified-author and role authorization facts. The docs explicitly label this as a target boundary, not an implemented Registry catalog. This matches Leslie's later decision in this conversation: **Registry catalog; Identity authorizes**.

The live source confirms the gap rather than closing it. At Platform head `a98770ad` (Oct 22), Registry is still schema v1 with tables for metadata, provider accounts, repositories, ecosystems, and repository membership only. Its Axum API has health/status plus two public GET lookups; there are no catalog records, Workshop binding/version routes, write handlers, auth middleware, or Identity client. The Registry README still describes its deliberately small current responsibilities as provider accounts, repositories, and ecosystem reconstruction. Identity has sessions, linked providers, profiles and roles, but its exposed routes are auth/session operations and administrative profile/role operations; the inspected API has no Registry-oriented authorization-check contract. Thus the accepted ownership model is soundly recorded but not operationally enforced by these services yet. Current client Workshop tags remain hints, as the decision doc itself says.

**Consequence:** do not describe Steam Workshop type filtering as canonically enforced, nor say Registry authorizes publication. The next implementation boundary needs an authenticated Registry write path and a deliberate Identity authorization protocol, while preserving Steam as file transport. Until then, existing Steam tags and client-side catalog assumptions remain provider/client behavior rather than server authority. This is a confirmed implementation gap, not a claim that the accepted design is wrong.

The per-file Registry pass confirms that boundary across the entire small repository: the router exposes only health/status and two read handlers ([`main.rs`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/main.rs>)); SQLite creates provider/repository/ecosystem topology and re-seeds a fixed three-root checkout list on startup ([`db.rs`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs>)); response DTOs describe those same facts, with no canonical Vapor content or release types ([`types.rs`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/types.rs>)). The user-facing README's “register” wording exceeds the actual read-only API ([`README.md`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/README.md>)); its remaining files are a private Axum/SQLx package ([`Cargo.toml`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/Cargo.toml>)), its format-4 lockfile with 136 resolved packages ([`Cargo.lock`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/Cargo.lock>)), a stable 1.97.0 workspace declaration ([`Workspace.vapor.toml`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/Workspace.vapor.toml>)), and the `target/` ignore rule ([`.gitignore`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/.gitignore>)). These eight files are now dispositioned individually in the whole-repository inventory; path mentions elsewhere remain unreviewed until that per-file status says otherwise.

## October 15-19: Steam discovery grows into a separate subscription and Library lifecycle

The sequence is more consequential than “Workshop search was added.” On October 15, Vapor introduced a `vapor_steam` provider for Steamworks UGC search, subscription changes, and subscription-state reads ([initial provider](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/blob/379615f37083644551889b3d94f82c7371cc0c67/crates/vapor_steam/src/lib.rs)). It initializes a Steam client for each operation, runs the callback pump on the caller's thread, and returns owned records so frontends do not retain Steam API handles. Search is bounded to pages 1–1000 and permits a 60-second cached Steam response; callback operations time out after 30 seconds. The commit's API comment says callers should use a background worker, and the later service does so. This is an actual provider boundary, but it was initially Steam-specific rather than a provider-neutral canonical catalog.

The October 15 subscription snapshot then grew beyond IDs to include display metadata and Steam's installed, update-needed, downloading, and sampled-progress flags ([metadata expansion](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/523e580140b25a50dfb4b0d20f7dcd18190faca5)). Metadata is queried in batches of 50 and missing metadata becomes a placeholder row instead of dropping the subscription. The flags are a point-in-time read from Steam; they are not a durable Vapor acquisition record, an install-plan result, or a continuous progress stream. That distinction matters because the UI can show “subscribed,” “Steam installed,” and “present in Vapor's Library” as separate facts. It is a useful separation in data, but not yet one unified lifecycle.

October 16 added a common `OperationId`, phase/progress event, and context, plus `remember_source` as a non-selecting workspace-registration action ([operation contract](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/blob/aef5d98b903f505837dace8fd32c2c4e3b878ac0/crates/vapor_core/src/operation.rs), [source registration](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/blob/aef5d98b903f505837dace8fd32c2c4e3b878ac0/crates/vapor_core/src/source.rs)). The contract explicitly leaves scheduling to its host. `OperationService::run_observed` emits `Queued` and then immediately emits `Running` before synchronously invoking the operation body. So that early event is a lifecycle label, not a service-owned waiting queue. In the same period the Studio service rejects Workshop actions whenever one operation is active; the later resource registry permits unrelated concurrent work but still returns retryable conflicts rather than persisting them in one shared queue. This chronology explains how a common operation vocabulary could coexist with “wait for the current operation” behavior.

October 16 also added batch subscribe/unsubscribe, capped at 50 IDs, deduplicated, and awaited each Steam callback ([batch implementation](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/50056aa872be4edb9e6e9d1d24366040a9bd248b)). It aggregates failures into one `Err` string and does not return a per-item outcome. This becomes a cross-boundary partial-success defect in the current source: the callback loop counts successes and reports the number of failures, but `execute_workshop_operation` applies `change?` before refreshing the subscription snapshot ([Steam result aggregation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_steam/src/lib.rs:472>), [service caller](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workshop.rs:1230>)). If Steam completes some IDs successfully and others unsuccessfully, external subscription state has already changed, yet the operation returns before Vapor reloads the actual subscription list. The UI can therefore retain an old snapshot until a separate reload. A timeout similarly reports only the number completed, not which IDs completed. This is source-confirmed partial mutation with stale projection potential, not a reproduced Steam account incident; the correction belongs at the provider result contract and service reconciliation boundary, not in a cosmetic retry button.

October 19 moved Workshop acquisition toward the owner's later “subscription versus Library” semantics. `971ab112` added cache staging/replacement, Workshop-ID-to-content identity checks, preservation of a prior cached version when the new version violates the active compositions' requirements, content forking, and composition updates after acquiring an Auto-Install-managed item ([lifecycle implementation](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/971ab1126b531a6f79146e652219b54e151c7b2a)). The subscribe operation first changes Steam state, then reloads subscriptions, then downloads/imports the item into Vapor's app-owned cache; an acquisition failure is represented separately as “subscription active, but not added to Library.” A successful item import is still not identical to installation into a playable composition. This is a valuable explicit lifecycle split.

The failure edges are asymmetric. On mixed batch results, no refreshed subscription list is returned as described above. On a fully successful subscribe followed by download/import failure, the service does preserve the new subscription snapshot and reports acquisition failure. On an incompatible Auto-Install update, import preserves the prior Library cache copy; composition update results are checked against captured composition inputs before state changes are applied. However, cache replacement and composition state persistence are separate filesystem/state transitions: if composition persistence fails after cache activation, the downloaded Library copy can remain newer while the old composition state remains. The operation reports this partial outcome, but there is no single transaction spanning Steam, cache, composition records, and installed runtime files.
