The path is recoverable by retry/reconcile in principle; source does not establish automatic recovery or a durable intent log.

**Causal reading:** the early “Workshop item” concept was used for at least three distinct states—Steam search result/subscription, acquired Library copy, and installed dependency. The code progressively split these states, while auto-install added a fourth relation: a Packagepack/composition owns a dependency's subscription and cache lifetime. Later October findings in this review show that this owner graph still uses content IDs in places where exact selected versions matter, and that some real-service Auto-Install controls fail. The chronology is therefore not a clean one-way migration; it is an evolving boundary with later corrections and remaining joins. No commit in this sequence establishes public second-account discovery, reliable Steam-side type enforcement, or a complete transactional subscribe/acquire/install lifecycle.

## October 25 — authored content conflicts disappear from the Library projection

The source manifest has a dedicated `conflicts` list ([authored fields](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/authored_manifest.rs:91>)). The provider preserves those references separately from dependencies when it reads source and deployed manifests ([source conversion](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/packaging.rs:145>), [deployed conversion](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/packaging.rs:648>)), and the launch verifier rejects an artifact if its declared conflict is currently installed and enabled ([launch check](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/launch.rs:378>)).

The player-facing local Library conversion does not carry that data forward: both cached and installed `CatalogContent` entries copy `artifact.dependencies()` and set their separate `conflicts` field to an empty vector ([cache projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/catalog.rs:15>), [installed projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/catalog.rs:43>)). That `CatalogContent.conflicts` field is defined as same-version metadata disagreement between local observations, not as the artifact's authored incompatibility declarations. Downstream composition eligibility and Auto-Install checks use this catalog field as the conflict-free gate; for example, Auto-Install passes `entry.conflicts.is_empty()` ([owner seeding](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workshop.rs:567>)).

**Result:** source-authored incompatibilities survive packaging and can stop launch, but normal Library entries do not expose them to the user or use them to gate composition creation and automatic ownership. Installation planning does independently block a planned graph containing declared conflicts or an enabled installed conflict, and it blocks multiple versions of one ID before materialization ([plan checks](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/install_plan.rs:240>)). So the supported consequence is narrower: a conflicting item may appear selectable and receive Auto-Install ownership, then fail when setup builds its install plan; it is not established that the current installation path silently installs that graph. This is a source-confirmed Library projection and preflight gap, not a reproduced Steam install failure. The same word “conflict” currently covers two different concepts—authored incompatibility and conflicting local metadata—which should remain distinct in the canonical model. The launcher checks a declared conflict by content ID and enabled state; it does not inspect the reference's version constraint in the checked launch loop, so version-qualified conflict semantics are not demonstrated here.

The dependency resolver makes a second boundary explicit. The generic `DependencySpec` holds an ID, version requirement, and optional flag, but no conflict edge or alternative/cardinality declaration; optional edges are omitted from automatic resolution. The local adapter selects the highest satisfying dependency independently per edge, and the resolver explicitly defers global version unification/backtracking. Its intermediate graph may therefore contain multiple versions of one shared ID; the downstream install-plan builder detects and blocks that before materialization. No such result is claimed to have occurred in a current composition. The type/docs and selection rule are in [content vocabulary](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/content.rs:126>) and [resolver](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/resolution.rs:313>); no direct `vapor_content` resolver test module was found at this head, and no direct install-plan test for these blockers was found in that module. This is consistent with the Oct 24 local content-graph proposal being design work rather than implemented graph semantics.

One important current-state refinement: Core also exposes a generated Engine+Game Cargo realization in [`cargo.rs`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cargo.rs:355>). It generates a small app crate, resolves the local Engine and Game packages, and offers build/run functions; the implementation explicitly rejects all resolved mod kinds and its generated manifest has only those two dependencies ([graph restriction and generated manifest](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cargo.rs:442>)). The API is re-exported from [`vapor_core::lib`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/lib.rs:38>), but a source search at this checkout found no product callsite beyond that definition/export. Keep this separate from `cargo_reconciliation.rs`: that other public Core slice reconciles direct Cargo edges for a Crate root only ([Crate boundary](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cargo_reconciliation.rs:1>)). These are real, narrowly scoped implementations, but neither currently forms the Composer-to-Packagepack build, artifact, and service lifecycle. This changes the precise diagnosis from “no generic realization exists” to “two Core proof paths exist without a current product integration or the owner's full graph.”

## October 25 — pack and code artifacts share an unrestricted packaging path

The current schema has the same `binaries` and `libraries` fields on every authored content kind, and source loading copies them without a kind-specific policy ([shared authored payload shape](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/authored_manifest.rs:77>), [conversion](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/packaging.rs:145>)). The content-kind layer primarily constrains dependency roles; `Enginepack`, `Gamepack`, and `Modpack` do not receive a separate manifest-only representation ([pack kinds and child tables](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/content.rs:141>)).

`stage_deployed_artifact` applies the same packaging path to any `ContentArtifact`: it copies the authored project tree, excluding only `.git`, `target`, and `output`, then stages any declared binaries and libraries ([generic staging](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/packaging.rs:275>), [tree exclusions](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content.rs:2422>), [runtime outputs](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/packaging.rs:306>)). The checked validation path enforces dependency/cardinality rules but does not reject payload declarations by content kind. Thus non-Packagepack kinds can be staged with binaries/libraries, and authored project files can be copied into each deployed artifact. Existing examples confirm that the vocabulary is used heterogeneously: Engine declares a binary, Game declares a library, and Crate declares a library.

This is broader than the owner’s clarified model: other pack kinds are typed composition manifests, Packagepack is the playable executable root, and reusable Engine/Game/mod/Crate content supplies compiled modules/libraries. The implementation currently represents packs and code artifacts through one payload-bearing artifact schema and one generic copier. The Workshop path then points the SteamCMD `contentfolder` at that staged output ([VDF generation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/workshop.rs:670>)); the upload source is therefore the same directory containing the copied project files and staged payloads. The code review confirms what is handed to SteamCMD, though no remote upload was performed in this audit. Since the copy policy is an exclusion list rather than a publish allowlist, any non-excluded file present in a source project also enters the staged tree; this creates a conditional accidental-file disclosure risk, not evidence that a secret was present or published. This is a confirmed mismatch in current staging behavior and a potential publication hygiene risk. It is related to, but distinct from, the authored-conflict projection and resolver behavior documented in the preceding section.

The newer source/release wording sharpens the consequence: authors must be able to reach the Packagepack's editable/forkable source closure, but a Pack manifest must not physically contain constituent code or libraries; the runnable Packagepack release separately carries the linked executable. Current generic staging copies the authored project tree and its declared payloads into one Steam Workshop input, with no kind-specific split that binds an independently acquired source closure to the same Packagepack release. Therefore today's pipeline cannot establish either “players receive only the ready executable” or “composers can recover the exact source closure for this executable” as one coherent release guarantee. The October 24 local design note and architecture draft agree that source and runnable bytes are separate projections, but differ on whether source belongs to the Packagepack identity or to its referenced Content closure; that binding remains open rather than settled by this implementation.

The same generic copier has a source-root confinement gap: it calls `fs::metadata`, which follows symlinks, then recursively walks anything that resolves as a directory and copies anything that resolves as a file. Its exclusion/root checks use the lexical path; this copy path does not canonicalize each source entry or reject symlinks. A symlink inside a project can therefore cause packaging to read and stage a file or directory outside the declared content root. This compounds the source-copy policy: non-excluded external data can enter a package and its Steam upload input even though the authored manifest itself was safely found inside the root. The helper also serves provider-root observation, cache staging, and installed-copy paths; exposure to an untrusted downloaded symlink depends on whether that provider materializes it, which was not checked. A symlink loop can also recurse until an OS/path error or resource exhaustion. This is a source-level filesystem-boundary risk; no symlink fixture, Workshop item, external-file read, or recursion failure was exercised. Evidence: [`copy_tree`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content.rs:2422>) and its use by [`stage_deployed_artifact`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/packaging.rs:275>); role-manifest containment in [`manifest::read`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/manifest.rs:97>) does not validate every copied descendant.

## October 25 — Auto-Install ownership traversal drops exact versions

The October 22 ownership change correctly narrows the owner concept to installed or subscribed Packagepacks and follows only required, non-conflict edges. Its current traversal nevertheless reduces roots and dependencies to stable content IDs. `installed_packagepack_roots` discards the saved root version ([root projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/library.rs:221>)); subscribed roots likewise become a set of `entry.id` values ([subscription root projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workshop.rs:1352>)). `packagepack_dependency_owners` finds the first catalog row with that ID, marks visited nodes by ID, and follows each required dependency ID without checking its `version` requirement ([traversal](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workshop.rs:1396>)). The subsequent cache lookup again chooses the first matching ID that has a cached location, not the exact node selected by the installed composition ([owner materialization](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workshop.rs:557>)).

The persisted composition already carries root version and resolved graph data, and each catalog dependency carries a version requirement. The ownership pass does not consume either exact graph binding. With multiple cached/installed versions of one ID, or a dependency range selecting a version other than the first catalog row, the derived owner set can reflect a different graph than the playable composition. The current focused test checks required versus optional edges for one version of each ID, not multiple-version selection ([test fixture](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workshop.rs:1968>)).

This is a source-confirmed exact-identity gap in the Auto-Install reconciliation path, not a reproduced unsubscribe/uninstall incident. Its consequence is conditional but direct: the owner-edge set is used to retain/remove persisted ownership, then unreferenced Auto-Install items are collected and their Workshop subscription IDs removed. Version-aware composition updates and cleanup therefore need to derive ownership from the exact installed/resolved graph rather than a first-by-ID catalog walk. The intended user semantics for Auto-Install were clarified in this conversation: a Packagepack owns its required dependency closure, while manual installation and explicitly disabled Auto-Install have different authority.

## October 25 — enabling Auto-Install has no successful real-service path

The non-fixture service branch accepts `SetAutoInstall` by starting a background Library operation ([dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs:1098>), [operation setup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/library.rs:14>)). For `enabled: true`, `start_library_operation` does not set `retained_subscription`; its worker therefore calls the generic application handler ([worker branch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/library.rs:124>)). That handler explicitly returns an error for every `SetAutoInstall` action because policy changes are expected to be handled by the client state service ([application rejection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/content.rs:190>)). The operation is accepted initially, then completes as failed; the completion handler persists policy only for the `enabled: false` case ([completion branch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/library.rs:226>)).

The inverse action has a dedicated real-service route: disabling automatic updates first subscribes the Workshop item, then stores `auto_install = false` after the subscription succeeds. Studio offers the enable control for cached eligible content referenced by a composition; Launcher offers it for content already Auto-Install-owned or owned by a Packagepack ([Studio gate](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/components/content_detail.rs:108>), [Launcher gate](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_launcher_ui/src/lib.rs:756>)). Those user-visible paths submit the action to the failing real-service branch. Moreover, `validate_auto_install_target` checks cache, Workshop identity, ambiguity and Packagepack ownership, but is called only from the fixture branch ([validation call](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs:1135>), [validation rules](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/library.rs:150>)). The current failure masks that missing production validation; removing the generic rejection without routing through equivalent validation would create a second defect. A search of the service action and completion code finds only helper-level eligibility tests, not a test of this real-service dispatch/completion path. Thus fixture mode can make this state transition while the real service cannot, despite the frontends exposing it. This is a source-confirmed non-fixture functional defect; no UI or Steam runtime reproduction was performed, and the finding does not imply that dependency-driven Packagepack ownership is broken in the same way.

## October 21–22 — host-specific verification becomes an explicit composition update

Vapor commit [`7accd549`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/7accd549f4f9366a296e9e440cd4928d2e9ceba0) addresses the reported Windows state where all content appeared verified but the Packagepack had no `x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm` executable. Verification now separately checks whether the installed graph can produce a launch plan for the current host target and carries an `update_required` explanation alongside content-integrity success ([verify projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/content.rs:484>), [host-target executable lookup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/launch.rs:532>)). The service retains `verified: true` but marks the composition `OutOfDate` when that launch preparation fails ([state transition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/composition.rs:713>)); that distinguishes integrity of installed files from playability on this device.

Explicit Update now refreshes the installed graph's Workshop-backed artifacts, respecting dependency constraints during import, then reinstalls the root by stable ID so the updated root manifest can resolve a current graph and host build ([update workflow](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/content.rs:604>), [constraint-aware Workshop refresh](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/content.rs:668>)). This is an end-to-end source path, not proof that every constituent publishes a target-compatible library or that every Workshop item is refreshed correctly. The update-required field currently wraps any launch-plan error, not only a missing host binary, so a malformed/missing Engine presentation manifest can also be classified as “update required.” The commit adds a service-state test for this classification, but the inspected test does not exercise Steam acquisition, artifact refresh, target build availability, or launching. Leslie later reported that Windows launched Loo-Cast successfully; that owner-run result is separate evidence for the tested build, not a broad cross-target guarantee.

## October 25 — shared-service lifetime is intentionally idle, not invocation-scoped

The local service is a singleton for one app/state endpoint and deliberately stays alive while any clients are connected or an operation remains active. After the last client disconnects and active work ends, it exits after a 15-second idle grace ([timeout definition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs:26>), [stop condition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs:516>)). It also stops a disconnected client's Rust Analyzer process. This means a short-lived `vapor launch` may leave the service visible briefly; a longer-lived Launcher/Studio/IDE client keeps the same process alive by design. This source contract explains a bounded process tail but does not prove that the user-reported lingering instances were within the grace period.

The first client starts the sibling service binary with `--serve`; stdout is discarded and stderr goes to a rotating service log. The spawned child is detached from the frontend's child guard only after the service endpoint answers ([startup handoff](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs:622>), [spawn/log routing](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs:685>)). Windows uses `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` for this background service spawn ([Windows creation flags](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs:829>)); the Rust Analyzer child uses the same flag and has explicit kill-and-wait ownership on failure/disconnect. These are intentional process boundaries with source-level safeguards. No Windows run or process inventory was performed during this review, so they do not establish that every Steam entrypoint starts the correct child or leaves no orphan.

The packaged Linux launcher wrapper is not itself a daemonizer: it resolves the app root from its packaged script location, changes into that root, and invokes Installer, Steam Entrypoint, or `vapor` synchronously; `run_command` waits for the child and returns its status, except that `--hold` opens an interactive shell after the child exits ([wrapper routing and wait](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/shell-scripts/linux/vapor-launch.sh#L6-L55>), [target dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/shell-scripts/linux/vapor-launch.sh#L63-L109>), [app-source packaging](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/App-Source.vapor.toml#L59-L60>)). On October 21, `772e487` removed the unconditional `vapor-installer install` attempt from both platform wrappers and routed Launcher/Studio/IDE/Chooser through the native Entrypoint; first-launch setup is now an explicit gate owned by the Entrypoint/Installer flow, not repeated by this wrapper. This narrows where an unexplained surviving process can originate, but the service's intentional 15-second grace remains, and neither the foreground contract nor source review establishes actual process-tree behavior under Steam on Linux or Windows.

## October 25 — workspace switching can invalidate completed edits after they write

This is a cross-client current-source review of Vapor `5743065` and Vapor-GUI `972a3f6`, not a later repository commit. The central issue is that the service models one globally selected source root, while each IDE client keeps its own displayed root and editor state.

**A root switch is immediate and outside operation scheduling.** `WorkspaceAction::Open` canonicalizes the requested directory, replaces `bootstrap.workspace_root`, persists it, resets selected content/catalog state, and returns a snapshot synchronously ([service dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs:953>)). It does not reserve a workspace resource or wait for active file operations. In contrast, `start_workspace_operation` copies the selected root into `root_for_worker` before spawning a background operation ([workspace request capture](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs:37>), [worker capture](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs:253>)). Save/create/module operations therefore still act on the original directory after another client changes the global selection.

**The side effect can succeed while the service reports failure.** The worker writes to the captured root ([save execution](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs:736>), [create execution](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs:748>)). On completion, the service compares that root to the currently selected root and overwrites a successful result with “The selected source folder changed…” when they differ ([completion guard](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs:290>)). It builds the `WorkspaceFileResult` only from the result after that guard; a rejected save/create therefore emits the failed `OperationChanged` event but no file-result event ([result creation and publication](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs:315>), [event push](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs:536>)). This is a source-proven possible “written, reported failed, editor not reconciled” outcome. No concurrent runtime reproduction was performed.

**Global event fan-out adds cross-project ambiguity.** The service broadcasts background operation events and a single current snapshot to all authenticated clients ([broadcast loop](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs:474>)). Each IDE stores its own root and accepts a `WorkspaceFileResult` only when its one pending request matches the operation ID ([IDE request correlation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs:490>), [file-result matcher](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs:541>)). That request correlation is useful, but it does not give every event a workspace identity. For operation diagnostics, the IDE fills `diagnostic.context.workspace` from its own current root before presenting the shared event ([diagnostic projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs:411>)). A different IDE client can therefore label the same operation diagnostic with the wrong local workspace. The operation event/output protocol needs a stable workspace identity supplied by the operation; frontends should not infer it from their own selected tab.

**The workspace-switch reset is incomplete in another way.** The IDE refuses a switch with dirty buffers, stops its Rust Analyzer, clears problems, code actions, symbols, documents and semantic selections, then sends `Open` ([switch setup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs:58>), [open response reset](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs:383>)). Neither path clears stored hover text or the Rust Analyzer reference list/count. The Inspector renders both whenever present ([stored result presentation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/inspector_view.rs:353>)). Thus even a successful switch can retain semantic observations from the previous workspace until another request replaces/clears them. This is directly visible in the state transitions; no UI reproduction is claimed.

**Explicit-root Run Configuration reserves the wrong key.** The request is canonicalized and executed from its explicit `workspace_root` ([root selection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs:15>)), and its completion is exempted from the “currently selected root” rejection. But operation reservation is computed from `self.bootstrap.workspace_root` for every `studio-workspace` operation ([resource derivation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs:711>)); the Run Configuration branch does not carry the requested root into `BackgroundOperationSpec`. A CLI run against workspace B can thus reserve workspace A's key: it may conflict with A's work when B is independent, or fail to conflict with B's work when A is independent. This is a narrower scheduler-identity defect, separate from the post-write completion race.

**The scheduler and IDE have different admission policies.** `OperationRegistry` supports multiple active operations and returns a conflict error for an overlapping resource; it does not retain a queued request ([reservation behavior](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/operation_registry.rs:67>)). The IDE stores one ordinary workspace request in `workspace.pending` and disables file, save, tool, authoring and switch controls while it is set ([single pending slot](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/lib.rs:199>), [save/run request](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs:84>), [workspace controls](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/workspace_view.rs:37>)). The console takes a different path: its requests are tracked by request ID in a map and can be sent while a workspace operation is pending ([console response correlation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs:318>), [console action dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/console_view.rs:344>)). This makes unrelated console actions more concurrent than ordinary IDE controls, but a resource conflict is still rejected by the service rather than queued. So the system has concurrent execution machinery, blanket frontend gating for one pathway, and a separate console pathway with no common user-action queue. That is confirmed from the current UI/service structure; whether every disabled action should be queueable remains a product policy question, while the owner has already stated the preferred general model is “queue actions unless they truly cannot run together.”

The service-level remedy is not simply “add another lock.” Each accepted operation needs an immutable workspace identity that flows through resource reservation, execution, diagnostics, snapshots/results, and completion routing. A switch should update one client's selected workspace without changing another client's operation context. If the product instead intends one globally active workspace, the protocol/UI must enforce and expose that invariant, and switching must coordinate with in-flight mutations. Existing tests cover operation-key conflict primitives and ordinary workspace file results, but the inspected tests do not exercise switching roots during a write or explicit-root run reservations. No tests were run for this review.

## October 25 — a 30-second service-start timeout is a readiness failure, not a launch confirmation

For Steam routes, Entrypoint selects a sibling `vapor-client-service`, supplies the app frontend executable, Steam app ID, app-root working directory and `VAPOR_HOME`, then synchronously invokes `--ensure` before launching Play, Launcher, Studio, IDE or Shell. Chooser is service-free. Installer is excluded only from Entrypoint pre-bootstrap so recovery can open; its UI still calls `Client::connect_or_start` and starts or joins the same service itself ([route callers](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L68), [service ensure invocation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L359), [frontend service connection](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L528)). Windows requests `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` for bootstrap children.

Installer still reaches the same service lifecycle by another caller path: it resolves the sibling service beside its *running target-specific executable* and invokes `Client::connect_or_start` on the role action. That connects to an existing endpoint or delegates to the same `ensure_service` readiness routine and its 30-second deadline ([Installer caller](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L518), [Client connect-or-start](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L165)). This explains why Installer can be opened without an already-running service yet still fail while promoting a role; it does not show that its target-specific sibling path is correct in every Steam depot or on Windows.

`--ensure` serializes concurrent starters on the app's state endpoint, first attempts to connect to an already-running local service, rejects an incompatible protocol endpoint, removes a stale endpoint where permitted, and spawns `--serve` when no service is reachable. It polls until the local endpoint accepts a Client connection. The readiness deadline is 30 seconds; at expiry it captures recent lines from the service log and stops the still-owned bootstrap child ([startup contract and deadline](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L31), [ensure loop](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L584), [child log and spawn](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L685)). A reported wait of roughly 30 seconds followed by “timed out during shared service startup” therefore identifies this readiness loop. It does not tell us whether the child was missing, exited, blocked during session initialization, bound a different endpoint, or encountered an OS-specific path/permission problem; the error's attached diagnostic tail and a Windows reproduction are needed to choose among those causes.

There is an important UX dependency here: Entrypoint does not hand off to the UI or game until `--ensure` returns success. A bootstrap failure is therefore a real launch gate, not a frontend that opened but appears unresponsive. The separate “service lives for a 15-second idle grace” behavior begins only after a frontend has connected/disconnected; it cannot explain a failure before readiness. This is a source-level lifecycle explanation of the delay and boundary, not a diagnosis of the user's historical Windows timeout. No process was launched or log read during this documentation pass.

## October 25 — Installer role and setup state do not share one authority

The Steam-installed app root is identified by `App.vapor.toml` with `[root]`; source workspaces use other marker manifests. The user’s Windows report that Installer demanded `Workspace.vapor.toml` inside the Steam folder was therefore a real semantic boundary failure when reported. Current discovery code explicitly models the app marker separately ([installation identity](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/installation.rs#L54), [provider discovery](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/discovery.rs#L171)). The current source no longer establishes that exact historical failure; no Windows reproduction was done here.

The present first-launch and role flow has at least four pieces of state/authority:

1. **Player setup receipt:** Entrypoint and Installer UI independently read `<app-root>/.vapor/state/installer/player.toml` and consider it ready when one line says `state = "ready"` ([Entrypoint gate](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L144), [Installer UI gate](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L488)). This is not the persisted role.
2. **Local role:** `role.toml` is written through `VaporInstallation::ensure_state_root()`, which normally resolves to OS user data and migrates the older app-root `state` directory. Missing role means Player. Promotion is strictly upward, and demotion changes the role without removing tools or caches ([role persistence/transition](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/role.rs#L98), [root state migration](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/installation.rs#L109)).
3. **GUI promotion:** Installer sends a typed service action. The application invokes `promote_role_with_context`; that reconciles the managed DeveloperEnvironment first and persists role only after success. Fixture sessions reject this write path ([service dispatch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L1307), [application adapter](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/lib.rs#L205)). A failed setup can therefore leave the user at the previous role, as intended, but the GUI and logs must expose which capability failed.
4. **A second bundled setup system:** `vapor-installer install` dispatches through `script_bridge` to `setup_player_main`; the production `app_setup.rs` scripts can also install development tooling. That older path installs Rustup/Cargo, target components, Zig, LLVM-Mingw and wrappers into app-root paths and writes its own `dev-env.toml` receipt. The service DeveloperEnvironment instead stores Rustup/Cargo/Tracy in OS user data and LLVM-Mingw under the app root. The two paths use different roots, status predicates, target matrices and cleanup rules ([CLI script dispatch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer/src/script_bridge.rs#L1), [legacy setup implementation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/app_setup.rs#L1), [service developer environment](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L1)).

The role/UI vocabulary is also explicitly not one authority: local `VaporRole` selects installed setup; per-action `WorkflowTier` describes experience/prerequisites; Identity and Steam decide remote publishing permissions. `EcosystemDeveloper` can be selected locally, but this does not authorize protected server actions. This follows the owner’s decision that local capability promotion and external authorization remain separate.

The source-level root cause is therefore **split setup ownership**, not a proven explanation for one reported promotion failure. The GUI role path always reconciles the Windows GNU target and linker for Composer-or-higher; the legacy script path installs both Windows GNU and Linux cross-build tools. `install_windows_gnu_linker` rejects unsupported architectures/operating systems, and neither the Installer view nor the service translates all readiness fields into independent install operations. This could explain a broad “unsupported host” class of failure on non-x86_64 or unsupported OS hosts, but that is an inference from the guard, not evidence that it caused the user’s Windows report. Exact machine/runtime diagnosis requires the corresponding operation error/log and a reproduction.

**The newer flow also fails to enforce its readiness postcondition.** `DeveloperEnvironmentStatus::is_ready()` defines one aggregate condition, and maintenance health checks consult it, but `promote_role_inner` discards `report.status` and persists the higher role after any successful reconciliation call. The application snapshot exposes readiness fields as booleans but sets `error: None` whenever status discovery itself succeeded. Installer's first-launch `role_ready` predicate checks `role.error.is_none()` and `installed >= selected_role`, not the readiness booleans. Thus the role can mean “promotion was attempted successfully” while the UI treats it as “all selected-role tools are ready.” A partial-but-Ok tool install/status is the condition that would reveal this; no such runtime case was constructed in this review. This is a code-contract defect, not a claim that the user's observed promotion failure was this exact defect.

The immediately preceding history makes the seam clearer. `Vapor-Client/92ab2b9` added Rust Analyzer to the readiness contract and expanded the reconciliation trigger; `3b692e7` added per-action capability profiles while explicitly saying they are not authorization; Installer `2592142` made first-launch setup and role selection a mandatory gate; then `b3ddcf9` intentionally kept role choices available when readiness discovery fails, so an error would not trap the user. That last change correctly separates a readable current role from tool readiness, but the current continuation predicate only partially preserves that distinction: it lets an error leave promotion available, yet does not require the chosen role’s actual capability fields to be ready before continuing. See the commit-level [`b3ddcf9` change](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/b3ddcf909218284de0f5c89fb9a2035a514d526) and [Installer transition code](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L291).

The per-action layer compounds this rather than closing it. The service enforces `ActionProfile.local_capabilities`; the profile's workflow tier is intentionally not a permission gate, and the external authority list is resolved by each publish handler. Yet the local capability vocabulary has only generic Rust, Rust Analyzer, and Tracy, with no target-specific capability. For example, workspace build/check/doc/release operations declare generic Rust readiness, even though target support also depends on Rustup target installation and a native/cross linker. A role snapshot can report those target/linker booleans, but action admission cannot express which target is required. So “role is ready,” “this action is in a workflow tier,” and “this specific target operation can run” remain three different predicates with only partial wiring between them. [Action capability validation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L68), [capability vocabulary](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/workflow.rs#L28), and [build action classification](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/actions.rs#L435) show the current contract.

This is also a lifecycle mismatch worth keeping visible: first-launch setup readiness is app-root-local while role state normally follows the OS user across app roots; developer tool state is split across both. No single “installation readiness” object atomically owns these receipts, tools, user-data retention and demotion/uninstall behavior. That makes fresh-install, repair, role promotion, app-root replacement and full uninstall separate test cases. No setup script or platform was run in this review.

There is a narrower first-launch deadlock even for Player. `installation_role_snapshot()` always discovers the full `DeveloperEnvironment` status, regardless of the installed/selected role. If that status lookup returns an error, `installation_role_snapshot_for` preserves the readable role but sets `error`; after the app-root Player receipt becomes ready, the first-launch UI still defines `role_ready = role.error.is_none() && installed >= selected_role`, then disables “Continue to Loo-Cast” when it is false. Thus a Player who completed Player setup can remain blocked by an unavailable developer-tool readiness probe, even though `VaporRole::Player` explicitly requires no developer tools ([unconditional readiness snapshot](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/lib.rs#L159), [Player role policy](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/role.rs#L24), [receipt plus first-launch gate](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L229)). Current Installer tests cover the Player default and that a readiness error preserves role parsing, but not the resulting enabled/disabled continuation decision ([focused tests](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L810)). This is statically demonstrable control flow, not a reproduced screen failure; no GUI or test was run.

Player setup also performs broader installation side effects than its UI description suggests. Both first-launch and later promotion call `vapor_core::install_installation_for` before the Player receipt/setup script. That core routine ensures the canonical Superworkspace (default `~/Vapor`) and installs machine command integration: Unix shell profile blocks or Windows user `VAPOR_HOME`/PATH values ([first-launch caller](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L190), [install routine](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/install.rs#L34), [default Superworkspace](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/install.rs#L54), [machine integration](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/install.rs#L72)). The separate Player setup then creates app-root directories, installs app-local SteamCMD if absent, writes an app-root anchor and records the Player receipt ([Player routine](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/app_setup.rs#L1)). So the first-run “Player setup” mutates OS-level command discovery and creates the developer Superworkspace as well as preparing player files. This may be intended as shared Vapor bootstrap, but it couples player onboarding to a developer-oriented location and global user shell/registry state; it should be made explicit in the product contract. No fresh installation was run.

There is also a bypass between that GUI gate and Steam's direct Play gate. The owner-directed first-launch flow asks for a role and says setup is required before play. But the Entrypoint's direct Play path checks only the app-root Player receipt; once that receipt says `ready`, it launches the persistent selected composition without checking the selected Creator role or its tool readiness ([Steam Play branch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L68)). In Installer first-launch code, the Player setup receipt is written before the service promotes a higher selected role; if developer reconciliation subsequently fails, the receipt can remain ready while the role remains lower. Closing Installer and invoking Play again then satisfies Entrypoint's only gate. That makes “Player prerequisites complete” and “the user's selected first-launch setup completed” observably different states, but only the first is enforced by Steam Play. This is statically derived sequencing, not a reproduced bypass; no entrypoint or Installer was run.

### October 22 — Steam direct launch follows the persistent selection; reference docs lag

`Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/c6e178fa` changes the no-argument Play route from `vapor launch default` to `vapor launch selected`, renames the helper/log messages, and updates the focused entrypoint test name. This follows the owner’s product decision that one persistent selected composition should replace a redundant “default” selection concept. The current CLI confirms that `LaunchCommand::Default | LaunchCommand::Selected` both route to `launch_selected_composition`; `default` is now a compatibility spelling, not a bypass to an app-manifest default. If selection is absent or stale, the CLI returns a user-facing error directing the user to choose a playable composition in Studio.

The cross-repository docs have not converged on that behavior. The Entrypoint README still says its default route runs the app manifest’s default composition and prints `launch default` in its route tree. The Vapor CLI command reference describes `launch default` as resolving the default Packagepack seed, while the Launcher workflow book says `launch default` means manifest default and `launch selected` means the Studio selection. Those descriptions contradict the current CLI implementation and the EntryPoint patch. This is a confirmed documentation/contract mismatch; it is not evidence that runtime launch itself is broken. The full Steam route still depends on the selected-composition record being present and on the Client service’s launch operation succeeding; no launch was executed during this review.

### October 22 — progressive workflow labels and resource-aware concurrency are introduced

Vapor commit [`3b692e7d`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/3b692e7d8f89d6b07f51dcb2befd8698e8ed9b16) makes two cross-cutting changes in one 21-file patch: it assigns `Player`, `Composer`, or `Developer` workflow profiles to every `ClientAction`, and replaces the previous single-operation gate with an `OperationRegistry` that can track several active operations and reserve resource keys. `ActionProfile` also names local prerequisites (managed Rust, Rust Analyzer, Tracy) and external authority requirements (Workshop or root publisher). The service checks local capability readiness; publishing handlers are expected to perform account/target authorization. The tier is explicitly classified as progressive UI navigation, not a credential or installation role, and the shown service dispatcher does not reject an action based on tier. This is a useful separation in the type model, but by itself it does not enforce the broader Player → Composer → Developer → first-party authority ladder in the product.

The registry allows unrelated work to run at once and rejects resource conflicts with a retryable `OperationInProgress` error. Resource selection is derived from string `domain`/`action` pairs: composition run reserves a composition plus workspace; workspace scan and edit get special keys; broad authoring/workspace work reserves the workspace; Workshop actions reserve one account; publishing reserves one global publication key; unknown domains fall back to an exclusive key. The conflict relation explicitly handles same keys, scan-versus-edit, and workspace-versus-edit. Its in-file tests prove a few representative combinations, including that a workspace build may coexist with a scan, but do not enumerate every action-to-resource mapping or show multi-frontend scheduling. Studio later adds its own bounded request queue, while the service's conflicting request is still rejected for the caller to retry/queue. Therefore the concurrency foundation is real, but the resource taxonomy remains partly string-adapted and queuing is not yet one service-owned behavior shared by every client.

A related commit, [`f2058b8b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f2058b87818f090bf59c06ef1489e2b99750391c), carries request-scoped operation identity through service events and corrects response association. It reduces a real ambiguity when several operations coexist: a request ID is no longer enough to identify which accepted operation's later output belongs to which action. The evidence establishes protocol/source changes and focused tests in the commit, not a running multi-client stress result; tests were not run during this historical review.

### October 22 — a shared Vapor console model reaches Studio and IDE, but not the game F2 console

Vapor commit [`8e3d1bac`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/8e3d1bac841d05faacbca9ce3309ac71277c6bf9) adds `vapor_console_core` record/tokenizer types and `ConsoleCommand`, which parses a small fixed vocabulary into existing typed `ClientAction`s. It also extends managed operation output with timestamp, severity, source, action and process fields; removes terminal control sequences before recording output; bounds individual output text; and forwards Rustup toolchain/target installation output through `OperationContext`. The output contract correctly keeps stream (stdout/stderr) separate from semantic severity—stderr alone is not declared an error. Producers still need to choose a level and populate origin/process fields; the record schema does not infer those facts.

The GUI follow-ups are [`Vapor-GUI/dab912cd`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/commit/dab912cd0dca488f5d3011ef1648a09c11e7bf41) and [`Vapor-Studio/13b829df`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/13b829df49d3f50439768d9eac9825c544da8b1f). They adapt the shared console records/view into the IDE and Studio, and both route parsed console commands through the Client service. This is real reuse across host UI and service intent. The command set remains small: help/status, catalog refresh, composition select/launch, and workspace format/check/test/build/validate. Launcher’s `LauncherReadOnly` catalog scope is declared in core but has no command-parse call site in the inspected GUI tree; the Launcher exposes a read-only operation view rather than that same in-app command vocabulary. The game’s F2 console and Rhai workbench remain separate command/editor paths, so the requested “clone F2 and bind CLI commands into it” is not yet the architecture achieved here.

This sequence is a valuable shared foundation with a clear boundary, not full console unification. It centralizes record shape, tokenization, a few service-backed commands and bounded rendering mechanics; it does not yet centralize all CLI commands, provide a common command registry for every product, or share the in-game F2 execution/visual implementation. No runtime UI or throughput verification was done in this historical review.

### October 25 — the shared console core is semantic data, not a shared console runtime

The local October 22 design is more specific than the implementation’s “shared console” label: one pure record/filter/history and language contract, while each product retains command authority, telemetry/process ownership and UI toolkit. The current crate obeys its most important isolation constraint—it has no process, terminal, GUI, game or persistence access—and it now contains several related primitives: shell-like command tokenization, console records/style roles/filters, bounded ConsoleHistory and PromptHistory, structured diagnostics, and Rhai lexical classification. It has no canonical command registry or executor, transport, durable log store, egui widget, rich-text span model, or syntax parser. That makes this a semantic adapter core, not the “clone F2” experience by itself ([core modules and record types](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_console_core/src/lib.rs#L1-L191>), [history and prompt state](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_console_core/src/lib.rs#L308-L426>), [Rhai lexical categories](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_console_core/src/lib.rs#L428-L533>)).

Several boundaries are looser than the design’s declared record contract. ConsoleSource, field keys/values, and message are open strings; the operation protocol separately carries typed ClientOrigin, but the GUI adapter copies it into an origin string field. StructuredDiagnostic has typed scope/domain/context/spans, yet the console adapter flattens those facts into fields for ordinary filtering/rendering. This is a reasonable interoperability view, but it is not one typed, queryable event schema end-to-end. The accepted design also calls for formatting spans; current ConsoleStyleRole expresses record-level severity styling only. For process output, ANSI CSI/OSC controls are removed and carriage returns become newlines; the GUI splits resulting text into nonempty lines and makes one row per line. This preserves readable logs and structured Cargo diagnostics, but it cannot preserve terminal redraw semantics or inline color/progress styling. records_from_operation_output uses only the first diagnostic message line as its row text and retains the rest as structured fields, so detail remains available but is not shown in the default row ([operation-to-record adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/console.rs#L444-L563>), [process event shape](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/state.rs#L558-L583>)).

“Bounded history” needs a precise reading. ConsoleHistory limits record count, not bytes per record. Service output has separate protections—a 512-event operation queue with an omission notice, byte-bounded protocol/outbound queues, and producer-specific limits such as 64 KiB retained Cargo JSON payloads—but the history type itself cannot guarantee a memory budget for arbitrary host-inserted records. Clearing removes this view’s retained records and leaves the dropped counter; it does not erase a persistent archive because the core has no persistence. Each GUI console state owns a separate history and prompt history, so shared widget/model code does not make one unified transcript ([history capacity](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_console_core/src/lib.rs#L308-L377>), [service event bound](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L50-L58>), [protocol frame bound](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/lib.rs#L61-L62>), [Cargo payload bound](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/cargo_output.rs#L8-L20>)).

The timeline is a real staged build-out. 7ab704b introduced the host-neutral record/history/filter and Rhai token-category foundation on October 22; 8e3d1ba added command-line tokenization and operation output fields, but left command parsing as a small separate fixed vocabulary. On October 23, 1a5796a added typed diagnostic context and domain/scope filters; the GUI adapter then bridged that typed context through string fields. This is useful convergence, while the accepted design’s end-to-end event semantics, terminal progress behavior, and same-record comparison across game/GUI/CLI remain unverified or incomplete ([shared-core design](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-shared-console-editor-core-design.md>), [diagnostic context](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_console_core/src/diagnostic.rs#L1-L100>)). The design lives in untracked docs/superpowers/ in the preserved source worktree; it is treated here as an accessible proposal, not a committed or runtime-proven contract. No tests, UI, process stream or memory profile were run during this inspection.

### October 22 — Packagepack-owned Auto-Install begins as a persisted lifecycle graph

Vapor commit [`25aeced4`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/25aeced4d8be2f2ecf05b531f11760649d559919) replaces dependency display strings with `CatalogDependency` records and adds per-item Packagepack owner IDs plus an explicit-user-choice bit to `LibraryItemPolicy`. A subscribed/acquired Packagepack contributes default Auto-Install ownership to eligible dependencies; a previous user choice is preserved. Disabling Auto-Install goes through a service operation that subscribes the item for manual retention before changing policy. Unsubscribing a Packagepack removes that owner, and cleanup removes eligible unreferenced cache entries and calls the Steam unsubscribe API for those dependencies. The tests cover default ownership, explicit opt-out surviving owner removal/reacquisition, and the “only package-owned content may use Auto-Install” rule in the surrounding service code.

The model is materially closer to the owner’s stated lifecycle semantics than a boolean preference alone, but its typing is partial: `CatalogDependency.relationship` and `CatalogContent.kind` are strings, so the service still has to interpret semantic categories at runtime. It also distinguishes package-owned subscription lifecycle from installed composition ownership only in follow-up [`28cc768c`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/28cc768c8d31c03f57c32ea00e59d0ac5366e87d), which ensures installed/out-of-date/repairable compositions keep the resolved graph and root alive after the Workshop subscription disappears. Together these changes express two separate owners—subscribed Packagepack and installed playable composition—rather than equating “cached,” “subscribed,” and “installed.” They remain source-level behavior: no real Steam unsubscribe plus cache deletion was exercised here. External subscription, filesystem removal and local-state persistence span separate systems and can yield partial outcomes, which the operation result must explain.

### October 22 — Windows GNU-LLVM runtime is separated from the Rustup host identity

Vapor [`1c92bd78`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/1c92bd7822949e8823ac279245135c2fadf5109c) changes managed-toolchain host selection to use `HostTarget::rustup_host_triple()` instead of the Vapor executable's target triple. This matters for the distributed Windows GNU-LLVM app: its runtime target is `x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm`, while Rustup's Windows host toolchain identity is `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`. The source test asserts exactly that mapping and still rejects unknown host combinations. This resolves a specific target/host vocabulary mismatch; it does not prove that the required GNU-LLVM linker, target standard library, or a package's target artifact is installed and usable.

A later same-night patch, [`2897a810`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/2897a810a5d002bd81f411ab772603a76d53cd48), appends existing Unix host utility directories to the managed Cargo subprocess `PATH`, deduplicating entries and skipping absent directories. That addresses managed builds which need ordinary host utilities beyond Vapor's Rust/Cargo paths. It broadens subprocess executable lookup to system paths by design; on non-Unix hosts this helper adds no directories. Its focused test checks `/usr/bin` and `/bin` only when present. These source changes explain the intended toolchain-host fix and Linux utility fallback but are not cross-platform build evidence.

### October 22 installed app roots and source workspaces have distinct markers

The current manifest module gives four root concepts different filenames: installed runtime app `App.vapor.toml`, app source `App-Source.vapor.toml`, general source workspace `Workspace.vapor.toml`, and Registry `Registry.vapor.toml`. `source_root_marker_candidates()` accepts only the latter three; its documentation says installed app roots are intentionally not source roots. Separately, [`InstallationPaths::from_executable`](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/discovery.rs#L171>) requires `<app-root>/App.vapor.toml`. These are two different discovery contracts, not alternate spellings for one root type.

[`8259961`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/825996195c054ed2808573ca4bee7e6e4e5a5153) adds `is_installed_application_root`: when a persisted authoring root contains `App.vapor.toml` and lacks `Workspace.vapor.toml`, service initialization clears that stale authoring selection and persists the corrected state. The regression test creates this fixture and starts a Linux-configured service in fixture mode; it does not exercise Windows Installer startup or a real Steam depot. A separate [`60ff4eee`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/60ff4eee92a02f768d14625a51b77e3eee385027e) changes Rust Analyzer toolchain discovery to use the selected source workspace rather than the installed app/service working directory. This is evidence the code recognizes the same boundary class as the reported Windows message about a missing `Workspace.vapor.toml` under `steamapps/common/Loo Cast`. It is not proof that Installer role promotion, service startup or toolchain provisioning succeeds on Windows; no such runtime path was tested here. The root predicate also uses the specific “App marker present, Workspace marker absent” test, so a depot carrying both markers would not be cleared by this branch. Whether both should ever coexist is not specified by this code.

### October 21 — CLI gains explicit composition lifecycle commands

Vapor-CLI [`061eb7ba`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/061eb7baf22139c815898196ae7a5572d1aa1aab) introduces typed `composition list|install|verify|repair|update|launch` commands. Mutating operations are translated to `CompositionAction` and sent through the shared Client service; the CLI does not duplicate content resolution or installation. The list reads the service snapshot, marks its active composition, and prints an installation-state label. It does not refresh or verify during listing, so after service restart an item can correctly show “not checked”; the docs direct the user to `verify` to obtain fresh state.

The same patch redefines `client launch play` as an alias for the player Launcher entrypoint, removing the earlier meaning “play active profile.” A specific composition launch now has its own explicit lifecycle command, while Steam’s no-argument Play path is a separate direct launch route. This is a cleaner separation of app routing and composition operations. The CLI still prints a completion sentence after `send_client_action`; correctness depends on that helper waiting for the service operation’s terminal result, while `composition list` is intentionally a snapshot rather than a live Steam query. No CLI command was executed in this historical review.

### October 23 — LSP edits gain explicit safety rails; the IDE grows into a separate subsystem

The later IDE changes deserve a deeper pass than the older prototype history. From `Vapor-GUI/220cc867` through `972a3f6`, 25 files change by about 11,302 insertions and 5,759 deletions. This includes a moved test suite and extracted modules, so net line growth is not all production behavior; it nevertheless marks a large new product subsystem rather than a mere cleanup.

The Rust Analyzer path is intentionally constrained before it mutates editor state. The IDE accepts only direct code-action edits and hides `command` actions. Workspace edits reject malformed/file-operation entries, non-local URIs, paths outside the canonical workspace, duplicate targets, more than 64 files, edits to closed files, and proposals above 4 MiB. They must match captured in-memory document revisions, are shown as previews, and update buffers only; the user saves afterward. These are source-confirmed guardrails and a good boundary for untrusted language-server output.

That is not full LSP workspace-edit support. Closed-file edits and create/delete/rename operations are refused; freshness is checked against open editor buffers, not a universal snapshot of disk and every workspace file. The IDE therefore offers reviewable refactors with explicit limits, not arbitrary Rust Analyzer mutations. Tests in the source cover selected parsers, ranges, staleness, and edit cases, but none were run for this review.

The current workbench now has several cooperating but distinct semantic authorities: local syntax projections for immediate outlines, Rust Analyzer for Rust workspace intelligence, Cargo for build diagnostics, Vapor’s index for addressable navigation, and the Client service for filesystem authoring and the language-server child process. Request IDs and document versions connect these layers, yet the parsers do not share one semantic model; context fields are only as complete as each producer makes them; and semantic content navigation currently resolves registered local source projects. The overall system is substantially integrated, but it does not yet provide one domain model across Rust, Rhai, Vapor manifests, service operations, and the in-game editor.

The phrase “addressable Rust objects” needs a narrower reading. The immediate outline is a best-effort `syn` syntax projection over an open buffer, deliberately used before Rust Analyzer replies or while it is unavailable. It handles selected declarations, fields, enum variants, trait/impl members, inline modules, and macro invocations; unsupported `syn::Item`/member forms are silently skipped. It does not resolve names, macro expansions, conditional compilation, or type identity. A parse failure yields an empty projection, which is presented as “No semantic outline is available”; the UI does not distinguish invalid/incomplete Rust from a valid file with no projected items. Rust Analyzer can later replace this local outline with its document-symbol result, so this is an immediate-navigation subset, not the IDE’s complete Rust model. [Parser and projection](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/rust_semantics.rs#L498-L525), [supported item cases](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/rust_semantics.rs#L560-L750), [empty-outline presentation](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/workspace_view.rs#L584-L603).

Several “semantic” labels are conventions, not compiler facts: functions in files named `systems.rs` or `run_conditions.rs` receive those kinds, and a struct is labeled Component/Resource/Event when a matching attribute or the final path segment of a derive token has that spelling. The canonical-module diagnostic is only a warning on the open file; it does not move items, reject the build, or establish a crate-wide rule. Tests cover representative fields, methods, Unicode positions, one nested module, filename-based system classification, and projection budgets; they do not establish coverage of the full Rust grammar or semantic correctness. This makes the new structure useful for navigation and future domain tooling, but its kind labels should not yet drive authoritative content/build behavior. [Filename rule and derive-name heuristic](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/rust_semantics.rs#L501-L520), [kind inference](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/rust_semantics.rs#L1009-L1034), [canonical layout warnings](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/rust_semantics.rs#L280-L334), [representative tests](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/tests.rs#L684-L760).

This projection is also run synchronously from the editor’s changed-buffer path. `did_change_document` invalidates the previous outline and invokes the parser on the new contents; the local parser accepts files up to 2 MiB but the inspected path has no debounce, incremental parse, or worker handoff. Therefore a 2 MiB syntactically dense file can consume UI-frame time on edits, and a transient syntax error removes its outline immediately. This is an unmeasured scaling risk, not a measured editor stall; Rust Analyzer’s later response may restore symbols. [Editor update path](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/editor_view.rs#L236-L270), [invalidation and local parse](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/language_server.rs#L1242-L1275).

The same date’s content-creation path illustrates a separate product-level limit: the IDE offers all ten kinds through one “New Vapor content” flow, although backend scaffolding correctly gives Packs metadata-only projects and code-bearing kinds Cargo projects. This one dialog does not express pack composition as distinct from implementation authoring, and the resulting scaffolds are not yet evidence of the owner’s target static composition build. See the [semantic content-model review](#cross-check-against-the-canonical-ten-kind-model).

The service owns one Rust Analyzer process per connected Client ID, not one shared process per workspace. This isolates JSON-RPC streams and gives disconnect a clear cleanup path, but two IDE-capable frontends on the same workspace can each start a separate analyzer and duplicate its indexing/memory cost. Startup discovers the toolchain from the selected source workspace, then requires the pinned Rust Analyzer executable and toolchain to already exist; it reports a repair/promotion hint instead of installing on demand. That keeps compilation/tool installation out of an editor-open side effect, but makes Developer setup a real prerequisite for LSP rather than a self-contained IDE capability. Process stop kills and waits for the direct child; process-tree cleanup and worker-thread joins remain unproven, as noted in the earlier lifecycle review.

The protocol crate adds one deliberate semantic seam rather than a typed LSP client: it recognizes `textDocument/publishDiagnostics`, validates and bounds the payload, converts positions/severity into Vapor's diagnostic record, and emits an omitted-item count. The limits are concrete (256 diagnostics per notification, 16 KiB each for diagnostic text and retained raw payload, eight related locations, 4 KiB URI); other JSON-RPC methods and responses stay generic `Value` messages and are interpreted by the IDE. The frontend accepts an unversioned diagnostic batch; if a version is supplied, it rejects a mismatch only when that URI is also present in the open-document map, then separately requires the canonical file path to remain inside the selected workspace. Missing document state therefore does not cause version-based rejection. This is useful structured integration, but not a uniformly typed protocol or unconditional freshness guarantee. LSP diagnostic context is therefore stronger than generic console output, while request lifecycle, edits, symbols and other messages still depend on GUI-owned JSON handling. [Bounded diagnostic decoder](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/language_server.rs#L32-L139>), [generic LSP event variants](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/state.rs#L780-L790>), [version and workspace checks](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/language_server.rs#L1319-L1368>).

#### The semantic object is a shared wire shape, not yet a shared semantic authority

The domain-neutral `SemanticObject` contract arrived in [`4fe3ab21`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/4fe3ab2121b81c4eaeb62effaf16ac298607d6da), inside a 32-file, 1,591-insertion service/diagnostics/workbench change. Its ID is a free-form domain string plus document path, a vector of name-like path segments, and an optional discriminator; the node adds a closed `SemanticObjectKind`, display/detail strings, UTF-16 range pairs, arbitrary string attributes, and recursively nested children. This is a useful transport envelope for IDE selection and diagnostics. But `qualified_name()` only special-cases the literal `rust`; every other domain gets dot separators plus a heuristic that appends segments beginning with `[` as array indices. Neither that display rule nor the shared `Other` kind defines the underlying TOML/XML/Rhai/Rust object semantics. [Protocol DTO and name rendering](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/semantic.rs#L5-L184>).

The indexing authority is still inside `vapor_gui_core`: it re-exports the protocol types, owns a serializable `BTreeMap<PathBuf, SemanticDocument>`, rejects older document revisions and nodes whose ID names a different document, and truncates trees at 4,096 objects or 64 levels. It does not validate unique IDs, range ordering/bounds, or identity stability across edits. References resolve only when the stored document version exactly matches, so this is a revision-scoped editor address, not a durable semantic identity. Local Rust/TOML/XML/Rhai adapters and Rust Analyzer create nodes; the IDE renderer separately caps visible nodes at 2,048. Thus the code has a real shared representation and stale-anchor boundary, but the parsers remain separate authorities and the index does not centralize their meaning. [GUI index, checks and bounds](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/semantic.rs#L1-L116>), [IDE semantic renderer and display cap](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/semantic_view.rs#L8-L18>).

There is also a scaling seam: byte-to-UTF-16 conversion rescans the source prefix to compute a position. Domain adapters invoke it repeatedly for object ranges, so a large file with many objects can revisit much of the same text; the 2 MiB document and 4,096-object caps bound input size but do not make the repeated work incremental. This is a source-derived worst-case concern, not a measured slowdown. `4fe3ab21` creates the protocol shape; [`e30cdac`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/commit/e30cdac915397f95107eff63f2f20e5402a034bb) installs the GUI semantic index/adapters; [`16df77e`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/commit/16df77eadc55967bedbe288f05933d940b26f258) then expands local Rust projections and integration. This chronology is a move toward multi-domain navigation, not evidence that Rust, Rhai, manifests, and the runtime now share one semantic model.

The IDE’s Rust file labels and tree also have unmeasured scaling edges. [`shortest_rust_label`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/workspace_navigation.rs#L253-L287) checks candidate paths repeatedly to find a unique suffix, and its fallback qualifies with the Cargo crate directory name. Two distinct crates with the same directory label and the same in-crate module suffix still produce identical labels; the `mod.rs` fallback appends the same literal `mod` to both and does not resolve that collision. The tests exercise duplicate suffixes across differently named crates, not duplicate crate labels. The [file tree renderer](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/workspace_navigation.rs#L12-L60) recursively constructs its `ScrollArea` contents without row virtualization. `matching_file_count` recursively traverses the full tree from the per-frame Explorer draw ([tree count](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/workspace_tree.rs#L124-L140), [Explorer call site](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/workspace_view.rs#L480-L493)); when filtering, each visited directory recursively checks whether it contains a match ([directory predicate](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/workspace_tree.rs#L109-L122)). Every visible Rust filename also invokes a candidate-wide uniqueness search, recomputing path parts for each candidate ([label call](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-GUI/blob/972a3f607a26b696d17579b731dbd57047577dcc/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/workspace_navigation.rs#L35-L50)). Consequently normal Explorer frames have at least a full-tree count pass, and a fully expanded/filter-open tree can add repeated subtree scans and roughly quadratic candidate comparisons. This is a source-derived complexity risk, not a measured freeze or benchmark; the current example-workspace size has not been shown to trigger it.

### October 23 — Installer separates known role from tool-readiness failure

`Vapor-Installer/b3ddcf9` fixes a consequential presentation/control-flow bug in the role screen.
