A snapshot can report the current role while separately reporting that tool-readiness inspection failed; the old UI treated any error as if the role were unreadable and returned before showing promotion controls. The new path parses and displays the role, labels readiness as unavailable, and keeps promotion choices available. Promotion itself now calls the app-root installation/setup path before submitting the service role action, and PATH registration is reported after success. Focused tests specify “role known despite readiness error” and “unreadable role still requires refresh”; these tests were not run here.

This is a recovery-path improvement, not evidence that every promotion failure is fixed. It intentionally allows the user to attempt promotion despite an incomplete readiness snapshot, so installation/setup and service-action errors remain the authoritative result. The patch does not establish successful Windows or Linux promotion, Rustup target installation, user PATH visibility, or correct behavior when the service executable is missing. The distinction matters: **the controls becoming reachable** and **the operation completing** are separate facts.

## October 25 — shared GUI base and Studio-specific palette remain duplicated

`vapor_gui_core::run_product` sets `ThemePreference::Dark` and `Visuals::dark()` before creating every product. Studio then independently replaces much of the same dark palette and style in `configure_studio_visuals` ([host initialization](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/lib.rs#L53), [Studio palette](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/app.rs#L434)). The double ownership means the shared host establishes only the base; Studio remains the owner of a second palette and spacing scale. Source does not prove Windows rendering now matches Linux or every secondary window uses the same colors; no GUI was launched for this audit.

## October 25 — GUI products have distinct binaries, but share one host package and overridable mode router

Correction to the earlier “one executable” conclusion: `Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui/Cargo.toml` declares five distinct binary targets—`vapor-gui`, `vapor-launcher`, `vapor-studio`, `vapor-ide`, and `vapor-installer-gui`—in one Cargo package. Each product wrapper calls the same `vapor_gui::run(default_mode)` host with its own default mode; the shared argument parser also accepts `--mode`, so binary identity is not a hard mode restriction. The Steam Entrypoint maps chooser/launcher/studio/ide/installer to those sibling executable names, forwards the selected `--mode`, checks the chosen file exists, and waits for its exit status ([binary targets](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui/Cargo.toml#L1-L26>), [mode/default dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui/src/lib.rs#L10-L58>), [Entrypoint selection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L405-L460>)). The current distribution design therefore already provides separate product process images and launch routes, correcting the owner’s earlier uncertainty about how Launcher and IDE are opened.

The remaining boundary is substantial but different: those process images are built from one GUI package and one host/router, which directly depends on Launcher UI, Studio UI, IDE UI, and Installer UI crates (some in separate repositories). The integration is shared and compile-time, not an IPC-separated frontend architecture. This may be the intended lightweight facade over one Client service; it is not evidence that product state/operations live in separate services. The package’s deployment manifest and Steam provider stage each named binary for supported targets, but source staging is not proof the current public depot contains them or that launch works on both machines. A text search found vector-drawn status marks and syntax highlighting but no explicit application-wide font registration in the reviewed GUI core/Studio path. The earlier missing-glyph report therefore remains unverified: absence of a custom font call alone does not prove a glyph failure, and no visual pass ran.

## October 25 — product launch images converge on one short-lived local Client service

The process topology is now clearer than “one GUI executable” or “each product owns its backend.” Steam Entrypoint starts the service bootstrap for direct Play, Launcher, Studio, IDE and Shell; it skips pre-bootstrap for chooser and Installer. Installer still calls `Client::connect_or_start` itself, while Launcher and IDE have their own connection paths and Studio connects in its app startup. All these paths resolve the service beside their app executable and use the shared local protocol/domain. Therefore service use is shared, but bootstrap authority is duplicated across Entrypoint and frontend crates; chooser is the clear service-free product ([Entrypoint branch and mode gate](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L68), [service bootstrap](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L359), [Launcher connect](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_launcher_ui/src/lib.rs#L1539), [IDE connect](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/service_session.rs#L802), [Studio connect](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/app.rs#L271), [Installer connect](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L528)).

The bootstrap path is a two-process handshake. Entrypoint runs the sibling service with `--ensure`; `Client::ensure_service` takes a filesystem bootstrap lock, probes the socket, removes a stale endpoint if appropriate, spawns the long-lived service with `--serve`, and waits for its local endpoint. Windows background spawning explicitly uses `CREATE_NO_WINDOW`; service standard output is discarded and standard error appends to a bounded service log. The service runs until all clients disconnect and no operation remains active for a 15-second idle grace. This is not Steam-close detection, an OS daemon, or installer-managed lifetime; it is client-count/operation based. The detached service gets a reaper thread in the short-lived bootstrap host, so the process relationship is supervised only while that parent process remains alive; whether this pattern behaves identically under Steam shutdown and Windows process-tree rules is not established by source review ([ensure handshake](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L584), [service spawn/logging](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L687), [idle exit](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L516), [Windows hidden process flag](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L827)).

This closes one claim and exposes a remaining ownership seam: the app experiences are distinct launchable process images, but all UI binaries share one host package; service startup can be initiated by Entrypoint or by a frontend; and service lifetime follows local sockets rather than Steam session lifetime. The architecture broadly matches the owner’s request for separate player/creator products over one local Client service, but the bootstrap/lifetime contract is not singular or tied to Steam’s lifecycle. No process trace, Steam launch, Windows child-process inspection, or shutdown rehearsal was run in this audit.

### October 26 — Steam Entrypoint is a real host router, not just a launch-string shim

The current Entrypoint resolves the installed App root from its own executable location (`bin/` or `bin/<target>/`), then routes no-argument/`play`/`game` launches to the persistent selected Packagepack. It deliberately does not require a source `Workspace.vapor.toml` in Steam's installed App directory. If the Player setup receipt is absent, it opens the sibling Installer GUI with `--first-launch`; otherwise it ensures the shared Client service and invokes sibling `vapor launch selected`. `launcher`, `studio`, `ide`, `installer`, and `chooser` are distinct sibling executables selected by mode, while arbitrary non-GUI arguments enter the Shell route. `chooser` and `installer` skip EntryPoint pre-bootstrap so the recovery/setup UI remains reachable without a ready service; Installer can then connect-or-start it itself. These are source-visible route contracts, not proof of Steam launch options or depot payload on either OS ([root discovery and mode dispatch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L35-L123), [sibling image mapping and GUI launch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L359-L455), [App-root inference](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/entrypoint/app_root.rs#L1-L22)).

Host responsibilities are not uniform across platforms. Linux launches a held Konsole and has a special Pressure Vessel escape through the host dynamic loader and host Qt paths; absent a display server, it returns an explicit error, and there is no adapter for other non-Windows/non-Linux targets. Windows launches `cmd.exe /D /C` with a manually constructed quoted payload. The route tests exercise argument/mode decisions and receipt text, but neither Windows `cmd` quoting nor Steam/Pressure Vessel behavior is exercised by those tests; this review ran none. The EntryPoint log appends to `<App>/.vapor/logs/entrypoint.log` without a visible size/rotation policy, and direct selected-composition stdout/stderr append to that same file. This is a source-confirmed unbounded retention path, not a measured disk-growth incident ([platform terminal adapters](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/entrypoint/terminal.rs#L1-L205), [routing tests](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L238-L357), [append-only log](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/entrypoint/log.rs#L1-L26), [composition output redirection](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L175-L210)).

The current root-resolution shape is a good fit for Steam-installed Apps: the EntryPoint is colocated under the App's `bin` tree, so it can derive its root independently of the current working directory and source-workspace vocabulary. The path check is structural rather than manifest-validated: it does not parse `App.vapor.toml` or confirm that the inferred directory is an installed Vapor App before writing the log or looking up sibling binaries. That is a bounded trust assumption about the depot layout, not evidence of the earlier reported `Workspace.vapor.toml` Windows failure. The route's setup gate also remains weaker than “the selected setup completed”: it checks only for one exact `state = "ready"` line in the Player receipt before Play, while Installer writes that receipt before higher-role promotion completes; the mismatch is described above and remains statically inferred, not reproduced.

The route's present meaning formed through repeated owner corrections rather than a single stable chooser design. October 14 first routed Steam launches through Studio, then moved dispatch into Vapor-GUI; October 18–19 added shared-service bootstrapping; October 21 separated direct Play from the chooser/Launcher, added the first-launch setup gate, and routed the IDE; October 22 changed the default path to the persistent selected composition ([Entrypoint history](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/commits/main/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs), [selected-composition change](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/commit/c6e178fa9e6d244cfe315a04a3d0a83099533e5a)). This sequence reflects the owner's clarified product shape—one Steam option plays, another chooses Launcher/Studio/IDE/Installer/Shell—not proof that the currently published launch configuration matches it. The current Entrypoint source is clean at `c6e178f` and matches `origin/main`; no binary or Steam configuration was inspected in this slice.

## October 25 — operation origin is typed, but inferred from the frontend executable name

`ClientOrigin` is an enum attached to requests and output events, with values Launcher, Studio, IDE, Installer, CLI and Unknown. Each service client computes it from `ClientHostConfig.application_executable`’s filename: the `vapor-gui` binary is hard-mapped to Launcher; names containing product words select that product; `vapor` and names containing `cli` select CLI ([origin mapping](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L509), [protocol enum](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/message.rs#L24)). Since the shared GUI parser permits `--mode` to override a binary’s default product, the reported origin can disagree with the visible product for cross-mode invocation. The enum also has no Chooser or Game/Composition value, and does not encode which launched composition produced output.

The operation pipeline does preserve the request origin into structured `OperationOutputEvent`s, so this is more than an unimplemented filter concept; the gap is the source and granularity of identity. The game F2/telemetry path remains a separate process and record transport, so the service’s typed origin does not automatically label live game output. This falls short of the owner’s requested Launcher/Studio/IDE/launched-composition provenance and filtering, despite having a useful first-party operation-origin field. No event stream from a running composition was captured; whether game-origin fields enter some other local diagnostics feed is not established by this path ([event propagation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L1834), [separate console trace](#latest-state-console-trace--game-command-runtime-versus-vapor-operation-console)).

## October 25 — startup, snapshots and Library refresh repeat filesystem work

On the service's first authenticated connection, `ClientSession::with_persistent_state` runs synchronously before the first snapshot. It discovers the Vapor installation and calls `ensure_canonical_superworkspace`; absent a saved location, this initializes `~/Vapor`. Setup creates/adopts the directory and manifest, scans its immediate entries and declared `.gitmodules` paths, and loads recognized workspace/project manifests ([session path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs:609>), [default root](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/install.rs:54>), [superworkspace scan](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/superworkspace.rs:134>)). It is bounded topology discovery, not arbitrary recursive search; the inspected path does not spawn Git or access the network. A setup error is retained as status rather than aborting service session creation.

After that synchronous setup, the Library catalog refresh is dispatched in a background operation. It reports 0/1 before scanning and 1/1 after the entire catalog returns; the scan has no inner progress/cancellation context ([operation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/catalog.rs:117>)). The projection reads the cache index, then calls `cached_artifact` for each ID; each call reloads and reparses the complete index. It repeats this pattern for installed content via `installed_index` and one `installed_artifacts` call per selector ([catalog projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/catalog.rs:9>), [cache lookup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content.rs:1238>), [installed lookup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content.rs:1344>), [index parser](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/storage.rs:101>)). For N cached plus M installed identities, this entails N+M repeated whole-index reads/parses, plus per-artifact manifest reads and merging. That is source-confirmed superlinear refresh work as the index grows; its practical cost depends on catalog size and storage speed and has not been measured.

There is a repeated-scan path on top of those bootstrap and refresh costs. Every `ClientSession::snapshot()` calls `superworkspace_snapshot()`, which rediscovers the app root/source-state and reloads the immediate repository/workspace topology from disk ([projection method](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/snapshot.rs#L18-L25>), [Superworkspace projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/snapshot.rs#L367-L429>), [discovery walk](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/superworkspace.rs#L178-L285>)). `ClientSession::dispatch` builds a response snapshot, then the server broadcasts a second snapshot after the request ([response projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L1607>), [request broadcast](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L264-L350>)); it also builds/broadcasts a snapshot after background-operation event batches ([event polling](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L474-L500>)). Ordinary actions therefore repeat this Superworkspace scan at least twice, and background events repeat it again. These scans run synchronously in the service loop that handles client frames and broadcasts, so slow workspace reads can delay unrelated clients/actions. This is a source-confirmed repeated-I/O path; its latency and relation to any one reported hang are unmeasured.

The exact handshakes matter when relating this to the reported Windows “timed out during shared service startup.” The Entrypoint's `--ensure` probe connects without the legacy-state seed and requires only `ServiceReady`; the server sends that event before it synchronously initializes the persistent session. The actual frontend connection supplies the seed and requires both readiness and the initial snapshot ([handshake condition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L98-L161>), [readiness before session initialization and snapshot](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L168-L253>)). Therefore the Superworkspace initialization/projection can delay the full frontend handshake after service readiness, but does **not** by itself explain the specific 30-second `ensure_service_with_timeout` error, which means the endpoint did not answer its readiness probe before that deadline ([ensure deadline](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L593-L660>)). No Windows reproduction or timing was performed.

These code paths can make first-connection setup, repeated snapshot construction and later Library refresh feel like one opaque wait, even though they are distinct operations. The coarse progress model can also make the scan appear complete only at its endpoint. They are plausible contributors to refresh/UI stalls, not a reproduced diagnosis: no runtime timing, catalog-size benchmark, or hang reproduction was performed.

## October 25 — a crashed content mutation can leave a permanent index lock

The app-owned content index uses a marker file as an exclusive lock. `acquire_content_index_lock` opens `<index>.lock` with `create_new(true)` and returns a guard whose `Drop` removes that marker ([acquire/release](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/storage.rs:169>)). There is no owner PID, timestamp, lease/expiry, OS advisory lock, or stale-lock recovery in this implementation. If the process is killed or crashes after creating the marker, Rust does not run the guard's destructor; subsequent index mutations fail at `create_new` with “already exists” until someone removes the stale file. Normal process shutdown drops the guard, so this is conditional on abnormal termination, not a claim that ordinary launches leak locks.

That lock covers Workshop cache replacement and collection as well as other index writers. The replacement path stages an incoming artifact, renames the old cache to a nonce-named backup, activates the new directory, saves the index, removes the backup, and then writes a receipt ([replacement transaction](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content.rs:576>)). It restores the old cache on an immediate activation or index-save error, which is a meaningful safeguard. It is not a crash-recovery journal: interruption between the directory rename and index save can leave an orphaned `.previous-*` directory or an index/path mismatch, and interruption while holding the marker can block future index writes. Even on the ordinary error path, failure to remove the old backup or write the receipt occurs after the new cache/index has been activated and is returned as operation failure. Therefore operation failure does not always mean “no state changed.” These are source-derived failure states; no process-kill, disk-full, or recovery rehearsal was run, and the exact durability behavior of directory renames depends on filesystem/platform semantics.

The direct repair target is an owned, recoverable mutation protocol: lock identity/reclamation, staged-cache/index promotion, receipt ordering, and startup reconciliation need one defined recovery story. This is separate from the Steam-side partial subscription result: there are at least two external/persistent boundaries in the same user flow, and the current operation status can report failure after one or more of them already changed.

## October 25 — Workshop acquisition is serial, silent, and reserves the whole Workshop account

`with_workshop_items` loops through selected PublishedFileIds in order. For each item not already installed/up-to-date in Steam, it starts one download and pumps callbacks until the result arrives or a 20-minute deadline expires; only after that item is consumed does the loop start the next one ([serial download loop](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_steam/src/lib.rs:115>), [timeout](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_steam/src/lib.rs:163>)). A single stuck item therefore holds that operation until its timeout. A batch whose items each complete just before timeout has a theoretical source upper bound of nearly 20 minutes per item—just under 16 hours 40 minutes for the 50-ID service cap. This is not an expected duration or measured performance; it follows from sequential loops and per-item timeout reset.

The service passes an `OperationContext` into `execute_workshop_operation`, but search/subscription/acquisition branches do not set download phases or report progress; the explicit phase changes in that function are on Stage/StageBatch only ([operation branches](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workshop.rs:1196>)). The provider polls Steam callbacks but notifies no operation sink. Subscription metadata can include a sampled `steam_download_progress`, yet that is loaded as part of the separate subscription-list query and is not wired to the in-flight download loop ([subscription snapshot](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_steam/src/lib.rs:70>)). Therefore an active acquisition may remain visibly “running” without identifying the current item, bytes, or completed-item count. The source supports missing progress events; it does not establish that every frontend fails to show other logs or status.

At the scheduling layer, every `studio-workshop` action maps to the same `WorkshopAccount` reservation ([resource mapping](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs:711>)). The registry rejects conflicting reservations instead of retaining them ([conflict path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/operation_registry.rs:79>)). Thus a long acquisition also makes a new Workshop search, subscription refresh, or independent subscription action conflict with the active operation. This joins three user-visible concerns that otherwise look unrelated—slow acquisition, opaque progress and a Workshop screen that cannot continue browsing—at the operation/resource boundary. Whether the UI queues one of those requests is frontend-specific; the service does not own a waiting queue. No Steam download or multi-client workload was executed.

**Shared acquisition state also triggers a frontend-local navigation effect on every connected Studio.** A successful batch is stored once in `ClientSession.workshop.acquisition`; the protocol snapshot has a service-wide revision and contains no requesting client ID or originating action ID ([session-owned projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L168-L183>), [snapshot fields](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/state.rs#L279-L365>)). After each applied client request, the server broadcasts the same session snapshot to all connected clients ([broadcast call](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L345-L349>), [broadcast fan-out](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L800-L813>)). Each Studio instance independently applies any higher acquisition revision and unconditionally invokes `apply_workshop_acquisition`; the successful branch navigates that window to Library, even when its own `pending_acquisition_ids` is empty ([snapshot adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/workshop.rs#L178-L205>), [unconditional success navigation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/workshop.rs#L297-L323>)). This makes a shared durable/result projection own a local UI side effect: acquiring from one Studio can redirect another connected Studio on the next snapshot. The exact active item and success status may also be repeated in each window. This is a source-confirmed multi-client behavior path, not a reproduced user incident; an origin/action correlation or a strictly state-only snapshot consumer would be needed to distinguish “my completed action” from “another client changed shared state.”

## October 25 — the example graph is not the composition build input

The current `Vapor-Examples` workspace has six Cargo projects and six authored content manifests. Its authored Packagepack manifest declares Terminal Engine, Wheel Salvage Game, Wheel Booster GameMod, and a Cargo dependency chain through Wheel Rules and Wheel Core. The corresponding Cargo Packagepack project directly depends on the Engine, Game, and Mod by relative path. Its `main.rs` calls `terminal_engine::run` with a closure that directly installs the Game and Mod. The workspace README describes this as a Packagepack-owned composition entrypoint, and a unit test asserts that the hardcoded selection should produce nine wheel sectors; the test was not run in this audit ([authored graph](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Examples/content/hello-world-packagepack/Packagepack.vapor.toml), [Cargo graph](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Examples/Cargo.toml), [Packagepack crate](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Examples/content/hello-world-packagepack/Cargo.toml), [entrypoint](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Examples/content/hello-world-packagepack/src/main.rs), [selection test](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Examples/content/hello-world-packagepack/src/lib.rs)).

This proves a small, static Rust composition across Engine/Game/Mod crates. It does **not** prove the Vapor manifest graph drives Cargo membership or the chosen install closure: changing the manifest’s selected Game or Mod would not change the hardcoded Rust imports/installer calls shown here. It also does not prove that a player-facing Workshop payload contains only a ready-to-run Packagepack executable while source remains separately obtainable. That distinction matters because the Packagepack is declared both as a binary-bearing authored artifact and as a Cargo project, while the example’s Steam metadata is only local configuration. Current `visibility = "public"` values and PublishedFile IDs do not establish the live Workshop visibility or contents.

The example workspace and Cargo crates use independent version schemes: authored manifests inherit `0.5.0` from `Workspace.vapor.toml`, while Cargo packages are `0.1.0`. The owner’s alpha policy explicitly allows Vapor content versions to remain at `0.5.0`; current files do not state how those versions map to the Cargo crate versions. This is not automatically a defect—content identity and Rust package version may be intentionally distinct—but it is a provenance and compatibility contract that the published artifact and IDE need to make explicit.

## October 25 — SDK content command types are specifications, not an authoring executor

`vapor_sdk_core::commands` defines typed request variants for content `new`, `init`, `build`, `package`, `publish`, pack membership changes, and Packagepack `lock`. But the corresponding `spec/content.rs` reports effects as future behavior (“when implemented”) and models read requests as displaying information. The `vapor sdk` CLI parses these requests and its output dispatcher routes unimplemented content cases to a stub that prints `status: not_implemented` ([request enums](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/commands.rs), [content command descriptions](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/spec/content.rs), [SDK CLI dispatch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/output/mod.rs), [stub](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/output/stub.rs)). Separately, the main `vapor` CLI implements service-backed build/deploy/package/publish routes through `ClientAction`s ([main CLI content commands](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/content_commands.rs)).

The distinction matters: Vapor does own some real content lifecycle operations, but the newer typed SDK authoring surface does not execute them and the main CLI follows a parallel command model. This is consistent with the owner’s repeated goal that products act as facades over one service, while exposing a present split between a promising typed vocabulary and the operational service-backed workflow. It is not evidence that every GUI operation duplicates business logic; the specific overlap between the SDK command model and main CLI deserves a command-by-command mapping.

## October 25 — a Vertical-Slice-0 content host remains in the Steam payload

The active authoring/package path parses role-specific manifests (`Engine.vapor.toml`, `Game.vapor.toml`, and so on) through `vapor_content::AuthoredContentManifest`; the provider emits the deployed role section to that kind's manifest filename and reads deployed releases through the same schema ([source read](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/packaging.rs), [role manifest path](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/content.rs)). The current Client Library projection is a separate provider/application catalog over cache and installed records.

Alongside that path, `vapor_core::manifest` still defines the earlier minimal `[content]` schema with `deny_unknown_fields`; `vapor_core::local` scans only for a file literally named `Vapor.toml`; and `vapor_core::resolution` adapts that local catalog into `vapor_content`'s candidate graph. The `vapor-ide-host` binary exposes JSON-lines `content.discover` and `content.resolve` using those APIs. A source search across Client, GUI, Studio, CLI and core found no current invocation site for the host/protocol, yet the binary remains a required Linux and Windows Steam-depot file and part of the distribution binary list ([old schema](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/manifest.rs), [old scanner](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/local.rs), [host protocol](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ide_host.rs), [depot requirements](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/steam.rs), [distribution list](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/development.rs)).

This finding narrows “two content systems”: there is one shared current authored resolver, plus a legacy generic schema/catalog and host still built and shipped. Whether that is intentional compatibility or orphaned product surface is unresolved; no deletion is proposed by this audit. The potential consequence is concrete: the shipped host scans a manifest layout that current source projects and current role-specific package output do not use, and it duplicates IDE discovery/resolution capabilities that are now available through the service. No Steam payload or installed app directory was inspected during this pass, so source staging requirements do not prove the actual current depot contains the host.

## October 25 — Steam kind filtering exists as a tag contract, not a catalog query

The Launcher and Studio both expose a kind selector and pass the selected `ContentKind` to the service. `vapor_steam::search_workshop` maps it to the canonical lower-case/kebab-case kind spelling, sends that tag to Steam UGC with `require_tag`, then applies a case-insensitive exact tag filter to the rows Steam returned for that page ([canonical kind spelling](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/content.rs#L88), [UGC query/filter](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_steam/src/lib.rs#L221), [Studio selector/action](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workshop_search_panel.rs#L21), [Launcher selector/action](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_launcher_ui/src/lib.rs#L922)). Workshop publication also emits the Vapor kind as a tag before authored tags ([publish tag construction](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/workshop.rs#L689)). Thus this is not a missing UI control or absent source filter.

The current contract still depends on external tag data: old/manual items without the canonical tag will be excluded, and post-filtering one provider page cannot refill that page with later matching rows. `total_results` remains Steam's query count while the returned `items` can be fewer after Vapor's local exact-tag pass. The checked-in tests cover tag normalization and predicate behavior, not a real UGC response across the published catalog. This narrows the owner-reported “type filtering does not work” to an unresolved Steam-data/integration behavior; source inspection does not prove that report fixed, nor prove a current bug in the canonical path. No Steam client query or current item-tag audit was performed.

The current Studio panels add a real but frontend-local paging/selection layer: Steam results arrive in 50-item pages, the UI can display 10/20/50 at a time, supports visible-page selection plus a selection set spanning pages/searches, and caps batch subscription changes at the provider limit. The subscriptions page supports ID/title/Steam-state search and visible-set bulk actions, displays Steam download state and local Library/composition context, and warns when local copies conflict ([Studio search/page selection](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workshop_search_panel.rs#L21-L220), [cross-page selection/actions](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workshop_search_panel.rs#L221-L360), [subscription projection and bulk actions](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workshop_subscriptions_panel.rs#L95-L275), [subscription rows and actions](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workshop_subscriptions_panel.rs#L276-L509), [actual search predicate](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workshop_subscriptions_panel.rs#L511-L533)). Steam tags are preserved in the subscription protocol record, but this UI never displays or searches those tags; `ContentKind` filtering exists only in Browse. Subscriptions are materialized into a complete in-memory list and each row is drawn in the same pass; the panel has no equivalent page-size/virtual-row policy. This is a confirmed incomplete frontend path, separate from the unresolved report that Browse filtering fails against live Steam. No large-subscription UI was rendered or profiled.

**The history separates the filter's several meanings.** October 16's [`9ee075a`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/9ee075a645d9dfce6a71df95a127e71cd92fee2f) split the Workshop browser into acquisition, search and subscription panels, but left search behavior in place. October 21's [`30037ea`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/30037eadd18a7f6c5c5d419dd48d3f5dd9aa8349) added the “Vapor content type” selector and initially represented its value as a string tag. October 22's Vapor commit [`7ab704b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/7ab704bf7978a9e387e29236b750f9002135b64a) made `ContentKind` a typed domain/protocol/service field, then translated it back into a canonical Steam required tag and locally checked returned tags; it did not introduce Registry lookup. Studio's October 22 [`b47056c`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/b47056cf269510a3420591058f85739281d06247) preserved the typed field and added local 10/20/50 slicing and cross-page selection. The same day's Vapor [`b32fec7`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/b32fec76eaa5d49e9fadad31b5557764a29bd8e4) added Steam tags to subscription snapshots, but the current subscription panel does not consume them. These diffs establish feature intent and implementation sequence, not that Steam's live tag query works correctly or that all existing Workshop items were tagged consistently.

## October 25 — the Rust toolchain pin is not a shared build authority yet

The Client's installed-workspace path has a real managed Cargo wrapper: it finds app-packaged Cargo beside `rustc`/`rustdoc`, installs Vapor-root Cargo/Rustup environment values, prefixes managed binaries, removes selected ambient Vapor paths, and preserves other PATH entries (plus standard Unix host tool directories) ([Client wrapper](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/managed_cargo.rs#L21)). Workspace operations choose operation-owned output roots ([workspace build](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/workspace_build.rs#L42)). This supports reproducible tool selection inside that path; it is not a sealed or universally shared environment.

The Platform Server subprojects each record Rust `1.97.0` in `Workspace.vapor.toml`, but its GitHub Actions CI installs the moving `stable` channel and deployment/test scripts execute host `cargo` directly ([service pin](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Docs-Server/Workspace.vapor.toml#L1), [CI toolchain](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/.github/workflows/ci.yml#L1), [test script](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/deploy/scripts/test.sh#L1), [deploy build](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/deploy/scripts/deploy.sh#L65)). The Toolchain Backend book's broader rule (“all Cargo execution paths”) is therefore ahead of current cross-repository practice; its own hermeticity roadmap still lists PATH and command-specific policy as open questions. The historical move from SDK toolchain helpers to Client-owned operations has unified a substantial local path, but did not absorb server CI/deploy. This evidence also explains why “Vapor pins Rust” cannot stand alone as a blanket claim: every build, test, release, documentation, and server path needs its actual executable, environment and output root checked. No command was executed for this finding.

## October 25 — Workshop publishing bypasses the accepted Registry/Identity boundary

The owner selected a specific division: Registry is the Vapor catalog of typed content identities, Workshop bindings, discoverability and release/channel records; Identity is the authority for linked people, roles and authorization. Steam remains the transport/provider. The Platform Server decision record says this is the target boundary and explicitly distinguishes it from the current implementation ([accepted boundary](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/server-domain-boundaries.md#L33)). The owner’s choice is therefore stronger than “use Steam tags and add a registry later”: Steam’s metadata must not become the semantic authority.

The current Registry is already a real service and is already consumed by the local shared Core, but its implemented domain is narrower. The server exposes only status, provider-account/repository, and ecosystem/repository reads; its schema stores those topology records. `vapor_core::RegistryClient` fetches an ecosystem record so the developer environment can clone registered repositories into a Superworkspace. This is a useful and integrated bootstrap registry, but it does not publish, index, or resolve Workshop content. It has no content-kind/version record, Steam PublishedFileId binding, release/channel pointer, artifact provenance, or protected catalog-write route ([Registry server routes](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/main.rs#L51), [schema and seed](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs#L1), [shared Registry client](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/registry.rs#L50), [ecosystem acquisition](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ecosystem.rs#L86)). Calling Registry “not implemented” would be false; calling the selected Workshop catalog boundary implemented would also be false.

This topology feed is also a trust boundary because an explicit Developer workflow uses it to choose repositories that `git clone` will acquire. The checked-in Client manifest configures `https://vapor.ghf-studios.site/api/registry`, and the client validates response schema, requested ecosystem ID, provider label, repository kind, and a one-component checkout path. But `RegistryClient::new` allows both HTTP and HTTPS; the ecosystem response omits the `verified` flag present in provider-account records; and repository validation does not verify that `clone_url` is hosted by the claimed provider/account or corresponds to the claimed repository before invoking Git ([configured endpoint](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Client.vapor.toml#L6), [URL policy](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/registry.rs#L52), [response validation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/registry.rs#L113), [repo validation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ecosystem.rs#L341), [clone invocation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ecosystem.rs#L409), [seeded provider record](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs#L129)). The checked-in official endpoint is HTTPS and the deployed seed contains fixed first-party GitHub URLs. This is a source-level response-validation hardening gap, not evidence of an unsafe current endpoint or an observed malicious clone. It also shows why “Registry-authorized developer” must not be conflated with “the current bootstrap Registry returned a topology row.”

The bootstrap resolver has a separate CWD fallback: after checking the installed `metadata/ecosystem.toml`, `load_bootstrap` walks upward from `env::current_dir()` for `Vapor-Client.vapor.toml`. Yet the service's `DiscoverSuperworkspaceRepositories` operation passes only the discovered installation into Core; it does not pass the selected source workspace. If installed metadata is missing, the source fallback therefore reflects the shared service process's CWD, not an explicit workspace identity ([bootstrap resolution](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ecosystem.rs#L172), [service caller](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L684)). This is conditional and may support source-launched development; no failure was reproduced. The risk is the implicit context, not the mere existence of a CWD fallback.

Identity is likewise implemented for a distinct subset: provider-authentication attempts, Steam/GitHub profile linking, root dashboard sessions, and admin/root role operations. The public authentication-attempt flow currently accepts only the `root-dashboard` purpose; completion requires an active root role and returns a root-dashboard cookie plus that profile's effective roles. This is authenticated state, but it is not a general current-user session or publisher proof. The route table has no general authorization-introspection endpoint for a separate publish service to ask whether a caller may publish a particular Vapor identity/version/target. The publish design itself recognizes that the cross-service JWT/introspection contract is not mature and leaves the normal publish pipeline unimplemented ([Identity routes](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/main.rs#L43), [attempt scope](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/session_handlers.rs#L16), [root-only session completion](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/session_handlers.rs#L470), [publish contract status](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/publish-pipeline-authority-model.md#L1)). This is a missing integration contract, not evidence that Identity lacks all role/session enforcement inside its own service.

Today’s Client publishing path is materially different from that accepted target. The Workshop service handler requires a currently staged review, validates a supplied account string, and checks an exact phrase such as `PUBLISH <content-id> TO <account>`; the batch path does the analogous checks. The root Steam upload checks a staged root review and an exact app/branch confirmation phrase. These are valuable freshness and destructive-action gates. They do not call Identity, send an Identity session/proof to another service, or resolve a Registry catalog record. The provider then invokes local SteamCMD with the supplied account ([Workshop action](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workshop.rs#L225), [root action](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/publishing.rs#L10), [SteamCMD provider](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/workshop.rs#L726)). Steam can still reject an account lacking Steamworks rights; that provider-side check is not the Vapor Identity authorization the owner chose.

The root-release application API does implement a meaningful review-before-upload protocol. A stage call validates account/branch/target inputs, builds the documentation bundle, synchronizes release assets, and runs a dry-run Steam staging operation that returns the exact file list/fingerprint. Publish requires the service-marked `release_build_validated` flag, repeats the dry-run staging and compares the complete review value, then invokes Steam staging/upload again with the expected fingerprint. This catches ordinary workspace/payload drift between review and confirmation and keeps the provider effect behind a second reviewed call ([application staging and publish](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/publishing.rs#L392-L530)). The stage is not read-only: it builds documentation and synchronizes assets before displaying its review. Its five local unit tests cover input validation and runtime-target inheritance only; they do not exercise the stage/review/upload state machine or validate the boolean review marker against an unforgeable build record ([limited tests](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/publishing.rs#L845-L891)). The robust local Steam confirmation is therefore real, while the more important catalog/Identity authority boundary remains absent; neither conclusion should erase the other.

This boundary is not just a missing extra API call. The per-action `AuthorityRequirement::WorkshopPublisher` / `RootPublisher` vocabulary is declared in the local Client protocol, while the service-level validator intentionally defers those requirements to concrete handlers. Those handlers currently implement local confirmation/account gates rather than consulting Identity. The server-side future design adds a protected publish request, Identity verification, publish policy, an immutable job, and a distinct execution plane; none is present in this local direct-SteamCMD route ([workflow requirement](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/workflow.rs#L40), [publish server target contract](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/publish-pipeline-authority-model.md#L52)). Therefore a staged-and-confirmed upload can be operationally successful while still lacking the Vapor-side author identity, catalog binding and auditable release authority that the platform model intends.

The distribution book currently narrates a stronger system than the code: it says Registry validates namespace/source claims and publication checks that authority at the mutating operation, and that manifest identity is connected across Workshop, Library and Composition ([authority](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/distribution/src/registry/authority.md#L1), [identity](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/distribution/src/registry/identity.md#L1), [permissions](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/distribution/src/registry/permissions.md#L1)). Those are plausible intended invariants, but the Registry schema and routes do not implement content namespace/release records, and the local Publisher does not call Identity or Registry. The Workshop page also describes the staged artifact as one typed item with version/dependency metadata, while the current generic package path copies the project tree and payload into the same upload folder (see [pack/code packaging trace](#october-25--pack-and-code-artifacts-share-an-unrestricted-packaging-path)). This is a concrete “docs overstate current behavior” instance, not a reason to discard the desired architecture.

### A second public Steam deployment path remains in Core with different manifest and preview semantics

`vapor_core::steam::deploy_ecosystem_to_steam` remains public and re-exported, but a repository-wide source search finds no in-workspace caller beyond its definition/re-export. It loads the older `Vapor-Client.vapor.toml` ecosystem manifest, stages one common plus current-host depot under the app user's development directory, then invokes SteamCMD even when `preview` is true; in that mode it writes a SteamPipe `Preview=1` VDF and still runs `+login` / `+run_app_build`. This differs from the current Application/Provider root release path: that path loads its distribution policy from `App-Source.vapor.toml`, stages the declared common/Linux/Windows depot matrix, and its `dry_run` returns after staging/VDF generation without launching SteamCMD ([legacy Core path](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/steam.rs#L1-L165), [current manifest ownership](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/distribution.rs#L12-L15), [current dry-run boundary](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/steam.rs#L94-L154)). These are not proven to be duplicate responsibilities—the older API deploys the “Vapor ecosystem” payload, while the newer one packages the app's allowlisted source/install inputs—but they are two exported root Steam workflows with distinct manifests, target models and meanings of “preview.” No test was found for the legacy public function, and no deployment path was executed. External downstream users of the public Core API were not searched.

## Cross-reference supplement — October 18–20: service extraction, templates, and documentation

This source hunk pass ties the current Packagepack/Composition and code-artifact seams to the commits that first formalized them.

### October 18 — `f9e8b13`: content domain, local Composition aggregate, and starter generators arrive together

The shared Client extraction is a large boundary move, not a narrow rename: it introduces `vapor_content`, Client domain/application/provider/protocol/service crates, moves content operations behind a shared host, changes the `Library` content kind to `Crate`, and creates a durable `Composition` record model. The record has its own `id` and `name`, references a `root_package`, stores a `resolved_graph`, source-workspace association, launch settings, and installation state. The default record is literally ID/name `default`/`Default`; these facts are source-confirmed at the current head ([Composition model](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/composition.rs#L304), [default value](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/composition.rs#L338)).

That record is a durable application model, but the owner later clarified that Packagepack itself is the playable-selection identity and “composition” is an informal synonym. The code’s extra launch/installation observations may still need a persisted per-user object; the mismatch is that current UI/docs elevate this state to a second playable identity rather than projecting settings/resolution/installation around a selected Packagepack. Do not read the model alone as proof the proposed content kind `Composition` exists: it does not; conversely, do not pretend the implementation already satisfies the owner’s simpler single-selection identity.

The same extraction introduced two authoring mechanisms with different generated shapes:

- `init_basic_content` creates Engine, Game and Packagepack directories, writes all three into `Workspace.vapor.toml`, and sets the Cargo workspace members glob to `crates/*`. The separate legacy `[[project]]` list records only Engine and Game, while its generated README says Packagepack is not a Cargo member. Packagepack has a Vapor manifest and workspace-project path but no Cargo `Cargo.toml`, so it is not itself a Rust package; whether Cargo's glob tolerates that metadata-only directory was not tested here ([starter workspace generation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/source.rs#L128), [starter Packagepack writes](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/source.rs#L283)).
- In that starter, Engine’s authored manifest declares a runtime binary. Its Cargo directory nevertheless has both `src/lib.rs` and `src/main.rs`; Game declares a library and a relative Cargo dependency on Engine. This produces a Rust package graph whose engine library is linked by Cargo, while the authored Vapor graph separately says Engine binary + Game library ([Engine manifest/files](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/source.rs#L240), [Game manifest/dependency](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/source.rs#L283)).
- `scaffold_content_project` for individual content has a different mapping: Engine → binary; Game/EngineMod/GameMod/ExtensionMod → `rlib` + `cdylib`; Crate → `rlib` + `staticlib`; Packagepack/Enginepack/Gamepack/Modpack → metadata only ([output mapping and scaffold](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/source.rs#L395)). This is the generator’s actual current contract, not merely a documentation paraphrase.
- Adding Rust-bearing content separately mutates Cargo workspace membership if `content_project_output` says it has a Rust output. It does not derive Rust dependencies or link order from the selected Vapor manifest graph ([Cargo member transaction](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L498), [manifest composition write](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L1311)).

The contrast with Loo-Cast’s current source is revealing: its Engine manifest declares a library and its Packagepack is the Cargo binary that calls the Engine host with the Game installer ([Engine manifest](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/Engine.vapor.toml), [Packagepack Cargo graph](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-packagepack/Cargo.toml), [entrypoint](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-packagepack/src/main.rs)). Thus the actual flagship content and the generic `basic-content` generator model different Engine/Packagepack roles. Both compile, but the templates are not an authoritative expression of the user’s content model.

### October 20 — `a194167`: 103 documentation files turn provisional semantics into a full tutorial surface

The diff changes 103 docs files (+2,801/-235) and turns multiple `Status: target outline` placeholders into concrete workflow guidance. The four pages most directly implicated are [SDK content authoring](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/sdk/src/workflows/content-authoring.md#L1), [SDK packs](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/sdk/src/workflows/packs-and-packagepacks.md#L1), [Packagepacks](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/vapor/src/concepts/packagepacks.md#L1), and [Content Types](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/vapor/src/concepts/content-types.md#L9). The new prose says Engine/Game “typically contribute crates,” uses a generic `Mod` not in the ten-kind enum, describes the Packagepack as metadata that is not compiled, creates a separate durable player Composition, and says exact legal parent/child relationships and required slots are checked by the shared model. These are not equal in status: some describe the code of that week, others generalize beyond it, and several were later superseded by owner clarification.

The current implementation supports only parts of those broad claims. The fixed enum and manifest names are centralized. Pack child allowlists and fixed Engine/Game choice helpers exist. But `dependency_kind_allowed` has a permissive fallback for kinds outside Pack/Game/Crate; generic `resolve_from` skips optional edges; semantic graph validation is a separate explicit step; the generic staging path copies the authored tree and permits runtime payloads for all kinds; and there is no one Pack-kind payload rule. These are the concrete checks behind the [October 25 lifecycle-stage matrix](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#0-ten-content-kinds-owner-meaning-versus-current-contracts) and [current Packagepack staging trace](#october-25--pack-and-code-artifacts-share-an-unrestricted-packaging-path).

**Glossary lineage and current-state mismatch:** the Aug 30 USF glossary (`c8b91a3e`) is a 43-term ontology snapshot; the Sep 9 Premium Docs split (`5b7ef29a`) creates a separate 62-term Vapor lookup glossary and says each concept should have one normative owner. The current Vapor book glossary began as a six-line stub in July (`9134d3ff`) and was expanded in the Oct 20 documentation pass (`a1941677`). It remains a compact summary rather than a migration of either glossary, and still says Composition is the user’s launchable selection while deferring to a future “canonical glossary.” That is especially consequential because the owner later clarified Packagepack itself as playable-selection identity. The three epochs should remain distinguishable: old vocabulary is evidence, the current book is still interim, and later owner decisions need a new canonical home. See the [all-term crosswalk](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#archived-vapor-glossary-cross-check--2026-10-25) and [USF crosswalk](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#the-archived-usf-glossary-against-the-current-implementation).

### What this chronology establishes—and does not

The commits establish that the separate Composition model was designed and documented as an intentional system in mid-October, not an accidental label that appeared only in the latest GUI. The later owner explanation is a real model correction, and the default identity duplication reported in the UI has a traceable semantic source. The same commits established real shared service, content types, resolver, staging, fingerprints and state that should be evaluated as foundations, not erased by calling the whole pass fake.

They do **not** establish that the October 20 documentation claims were deliberate final doctrine, that all users ran the `basic-content` starter, or that a Rust Engine binary is inherently wrong in every project. The conclusion is narrower: both template paths and current guidance fail to express one current, owner-approved, artifact-level contract for Engine, Game, Crate, Pack and Packagepack; the owner has explicitly set constraints that future work must reconcile against. No docs or source code in these repositories were edited during this audit.

**Historical cross-reference:** the current topology service begins with [`12c2e5a5` on September 7](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Registry-Server/commit/12c2e5a5d454fe9cf91a9e0f37088f9704389f5c) as an ecosystem/source-repository API, then receives repository-renaming and ecosystem updates through September 15 (`0f4500ec`, `566130c7`). The first commit also accidentally tracked the just-built `target/` tree: it adds 1,520 files / 8,937 insertions, most of the file count being generated Cargo output; [`7f5fb1e5` about twenty minutes later](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Registry-Server/commit/7f5fb1e5f4f0357b7215ffb041b2a8d322b1662) removes that tree and adds the ignore policy. Those generated blobs remain part of Git history even though no target files are tracked at the current head. On October 22, [`d02a0c6a`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Platform-Server/commit/d02a0c6acf083a00f06d62b35cff49852ed3cab1) records “Registry catalog; Identity authorizes” as an accepted target, but its diff changes only the server boundary document; it does not update the Registry submodule or client contracts. The implementation has since grown both a Registry topology API and local publishing confirmation workflows, but the evidence reviewed here shows no connection between them. Treat the current Steam path as a local development publisher, not as the eventual public release/catalog authority. No upload or identity service request was made during this audit; no end-to-end authorization behavior was exercised.


## October 25 — thermal subsystem cross-check against its deleted architecture note

The source-level subsystem review is recorded in the [latest-state atlas](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#6a-thermal-and-combustion-a-coherent-slice-with-a-two-level-state-model). The chronology matters: [`ebd9643`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/ebd9643) introduced the September 12 systemic fire/health vertical slice; follow-on September changes reorganized the domain and developer inspection; later changes added local finite-volume spatial refinement and point impulses. The October 6 [`0e48843`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/0e488433dd26b35a937dba8c5f755b52615e8eaf) cleanup removed `spacetime-engine/src/thermal/ARCHITECTURE.md` (99 lines), including explicit ownership, approximation, solver and non-goal statements. Those claims were recovered from the parent commit and checked against the current source rather than assumed to remain true.

The documented two-state compatibility bridge is still what the code does: aggregate `ThermalBody` remains the authority for older combustion/cooling/game injury consumers; optional `ThermalField` refines internal gradients; localized point impulses update both; aggregate-only changes are projected uniformly back into the field. Combustion ignition can inspect a field's maximum temperature, while injury reads aggregate temperature. This is a deliberate approximation with a predictable information-loss seam, not evidence of a fire solver bug. Spatial interaction samples map split manifestations back to a semantic body and use scale-to-metre positions, but pairwise candidate discovery is O(n²) and does not establish a world-scale USF distance contract.

The earlier architecture note's stated non-goals—radiation, convection, phase changes, contact conduction, variable/anisotropic material properties, large-world acceleration and material-accurate tuning—remain limits of this slice, not implicit promises. The current source has no thermal-local test module in the inspected engine test locations; no build, test or runtime was performed. This subsystem is therefore source-cross-checked, not empirically validated. The archived note is represented as historical evidence in the atlas; it was not restored into the source repository.

**Test-history correction:** the current source absence is not “thermal was never tested.” `7402cc6` carried three focused test modules for bounded fuel consumption, aggregate heat-capacity conversion, field capacity, localized heating/conduction and energy conservation. The October 5 [`dc69de6`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/dc69de6) change removed the domain, simulation and spatial thermal test modules (91 lines total); current source/test inventory has no thermal-local replacement. This is a concrete test-coverage regression associated with the larger source cleanup, although the reviewed history does not establish the author's reason. The old assertions remain useful historical evidence but were not run in this audit.

## October 8 — worldgen's typed phenomenon evaluator is replaced by construction provenance

At the October 6 head `0e48843`, worldgen was no longer just a seed helper: it had a typed `PhenomenonRule` registry, type-erased per-domain snapshots, canonical-address cache keyed by spatial scope / temporal label / epoch, root-to-fine contextual evaluation, seeded noise and nine built-in phenomenon families. But its own module header explicitly limited the result to descriptive snapshots: it did not construct celestial identities, terrain, ecology or material state, and the Loo-Cast fixture did not consume it. Its `TemporalScale` documentation says it is an opaque parameterization/model-resolution label, expressly not seconds, tick duration, a timestep or integrator policy. The approximate planetary model biases toward Earth-like values and emits scalar descriptions; this was a broad speculative model layer, not a functioning authored-to-live world pipeline ([historical model](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/0e488433dd26b35a937dba8c5f755b52615e8eaf/spacetime-engine/src/worldgen/model.rs), [historical store](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/0e488433dd26b35a937dba8c5f755b52615e8eaf/spacetime-engine/src/worldgen/store/mod.rs), [historical rule contract](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/0e488433dd26b35a937dba8c5f755b52615e8eaf/spacetime-engine/src/worldgen/phenomenon/mod.rs), [example planetary rule at `0e48843`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/0e488433dd26b35a937dba8c5f755b52615e8eaf/spacetime-engine/src/worldgen/builtin/planetary_body/mod.rs)).

On October 8, `d806e3d` deletes 1,382 lines across the cache, temporal/epoch model, registry, noise and all nine built-ins. It is followed that day by `0f153c5`, which introduces the current 206-line deterministic `WorldSeed` / stable phenomenon-field seed / exact-or-procedural constraint / provenance kernel, then `b77a397`, which adds `SparseConstructionAtlas`. The current README marks the catalog experimental and explicitly says it is not live world construction. The reversal narrows implementation toward explicit authored facts and stable provenance before a live generation mechanism exists. It should neither be described as “the old generator worked and was removed” nor erased from the future plan: it shows one earlier approach, its explicit disconnect from runtime, and a real exploratory temporal-scale label that stopped short of physical time semantics. The old worldgen tree has no checked-in test functions; the narrower successor has focused seed and catalog tests. This review did not run either version. The full current cross-check is in [atlas section 7a/7b](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7a-worldgen-means-deterministic-construction-inputs-today-not-procedural-worlds).

## September 30 worldgen megapass design versus current celestial source

This review crosswalks the archived [September 30 architecture spec](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/5021345a88ad935a8cea460adb1b9feda02e792e/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-30-usf-sparse-procedural-celestial-worldgen-design.md) and its companion plan (`d44b3407`) against current Loo-Cast source at `c070bf3` (October 22 commit; inspected October 25). It is a current-state comparison against intent, not a declaration that the deleted spec was approved or that its checkbox plan was completed.

The spec's target was one integrated semantic world: movable canonical celestial bodies; demand-based sparse realizations; an adaptive coarse whole-body surface composed with local volume; hierarchical continental and mountain morphology; an Earth-relative moving Moon; and a future-safe high-speed collision seam. The ordered tranches make the surviving implementation easier to understand: body-frame ownership and sparse realization preceded the missing whole-planet presentation and terrain morphology work.

| Tranche / invariant | Current evidence | Status and caveat |
|---|---|---|
| A. One movable semantic frame; body-local edits | Current body ECS owns canonical position/frame/motion; voxel scale realizations bind to that authority. Semantic edits are frame-local ordered `VoxelFrameEdit` records. | **Partly realized.** Rotation currently retires and recreates a realization because the lattice cannot preserve arbitrary rotation. Save/reload and edit continuity through body movement were not exercised. |
| B. Sparse scale-local realization | `reconcile_celestial_voxel_realizations` creates containers only for demanded targets; dense residency is separately budgeted and can be parked. | **Implemented structurally.** No runtime proof of bounded memory/work or demand proportionality. Target identity remains authority + scale, not the spec's generalized region-cover planner. |
| C. Adaptive cubed-sphere body presentation and make-before-break coverage | No cubed-sphere/coarse planetary patch renderer or body-wide coverage handoff was found in current source. A generated 256×128 tectonic/biome-like texture and `planet_surface` material are initialized, but no current consumer was found; the asset is not a geometry backend. Local voxel streaming/meshing is not equivalent to that backend. | **Absent from inspected source.** The orphaned material is a presentation remnant/direction, not a wired far-body renderer; rendered appearance was not assessed. |
| D. Planet-scale terrain bands and long morphology | `CelestialVoxelField::sphere` holds radius/detail-floor; signed distance is radial length minus radius; sampling chooses rock/void. | **Absent.** No province, orogenic, residual-band, cave or kilometre-relief field is in the current authority. |
| E. Generic Earth/Moon construction and canonical Moon orbit | Both authored records use the same celestial constructor. Moon gets `KeplerianOrbitPropagation`, which writes canonical position and motion from analytic elements. | **Core ownership model present; proof incomplete.** Earth/Moon values are exact authored facts; procedural fallback is unused. Epoch uses Bevy virtual elapsed seconds. No runtime orbit, time-scale, visual or collision validation was performed. |
| No worldgen god-manager; keyed deterministic construction | Seeded keyed constraints, provenance and sparse atlas feed fixture construction. | **Narrow substrate present.** No phenomenon-to-phenomenon rule graph, continuation system or generated-world persistence was found. Atlas region lookup filters known entries. |
| Swept collision consumes moving semantic bodies | Canonical sweep and semantic voxel authorities coexist with local Avian motion. | **Enabling structure only.** The separate collision review finds readiness/completeness and bounded-work gaps; radial TTC does not account for target-body velocity. No high-speed acceptance run was performed. |

The September 30 proposal was deleted on October 6 by `0e48843` as part of a cleanup removing 404 paths / 9,786 lines overall. The separate October 6 phenomenon-evaluation prototype was then removed on October 8 by `d806e3d`. Later that day, `0f153c5` and `b77a397` introduced the much narrower present construction-input substrate. These are three distinct layers: ambitious architectural target, descriptive-but-unconsumed procedural model, and current construction-fact mechanism. Newer source did implement meaningful pieces of the target's ownership and sparsity principles, but not the conspicuous planetary presentation/morphology result. Thus the reset is neither “a working planet generator was deleted” nor “the plan was completed under another name.”
