## October 2 segmented materialization design versus current store and scheduler

The archived [October 2 design](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/020877577d1c1c0f86b69a519b43d5af2dcea844/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-02-segmented-voxel-materialization-design.md) states that it was approved and frozen before implementation. It is therefore stronger than an exploratory TODO, but still historical: the owner can and did revise direction, and its deletion does not make every clause current doctrine. The design's key acceptance pressure was to make demand/address, occupancy proof, dense data, surface, rendering, collision and editing independently owned—especially compactly representing proven empty space before dense allocation.

### Present source matches

- **Store/entity split:** `VoxelMaterializationStore` owns address-keyed dense entries and optional surface caches; inactive dense entries form a bounded warm cache. Bevy manifestations are disposable downstream products.
- **No empty render entities:** manifestation reconciliation publishes a `VoxelPresentationManifestation` only when presentation is requested and the current surface has triangles. No-surface facts instead use `UsfCapabilityCoveragePublication` batches on a scale-realization entity. The generic spatial snapshot consumes both batch-published and entity-backed facts.
- **Role separation:** demand roles distinguish presentation, collision and editing; collision aggregation checks rigid triangles independently of presentation, and editing readiness can be satisfied from dense semantic data.
- **Real prioritization:** per-address rank includes role priority, semantic priority, boundary-focus distance, trajectory distance and observer distance. Generation re-ranks candidate worlds and gives each one batch per round; per-world pending queues are sorted by rank. Worker lanes have critical/normal queues, weighted-fair service across generation/derivation/planning, and a bounded critical burst to prevent permanent starvation of normal work.

### The primary compactness contract is still absent

`VoxelMaterializationRecipe::materialize` always calls `DenseVoxelMaterialization::generate`. That method loops across the full padded sample lattice, pushes every distance and material into arrays, and only then records `surface_transition`. `VoxelMaterializationStore::insert_dense_active` treats a no-transition result as already derived and skips surface generation; presentation membership then removes or never creates its render manifestation. But the store retains the dense arrays as `VoxelMaterializationState::Dense`, including for a chunk whose known samples are all air. Current “empty” is therefore a **no-surface result**, not the design's compact pre-classification state.

There is no current `UniformAir` / `UniformSolid` store variant, no pre-generation `VoxelBase::Empty` fast path, and no per-address celestial AABB/radial occupancy classifier before dense generation. There is a different, useful optimization upstream: demand-region traversal rejects whole nodes outside a spherical surface shell, with margin of two local materialization chunks. That reduces which addresses become demand at all in this radius-only terrain model. It is not an occupancy result carried by a demanded address; it does not prove/store compact air for addresses that make it through traversal, and a terrain-envelope margin will need to account for real relief before the field becomes non-spherical. `VoxelBase::Empty` sampling itself is trivial, but if an address reaches the recipe, it still visits every sample and stores it. A uniform result therefore avoids Surface Nets and ECS presentation cost, but not the planned dense sample generation/allocation cost. This is the clearest surviving reason the Oct 2 design matters.

### Priority exists, but it is not the proposed scheduler

The current design does **not** simply use one unranked global FIFO: demand deltas are incrementally applied, rank values are retained by address, pending desired work is sorted, and generation re-ranks the world's front work item each admission round. Separate worker lane fairness is also implemented. Those are substantive implementations of priority and bounded service.

The accepted design proposed a different layer: keyed current demand/revision state plus versioned tickets per capability segment (`classify`, `dense-generate`, `surface-derive`, publication), compared globally before expensive work. Current generation scheduling is still chunk-first. It does not have a classification ticket because no classifier exists; derivation then uses a separate dirty queue that scans for its best item only when a slot opens; publication has a frame budget. These stages are prioritized locally but are not one global capability-work scheduler. This distinction matters: broad “priority scheduling exists” claims are true at the chunk/work-lane level, while the more ambitious capability-ticket contract remains open.

### Instrumentation and verification are smaller than the accepted checklist

The present `VoxelMaterializationTelemetry::summary` reports worker capacity/in-flight counts and generation/derivation totals, cancellations, failures and empty-surface skips. It does not report compact occupancy counts, dense-versus-demand ratios, avoided dense generation, presentation entity ratios, queue age, or useful completions by capability stage. The inspected current `src/voxel` tree has two inline tests (region traversal and realization intent) and no separate `spacetime-engine/tests` directory; no Cargo tests or runtime checks were run here. This is weaker than the design's extensive classification, coverage, scheduler and scaling checklist, though an exhaustive test search outside the inspected paths is not claimed.

The October 6 cleanup (`0e48843`) deleted the 709-line design, but current source later grew several of its ideas organically: store-owned materialization state, compact batched coverage, no-surface presentation elision, explicit role masks and ranked demand. The specific design's highest-value first-stage objective—proof-driven compact occupancy before dense generation—did not survive into the current architecture. Thus the right summary is not “the plan was implemented” or “the cleanup discarded it”: the implementation retained selected ownership and manifestation contracts, while its main memory-saving algorithm and cross-stage scheduler are missing. See [atlas section 7c](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7c-october-2-voxel-design-which-sparsity-contracts-survived).

## October 25: Three scale models: worldgen atlas, descriptive evaluator, current USF

The archived [`USF_WORLDGEN_SCALE_ATLAS.md` at `020877577d`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/020877577d1c1c0f86b69a519b43d5af2dcea844/spacetime-engine/USF_WORLDGEN_SCALE_ATLAS.md) explicitly labels itself a historical proposal. It defines 36 non-negative spatial domains, S+35 through S0, and proposes an every-scale top-down generation path. Its temporal contract says spatial and temporal scale are orthogonal, while the deleted October 6 evaluator's `TemporalScale` was only a model-resolution label and its epoch was fixed. Neither proposal was a physical clock or operational time-scaling system.

The current numerical USF has 71 **spatial** exponents S−35 through S+35. Its unit conversion is explicit in `usf::SpatialScale`; `spatial` owns runtime partitions, projection, demand, coverage and transitions. The present worldgen module contains keyed deterministic sampling, constraints and sparse authored facts, not the archived evaluator or the proposed +35→0 chain. The fixture authors exact Earth/Moon data; the Moon's Keplerian propagation consumes Bevy virtual elapsed time. Current source does not define a temporal scale coordinate, common space-time scale index, cosmological epoch model or generated terrain chain.

An October 9 owner-directed plan records a newer future constraint: one authored scale index with baseline spatial and temporal units coupled by ×10 per step, potentially adjusted by local gameplay clock rates. That plan explicitly places canonical world time and event ordering before implementation, and labels coupling future work. Therefore the older atlas's orthogonality is superseded as intended design, while the newer coupled model is **not implemented**. This distinguishes an old proposal, an experimental/disconnected prototype and the latest owner direction from one another, rather than treating all uses of “scale” as the same contract.

The current source evidence for the numerical split is [`usf/mod.rs`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/usf/mod.rs#L1) and [`spatial/mod.rs`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/spatial/mod.rs#L1); the historical future constraint is in the [October 9 plan](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/blob/c070bf3/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-09-usf-spatial-authority-megapass.md#future-constraints-not-current-implementation). This is a source/document crosswalk only; no world generation, time behavior, build or runtime was exercised. See [atlas section 7d](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7d-the-old-world-generation-scale-atlas-is-not-the-current-scale-model).

## October 25: The Client service extraction still routes through broad Core

The October 18 [`f9e8b13`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f9e8b13) “Extract shared Vapor Client service and domain” is a meaningful architectural transition, not a cosmetic crate move. It creates the local Client transport, protocol, service, application, provider, domain and content packages in an 85-file diff with 27,021 insertions, adds a substantial service process/session, and writes a 309-line service-boundary guide. On October 19, [`d7e21dc`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/d7e21dc) moves more operations behind the service and removes the prior 2,704-line Core CLI. The current dependency graph shows that this extraction established a new service boundary around many operations but did not make the older `vapor_core` a leaf/static kernel.

At the current October 25 source snapshot, `vapor_core` still has 32 public modules. It depends on content, console and telemetry libraries plus Clap, blocking `reqwest`, CSV, TOML and other host-level dependencies. It exposes toolchain/process/installation/role, workspace/source/superworkspace, content resolution, Cargo build/deploy, Steam, documentation, profiling/Tracy and Registry operations. The new Provider crate depends on Core and contains call sites from Cargo output and builds, authoring, launch, Workshop, cross-target tools, discovery, docs publication, managed Cargo, process output and release. Application depends on Provider and Core; Service depends on Application, Core and SDK Core; SDK Core also depends on Core. These are verified manifest and import edges. They do not by themselves establish harmful duplication: a broad library can be a deliberate shared implementation substrate. They do establish that the service boundary delegates into it and does not yet encapsulate all those responsibilities behind a narrow, provider-neutral API.

The frontend call sites confirm that bypasses persist. The Installer UI directly executes Core install/status/repair/uninstall and role operations. The regular CLI's local deployment command directly calls Core while content lifecycle commands use the service. The SDK CLI directly executes SDK Core in process, and that dispatcher still has an explicit generic `not_implemented` fallback. Therefore “one local service powers every frontend operation” is only partly implemented. The exact statement supported by source is: **many common Client workflows use a shared local service; the old broad Core remains a cross-layer implementation dependency, and some installation/development/SDK paths still bypass the daemon.**

This is especially relevant to the owner's size concern. The current shared Vapor checkout is 68,460 physical source lines; `vapor_core` accounts for 16,907 and `vapor_client_service` for 16,207, while Provider is 15,874. Those counts show that extraction added substantial ownership surfaces without shrinking Core to a small kernel. They do not prove that any line is useless or that a 30k target would be sound. To judge necessity, a future review would have to classify each Core responsibility by canonical owner, caller, duplicate behavior and lifecycle; line-count pressure is a diagnostic prompt, not a deletion criterion.

The 32-module `lib.rs` surface has a second implication beyond size: public module paths allow downstream crates to depend directly on host effects as well as semantic models. A current module inventory groups into content/schema (`authored_manifest`, `content`, `identity`, `manifest`, `local`, `resolution`); installation and role (`installation`, `install`, `role`, `developer_environment`, `maintenance`, `uninstall`); workspace and development (`workspace`, `superworkspace`, `source`, `ecosystem`, `development`, `run`); build/tool/process (`cargo`, `cargo_reconciliation`, `toolchain`, `cross_target_toolchain`, `managed_tool`, `managed_process`); integrations (`ide`, `ide_host`, `steam`, `registry`); and host/observability (`host`, `operation`, `profiling`, `tracy`). That inventory is an API map, not a modularity verdict. It sharpens what a genuine service-boundary review must answer: which data contracts are provider-neutral, which effects belong behind service operations, which are intentionally local bootstrap exceptions, and which public APIs survive only as compatibility/VS0 paths. The [atlas groups the same current surface against the product/service direction](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#3-shared-service-operations-logs-and-cross-frontend-behavior).

Several source comments make the transitional split unusually explicit: `manifest.rs` calls its `Vapor.toml` format Vertical Slice 0; `local.rs` discovers that catalog; `authored_manifest.rs` and `identity.rs` re-export canonical types from the newer `vapor_content` crate; `ide_host.rs` still exposes a line-oriented stdio host. Those facts show current and prior semantic layers co-resident in one public crate. They do not show that the legacy path is unused everywhere: the distribution still carries `vapor-ide-host`, although no current product caller was found in the source search. The evidence supports a stale-shipped-path concern and a compatibility audit, not deletion without a complete caller/package/release trace.

Evidence: current [`vapor_core` facade](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/lib.rs#L1), [Service manifest](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/Cargo.toml), [Application manifest](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/Cargo.toml), [Provider manifest](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/Cargo.toml), [Installer direct Core use](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L90), [regular CLI local deployment](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/client_commands.rs#L1), and [SDK CLI dispatcher](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/output/stub.rs#L1). No build, test, profile or runtime was performed.

## October 25: Identity owns local roles but does not yet authorize downstream publishing

The current Identity service is more than a future placeholder: the source registers Steam OpenID and Steam ticket verification, GitHub browser OAuth/device/token verification, auth-attempt completion, profile/account linking, session creation/revocation, role grant/revoke, audit listing, and root dashboard routes. Its SQLite schema gives the role/profile/session records clear persistence ownership. A successful browser session is an opaque random token; only SHA-256(token) is stored in `identity_sessions`, while the raw token is sent as an HttpOnly cookie. Root dashboard authorization rechecks session expiry/revocation, enabled profile, active root role, and both linked providers at request time. `root` implies `content-developer` in effective-role projection. This is a real local authority boundary for Identity's own admin operations.

The 19-commit Identity history has 17 implementation/role/admin commits between July 23 and July 24, followed by the September repository rename and October 22 Vapor workspace metadata. That short build-out creates Axum/SQLite persistence, provider verification, dashboard sessions, role grant/revoke and audit. The cross-service authorization contract is recorded July 25, and the Registry-as-catalog / Identity-as-author-authorization boundary is reaffirmed October 22 ([July server QA/contract commit](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Platform-Server/commit/709cca7df40493b3e9217c05c706c6a5dc89549e), [October Registry ownership decision](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Platform-Server/commit/d02a0c6acf083a00f06d62b35cff49852ed3cab1)). The current routes and Client consumers still do not implement its introspection handoff. This is a boundary that was built locally in a short burst and later assigned wider ecosystem authority without yet completing the integration. The [timeline's Identity commit register](loo-cast-vapor-history-timeline.md#vapor-identity-server--19-commits) supplies the full dated sequence.

That boundary has not yet become service authority. The accepted cross-service contract explicitly says its transport is not implemented and describes audience-bound introspection as the target. The current Identity route table contains no introspection route, no service audience type, and no downstream authorization endpoint. The Platform Server docs likewise say Docs/Diagnostics and publishing still use token/bootstrap scaffolds. The Client's local Workshop and root-publish handlers do not ask Identity for current roles; Registry has no authoring/release catalog route to receive a publication record. SteamCMD remains the actual provider authorization gate. Accordingly, “Identity is the authorization source” is true as architectural ownership and true for Identity admin routes, but not yet true for Client/Registry/Docs/pipeline decisions. The service is useful and in operation; it is the connector contract and adoption that remain missing.

The sources also disagree about the token model. The Identity README says “JWT issuance”; source instead issues opaque random session tokens and persists their hash, and the newer vertical-slice contract explicitly states there is no JWT or service-to-service authentication. This is a documentation error, not merely a future design mismatch. The README's generic “Protected routes expect” block also lists only the admin bearer token, although root sessions are accepted by several `/v1/admin/*` operations; later sections document that alternate path, so this is imprecise local wording rather than a missing implementation. The target docs are clearer than the older README here and should be the authority for present implementation status.

The remaining Identity source modules clarify what the July 24 extraction actually established. `api_handlers.rs` and `persistence.rs` are three/four-line wildcard re-export facades; they shorten the imports in `main.rs`, but do not themselves implement an API layer or a persistence abstraction. The behavior remains in the concrete handler, attempt, profile and database modules ([API re-exports](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/api_handlers.rs>), [persistence re-exports](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/persistence.rs>)). `provider_handlers.rs` retains two registered legacy verification probes alongside the newer session flow: direct Steam verification can persist/link a Steam profile but returns no session; direct GitHub token verification returns an empty `profile_id`, does not link an account and does not create a Vapor session. The README labels them legacy probes, and repository search found no first-party caller beyond route registration and operator documentation. Their `/v1/auth/*` naming can therefore look more complete than their actual contract ([legacy handlers](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/provider_handlers.rs#L10-L163>), [route registration](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/main.rs#L80-L85>), [README qualification](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/README.md#L188-L198>)). `status_handlers.rs` combines liveness/readiness, the authenticated one-time database initializer, and an authorization-gated metadata/count export; the latter is not a database backup and the public readiness fields reflect configuration predicates rather than provider reachability. `types.rs` is the shared transport/state vocabulary for these paths: `AppState` holds the pool, admin-token option, provider config and HTTP client, while the DTOs cover both legacy direct probes and the multi-step auth/session flow. This is a real extraction from the former monolith, but the re-export facades and shared DTO module do not create strict API/domain ownership boundaries by themselves ([status/init/export](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/status_handlers.rs>), [state and DTOs](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/types.rs>)).

The history explains this shape: `b8b1671` moved roughly 3,200 lines out of the 3,262-line `main.rs` in one extraction commit, introducing the handler, persistence, state and utility modules together. That materially improved navigation and assigned code by responsibility; it did not add contracts around the re-export modules or remove the direct provider routes ([extraction diff](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Identity-Server/commit/b8b1671)).

### Source-level concurrency and deployment properties

These are review findings from control flow, not reproduced incidents:

| Property | Current code path | What the evidence supports |
|---|---|---|
| Browser callback one-time use | Steam and GitHub callback handlers query a valid, unconsumed state row; they then verify remotely and create/link identity/session state; only afterward do they issue an unconditional `consumed_at` update. | There is no atomic “claim this state if still unused” before side effects. Two concurrent callbacks with the same valid high-entropy state can both pass the read. The Steam flow can create duplicate sessions if the callback is accepted twice; GitHub additionally relies on its provider authorization code exchange, which may reject a second use. This is a race candidate, not proof of account takeover or replay in deployment. |
| Last active root invariant | `revoke_role` reads active-root count before opening its transaction, then revokes within the transaction. The count filters active role rows but not disabled profiles, while root-session authorization rejects disabled profiles. | The single-request invariant is tested; concurrent root revocations could both observe more than one root and each remove a different root. If disabled profiles are introduced/used, a disabled root row can also count as the remaining administrator although it cannot authorize a session. No service path currently sets `disabled_at_unix`; neither condition was reproduced. |
| First-root bootstrap | Auth completion checks active-root count, then separately grants root. | Two bootstrap completions could race on an empty-root state unless the storage transaction or a uniqueness invariant prevents it; the schema has no single-active-root constraint. Conditional concurrency concern only. |
| Secure cookies | `SameSite=Lax` and `HttpOnly` are always set; `Secure` depends on `VAPOR_IDENTITY_COOKIE_SECURE`, whose parser defaults to false. The checked-in VPS bootstrap sets it true. | The template is correct for HTTPS, but the live VPS environment value was not inspected. |
| Dashboard password setting | VPS bootstrap writes a random `VAPOR_IDENTITY_DASHBOARD_PASSWORD`; Identity reads it and reports only `dashboard_basic_password_configured`. No handler authenticates against or otherwise reads the value. | It is retained configuration/status residue, not an active login mechanism. The dashboard correctly says it uses Identity sessions instead of Basic auth, but the generated secret and readiness field can imply a password path that does not exist. |
| Privileged browser forms | Grant/revoke forms use POST and root-session cookies; no per-form CSRF token or explicit Origin check appears in these handlers. Cookies are `SameSite=Lax`. | SameSite=Lax mitigates ordinary cross-site form POSTs in current browsers, but there is no second request-origin check visible here. Whether same-site subdomains or supported browser edge cases matter is unassessed; no CSRF was demonstrated. |
| Provider-call availability | One shared `reqwest::Client` is constructed with a user agent but no explicit request/connect timeout; the Axum router has no visible request-rate limiter. Caddy's checked-in route is a plain reverse proxy. | A stalled provider call may retain a handler task without an application deadline, and repeated public auth attempts are not throttled by an observed service/proxy rule. This is a source-level availability concern; deployed proxy configuration and live behavior were not inspected. |
| Readiness reporting | `steam_browser_login_ready` is hard-coded `true`; Steam identity readiness is based on API-key presence; GitHub identity readiness and GitHub browser-login readiness use different configuration predicates. No provider reachability probe runs. | These fields describe local configuration or route availability, not successful end-to-end provider authentication. A consumer that treats them as live service readiness can overstate actual capability. |
| Logout | `/logout` is a GET route that revokes the session and expires the cookie. | Logout has a state-changing GET shape. The evident impact is cross-site sign-out nuisance; no elevated action is exposed by that route. |

The Identity tree contains four inline Tokio tests, all in `profiles.rs`, for role aggregation, refusal to remove the last root in a sequential case, no-op revocation, and audit behavior. Platform Server also has a manual `smoke-identity-auth.sh` flow and unauthenticated HTTP contract checks for health/status/admin rejection; neither was run here. These do not demonstrate the concurrent callback/root properties above, provider callback integration, VPS cookie settings, or downstream service authorization.

Evidence: [Identity routes and provider-client construction](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/main.rs#L49), [provider verifiers](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/providers.rs#L11), [cookie/session token construction](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/util.rs#L46), [configuration defaults](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/config.rs#L1), [browser state storage](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/auth_attempts.rs#L36), [Steam callback](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/browser_handlers.rs#L77), [GitHub callback](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/browser_handlers.rs#L208), [last-root check](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/profiles.rs#L125), [root-bootstrap flow](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/session_handlers.rs#L470), [Caddy route template](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/deploy/caddy/Caddyfile.template#L8), [cross-service target contract](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/cross-service-authorization-contract.md#L1), and [Identity README](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/README.md#L1).

## October 25: Diagnostics server exists, but the Client upload path is still a stub

The Platform server’s diagnostics API and the Client’s diagnostics command were developed as separate vertical slices. The earliest Client-side planning record (July 22) explicitly made *local diagnostics capture* the active topic and parked upload behind privacy decisions, schema design, consent UX and transport choice. The server binary appeared July 23; the July 25 server v2 commit added a structured schema beside a legacy upload route, then a second July 25 commit deliberately collapsed those into the current unversioned `/reports` API and removed the `schema_version` field. On that same date, Client commit `78ec93a` substantially revised local capture and added an explicit future transport object; later shell-to-CLI rename and Client routing commits retained the stub. That sequence produced a good local record plus a usable server service, but did not close the product decision between them. Current CLI `diagnostics.rs` still instantiates `FutureHttpServerTransport`, whose `configured()` always returns false and whose non-dry-run `upload()` always errors. `diagnostics upload` can describe or dry-run a local capture, but it cannot send it in this build. Conversely, the server source accepts a correctly shaped HTTP report. This is confirmed source behavior, not a statement that a CLI upload was attempted in the current runtime. The pre-alpha report contract explicitly says it is not a stable public API; because the endpoint is now unversioned, client/server schema evolution depends on coordinated releases rather than request-level version negotiation.

This gap protects a meaningful privacy boundary. Local capture records installation and executable paths, command arguments and source context; the server schema deliberately accepts only client version, coarse platform fields and an allowlisted set of text artifacts, and explicitly excludes hostname, machine ID, account and path fields. A future transport cannot simply serialize the local run directory or its metadata wholesale. It needs a deliberate preview/selection and schema projection, and should preserve explicit consent. The local CLI help says a future HTTP transport will attach here; current server deployment does not change that statement by itself.

The server-side protections and their limits are also uneven. Upload is unauthenticated by design, with `consent = true` as a caller-supplied field, a 2 MiB request cap and a 256 MiB default aggregate quota. There is no visible per-client rate limit or automatic retention worker in the service or checked-in proxy. The focused report contract explicitly rejects automatic destructive retention for now, while the older server README still says it enforces a retention policy and supports export/import. Current code has no import route; `GET /export` emits metadata summaries only, not the stored log contents. The deployment-level state archive is a different, root-operated full-state recovery mechanism. Without a public client implementation, those gaps are latent server-policy concerns; if anonymous upload is connected, anyone able to reach it can consume the finite quota by repeatedly asserting consent, and the service has no current cleanup policy to reclaim accepted reports.

Redaction is a best-effort transformation, not a privacy proof. It handles unquoted `token=value`, `token: value`, authorization/cookie header lines, selected URL query parameters and common GitHub token prefixes. A small read-only check of the exact regex patterns confirmed they do not redact ordinary quoted JSON such as `{"token":"sensitive-value"}` or common underscore names such as `api_key=...` and `client_secret=...`. This is narrower than arbitrary-secret protection and should be considered before any client uploads structured logs. The server contract already warns that arbitrary sensitive text may survive; the discrepancy is between that caveat and any stronger reading of the advertised “common sensitive forms.”

Storage handling has conditional partial-state behavior. A report is assembled in `.upload-<run-id>` and renamed to its final run directory, then `latest.txt` is written. A process failure during writes can leave an unindexed staging directory; it is ignored by listing, but `directory_size` counts it toward quota. A failure writing `latest.txt` can return an upload error after the final report has already been committed. These are source-derived failure windows, not reproduced. Status also maps a storage-usage read error to zero via `unwrap_or_default()`, which can under-report pressure; upload admission itself propagates the same size-read error.

The server has four inline tests for redaction, artifact-name allowlisting and quota parsing. The manual VPS smoke script uploads a synthetic report, downloads it with the admin token and checks a few fake secrets, then checks unauthenticated reads return 401. That script proves neither Client transport integration nor retention, rate limiting, JSON-key redaction, import/full export, crash recovery or the deployed state. No server test or smoke flow was run during this review.

This is a cross-repository ownership gap, not merely “diagnostics not finished”: the Client owns capture and user consent, Diagnostics owns public acceptance/storage and operator access, and Identity is the future reader-authorization authority. Current source implements the capture and server storage halves but no transport contract tying them together. The July planning record intentionally delayed transport; later creation of the server API did not implicitly approve sending the Client’s richer local metadata. See the [July planning source](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/planning-intake/source-corpus/raw-input/vapor-diagnostics/2026-07-22-diagnostics-registry-infrastructure-planning.md), [Client transport stub](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/diagnostics.rs#L880), [server schema/storage/routes](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Diagnostics-Server/src/main.rs#L31), [current report contract](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/diagnostics-report-contract.md), and [older README promises](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Diagnostics-Server/README.md#L1).

## October 25: the public homepage is still a deployment stub, not the product map

The latest checked-out `Vapor-Homepage-Server` head is `89155e9` (the metadata-only workspace-manifest commit; the preceding runtime commit is `a41aedc`). Its Axum router serves only `/`, `/index.html`, `/healthz`, `/license`, and `/impressum` ([router and handlers](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Homepage-Server/src/main.rs#L7)). The landing page is a short inline HTML literal with one sentence, a Docs link, License, and Impressum; both legal pages explicitly say their content is not finalized ([page bodies](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Homepage-Server/src/main.rs#L31)). There is no templating/static asset layer, product catalogue, release status, install/download path, identity link, or generated connection to current content kinds in this service.

The repository README's responsibility is broader: product/project overview, license/product text, legal contact and links to other public surfaces ([README](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Homepage-Server/README.md#L7)). The source has only the latter two placeholder pages and a minimal landing message. This is a concrete documentation/implementation gap, but it is also consistent with the Platform Server vertical-slice contract's explicit non-goal of a polished frontend: that document says the slice is meant to prove ownership, authority and deployment paths first ([vertical-slice contract](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/vertical-slice-contracts.md#L1)). Therefore “homepage unfinished” is a source fact; whether its thinness is presently a defect or an intentionally deferred product milestone depends on the product decision, not inference from the stub alone.

The reverse proxy sends `/docs/*` and each `/api/*` service prefix to its owning backend, then sends all other routes to port 7111 ([Caddy routing](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/deploy/caddy/Caddyfile.template#L1)). `/login*`, `/logout`, and `/admin*` are explicit Identity exceptions before that catch-all. Thus the homepage server is a narrow HTML root behind a broad multi-service origin; the route topology is intentionally centralized even though its service bodies remain separate. The Homepage README says it should remain mostly stateless and should not own Identity, diagnostics, docs publishing or orchestration, so adding those responsibilities to make the page feel complete would violate the stated boundary.

Deployment evidence is stale relative to the source head: the checked-in status document's last verification is July 25 and names runtime commit `a41aedc`, while current local source is `89155e9` ([deployment status](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/deployment-status.md#L1)). The Oct 25 checkout check found its local `main` matched `origin/main`, but no live HTTP request or VPS inspection was performed in this research pass. The status document is historical evidence that the earlier service was deployed, not evidence that the current route/content is live. This distinction matters because recent owner direction asks for trustworthy public documentation and a coherent creator/player path: the homepage currently does not explain that larger ecosystem, but the code alone cannot tell us whether that work belongs there, in docs, or in the Launcher.

## October 25: Registry's database is a seeded snapshot, not an administrable catalog

The Registry service has durable SQLite tables for provider accounts, repositories, ecosystems, and ecosystem-to-repository membership ([schema](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs#L34)). On every process initialization it runs idempotent table creation, writes the schema version, then calls `seed_official_registry` ([startup](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/main.rs#L45), [seed entry](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs#L27)). That seed upserts the GHF organization, Vapor ecosystem and six repository records from source constants, then deletes and recreates the ecosystem's three top-level memberships on each start ([seed data and membership reset](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs#L118)). The HTTP router exposes only health/status and GET ecosystem/provider reads ([routes](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/main.rs#L51)); there is no Registry registration/update API in this service.

So “Registry database” describes the persistence mechanism, not the current authoring authority. For the seeded official records, executable source code is the effective catalog input; SQLite materializes that seed for queries. A hand-edited membership would be reset at the next service start, and a new official repository needs a source/deploy change rather than a Registry API write. This may be an intentional bootstrap stage, but it is narrower than “canonical Registry catalog” can sound to a client or operator. The README's “register” verbs ([Registry README](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/README.md#L7)) overstate what the public service lets an administrator do.

The schema-version field is also only a marker today, not a migration gate. `run_migrations` always executes a fixed list of `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` statements, then overwrites `registry_meta.schema_version` with `REGISTRY_SCHEMA_VERSION`; it never reads the previous value or applies versioned transformations ([migration function](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs#L34)). The current single schema is simple and pre-alpha, so this is not evidence of an existing upgrade failure. It does mean the field cannot protect persisted Registry data when a later schema becomes incompatible; that needs to be decided before this service's SQLite state is treated as a durable user-administered catalogue. The only Registry test seeds an in-memory DB and checks the expected three roots and six provider repositories; it does not test restart behavior, writes, migration compatibility or returned URL trust ([seed test](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs#L483)). It was not run here.

The current top-level root set also records a meaningful evolution. Commit [`566130c`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Registry-Server/commit/566130cee3f3f2c455a1964e455625f2ca60a1) on September 15 added `Loo-Cast` as an independently acquired root and changed the ordering from the earlier two-root topology to `Loo-Cast`, `Vapor-Client`, and `Vapor-Platform-Server`; the `Vapor-Client` and Platform Server container repositories remain responsible for pinned nested workspaces through `.gitmodules`. The same commit adds the corresponding test assertions, so this is an intentional topology revision, not an inferred result from the current array. It makes Loo-Cast part of the official reconstructable ecosystem while preserving container repositories as submodule authorities. This still reconstructs **source repositories**, not all Vapor product/data: Steam depots, Workshop items, published package artifacts and runtime app installation are separate authorities and are not Registry rows.

This sharpens the accepted Registry/Identity direction: Registry has real bootstrap value, and Identity has real profile/role authority, but neither the database nor the current Client API yet forms the mutable, cross-service content release authority imagined in the owner's broader ecosystem plan. Any claim that Registry already registers arbitrary content, release versions, channels or publication policy is unsupported by this head. The source snapshot and migration limits are reviewed statically; no service restart, database mutation, API request or VPS check was performed.

### October 26: Registry repository renames can leave stale provider records

The September 12 seed update replaces `github:GHF-Studios/Vapor-Root` and `Vapor-Server-Root` with new IDs for `Vapor-Client` and `Vapor-Platform-Server`, but keeps the same insert-or-update-by-ID behavior. It does not delete retired repository rows. The September 15 change then inserts `Loo-Cast`, again without pruning removed records. Meanwhile `/v1/providers/{provider}/{login}` selects every repository linked to that provider account, not only the current hardcoded seed ([seed upsert](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs#L145-L199), [provider query](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs#L400-L457)). Therefore a persistent database initialized under the earlier seed can continue returning retired repository names/URLs after the new code starts. This is a conditional migration defect inferred from the SQL sequence; the current VPS database was not inspected, so presence of stale rows is unknown.

The sole Registry test creates a fresh in-memory database, initializes the latest seed and checks three ecosystem roots plus six provider repositories ([test](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Registry-Server/src/db.rs#L483-L523)). It cannot observe upgrade residue because it never starts from the older seed. The table-level behavior is small, but it connects the earlier `Vapor-Root` naming stage to current source-acquisition answers and demonstrates why a clean-database bootstrap test is not a persisted-state migration check. No test or database was run for this review.

## October 25: Steam's two routes are clear; the word “default” still names three different layers

The current Steam entrypoint source now implements the owner's simple product split: no arguments means **Play**, while `chooser` opens the small selector. Its README lists exactly those two launch choices for Linux and Windows targets ([launch table](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/README.md#L9)); the repository's Windows release proof repeats the Windows pair ([proof document](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/docs/windows-gnullvm-release-proof.md#L14)). The app chooser then offers Launcher, Studio and IDE as primary apps, with Installer and Shell in a setup/advanced group ([chooser UI](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui/src/lib.rs#L130)). This is a real improvement over exposing one Steam launch entry per app and aligns with the owner's explicit two-choice direction. Those checked-in tables describe intended Steamworks configuration; this source-only pass did not inspect the live partner configuration or verify either platform's launch UI.

The direct Play route first checks an app-root Player setup receipt. If absent, it opens Installer in first-launch mode; otherwise it ensures the shared Client service and executes `vapor launch selected` ([entrypoint branch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L68)). So the shipped route does not build the game or select a hardcoded Loo-Cast binary: it delegates to the service-owned persistent selection after required setup. The Entrypoint does not pre-bootstrap the service for chooser or Installer. Chooser is independent; Installer then connects-or-starts the same service from its own UI code. The other GUI modes are pre-bootstrapped by Entrypoint, and their frontends also have service connection paths. Thus the exception is who initiates startup, not whether Installer uses the shared service. This is a useful concrete alignment of direct player flow, setup gating and the shared-service model.

However, **“default” has not disappeared; it survives in several non-identical roles**, which the current docs blur:

1. `App.vapor.toml` declares `default-launch = "default"` on the root Packagepack seed ([manifest](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/App.vapor.toml#L24)). The service resolves that alias when it imports/seeds an empty legacy selection ([bootstrap call](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L573), [legacy-only migration](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L2128)). This is an initial bootstrap value, not a second live player selector.
2. Fresh state itself constructs a Composition with ID/name `default`/`Default`, then marks that ID as active ([fresh state](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/state.rs#L29), [Composition default factory](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/composition.rs#L329)). Startup bootstrap later fills a missing Packagepack root from the app seed and renames the display label while retaining the `default` ID ([bootstrap migration](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L2128)). So this is not merely legacy-data residue: the special identity is still minted for every fresh state document before the seed is applied.
3. CLI `launch default` is retained as a compatibility spelling, but the command implementation maps both `Default` and `Selected` to the same persistent selection ([dispatch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/client_commands.rs#L97)).

The Launcher book does not yet explain those distinctions accurately: `lock-and-launch.md` says `launch default` runs the app's default Composition and `launch selected` uses the Studio-selected Composition ([book text](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/launcher/src/workflows/lock-and-launch.md#L29)); Quick Start likewise instructs `launch default` ([quick start](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/books/launcher/src/quick-start.md#L15)). Current CLI code contradicts that documented semantic fork. The owner direction is to make persistent selection the one real player concept; current source still creates a named `default` Composition as its initial active selection, while the App manifest's seed alias and CLI compatibility spelling are separate mechanisms. The exact future deletion/rename policy for the initial object and app-root seed is not inferable from this code review, but the docs should not present them as separately selectable compositions.

The Entrypoint README itself also says no-argument Play starts the “default playable composition” ([README](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/README.md#L1)), whereas current code explicitly routes to `launch selected`; the root App manifest field and first-run seed explain why “default” remains in source, but not why this public-facing description still calls the active selection a default. The source README, Launcher book and CLI help therefore preserve three readings of the same word even though the code's launch dispatch has converged on selected state.

This is also a same-repository documentation divergence, not just old Launcher-book prose. The Oct 22 [Launcher content-coherence plan](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-22-launcher-content-coherence.md#L18) explicitly says Steam should use `launch selected` and `launch default` may remain only as a compatibility route that no longer bypasses selection. The top-level overview in current [`Vapor-CLI/docs/commands.md`](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/docs/commands.md#L51) records that distinction correctly, but its detailed `launch default` section later claims that command resolves the app-manifest default Packagepack seed ([contradictory detail](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/docs/commands.md#L80)). Thus even the updated command guide is internally inconsistent. `Vapor-CLI/docs/discovery.md`, `steam-development.md`, and the Entrypoint README still say “default playable composition”; the Launcher quick-start and lock/launch pages also retain the former two-composition story. The mismatch was therefore already resolved in an accepted plan and partly corrected in one guide, but not propagated consistently through the docs surface. No source behavior needs to be inferred from those stale pages.

The deeper identity issue appears across the books, not just in launch instructions. `docs/books/vapor/src/README.md`, `concepts/packagepacks.md`, `concepts/packs-and-composition.md`, `concepts/content-types.md`, `glossary.md`, `rationale.md`, `installing-and-launching.md`, and the service overview describe Packagepack as a metadata/root artifact and Composition as the user's separate durable selection. SDK pages `workflows/packs-and-packagepacks.md`, `reference-layout.md`, `workflows/content-authoring.md`, and `workspaces.md` likewise teach a metadata-only Packagepack and/or a separate Composition projection. Launcher pages for Packagepacks, content sources, removal and troubleshooting also present Composition as the distinct player-owned identity. Some pages correctly describe *local installation facts*—exact resolved versions, launch arguments, receipts and repair status—that still need durable storage; the error is treating that operational state as a second content/selection identity without the owner's authorization. Owner clarification instead says the playable identity is the Packagepack, “composition” is informal language, packs remain manifests, and separately distributed source plus compiled executable are projections/releases around that same identity. The Oct 24 content-graph proposal reflects that correction more closely than the published books, but is still a proposal. No source migration or accepted schema change follows from this documentation review.

There is also a Windows observability edge: this is a GUI-subsystem executable, and its main error path writes to `stderr`; the durable entrypoint log is only opened *after* executable/app-root discovery, and log-open/write failures are silently discarded ([startup order](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/main.rs#L24), [logger](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/entrypoint/log.rs#L1), [root discovery](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Steam-Entrypoint/crates/vapor_entrypoint/src/entrypoint/app_root.rs#L1)). Once the root is found, the entrypoint records decisions and child exit status; before that boundary, a Windows failure may have no visible console or log. This is a source-level diagnostic gap, not proof of a reported Windows failure. Routing tests exist in the entrypoint source, but were not run in this documentation pass.

## October 25 — the in-game Rhai workbench executes a narrow committed hook

Roadmap 07 says “No Rhai parser, executor, or capability implementation exists” ([roadmap page](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/roadmap/07-packs-capability-rhai-runtime/03-capability-rhai-runtime/README.md#L5)). The first two claims are too broad. Current Loo-Cast workbench code compiles Rhai documents. Its `FreecamSpeed` target requires `transform(f64) -> f64`, runs it for preview, rejects non-finite output, and supports candidate/committed AST state. Commit promotes only the AST compiled from the exact current editor buffer. A separate live-enabled flag gates runtime calls; when off or no script exists, the original scalar passes through. This is a functioning but narrow execution contract, not merely syntax coloring. Source: [document lifecycle](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/document.rs#L145), [target validation and call](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/document.rs#L210), [live runtime path](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/workspace.rs#L94).

The host sets operation, call-depth, expression-depth, variable, function, module, string, array and map limits, and rate-limits logging. But it uses `Engine::new()`, which includes Rhai's StandardPackage, then registers additional project math and log functions ([host](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/host.rs#L9)). That supports “bounded” and “small host API”; it does not establish the proposed zero-native surface or a security sandbox. The scratch target compiles without execution. The GUI IDE's Rhai parse diagnostics are another path and do not share this workbench's execution context.

The host contract runs at freecam movement as a scalar speed transform, after which Rust clamps the value to `[0, 1e9]` m/s and applies boost and delta time ([consumer](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/camera/freecam/movement.rs#L90)). `live_enabled` starts false for every loaded document; only the UI checkbox toggles it, and the exposed script console commands do not include a corresponding toggle. So the feature has real runtime effect but is opt-in and process-local; save/commit do not persist enablement. Startup materializes embedded defaults, seeds missing live files, then scans at most 256 `.rhai` files. It keeps existing live copies when shipped defaults change. The roots require both environment overrides or fall back to process-CWD repo discovery and then executable-relative deployed paths. Lexical traversal is rejected, but file operations do not canonicalize symlink targets; individual scan/read failures are silently skipped and script source size has no pre-compile cap. These are exact source properties; no hostile-file scenario or performance failure was reproduced.

There is a smaller lifecycle-label mismatch inside the workbench. `ScriptTarget::None` is explicitly “compile-only,” and it has no Live toggle or preview, but the common editor still offers **Commit** and **Revert Runtime** for that document. Commit promotes its AST to the document's `committed_ast` and increments a local revision; no host calls that AST, so this is a per-document compile snapshot rather than a live runtime revision ([target contract and document revision](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/document.rs#L25-L57>), [unconditional editor actions](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/ui/editor.rs#L116-L140>)). This does not create a safety defect, but it blurs “compiled snapshot” and “runtime behavior” exactly at the UI boundary. The freecam target has a real runtime toggle; scratch does not. No UI was run to inspect surrounding explanation or reproduce user confusion.

The source-to-runtime packaging boundary is explicit but broader than the live contract. `spacetime-engine/build.rs` embeds every `.rhai` file under repository `scripts/` as source text in a generated Rust table, sorting by logical path and allowing up to 1,024 files; this is not Rhai-to-Rust generation or a compiled Rhai AST ([build script](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/build.rs#L15)). Runtime materializes the full table as current-build defaults, then seeds only absent files in a separate live tree; existing live scripts persist until explicit reset ([storage lifecycle](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/storage.rs#L118)). The repository currently has two `.rhai` files: `debug/freecam_speed.rhai` and `scratch/experiment.rhai`. The source README says only the former has a live host policy and the scratch script is compile-only ([script contract](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/scripts/README.md#L37)). `loo-cast-game` depends on `spacetime-engine`, so this path embeds scripts through the Engine crate boundary ([Game manifest](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-game/Cargo.toml#L11)). There is a source-level budget mismatch: build collection caps at 1,024 while runtime discovery caps at 256; the present two-file tree is below both limits. Runtime collection does not sort directory entries, so which files are discovered at the 256-file ceiling may depend on filesystem enumeration order. This consequence is inferred from the implementation and was not tested at the limit.

The callable capability graph discussed by the owner is a different feature family: typed phases/schedules, caller/cardinality/signatures, scoped composed handles, retained data with later access reacquisition, recursive graph stages, and generated Rust/WASM load/unload boundaries do not appear in this workbench trace. The roadmap should keep its broader status deferred while recording the parser and narrow scalar executor as already implemented. “Capability implementation” should be split into host functions, spatial realization capabilities, and the proposed callable capability system; treating those three as one checkbox created this stale claim. This is source inspection only; no script was edited, executed or tested during the current documentation pass.

The current UI and command surface expose this lifecycle through two adapters. The Scripts tab is hosted inside the in-game F2 console, with a grouped explorer, scratch-document creation, dirty/runtime markers, contract tooltips, and a two-column editor/explorer layout ([UI shell](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/ui/mod.rs>), [explorer](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/ui/explorer.rs>), [editor actions](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/ui/editor.rs>)). The five `debug script` commands (with shorter aliases) operate on the active document and report status, compile, commit, revert or save; they do not carry a role/capability field of their own ([command adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/commands.rs>)). These are useful authoring affordances, but “Commit” and “Revert Runtime” remain available for compile-only documents, where they change only that document's committed AST snapshot. That is a vocabulary/authority mismatch in the UI contract, not a demonstrated runtime bug.

Storage's two-root requirement is a meaningful separation between shipped defaults and mutable live copies, but the selection logic is intentionally convenience-oriented: an environment override is accepted only when both roots are set; otherwise the code searches from CWD for a source checkout and then tries executable-relative deployed paths ([root selection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/storage.rs>)). This makes source and deployed launches behave differently by design. Path validation rejects lexical traversal and non-`.rhai` paths, yet file reads/writes do not resolve symlink components before operating in the live root; this is a source-derived escape risk if an untrusted actor can plant a symlink there, not an exercised exploit. Startup discovery silently skips invalid entries and caps the runtime set at 256, while build-time embedding allows 1,024 ([embedded source collector](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/build.rs)). The `rhai` dependency enables `sync` and the host creates one Engine resource for the workbench, rather than spinning up an Engine per invocation ([Engine manifest](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/Cargo.toml>), [workspace lifecycle](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/script_workbench/workspace.rs>)). No performance conclusion follows from that architecture without runtime measurement.

## October 25 — root package contents depend on a separate deploy step

Roadmap 03.01 says `sdk root package` includes `sdk_cli`, `launcher_cli`, and their binaries; Roadmap 05.03 says `sdk deploy` writes `sdk_cli` or `launcher_cli` aliases ([03.01](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/roadmap/03-steam-root-self-bootstrap/01-root-package/README.md#L1>), [05.03](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/roadmap/05-workspace-execution-hermeticity/03-deploy/README.md#L1>)). Current `workspace_deploy` accepts only the `vapor-cli` workspace, builds `vapor_cli`, copies that executable into the managed app root, and creates the `vapor` alias ([deploy path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/deploy.rs#L18>)). Separately, `root_package` copies the entire existing `bin/` directory plus one activation script; it neither builds nor verifies named product executables ([package roots](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/root/package.rs#L140>)). Therefore the roadmap's binary list is a package-content expectation, not a guarantee made by either operation in isolation. The exact contents of a particular published depot depend on prior deployment state and were not inspected or rebuilt here.

Roadmap 05.02's custom-content sync is narrower than its “Exists Now” list: `workspace_sync` reads declared project paths from `Workspace.vapor.toml`, requires exactly one already-present role-specific manifest per project, generates managed Cargo workspace/crate manifests, and seeds `src/lib.rs` only if missing ([sync entry](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/manage.rs#L54>)). It does not generate per-content `Vapor.toml` files, despite the roadmap saying it does. This is a useful constrained scaffold, not a general discovery mechanism or proof that every authored content kind has an appropriate Rust representation. The scaffold and deploy findings are source-level; neither the package command nor workspace sync was run.

## October 25 — SDK workspace identity can collide in the shared Cargo output root

The complete `vapor_sdk_core::workspace` subtree (seven files, 1,120 lines) was read as one workflow. Discovery accepts any string-valued `organization` and `name`, concatenates them with `/`, and finds the first `Workspace.vapor.toml` at or above the start path ([identity](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/identity.rs#L20>)). It does not canonicalize the workspace path or validate the identity components in this code. Cargo target storage is then `VAPOR_HOME/output/dev/<slug>`, where `slug` lowercases ASCII alphanumerics and maps every other character to `-` ([target selection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/cargo.rs#L22>), [slug](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/cargo.rs#L78>)). For example, IDs `a/b-c` and `a-b/c` collapse to the same slug `a-b-c`; no collision detection or stable disambiguator is present. This proves two workspace identities can share one output directory. Cargo's resulting artifact/cache behavior was not tested, so incorrect build reuse is a risk hypothesis, not a demonstrated corruption.

The Cargo wrapper selects Vapor's installed toolchain and dedicated CARGO_HOME/target directory, but builds PATH by prepending managed Cargo/Rustup paths and then retaining the ambient PATH; Unix system directories are appended too. This is a pinned compiler environment with host-tool access, not a hermetic build boundary. The only inline test in this subtree asserts that common Unix host-tool directories are present; discovery, path normalization, slug collisions, sync ownership, deploy replacement, and Windows behavior have no tests here. The command docs also drift internally: the enum calls Deploy promotion of the first-party “SDK CLI,” the public function calls it the unified `vapor` facade, and the implementation builds only `vapor_cli` and creates alias `vapor`. These are naming/coverage mismatches, not evidence that a second CLI binary is deployed. No workspace command or build was executed during this review.

Workspace sync has a separate filesystem-boundary gap: the manifest's `path` becomes `ContentEntry.path` and is joined directly to `workspace_root` during both reading and generation ([input and read](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/manage.rs#L136>), [generation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/manage.rs#L70>)). There is no requirement that it be relative, no rejection of parent components, and no canonical check that a symlink still resolves under the workspace. Thus an absolute or `..` path can point sync outside its declared root; it can create the `src` directory and write a managed `Cargo.toml`/seed `lib.rs` there if those paths do not already hold user-owned files. This follows directly from the input and write path but was not exercised. In contrast, the shared Client workspace provider rejects absolute/parent components in its source-project paths, and `manifest::read` canonicalizes role manifests and rejects a resolved path outside the source root ([Client relative guard](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/workspace.rs#L636), [canonical manifest check](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/manifest.rs#L106)). The two operations therefore implement different safety contracts for a Workspace-shaped manifest; SDK sync bypasses the stricter provider path. The July generator's managed-file protections are relevant precedent, not an equivalent confinement guard.

### How this workspace contract arrived

| Date / change | Semantic shift |
|---|---|
| July 2, [`f76060c6`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-SDK/commit/f76060c6ca7991bb179b4698f61f3d4888bf8486) | The earlier SDK generator creates one Cargo crate per declared content entry and generates role-specific `Vapor.toml`, Cargo manifests and `lib.rs` identity stubs. [`a0c92232`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-SDK/commit/a0c922329e8def7d6354b2651a157d7fe05782ed) then marks managed files, preserves seeded source after creation and rejects duplicate normalized Cargo package names. That protection is specific to crate names within one generated workspace. |
| October 14, [`0e5789bf`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/0e5789bfe8d7590d401f33f7617ae75a6a2f023c) | The present seven-file workspace subsystem enters shared Vapor in one 1,092-line addition. It already uses the lossy workspace-ID slug for the shared output directory; the collision risk is present from its introduction, not a later regression. The current identity is assembled from organization/name, and the current authoring model expects kind-specific manifests in declared project folders. |
| October 18, [`f9e8b135`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f9e8b135f3991f4eac43de6da964d0874504cde4) | The manifest enumeration delegates to the shared `ContentType::ALL` vocabulary rather than keeping a local nine-kind list; `Library`/`Crate` and manifest spelling now belong to the content package. The same extraction changes deploy's built package from `vapor_shell` to `vapor_cli`, retaining the single `vapor` alias. This update does not implement the old roadmap's claimed per-content manifest generation. |
| October 20–22, [`ef611da`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/ef611daafe8647a731a64cd7db10d3c1e2552557), [`92ab2b9`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/92ab2b9b075a3d52976b9ce5e2ec99ea4d0278a2), [`2897a81`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/2897a810a5d002bd81f411ab772603a76d53cd48) | Cargo environment setup is centralized, execution moves to the background-process helper, then standard Unix system directories are appended after a reported host-utility failure. The direction is a single pinned-toolchain setup with explicit host-tool fallback, not hermetic execution. The only test added in this sequence checks presence of `/usr/bin` and `/bin` when available; it does not test command resolution or builds. |

This history preserves two different collision questions: the July guard checks normalized *Cargo package names* within one generated workspace; October's sanitizer derives a *cross-workspace build-output directory* and adds no identity-collision check. The old guard therefore does not close the new namespace collision. This is a source/diff comparison; no old or current build was executed.

## October 25 — Roadmap 11 spans multiple, still-disconnected source workflows
Roadmap 11's onboarding transcript also names `vapor-installer role promote ecosystem-developer`. The Installer command parser has no `role` group, and the main Vapor CLI model has no role command; role transition is currently a `DeveloperAction` carried by the shared Client protocol and executed by its service ([Developer action model](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/actions.rs#L369), [service transition handler](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L1314)). The role workflow is available through Client frontends, but Roadmap 11's literal shell command is not implemented by either CLI. This is another product-surface mismatch, not absence of role promotion.


Roadmap 11 is not linked from the roadmap root, whose chapter list stops at 10 and whose “Current Active Work” still names glossary migration as the active branch ([roadmap root](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/roadmap/README.md#L1)). Yet its own execution ledger marks bootstrap, canonical marker creation, granular acquisition/removal, first-party registry roots, and RustRover reconciliation complete ([Roadmap 11](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/roadmap/11-local-install-source-lifecycle/README.md#L78)). These are conflicting planning-status signals in the same docs tree; neither alone proves a released workflow.

More materially, Roadmap 11's shell command transcript is not the implemented CLI surface. It proposes `vapor source setup`, `vapor source acquire loo-cast|vapor-client|vapor-platform-server|vapor-all|first-party-all`, and destructive `source remove`/`teardown` commands. The current Vapor CLI `SourceCommand` instead exposes `init`, `status`, `open`, `close`, `list`, `add`, `remove` (forget an index entry), `sync` (prints “not yet applied”), and metadata repair ([CLI enum](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/model.rs#L371), [dispatch and behavior](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/source_commands.rs#L8)). The precompiled Installer exposes `install`/`uninstall`, `superworkspace create`, and `source status|clone SOURCE_NAME` ([Installer CLI](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer/src/cli.rs#L61)). But that is not the whole current capability: the Client service has Registry-backed `DiscoverSuperworkspaceRepositories` and `AcquireSuperworkspaceRepositories` actions, and Studio shows available roots with a per-row `Download` action ([service action/operation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L12), [Studio panel](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workspace_registry_panel.rs#L36)). The service accepts one to 64 repository names, while the current Studio panel sends one name at a time; no group-selection UI is shown. A lower-level Core helper treats an empty selector as “all,” but the service rejects an empty vector before reaching that helper, so “acquire all” is not exposed through this route. So the Registry acquisition capability exists in Studio, but not as Roadmap 11's `vapor source acquire` commands, and the richer source removal/teardown workflow remains absent. The shared Rust core has guarded `UninstallOptions` for app-data and Superworkspace purges, but no current CLI/Installer parser path passes those options; that is an internal primitive, not an available danger-zone flow.

The duplicated surfaces have different semantics. CLI `source remove` calls `ForgetSource`, removing an index entry without deleting files. Installer `source clone` uses its compiled `SOURCE_PRESETS` table and fixed GitHub remotes; the displayed help requires `--super-workspace`, while its helper may infer a root through `VAPOR_SUPER_WORKSPACE_ROOT` or upward CWD search ([preset table](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools.rs#L103), [root resolution](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/discovery_paths.rs#L13)). It does not use the Client's persisted canonical-source selection or query Registry. Separately, Studio's registry flow reads repository definitions from the configured ecosystem endpoint, preflights checkout paths and existing remotes, then clones repositories and initializes their submodules ([Registry acquisition](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ecosystem.rs#L87), [path and remote validation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ecosystem.rs#L275)). That service path ensures the canonical Superworkspace during Client session initialization and has an explicit UI action to initialize it ([session initialization](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L613), [initialize action](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L885)). By contrast, Installer `install` delegates to Player setup; it does not call `vapor_core::install_installation` or acquire sources ([Installer dispatch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer/src/cli.rs#L26), [core install routine](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/install.rs#L28)). Roadmap 11 places automatic Superworkspace setup on Installer install, but current automatic setup occurs through Client session initialization. Its assertion that acquisition immediately repairs RustRover also does not match either clone implementation: the separate RustRover workflow must be invoked to patch the IDE. These are distinct operating paths, not one shared lifecycle; no acquisition or IDE action was run.

This is not merely stale syntax. The intended lifecycle spans Steam app bootstrap, persistent user data, one authored-source root, Registry selectors, Git acquisition, role/toolchain readiness, IDE projection, and guarded destructive removal. Studio already provides the central Registry-backed discover-and-download path; Installer still has a parallel preset-based clone path; the CLI `source` family manages active/indexed authoring roots; core contains purge APIs without a user-facing flag path. The roadmap root's omission and stale active branch make the mismatch harder to discover. This is static-source verification only; no acquisition, uninstall, purge, role promotion, or fresh-machine workflow was run.

Both current acquisition paths still depend on host Git, despite the app-local Developer installer managing Rust and cross-target tools: preset Installer clone uses `Command::new("git")`, while Registry-backed Studio acquisition gates on `git_available()` and launches Git through the managed-process helper ([Installer Git invocation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/source_workspace.rs#L16), [Registry Git prerequisite](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ecosystem.rs#L87), [host-PATH check](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/role.rs#L224)). Studio currently displays one Download button per unacquired Registry entry. The service accepts multi-name requests but rejects empty sets, so acquire-all is not exposed through this service. This is a machine setup prerequisite and a UI-capability gap, not absence of Registry acquisition. Neither clone path invokes RustRover reconciliation after acquisition; the separate IDE workflow must be used. No Git-missing or IDE state was reproduced.

## October 25 — Roadmap 08's child statuses mix stale absence with still-missing authority

Roadmap 08 says “No Workshop implementation exists,” and child 08.01 repeats that Workshop commands are not implemented. Both are now false as blanket current-state statements: Vapor has a Steamworks UGC provider for search/subscription-state changes, the shared Client service runs those operations in the background, and the provider contains SteamCMD Workshop package/create/update/delete-preview and download/acquisition paths ([current acquisition and scheduling review](#october-25--workshop-acquisition-is-serial-silent-and-reserves-the-whole-workshop-account), [provider module](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/workshop.rs#L1)). That does not mean canonical Workshop semantics are complete: the existing service/UI surfaces still have type-filtering, subscription/cache/install ownership and async scheduling gaps recorded elsewhere in this review, and the accepted Registry/Identity authority model is not yet implemented by those services.

Child 08.02 is more accurate but also needs precision: Registry does exist and does not gate Workshop publishing, but its current machine-readable authority is only provider/repository/ecosystem topology, not content types, Workshop bindings, releases, or permissions ([current Registry schema/API review](#october-25-registrys-database-is-a-seeded-snapshot-not-an-administrable-catalog)).
