Child 08.03's “No install ledger exists” is too broad if it means local acquired/installed state: the provider persists `ContentIndex` records for installed and cached artifacts, including version, Workshop ID, fingerprint, source and dependency/conflict snapshots; separate operation receipts record action/status/time ([content index](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/storage.rs#L20), [operation receipt](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/storage.rs#L91)). Those structures are not a signed provenance ledger or Registry-authoritative release record; no signing implementation appears in the inspected provider path. This is a naming/status correction, not evidence that trust claims or installation reconciliation are solved. No Workshop operation or Registry request was run.

The Registry-backed source workflow has its own incomplete batch semantics. The service validates that the request names 1–64 repositories, so it rejects an empty list even though the lower-level Core selector interprets empty as “all”; the service's public path therefore has no acquire-all request. Studio only dispatches a one-name vector per row. Core preflights all requested entries before the clone loop, which prevents an invalid later entry from being discovered only after earlier clones start, but then clones and initializes submodules sequentially with `?` and performs no rollback if a later clone/submodule fails. That can leave a partial but real source set after the operation reports failure. The selector resolves names with first exact match; current seeded repository names are unique, but if the catalog later allows same-name repositories from different owners, name-based UI/action identity becomes ambiguous. These are source-derived operational boundaries, not reproduced failures; see [service validation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L73), [preflight/clone sequence](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ecosystem.rs#L117), and [name selection](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ecosystem.rs#L308).

## October 25 — Roadmap 06's “no fingerprints or receipts” claim is stale; its general lockfile target is still absent

The July Roadmap 06 is not simply implemented or unimplemented: its named generated-state objects separated into several narrower mechanisms with different owners and persistence guarantees.

| Current artifact | What the code actually stores | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| Content-tree fingerprint | `fingerprint_tree` sorts regular relative file paths and hashes each path, a NUL separator, and file bytes using `vapor-fnv1a-64-v1` (64-bit FNV-1a) ([tree encoder](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content.rs#L2362)). Package staging, cache acquisition and installed trees carry this value; file count/byte count are metadata. | This is not cryptographic integrity or publisher authenticity. More specifically, the hash-input encoding has no file-byte length or terminator: tree `{a: "xb\0y"}` and tree `{a: "x", b: "y"}` feed the identical byte sequence `a\0xb\0y`. Install compares the full `Fingerprint` (including counts) and rejects that pair ([comparison](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content.rs#L2108)), but Workshop review stores and compares only `algorithm:hash` ([create review](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/workshop.rs#L149), [update review](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/workshop.rs#L564)), so its change-after-review guard does not distinguish them. This is structural ambiguity, separate from an FNV collision. The traversal also omits directory-only structure, filesystem metadata, symlinks and other non-file/non-directory entries. Relative paths use lossy, host-native strings and host-native sorting; Windows/Linux fingerprint equality is unproven. |
| Installed index record | App-owned `state/content/index.toml` maps each installed/cache ID to kind, optional version, Workshop ID, enabled state, path, fingerprint, dependencies/conflicts, install time and source. This is actively loaded and saved by content workflows ([index records](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/storage.rs#L20)). | Local realization metadata is not a Registry-signed release or a portable exact source/build provenance record. |
| Per-content `locks/<slug>.toml` | `write_lock` serializes the same `InstalledRecord` during install/enable/disable ([writer](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/storage.rs#L199)). | Search of current provider call sites finds a writer but no reader; the live index is separately loaded. The `locks/` directory therefore exists as a duplicate projection, not an independently enforced package lock authority. |
| Operation receipts | `state/content/receipts/` records schema, action, artifact ID, status, timestamp and optional detail ([receipt shape/writer](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/storage.rs#L91)). Packaging, install, cache and Workshop paths emit receipts. | A receipt can be written after external/filesystem changes and is not a transaction log guaranteed to replay/roll back every partial operation; the existing cache mutation review documents post-activation errors. No one receipt format captures complete build inputs, output identity, registry release and provider publication as one lifecycle. |
| Composition's resolved graph | The durable Client `Composition` serializes root, effective Engine/Game and exact node references/versions, kinds, per-node fingerprints/sources where known, and binding/dependency edges ([graph model](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/composition.rs#L8)). Successful install/verify/launch updates it. On Client-state save, runtime `InstallationState` is explicitly cleared, while the composition's `resolved_graph` remains serialized ([state persistence](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/persistence.rs#L78)). | This acts as a durable selected-closure snapshot, but is not a standalone `Vapor.lock`, does not retain optional candidates omitted by resolution, and is not a user-reviewed selection/lockfile workflow. |
| Resolved-graph fingerprint | `fingerprint_resolved_graph` canonicalizes exact identities, kinds, sources, payload fingerprints and dependency edges, then emits `vapor-graph-fnv1a-64-v2:<hash>` ([implementation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/composition.rs#L352)). | It returns `None` when node source/fingerprint facts are incomplete; like the tree value it is a 64-bit FNV consistency hash, not a cryptographic release identity. `resolved_graph_matches` tolerates missing legacy source/fingerprint facts in the expected snapshot, so partial historic state can be upgraded rather than immediately rejected ([comparison](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/composition.rs#L431)). |

Roadmap 06's categorical “no fingerprint implementation” and “package/publish reports only in memory” statements are false at this source snapshot. “No `Vapor.lock` implementation” remains literally true. The June 30 commit whose subject says “Add Vapor lockfile” (`Vapor/d0fd8773`) adds an 11-line root `Cargo.lock` for `vapor_core` and `vapor_macros`; it does not add a Vapor-domain lockfile ([diff](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/d0fd87730fcfb0f862ceb03c42c422d890b6157b)). The main CLI also has no such command/file contract: SDK request models include `Packagepack lock`, but SDK output remains `not_implemented`; current lock-like behavior is spread among persistent composition graph, content index, write-only per-content lock copies and operation receipts. This is not one cohesive lock lifecycle. The July monolithic `content.rs` already had tree fingerprint/index/lock/receipt behavior; October 18–19 extraction distributed it across provider storage plus durable Client composition graph. The roadmap's target “generated state records what was resolved, installed, built, packaged, published or selected” remains only partially represented, with no standalone lockfile or unified release/provenance record. No build, package, install or receipt replay was run in this review.

This fingerprint boundary matters to the wider reproducibility and trust goals: the current hash answers a narrower question—whether this traversal emits the same unframed path/byte stream under its own platform representation. It does not prove publisher authorization, Windows/Linux canonical identity, or equivalence of ignored filesystem objects. Because the Workshop review path compares only that hash string, the framing ambiguity can make a changed file layout appear unchanged even without finding an FNV collision. Those stronger properties need explicit format and trust rules before this value can serve as a release identity. This is code-derived; no publish, cross-platform comparison or adversarial test was run.

The same Roadmap 11 sentence says Composer-or-higher **role promotion** requires Git on PATH. Current role promotion instead reconciles managed Rust, Rust Analyzer, Windows GNU target/linker and Tracy through `DeveloperEnvironment`; it does not call `git_available()` ([promotion path](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/role.rs#L143), [role toolset](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L23)). The Git check is in `acquire_ecosystem_repositories`, after role setup ([Git gate](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ecosystem.rs#L87)). So the clean-machine limitation is incorrectly attached to role promotion: a user may become Composer/Ecosystem Developer and have the Rust toolchain provisioned, but source acquisition still fails until host Git is installed or otherwise made available. This is a documentation ownership error with concrete onboarding consequences; no clean machine was used to reproduce it.

## October 25 — small engine foundations: real reuse, partial generalization

This pass checks less-visible roots against the engine's own module map and the owner’s recurring demand for shared facilities instead of product-specific duplicates. These modules are small in line count but decide whether larger systems can be composed consistently.

### The crate root names a boundary that the plugin graph only partly realizes

`spacetime-engine/src/lib.rs` describes a reusable `SpacetimeEnginePlugin`, a standard host constructor, and `run(install_game)` as the seam where a selected game extends the engine app. It exports the concrete `bevy::App` as `EngineApp`; `engine_app()` installs Bevy defaults plus the engine plugin; `run()` then calls the supplied closure before entering Bevy's loop. That is a clear static-composition seam, but it is not itself a Vapor content boundary or a runtime-neutral game ABI.

The implementation's ownership map is less clean than the API description. `SpacetimeEnginePlugin` installs config, authored geometry, physics, reconstructible work, voxels, UI foundation, diagnostics, devtools and console. `LooCastGamePlugin::install_game_facilities`, however, installs further modules physically under the Engine crate—USF spatial, portal, thermal, procedural assets, flight, navigation, locomotion, orbit, player, spacecraft and scenario/world setup—alongside game-domain plugins such as inventory, item, health and combat. The distinct `loo-cast-game` crate remains a small adapter. Thus “EngineApp lets a game extend the engine” is a useful seam, while the present source tree still makes Engine the Cargo owner and much of the `game` subtree the effective gameplay implementation. This directly supports the owner’s concern that names and module paths are not yet aligned with Engine/Game/Mod/Crate semantics; it does not imply those facilities should be split mechanically by folder name.

### Input focus is one of the clearest successful shared mechanisms—and still a small one

`input_focus::InputFocus` stores separate pointer and gameplay claims under static string owner IDs and exposes a monotonic gameplay-resume epoch. The same resource is used by the console overlay, world-selection screen, developer palette and gizmo interaction, playground menu, player cursor and input dispatch. This is genuine cross-cutting reuse: overlays declare their claim, and player adapters consume the resulting state rather than each tool inventing its own cursor/input suppression path. The history links it to September 13 `8ef733b` and the October 6 root cleanup `0e48843`.

The realized use is narrower than the API's two claim channels: current callers use `set_modal_claim`; no current caller sets pointer-only or gameplay-only claims. The owner token is an untyped `&'static str`, and claims require explicit release when a surface closes/exits. Source therefore shows a useful shared arbitration point, not a scoped lease system or proof that every focus lifecycle is cleanup-safe. The older owner concern about capability handles and temporal scope is an analogy, not evidence that this Bevy input resource was intended to solve script-capability lifetime.

### Theme and viewport contracts solve distinct slices, not a shared UI toolkit

The October 6 `0e48843` cleanup adds the small `ui` foundation: `UiTheme` centralizes font sources, text roles, colors, spacing and panel padding, and `UiFoundationPlugin` initializes the resource. This gives in-game debug/editor UI one place to change those policy values. Its own source explicitly retains Bevy's default font because no Unicode-capable project font is shipped, which is consistent with—but does not prove the cause of—the reported missing-glyph squares. The theme does not provide reusable button, panel, navigation, docking, virtual-list or console widgets; screens such as world selection still define their own control colors and layout. It is a theme policy, not the custom egui/Bevy UI component library the owner later asked Vapor to build.

The `view` module is a more concrete integration contract. `PrimaryGameView`, `PrimaryViewPresentation::{Immersive, Embedded}`, `ViewportSpace`, and `ViewRay` keep viewport/world coordinate conversion in one place. The in-game editor shell computes its Game-tab rectangle from egui, converts logical pixels using the primary window scale factor, clips to target bounds, and assigns that physical viewport to the single `PrimaryGameView` camera; if the tab has no usable viewport it deactivates that camera. Cursor picking and developer gizmos consume the same viewport contract. This is a real embedded-game view inside the in-game editor, not evidence that the separate Vapor IDE embeds a Loo-Cast view.

### Reconstructible work is a soft admission heuristic, with one unclosed measurement path

`ReconstructibleFrameBudget`, introduced in Loo-Cast `cb094c1` on October 2, is used by voxel demand planning, generation publication, derived-surface publication/scheduling, manifestation-membership reconciliation and mesh rebuilding. The October 6 `0e48843` cleanup adds a closure-based `try_run` convenience and formats the module; its admission/EWMA policy remains the same. It estimates work-unit duration by class, adjusts next-frame allowance using observed frame overshoot/slack, and returns `None` when a later unit is unlikely to fit. The debt sample is wall-clock start-to-start time between `First` stages, not isolated simulation CPU time; it includes rendering cadence, waits and other work outside the budget. Admission checks elapsed wall time since the current `First`, against a fixed discretionary allowance after a configurable reservation; it cannot preempt a started unit, and it deliberately admits the first unit of each class even if the frame allowance has already elapsed. It is therefore a cooperative pacing heuristic, not a hard frame-time cap or measured guarantee that the rest of a frame stays within target.

The shared class model is coarser than the apparent coordination claim: one `Publication` EWMA mixes output draining, surface-result publication, dirty-membership reconciliation, and actual mesh construction. A cheap queue transition can therefore lower the same estimate used to admit a costly mesh build, while a costly path can throttle other publication work. Each caller defines its own token interval, so the samples do not represent one consistently delimited kind of work. In addition, every class receives one unconditional first start per frame, so prior-frame debt never prevents all reconstructible work from starting. These are source-level scope/policy observations, not performance measurements.

At the current head, `voxel/manifestation/rebuild/mod.rs::rebuild_dirty_presentation_manifestations` calls `begin(Publication)` in its configured loop but discards the returned token rather than passing it to `finish`. Its mesh-build path therefore contributes no sample to the publication EWMA; it runs against the initial estimate unless another publication consumer updates that shared class. The token is acquired before scanning the dirty set, and several cleanup/requeue branches also do not close a token. The configured `rebuild_budget_per_frame` still bounds the number of loop iterations, so this is not proof of unbounded work or an observed hitch. The source module has no focused tests for the admission/debt/EWMA behavior, and this review did not run tests or measure frame times. These are concrete integration and observability limits discovered by following callers, not by treating the abstraction's name as a guarantee. Source anchors: [budget implementation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/reconstructible.rs#L1>), [mesh rebuild admission](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/manifestation/rebuild/mod.rs#L90>), [planning sample](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/streaming/demand/systems.rs#L35>), [publication sample](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/async_pipeline/mod.rs#L45>).

### Cross-reference and historical weight

The three foundations have different maturity: input arbitration is used across several gameplay/tool surfaces; viewport conversion is actively used by the in-game editor; theme centralizes a few visual tokens but not components; and frame pacing is wired through important voxel paths but has a missed measurement closeout. Treating them all as either “shared machinery complete” or “mere scaffolding” would erase these differences. The timeline places the facilities' introductions at September 13–14 and the large October 2/6 integration/refinement, while current `lib.rs`/`game/mod.rs` source shows the remaining ownership split. The broader latest-state audit should use these narrow cross-cutting facilities as test cases for the Vapor-wide principle: one semantic owner and one reusable contract should be demonstrated by callers, not inferred from an umbrella name or module map.

## October 25 — portal subsystem: gameplay feature, collision protocol, and scale adapter

The current `portal` module is a useful stress test for the engine's semantic boundaries because one feature spans gameplay commands, collision topology, Avian solver integration, USF partitions and recursive rendering. Its module hierarchy is unusually legible (`domain`, pure `topology`, `simulation`, `rendering`, `devtools`), but the feature's original conceptual breadth is larger than the concrete implementation.

### Current contract and authority flow

The root exposes `PortalCommand::{Place, Remove, RemovePair}` as the intended mutation surface. `apply_portal_commands` resolves a placement against a `CollisionClipSource`, stores that support binding, and updates a generic `CollisionStencil`; stencil subtraction becomes enabled only while both endpoints are active and their support colliders still exist. This is a substantive separation: portal code chooses and publishes the aperture stencil, while physics owns host-collider reconstruction. Invalid placement is silently ignored by the command handler (`None`/failed query returns `continue`); the command has no result/diagnostic channel here, so rejected authoring intent is not observable through this API alone.

The normal traveler path detects a segment crossing in portal-local coordinates, maps position/orientation and optional velocity through the rigid portal transform, then commits the arrival position so it cannot immediately retrigger at the destination. This path excludes `PortalSplitTraveler` and runs in Bevy `Update`, sampling the transform's previous and current positions once per invocation ([system registration](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/portal/mod.rs#L107>), [crossing sample and commit](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/portal/simulation/traversal/mod.rs#L24-L123>)). That creates a conditional temporal-resolution risk: if a traveler crosses and returns between sampled updates, or motion is advanced in a separate fixed-step path without these samples, this conventional route may not observe the crossing. This is a schedule-derived possibility, not a reproduced traversal failure. The split path instead represents a traveler on both sides during an aperture crossing, orders preparation/materialization around character movement, and has a separate pairwise rigid-body adapter around Avian solver substeps. Its own types explicitly say that external forces, gravity, mass and inertia remain on the primary solver realization while peer contact deltas are reconciled afterward. The peer is a reserved solver slot associated with one generic USF authority partition; it is not the general 1:N semantic authority graph. This is an important adapter boundary stated in code, not an inferred generalization.

Presentation is a separate child: active portal endpoints produce directed faces; recursive views use a bounded render-target tree and dedicated render layers; collision/topology logic does not depend on the rendering subtree. `PortalConfig` defaults to a fixed two-endpoint demo pair and recursion depth 2, with maximum depth 4. Its public configuration is validated with assertions during startup setup. The portal module is installed by `LooCastGamePlugin`, not by `SpacetimeEnginePlugin` itself, further showing that a reusable-looking engine module is currently wired through the game composition.

### Cross-check against earlier concepts

The scattered Vapor glossary does not define merely “a game portal.” Its `Portal Traversal Semantics` entry is marked `WIP-draft` and describes continuity across portal links or wrapping worlds, coordinated with `Scale View`, `Observer-Relative Simulation`, `Entity Plane Split` and `Entity Proxy`. The related `Entity Plane Split` entry says backend authority and frontend presentation can be separate, including when traditional floating-point physics/rendering sits behind a scale-aware semantic boundary. Those are design pressures, not approved contracts, and the files are explicitly draft-state.

The present portal code partially realizes that direction: it separates semantic portal state from render views and treats an Avian solver peer as a disposable, bounded manifestation adapter. It does not establish a general wrapping-world topology, observer-relative portal traversal policy, or arbitrary multi-partition physical split. The gameplay pair uses Bevy `Transform`/`Vec3`, while the split adapter stores one active source/destination and one peer. The `PortalTraveler` and `PortalSplitTraveler` caches are refreshed/reset around USF chart rebases, so the implementation is not wholly disconnected from scale-local rebasing; nevertheless, the breadth of the earlier cross-scale concept exceeds the verified two-endpoint runtime contract. This is exactly where a current-state-first timeline must preserve the older conceptual lineage without declaring the WIP glossary fulfilled.

### A historical test-coverage regression is visible in the current snapshot

`e987230` (October 5, “AI Stuff (stuff)”) deletes the portal crossing tests for orientation-independent crossing, one-sided rejection and crossing fraction; the portal-mapping inverse round-trip test; and a split-visual mesh triangle-count test. The current `spacetime-engine/src/portal` tree contains no `#[test]` cases, and no replacements were found in that module. The deletion coincides with a substantial restructuring of portal splitting into character and rigid-body paths, not with a documented equivalent test migration. This does not prove the routines are wrong, but it means the current code has less direct regression coverage for core geometric invariants than a prior revision. No build or test was run for this review.

### Rigid split keeps one semantic owner through a pairwise solver adapter

The dynamic-body split has a sharper authority contract than its two physical solver entities suggest. A reserved peer maps the authority's transform, linear velocity and angular velocity through the portal; its collider is the complementary half of the projected physical box. The authority retains its full physical hull outside an active split. USF temporarily links that peer as a realization of a spawned authority partition, while `SpatialSplitPeer` lets generic ownership queries resolve it back to the authority and collision hooks suppress contact between the authority and its own proxy ([peer materialization](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/portal/simulation/rigid_split/peer/mod.rs>), [temporary partition ownership](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/portal/simulation/split/mod.rs>), [generic peer identity/filter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/physics/topology/hooks/mod.rs>), [runtime ownership mapping](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/physics/topology/query/mod.rs>)). The reserved slot persists while dormant; activation and retirement change its collision layers and USF relationship rather than create/destroy the physical peer on each crossing.

Avian solver synchronization is explicit and staged. Before constraint work, the peer's solver velocities are mapped from the authority and saved as a baseline. After constraints, damping and restitution, the code subtracts that baseline from the peer result, inverse-maps the resulting velocity delta into the authority, then immediately remaps the combined authority velocity to refresh the peer baseline. This avoids treating the solver peer as a second independently moving semantic body. Post-physics reconciliation maps the authority transform and both velocities through a completed center crossing, swaps the active source/destination pair, and restores the full collider/deactivates the peer once the box clears or the pair becomes invalid ([solver coupling](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/portal/simulation/rigid_split/solver/mod.rs>), [substep schedule](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/portal/mod.rs>), [crossing and completion](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/portal/simulation/rigid_split/reconciliation/mod.rs>), [completion policy](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/portal/simulation/rigid_split/reconciliation/completion/mod.rs>), [crossing transform](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/portal/simulation/rigid_split/reconciliation/crossing/mod.rs>)). The playground dynamic-cube spawn stores `RigidBody`, `Mass` and `AngularInertia` on both authority and peer; code comments describe authority ownership of mass/inertia/forces as the semantic policy, while the duplicated components are solver representation ([paired entities](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/items/damageable_cube/mod.rs>)). This distinction should not be simplified to “there is only one physics body.”

The kinematic-character bridge is separate: destination-side peer collisions with dynamic bodies are read after physics, but only the manifold's total normal impulse is mapped back; the shared character helper converts it with an 80 kg effective mass and caps the resulting velocity delta at 12 m/s. The shown bridge does not transfer a tangential impulse or torque to the character, consistent with its non-rigid motor model but narrower than full rigid contact response ([portal character contact](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/portal/simulation/rigid_split/character_contact/mod.rs>), [character impulse policy](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/physics/character/controller/pushing/mod.rs>)). These are source contracts and bounded approximations, not evidence of a specific failure. The current tree has no portal test module; the September 19 solver bridge was substantially restructured on October 5, and that patch deleted the earlier crossing/mapping tests. No solver run, portal traversal or contact scenario was executed for this review.

### Lineage and interpretation

On September 12, `62414407` adds the large collision-topology CSG/stencil and moves placement validation toward persistent support bindings; this is the point where a portal becomes a physics/topology change, not only a visual teleport. By September 19 the portal is a deeply nested subsystem in the new Loo-Cast repository. `eaf0454` adds the rigid split peer and solver coupling as a coherent 853-line cross-module tranche. October 5–6 restructures the character/rigid split machinery and deletes the prior crossing/mapping tests; October 8 `d806e3d` reorganizes the root rather than closing the broad semantic contract. The current code therefore carries both a successful concrete integration and a still-open conceptual expansion. The evidence supports “pairwise portal gameplay integrated with current spatial and physics machinery”; it does not support “general portal traversal semantics across the whole USF” or runtime-correct high-speed traversal.

## October 25 — USF identity graph and diagnostics: semantics split, persistence and observability still separate

### The manifestation graph is a real correction to the early “entity” knot

Current `ecs::manifestation` defines four different relationships: a `UsfEntity` semantic subject owns peer `UsfAuthorityPartitionOf` entities; each partition owns one or more `UsfLogicalRealizationOf` backend-local realizations; presentation projections target realizations; and `UsfPresentationViewOf` separately associates a concrete presentation with a view. `UsfConstituentOf` is another relation, deliberately independent of control and manifestation: a player can be a constituent of a ship without becoming the ship's identity or sharing its realization. The read-only `UsfOwnershipQuery` traverses semantic→partition→realization, while portal split comments explicitly place their one Avian peer inside this generic partition model. The October 9 spatial plan explicitly says to retain this graph and keep semantic editor grouping separate from transform-parenting. This is an unusually clear through-line from the old multi-scale/entity problem into a current implementation shape.

There are still important limits on what “semantic identity” means here. `UsfEntity` is an empty marker; its identity is the Bevy `Entity` ID itself. No stable external/save identity is represented by this graph, and no current-source evidence says that a semantic identity survives world reload or entity destruction. The relationship wrappers also store raw `Entity` targets: `UsfOwnershipQuery` returns `Option` when a link is absent, but there is no generic graph constructor or validator in this ECS module that proves the target carries the required role. This is a runtime ownership graph, not yet a persistent content identity or fully validated domain object model.

The lifetime policy is intentionally asymmetric and useful: semantic→partition and partition→realization relationships use `linked_spawn`, so the upstream authority owns downstream simulation lifetime. Presentation projection/view links do not use `linked_spawn`; their docs say view ownership and existing render hierarchy still control teardown, and centralized view retirement is future work. `UsfConstituents` likewise records containment without claiming it owns lifetime. This avoids accidentally despawning an identity when one backend realization or visual disappears, but leaves presentation cleanup split among consumers. The correct description is therefore “authority/lifetime ownership is partly encoded centrally; presentation and containment lifetime remain explicit elsewhere.”

### October 26 — call-site and regression audit

The graph's relationships are not equally operational. The `UsfPresentationViewOf` relation is currently attached to the two player/split-solver model projections, but no system reads `UsfViewPresentations`; the reverse index presently has no consumer or centralized retirement behavior. `UsfConstituentOf` is used for the direct player→spacecraft relation and one direct membership check for visibility; no current caller traverses `UsfConstituents` recursively or detects cycles. So “recursive constituency” describes a representable relationship shape, not a generic recursive traversal feature. Conversely, `UsfOwnershipQuery` is used widely, but it only follows realization→partition→semantic links. Its queries do not require the final entity to carry `UsfEntity`, and the module exposes relationship components directly rather than providing a validating graph-construction API. A malformed edge therefore yields `None` or an incomplete result rather than a typed graph error; consumer-specific fallbacks determine whether that absence is visible. These are source-confirmed API and call-site facts, not demonstrated bad runtime state ([relationship definitions](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/ecs/manifestation/components.rs#L5-L149>), [limited traversal API](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/ecs/manifestation/query.rs#L13-L49>), [only current direct constituency consumers](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/spawn.rs#L88-L90>, </home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/boarding/entry.rs#L119-L124>, </home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/boarding/visibility.rs#L10-L25>), [view relation assignment](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/spawn/mod.rs#L242-L263>)). The module root still labels constituency “recursive,” while the public module exposes only the relationship and its direct target collection ([ECS module map](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/ecs/mod.rs#L1-L20>), [constituency API](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/ecs/constituency/mod.rs#L1-L29>)).

The graph also has one real visualization consumer: the opt-in `world.usf_manifestations` draw runs in `PostUpdate`, walks marked semantic entities through linked partitions/realizations, then draws uniformly colored crosses and lines from the first available transform anchor. It does not visualize missing edges, distinguish partition roles, or expose view/constituency depth. This is a useful inspection aid but a geometric overview, not a graph-integrity diagnostic ([visualization registration and traversal](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/ecs/devtools/mod.rs#L1-L70>)).

The test history makes this an important documentation-and-regression gap: the September 27 graph tests exercised peer partitions, multiple realizations and downstream-only despawn; October 5 `e987230` deleted those tests (100 lines from the module) while performing a broad tree consolidation. The current ECS ownership files contain no replacement test module, and the spatial transition tests do not cover these relationship lifecycle rules. This does not establish that Bevy's relationship behavior is broken; it means the current repository no longer carries its prior direct assertion of the intended lifecycle semantics. No test/build/runtime check was run for this review.

History is part of this result. The `UsfEntity`/partition/realization files first appear in September 10 `e274357`; the traversal API is introduced September 27 `e6fe305`; the October 6 cleanup centralizes and documents graph roles, linked-spawn rules and view relationships. On October 9, the accepted spatial megapass plan preserves the graph while explicitly rejecting `ChildOf` as semantic grouping. Compare this with the September 2023 prompt seed, where a Phenomenon was simultaneously an observed experience, unique ID, ECS entity and model/archetype. The latest graph separates several of those roles, but still uses an ECS entity as the live semantic handle. This is a refinement, not completion of stable identity or storage semantics.

### Diagnostics are typed and separated from UI; their product surface is still narrow

`RuntimeDiagnosticsPlugin` publishes typed frame, world, physics and system snapshots. Runtime sampling runs every 0.25 seconds; the physics accumulator resets after that interval, making its `*_window` counters local windows rather than totals since process start. World/archetype and inline-component-memory sampling runs every 5 seconds, excludes resources, empty archetypes and entities marked `DeveloperArtifact`, and explicitly omits heap allocations inside component values. The in-game playground HUD currently consumes FPS/frame time and player-motion state; optional `TelemetryEmitter::from_env("spacetime-engine")` publishes runtime metrics and a world/component-memory snapshot. The EcsMemory snapshot is not read by an in-game diagnostics panel in the inspected call sites.

This is useful observability machinery, but it is not a general log/operation console and is not the Vapor Client service's operation stream. `spacetime-engine::console` separately transports tracing records and developer commands, while Vapor's `vapor_console_core` models operations/logs for Launcher/Studio/IDE. The shared names and visual aspirations must not hide that they are separate transports today. The diagnostics module itself states its data is owned independently of developer UI; that is a sound boundary, while the in-game F2 and Vapor consoles still need an explicit cross-process product decision to share presentation, record schema, or only selected adapters. Telemetry's existence also does not prove upload, server ingestion or profiling UI behavior; those are separate service paths reviewed in the Vapor sections.

## October 26 — SDK exposes a large typed command vocabulary, but many commands are still specifications rather than operations

The SDK command model covers all ten Vapor content kinds through generic leaf/pack/packagepack variants and also exposes workspace, toolchain, root release, Steam, repair and template commands ([command model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/commands.rs>), [content-type exports](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/lib.rs>)). The first-party CLI parses that model and dispatches in-process. Only environment status, workspace status/sync/Cargo/deploy, root package/publish, Steam status/login and toolchain status/install have concrete handlers in the dispatch match; the remaining commands route to `output::stub`, which describes the requested action instead of executing it ([CLI entry](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/lib.rs>), [command parser](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/cli.rs>), [dispatch table](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/output/mod.rs>), [stub renderer](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/output/stub.rs>)). The API surface and command help therefore overstate working breadth if read as an implementation inventory.

This SDK CLI is a deliberate exception to the otherwise shared-service product model: it calls `vapor_sdk_core` functions directly and has its own global options and destructive-action guard, rather than submitting commands to the Client service ([SDK CLI adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/lib.rs>), [safety guard](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/safety.rs>)). The guard is applied before dispatch, supports only selected command combinations, and is not inherent to `SdkCommand` or the SDK Core functions ([policy](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/safety.rs>), [global flags](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/options.rs>)). Consequently, migrating these paths behind a future service API must move safety policy with the operation; simply calling the existing Core function from another frontend would bypass CLI prompts.

The concrete developer workspace path walks upward from the process working directory until it finds `Workspace.vapor.toml`, unless `--workspace` changes the search start; it requires organization/name, then runs Cargo through the pinned Vapor toolchain with per-workspace output roots. SDK deploy accepts only the `vapor-cli` workspace and promotes a built executable into `$VAPOR_HOME/bin` ([identity](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/identity.rs>), [Cargo environment](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/cargo.rs>), [deploy](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/deploy.rs>)). This is not an App.vapor.toml discovery path and does not establish that installed app roots need a workspace manifest.

The SDK toolchain path declares only Linux GNU and Windows MSVC in its supported target list; it does not install the Windows GNU-LLVM target or linker ([SDK model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/toolchain.rs>), [SDK target plan](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/toolchain/plan.rs>), [SDK install](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/toolchain/install.rs>)). The broader Vapor role setup handles Windows GNU separately: host identity maps GNU Windows to the MSVC Rustup host, then managed Developer-environment reconciliation installs `x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm` and a pinned LLVM-MinGW bundle ([host mapping](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/host.rs>), [managed target install](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/toolchain.rs>), [role reconciliation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs>), [linker bundle](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cross_target_toolchain.rs>)). The actual finding is divergent support machinery and an SDK authoring path that does not express the same target contract—not blanket lack of Windows GNU support. No Windows installation or cross-target build was run. Repair and template remain enum/API models with future-effect specs; their visible CLI routes are stubs rather than completed workflows ([repair model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/repair.rs>), [template model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/template.rs>), [spec model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/spec.rs>)). No command was executed.

### Cross-domain reading

The graph and diagnostics demonstrate two distinct kinds of progress toward the owner's larger goal. USF manifestation uses semantic distinctions to prevent ECS identity, physics realization and presentation from collapsing into one object. Diagnostics uses typed snapshots to avoid UI-owned sampling and string parsing. Their unfinished edges are different: USF still has runtime-scoped identity and decentralized presentation teardown; diagnostics still has narrow consumers and a separate telemetry/console path. The next synthesis should connect them without generalizing either into an all-purpose abstraction: preserve exact domain authority, then expose shared identity/records only where a real cross-domain consumer needs them.

## October 25 — authored geometry and procedural assets: reusable pipeline, incomplete lifecycle and recipe authority

### Authored maps are a real constrained authoring facility

`geometry::AuthoredGeometryPlugin` registers `.spacemap` as a hot-reloadable RON asset. The schema covers primitives, ramps, repeated geometry, moving boxes, generic markers, materials, zones and lights; validation checks unique IDs, references, finite/positive constraints, convex cross-sections and a 20,000-generated-object cap. Compilation produces an internal geometry/light/marker IR, and runtime reconciliation realizes that IR as meshes, Avian colliders, lights and inspectable `AuthoredMapObject` / `AuthoredMapMarker` components. The playground map adapter interprets `player_spawn`, `portal_a` and `portal_b`; the generic geometry module itself does not assign those game meanings. This is an actual reusable engine facility with a documented authoring boundary, not merely a one-off scene script. The map README says it is designed to feed future editor/diagnostic/regression tools, which remain future-facing.

There is a concrete lifecycle hole in that otherwise coherent pipeline. `reconcile_authored_map_scenes` ignores `AssetEvent::Removed`; it also clears a dirty scene only after finding its source asset, and does nothing if the handle no longer resolves. So if a loaded map asset is removed while its `AuthoredMapScene` remains, the old generated entities are not despawned. Separately, generated entities store the source's raw Bevy `Entity` in `AuthoredMapManifestationOf`, but are not children or linked-spawn dependents of that source. Despawning the scene entity itself therefore has no cleanup path in the inspected code. These are source-derived stale-manifestation cases, not reproduced runtime failures. The source's “disposable manifestations” description is stronger than its current teardown wiring.

### October 26 — gameplay marker and IDE gap

The hot-reload promise also stops at runtime geometry. `place_player_at_spawn_marker` and `initialize_demo_portals_from_markers` each keep a one-shot `Local<bool>`; after their first successful marker read, later asset rebuilds do not reapply changed player-spawn or portal marker positions, and re-entering the scenario does not reset those system-local flags. Thus “save the map and all geometry rebuilds” is accurate for spawned map objects, but not for gameplay state derived from those objects ([asset reload path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/geometry/runtime/rebuild/mod.rs#L14-L70>), [one-shot playground marker adapters](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/map/mod.rs#L80-L151>)). The editor implications are also concrete: the authored root has no explicit schema version and derives `Deserialize` but not `Serialize`; the map README calls editor support future work, and no dedicated `.spacemap` editor was found in the current IDE source. This is a structured authoring format, not yet a versioned Vapor content artifact or integrated domain editor ([schema](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/geometry/asset/schema/mod.rs#L1-L35>), [map-tooling roadmap](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/assets/maps/README.md#L34-L50>)). The exported `AuthoredMapObject` retains zone/tag metadata, but a source-wide consumer search found no current reads of that component; these fields presently label generated entities rather than drive a generalized zone/tag behavior ([metadata definition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/geometry/runtime/mod.rs#L46-L52>), [geometry attachment](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/geometry/runtime/spawning/mod.rs#L64-L74>), [README explicitly marks editor/overlay consumers as future work](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/assets/maps/README.md#L36-L48>)).

### Test coverage was removed after focused behavior tests existed

The current geometry and procedural-assets trees contain no `#[test]` cases. This is a visible regression, not simply a feature that never had tests: `c187ac7` added compile/runtime-focused geometry tests during module extraction, but `e987230` deleted `geometry/asset/tests.rs`, `geometry/compile/tests.rs`, and `procedural_assets/tests.rs`. The compile tests pinned staircase expansion and ramp-top placement; the procedural test pinned generated texture byte storage. No replacement tests appear under these current modules. This does not establish a runtime bug, but removes direct guards around authoring validation, generated geometry, asset replacement and this subsystem's coordinate conventions. No test suite was run in this review.

### Procedural presentation recipes currently contain both used and orphaned outputs

`ProceduralPresentationAssetsPlugin` creates cracked-clay textures, star and planet surface materials, a lunar material, and an analytic debug-grid marker material. Only the debug-grid handle has a current consumer in the searched source tree; no current consumer was found for the cracked-clay, star, planet or lunar handles. The planet image is explicitly described in the fixture code as a fake tectonic/biome surface for far-body presentation, while current celestial geometry remains the exact `CelestialVoxelField::sphere` field. It is therefore a visual recipe/prototype, not terrain semantics or proof of a planet surface renderer. The height texture is generated, exposed through the PBR bundle and regenerated in place, but no current `StandardMaterial` field or consumer connects that image to displacement. These are identified future-capability remnants, not evidence the outputs are currently visible.

The `CrackedClayRecipe` is public, reflected and stored as a mutable Bevy resource. Its defaults are small (256×256), but there is no validation or maximum on its resolution or cell parameters; a changed recipe regenerates synchronously inside `Update`, with five surface samples per pixel and a fixed 3×3 neighborhood per Voronoi field. Thus arbitrary/large reflected settings can create a large synchronous CPU allocation and frame cost. This is a code-path bound/risk, not an observed hitch. The API needs a resource-budget/validation policy before this recipe becomes an unrestricted editor control.

### Current worldgen is keyed construction input, not an operational generator graph

The current kernel has a valuable small contract: a fixed `WorldSeed`; `PhenomenonGeneration` derives field-specific, revision-keyed deterministic seeds from world seed and stable phenomenon key; exact authored constraints bypass procedural fallback; and `SparseConstructionAtlas<T>` stores one canonical initial center, conservative radius and typed recipe per key. A failed bounded coordinate projection returns “may intersect” rather than incorrectly hiding a candidate. The Earth-Moon fixture registers two exact authored bodies, constructs them through the semantic body path, and records provenance. The source contains `#[test]` cases for deterministic key separation, exact-constraint bypass, chunk-boundary discoverability and the Earth/Moon exact values; however, the Engine manifest sets `[lib] test = false`, so these are not part of a Cargo unit-test target in the current workspace configuration.

The names can imply more than the implementation: the atlas is a `BTreeMap` keyed by identity, and `intersecting(region)` linearly filters every record through a geometric bound. It is sparse in stored semantic facts and avoids per-chunk duplication/residency; it is not a spatially partitioned query index or a demand scheduler. `WorldSeed` currently has one fixed default and comments defer save serialization until saves exist. The production fixture uses `ConstructionConstraint::Exact` for all present body parameters; the procedural fallback closures are demonstration paths, not an active celestial generator. There is no current procedural phenomenon tree, worldgen hook/registry, terrain algorithm or seed-persistent generated world to infer from these types.

### Cross-check against the proposal and the reset

This latest kernel follows a sharp two-step retreat from the September 30 proposal. The Oct 6 revision (`0e48843`) carried a descriptive typed `PhenomenonRule` registry and a sparse spatial/temporal evaluation cache with epochs and nine built-in state families; its own docs explicitly said this did not construct live identity, terrain or ecology, and that the Loo-Cast fixture did not consume it. On Oct 8, `d806e3d` removed that evaluator and its families. Same-day `0f153c5` established keyed deterministic construction inputs and authored-vs-procedural facts; `b77a397` added the typed sparse atlas. The older evaluator was not a functioning world-construction engine, so its deletion should not be counted as lost operational generation. However, the new implementation is also not completion of the September 30 design: it preserves the identity/constraint/position entry point while omitting the generative chain, body-wide terrain, broad-scale morphology and corresponding scheduler.

The September 30 plan specifically demanded that local voxel terrain and whole-body presentation derive from the same terrain semantics, with a moving canonical Moon and sparse realization. The present celestial path uses one semantic body and scale-demanded voxel field, which realizes part of the single-authority direction; the exact spherical field and orphaned planet texture leave the terrain/presentation unification target open. The Oct 6 deletion of three worldgen/voxel design documents erased an active planning corpus from the current tree, but their parent commit remains accessible in Git and is linked in the history artifact. The detailed scale-model reconciliation remains in the [worldgen crosswalk](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7a-worldgen-means-deterministic-construction-inputs-today-not-procedural-worlds).

### Evidence and limits

This is current-source, README, parent-commit and commit-diff inspection. It is not a runtime check of file-watcher behavior, entity teardown, procedural texture cost, or map authoring. The stale-manifestation cases follow directly from the event filter and lack of source-linked cleanup, but were not executed. No builds or tests were run. Relevant source anchors: [map reconciliation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/geometry/runtime/rebuild/mod.rs#L14>), [map validation and expansion cap](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/geometry/asset/validation/map.rs#L17>), [worldgen atlas/query shape](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/worldgen/atlas.rs#L70>), [synchronous procedural recipe regeneration](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/procedural_assets/systems.rs#L91>), [recipe sampling cost](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/procedural_assets/texture/mod.rs#L140>).

## October 25 — configuration: a sound precedence chain with a narrow domain surface

`EngineConfigPlugin` implements a real precedence model: compiled defaults, validated RON at an explicit `SPACETIME_ENGINE_CONFIG` path or under `VAPOR_ENGINE_ROOT/assets/config/engine.ron`, then typed transient `EngineConfigOverrides`. The shared Vapor launch plan currently sets `VAPOR_ENGINE_ROOT` to the selected engine content root, so installed launches have an explicit path contract rather than relying on Steam's working directory. Source-run fallback checks the current directory's `assets/config/engine.ron`, then `spacetime-engine/assets/config/engine.ron`. The README describes this chain accurately. File polling is 0.5 seconds; a valid reload replaces the source layer, invalid edits retain the last valid file config, and invalid effective overrides retain the last effective config. The three current tests cover only path precedence/fallback, not RON parsing, layer precedence, reload behavior or rejection. The top-level module exposes `EngineConfig`, `EngineConfigOverrides`, the loader plugin, and voxel policy types; the effective root itself currently has only a `voxel` field, and resolution clones the file layer, applies typed overrides, then validates the result ([module surface](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/config/mod.rs>), [root model and precedence](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/config/model.rs>)).

The declared “engine configuration” currently contains only `voxel` streaming and manifestation policy. It is not a system-wide policy registry: portal configuration is separately owned by the portal domain, and other facilities retain their own resources/config types. That can be a deliberate domain boundary; it does mean the root name should not be read as evidence of centralized configuration across the engine. The RON structs use `serde(default)` but not `deny_unknown_fields`, so an unrecognized/misspelled key is eligible to be ignored and the affected setting silently remains at its default. That is a source-level authoring-risk inference from the derive contract; no typo fixture was parsed in this review.

Runtime console bindings expose five of the seven typed override fields: load/publish budgets, warm-cache limit, max chunks/task and rebuild budget. `generation_group_base_chunks_per_axis` and `physics_interaction_radius_native` can be set by the RON layer or by programmatic resource mutation, but no console runtime-variable binding exists for them in the inspected registrations. This is a discoverability gap only if the intended contract is that all typed runtime overrides are player/developer console controls; the code does not state that every field must be exposed. The runtime-variable “default” callback returns `EngineConfig::default()`, while reads otherwise return the effective project-config value when no override exists, so a UI that distinguishes “current value” from “reset default” must preserve that distinction.

The October 8 cleanup flattened the earlier nested `config/voxel/{streaming,manifestation,overrides}` files into one `config/voxel.rs`, removing 215 lines while adding the combined file. The semantic boundary survived; this was mostly organizational compression, not evidence that configuration became a shared engine-wide architecture. The current implementation is clear and small; its limits are that it owns only voxel tuning, exposes a subset through console controls, and has shallow automated verification. No tests or runtime reload were performed here. Source anchors: [configuration loading and precedence](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/config/source.rs#L34>), [config fields and validation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/config/voxel.rs#L5>), [console override registration](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/console_commands/runtime_variables/voxel.rs#L60>), [Vapor engine-root environment handoff](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/launch.rs#L302>).

## October 25 — item, combat and health: a clear request chain with broken root teardown

The present code does have a useful gameplay ownership path: the local input adapter emits `UseItemRequest`; one built-in item plugin turns its semantic action into `FireWeaponRequest`; combat creates and advances a projectile; a hit becomes generic `Damage`; and Health alone applies `Damage → Health → Died`. The hit adapter resolves a runtime manifestation back to its semantic entity before sending damage. This is a genuine separation of input, item behavior, combat detection and health authority, though all of it is currently composed inside `LooCastGamePlugin`, not separately shipped Game content.

The orchestration chain is also real: `GameSet` orders action, simulation, consequence, cleanup and presentation; simulation orders motion before collision and phenomena; hit conversion is explicitly before Health application; player and Playground death adapters run in cleanup. This is a useful cross-domain schedule owner and should not be collapsed into each feature plugin. The incomplete part is lifecycle ownership beneath the semantic root, not absence of all integration structure.

The names overstate the persistence/domain depth. `game::inventory::Hotbar` is a fixed nine-slot selection resource, not an ownership/count/stack/drop inventory; the Playground explicitly clears and repopulates its first three slots in `PreStartup`. No persistence path is present in these modules. `ItemCatalog` stores an insertion-ordered `Vec` of definitions with `&'static str` IDs, labels and descriptions; registration panics on duplicate IDs, and there is no unregister or namespace/version contract. That is suitable for statically composed built-ins, not proof of a runtime content registry or module unload. The September 11 Playground note had called Hotbar authoritative gameplay state and item objects persistent, while also calling runtime registries future/static-first; the note itself says it is temporary and dislikes what it implies. Treat it as a historical experiment, not a durable promise. The current small module docs now say “local inventory-selection state” and “registered semantic item definitions,” which are more accurate. This is a gap between compiled item behavior and manifest-driven composition, not a proposal for an eleventh Vapor content kind. See the [September 11 architecture snapshot](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/ee432ee58d5941b923afc1c1edf9eaa4df752c1a) and [current hotbar/item APIs](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/inventory/mod.rs#L1>).

The October 25 callsite check sharpens the item abstraction's history. September 11's [`ee432ee`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/ee432ee58d5941b923afc1c1edf9eaa4df752c1a) left an explicitly provisional Playground architecture around item definitions, inventory selection and creative UI. On September 19, [`5489776d`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/5489776d43a453ded0911e8ae14e416d65c7cbc3) extracted the present generic `ItemAction`/`UseItem`-message shape and a metadata catalog, while adapting the concrete playground tools. Its comments explicitly proposed AI, replay, networking and mod producers, but repository-wide search at the October 22 head finds only one publisher: the local Playground adapter. On October 6, [`0e488433`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/0e488433dd26b35a937dba8c5f755b52615e8eaf) reorganized and grouped the item plugins; the diff does not establish Vapor content discovery or unloading. The trajectory is therefore a useful internal decoupling step—from device controls toward semantic item requests—whose comments describe a wider future extension surface than the repository currently integrates. That distinction matters to the owner's later request for content to be composed as separately managed artifacts: a generic ECS message is not itself a Workshop/content lifecycle or module boundary.

The most concrete lifecycle defect is in Playground object teardown. Erase and death despawn only the entity marked `PlaygroundRoot`. Damageable-cube and chunkloading-cube creation place Health and `PlaygroundRoot` on one semantic entity, then create authority partitions and physics manifestations as separate entities linked by raw `Entity` references (`UsfAuthorityPartitionOf`, `UsfLogicalRealizationOf`, `PlaygroundPickable::root`); they do not make those objects children of the root or register an explicit cascade. Only a model is parented to a manifestation. Consequently, root despawn does not itself despawn the partition, collider/rigid-body manifestation, or peer. In the erase path, the surviving pickable still points at the now-despawned root, so repeating erase cannot find a new live root to remove; spatial-demand components can also remain on the orphaned manifestations. This is source-confirmed orphan risk for both erase and lethal damage, not a reproduced runtime leak. It is the same identity-versus-lifetime distinction already found in authored geometry and USF: a semantic reference is not an ownership relation. Sources: [root-only erase/death cleanup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/lifecycle/mod.rs#L18>), [damageable cube root and manifestation construction](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/items/damageable_cube/mod.rs#L110>), [chunkloading cube construction](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/items/chunkloading_cube/mod.rs#L82>).

Combat is likewise a functional slice, not a robust collision contract. Projectile movement advances a point transform by `PortalVelocity * Time::delta_secs()` in `Update`; detection then asks whether that endpoint lies inside each eligible collider. It does not sweep the segment traversed between frames, so a sufficiently fast projectile or long frame can cross a target without any sampled endpoint inside it. The search scans each projectile against the damageable query, making the straightforward path proportional to projectile-count × target-count. This is a source-derived tunnelling/scaling risk, not an observed miss or benchmark. `DamageableBounds` is required as a target marker but the collision routine uses Avian `Collider::contains_point` rather than its extents. The path has no focused tests in the inspected item/combat/health modules; no game run or performance test was performed. Sources: [projectile integration and endpoint collision](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/combat/projectile/mod.rs#L5>), [fixed-size Hotbar](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/inventory/mod.rs#L7>), [item catalog identity and duplicate policy](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/item/catalog/mod.rs#L7>), [damage/death owner](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/health/damage/mod.rs#L5>).

Coverage cross-check: a repository search finds no current tests naming these Hotbar/item/combat/damage/lifecycle contracts. The nearby historical `portal_frame_points_out_of_surface_and_preserves_up` unit test in the Portal Gun adapter was removed in `e987230`; it only tested frame orientation, not the root cleanup or collision chain. This is narrower than saying all portal behavior is untested: separate portal topology test modules remain, as documented in the portal review. The test gap here is not “all of game has no tests,” but that these particular gameplay handoffs and teardown semantics lack a direct current guard.

## October 25 — control transfer and spatial handoff are separate transactions

The reference spacecraft path makes an important distinction visible in code: local control can be accepted before the destination interaction chart is ready. `resolve_local_control_transfers` validates that the controller is local, the target belongs to a semantic subject, and the manifestation has a scale affinity; it then moves `LocalControlSubject` and emits `LocalControlTransferApplied`. Its adapter consumes that event, immediately moves view/spatial-anchor markers to the new manifestation, and queues a `UsfSpatialTransition` for the subject's affinity scale. The spatial transition is applied later in `PostUpdate`, after the adapter runs in `Update` ([control resolver](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/control/runtime.rs#L17>), [adapter and queued transition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/control/runtime.rs#L110>), [spatial application schedule](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/spatial/mod.rs#L172>)).

That second transaction can wait: coverage failure requeues an exact one-shot relocation, while backend guards can delay continuous interaction requirements. The spacecraft affinity explicitly requires destination realization and collision roles. However, the accepted-control message is already emitted, view/anchor ownership has already moved, and the local-control audit checks marker cardinality, semantic relationship and focus identity—not whether the requested chart handoff has completed. The spacecraft entry action likewise hides/disables the player and changes constituency before writing the transfer request; exit changes pose, visibility, demand, locomotion policy and constituency before requesting the reverse transfer ([admission and requeue policy](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/spatial/transition/admission.rs#L90>), [spacecraft affinity](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/spawn.rs#L110>), [boarding](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/boarding/entry.rs#L30>), [disembark](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/boarding/exit.rs#L25>), [control audit](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/control/runtime.rs#L190>)).

This is not evidence of a default-game failure: the normal spacecraft bootstrap waits for the player's detailed chart and collision readiness, and boarding requires a landed ship within physical reach. It is evidence that “control transfer applied” means semantic authority/focus moved, not “the full spatial handoff completed.” If destination coverage is missing during a later handoff, the source permits an intermediate state with new control/focus and a pending chart transition; no inspected action gate or cross-stage completion result makes that state explicit. The schedule order makes this more than a presentation-only interval: the next `RunFixedMainLoop` is placed in `BeforeFixedMainLoop`, whereas the chart transition is applied in `PostUpdate`, so fixed simulation can sample the newly controlled subject before that frame's chart-admission attempt ([cross-domain schedule](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/mod.rs#L106>), [PostUpdate transition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/spatial/mod.rs#L172>)). This is a **source-confirmed transaction-boundary gap with conditional runtime consequences**, not a reproduced bug. The narrow transfer validations make rejection possible in principle, but the normal spacecraft caller establishes the required ownership and affinity first; the more direct concern is delayed spatial admission after accepted control.

This sharpens the existing USF finding: the graph cleanly separates semantic subject, authority partition, realization and view, but the cross-subsystem lifecycle transaction does not yet span those layers atomically. The concrete spacecraft, generic control, and spatial transition systems are all composed from `spacetime-engine::game`; `LooCastGamePlugin` installs `SpacecraftPlugin` there, so this semantic integration is not yet an independently distributed Game content artifact ([game composition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/mod.rs#L190>)). That links the runtime finding to the owner's separate Engine/Game/Packagepack distinction: semantic module boundaries are developing inside one compiled Engine crate, while pack manifests and content artifact boundaries remain a distinct layer. It also puts the older “semantic control first” comment in its proper weight: that ordering is an explicit policy, while readiness-gated arrival and control availability are not one joined state machine. No builds, tests or runtime reproduction were performed; the review found no focused test that joins transfer acceptance to later coverage wait/application.

## October 25 — Vapor-owned validation exists, but the Engine README bypasses it

`spacetime-engine/README.md` presents raw `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo check -p spacetime-engine` as the normal structural-validation loop ([README validation block](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/README.md#L32-L42>)). This wording is present in its first appearance, Loo-Cast `76d1d84` (September 18), and remained through later README edits that changed source/world claims but did not revisit validation. The current Vapor CLI exposes `fmt`, `check`, `test`, and `validate` as app-local Rust/Cargo commands ([CLI model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/model.rs#L54-L106>)); the router converts them to typed Client actions ([CLI dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command.rs#L96-L114>), [Client action model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/actions.rs#L151-L165>)), and the service delegates to Provider's managed build runner ([service dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L773-L788>), [Provider validation plan](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/workspace_build.rs#L180-L191>)). `vapor fmt` applies formatting, while `vapor validate` is non-formatting and runs format-check, workspace check, tests, Clippy with warnings denied, and Rustdoc. This is more than a naming preference: the README teaches a second toolchain path despite the owner's repeated single-Vapor-entrypoint direction, and it omits the service's stronger validation sequence. `git diff --check` is a separate Git whitespace check, not part of the Cargo wrapper.

The exact CLI source workspace must first be opened/selected; its project selector accepts a declared Cargo workspace name or `all`. The Loo-Cast workspace declares the `spacetime-engine` Cargo package, but this audit did not run or experimentally verify a command sequence. The README's note that test targets/doctests are disabled is consistent with current crate manifest flags, and the actual disablement is stronger than that sentence suggests: all three crates set `autotests = false`, the Engine and Game libraries set `test = false`, and Packagepack's binary sets `test = false`; the libraries also disable doctests. Thus `validate` includes a Cargo test invocation, but these manifests exclude the in-source unit-test harnesses described below. This is a confirmed documentation/authority mismatch, not evidence that raw Cargo fails or that the managed path is fully hermetic. The cross-repository toolchain audit already finds Platform Server CI/deploy invoking host Cargo, so this is one instance of a broader incomplete centralization contract. See the [toolchain and validation cross-check](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#october-25--engine-validation-docs-bypass-vapors-managed-command-path), [test-target finding](#october-25--loo-cast-has-test-code-but-disables-its-test-harnesses), and [chronological trace](loo-cast-vapor-history-timeline.md#october-25--engine-validation-documentation-lags-the-managed-toolchain-path).

### Evidence and limits

Read-only inspection of the Engine README, its Cargo manifests, Vapor CLI command model/router, Client domain operation, service workspace dispatcher, and Provider build runner. No Cargo/Vapor operation was run, and no current README edit was made. The finding establishes exposed implementation and documentation drift, not end-user success, complete command discoverability, or equivalent side effects across frontends.

## October 25 — Loo-Cast has test code, but disables its test harnesses

The current Engine source contains 28 `#[test]` annotations across inline test modules. The workspace has no `tests/` integration-test files, and all three member manifests disable automatic test discovery with `autotests = false` ([Engine](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/Cargo.toml#L5>), [Game](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-game/Cargo.toml#L5>), [Packagepack](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-packagepack/Cargo.toml#L5>)). More decisively, Engine and Game each set `[lib] test = false`; Packagepack sets `[[bin]] test = false`. The Engine and Game libraries also set `doctest = false`. Therefore these Engine unit-test functions are present as source but Cargo will not build them into the crate's normal unit-test harness under the current manifest settings. Vapor's service-managed `validate` sequence does include `cargo test --workspace --all-targets`, but that invocation cannot exercise test targets the crate manifests have disabled. The README's statement that automated test targets/doctests are disabled is accurate, though the nearby “tests are added where…” sentence can make the inline annotations look more active than they are.

This setting has a traceable history. Loo-Cast `e987230` (October 5) adds `autotests = false`, disables the Engine and Game lib harnesses/doctests, disables the then-Engine binary harness, and removes multiple test modules in a 176-file consolidation (14,108 lines deleted). Packagepack's original library harness is disabled in the same consolidation; `4551c53` changes it to a binary with `test = false` while moving the executable to Packagepack. Later October changes add 28 inline Engine `#[test]` annotations without reversing the manifest flags. The net effect is not simply “no tests were written”: executable test harnesses were deliberately shut off during the cleanup, then test-shaped specifications reappeared in code without being reconnected to Cargo. The repository and owner have both expressed test-free implementation preferences at points, so this review does not label the policy itself wrong; it records that `vapor validate`'s advertised test phase does not test those invariants.

This changes how several other findings should be read: “test code exists” is not evidence of executable regression coverage, and deleting a test module cannot be assessed only by counting remaining `#[test]` functions. For example, the worldgen cases are useful executable-looking specifications but currently disabled by the Engine manifest; the deleted geometry/portal tests still represent lost authored specifications, yet no present Cargo test run would have exercised their surviving neighbors either. This finding is source/configuration-derived; no Cargo command was executed. It does not assert that tests should be enabled—the project has at times explicitly directed test-free passes—but the state should be reported as **test annotations checked in, test harnesses disabled**, not “tests exist and were not run.” See the [Engine validation path](#october-25--vapor-owned-validation-exists-but-the-engine-readme-bypasses-it) and [atlas](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#october-25--loo-cast-test-annotations-are-disabled-by-crate-manifests).

## October 25 — the documented local content scripts are stranded on the old path

The Loo-Cast root README and Vapor CLI content guide both direct users to `script run content-roundtrip` and `script run content-publish-preview`. The actual tracked files live under `.vapor/scripts/`, first added by Loo-Cast commit `ff16e4c` (July 10) and revised by `2f87384` (July 17) to mark package/publish commands host-only.
