The current CLI `run_script` resolver does not search `.vapor/scripts`: it searches only `<active source>/resources/vapor/vapor-scripts/<name>.vapor`, then the installed app's corresponding `resources/vapor/vapor-scripts` fallback. The source-controlled Loo-Cast `.vapor/scripts` pair therefore cannot be found by the documented current CLI command; the Client payload has only `default.vapor`, not either proof script ([Loo-Cast README](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/README.md#L23>), [old proof scripts](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/.vapor/scripts/content-roundtrip.vapor>), [CLI resolver](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command.rs#L593>), [current script source contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/docs/scripts.md#L1>), [installed script payload](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/vapor-scripts/default.vapor>)).

There is also a safety-description mismatch if the old sequence is restored to the current path. `content-roundtrip.vapor` passes an authored Vapor identity to `content subscribe` without a dry-run/provider selector. The current CLI defines Subscribe as a Steam Workshop subscription action and requires a PublishedFileId; as written, the old authored-identity argument would fail `require_workshop_id` before dispatch, rather than demonstrate a local mock or a successful Steam subscription ([old script](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/.vapor/scripts/content-roundtrip.vapor>), [current command dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/content_commands.rs#L288>), [Subscribe command contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/model.rs#L588>)). `--host-only` restricts target selection for package/create/publish operations; it does not make Subscribe a fixture. If the sequence were updated with actual Workshop IDs, it would invoke account subscription through Steam, so the documented “safe local” guarantee would still need a deliberate policy. The exact effect of the original July-era command implementation cannot be reconstructed from the present CLI alone; no older executor was runtime-tested here. This is a **source-confirmed stale entrypoint and unresolved side-effect contract**, not a report that anyone ran it or changed a subscription. The two distinct `scripts/` systems compound the naming trap: Loo-Cast's visible `scripts/README.md` documents embedded Rhai defaults/live files, whereas Vapor CLI's `script run` reads line-oriented Vapor command files from a different root.

Historical source note: the proof scripts were added under `.vapor/scripts` in July. The current Client script contract and resolver use a release/runtime resource path instead, while the Loo-Cast README still documents the old names and the files remain where they were introduced. No inspected migration moves or rewrites those proof scripts. Neither script was run during this documentation audit; the path mismatch and current argument classification follow from resolver/dispatch source and checked-in script text.
## October 25 — the semantic IDE teaches Rust structure, but does not govern it yet

The October 23 semantic-workbench implementation is a substantial, real vertical slice: workspace files and declarations are addressable semantic objects; Rust Analyzer supplies language symbols; local syntax metadata projects fields, parameters, attributes and selected Bevy roles; diagnostics can target an object span; and the workspace tree applies Rust-specific labels/order inside detected Cargo crates. The source preserves ordinary file editing if Rust Analyzer is unavailable, and explicitly avoids implicit Cargo builds when opening a workspace ([semantic workbench plan](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-23-semantic-workbench.md#L13-L28>), [IDE guide](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/docs/ide.md#L100-L124>)). This is not merely a renamed text editor.

The process-ownership concern resolves positively on this slice: the IDE sends typed `LanguageServerAction`s over its Client connection; the service validates that the requested root is the Client-selected workspace, discovers that source workspace, resolves its `ManagedToolchain`, and spawns the pinned Rust Analyzer. The service holds one process per connected client ID and stops it on explicit stop, disconnect, or replacement; the GUI then performs the LSP initialize/message exchange through the same protocol. On Windows the service marks the child `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` ([IDE request path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/language_server.rs#L120-L180>), [service launch and managed toolchain](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server/language_server.rs#L60-L111>), [service workspace authorization and dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L540-L624>), [disconnect cleanup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L245-L266>)). Thus the design’s process ownership is implemented, not merely promised. Limits remain: source inspection proves direct-child lifecycle code, not descendant-process cleanup, successful Analyzer startup on either OS, or real-time responsiveness; those require runtime evidence.

The current Rust layout contract is narrower than the owner’s stated ambition. The shared Client domain defines nine canonical module kinds—components, constants, events, functions, resources, run conditions, statics, systems and types—with stable filenames and starter module docs ([vocabulary](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/canonical_rust.rs#L5-L61>)). The IDE’s “New canonical Rust module” invokes a typed Client action. The service checks that the selected Rust parent is under a Cargo crate’s `src`, verifies its fingerprint and syntax, rejects duplicate module declarations, creates the category file and updates the parent declaration; it removes the new file if the guarded parent update fails ([service operation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/workspace_files.rs#L312-L413>)). That is meaningful service-owned scaffolding with stale-write protection. Its scope is still “any detected Cargo crate,” not a Vapor content/crate role; no current policy says whether this dogma should cover the IDE’s own crates, authored Vapor crates only, or another selected set.

The vocabulary is not fully framework-neutral either. `systems.rs` documentation calls out Bevy systems and system sets, and the generated Component/Resource/Event declarations use Bevy derives. The “System” item template is an empty public function, while local classification infers System/RunCondition from the source filename and recognizes ECS roles from the final identifier in a derive path. These are convenient conventions for current Bevy-oriented code, not resolved Rust type semantics; a template can parse while being semantically unusable in a crate without the matching framework/dependency. Generated item and module declarations also default to `pub` without a visibility contract. No compilation or cross-framework test was run. [Module starter text](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/canonical_rust.rs#L50-L62>), [template bodies](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/rust_semantics.rs#L196-L229>), [syntax classification](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/rust_semantics.rs#L365-L481>), [parent declaration](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/workspace_files.rs#L363-L389>).

But creation is not repository-wide enforcement. The IDE’s `convention_diagnostics` emits **Warning** diagnostics when a recognized semantic declaration is in the wrong filename. The diagnostic is produced in the IDE’s Rust Analyzer/local semantic paths; the reviewed service module-creation operation does not inspect or normalize all existing declarations, and the reviewed build/provider contract does not turn these warnings into compile/CI gates. The rule checks the declaration’s filename, not all module-graph structure, visibility, ownership, allowed declaration categories, or whether a nearer category is warranted. Classification also depends on Rust Analyzer symbols plus local syntax heuristics—for example, derive recognition checks the final path segment for `Component`, `Resource` or `Event`—so it is not a complete Rust semantic authority ([warning implementation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/rust_semantics.rs#L280-L339>)). This is therefore advisory IDE guidance, not a Vapor-wide invariant.

The workbench does fulfill several exact navigation ideas from the owner’s request: non-`.rs` display labels are used; `mod.rs` is labeled by its shortest unambiguous module suffix and expanded on collision; Rust crate subtrees sort alphabetically while ordinary workspace trees sort folders before files. Tests in Vapor-GUI source assert those behaviors ([navigation implementation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/workspace_navigation.rs#L125-L160>), [crate ordering and disambiguation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/workspace_navigation.rs#L239-L295>)). This review did not run those GUI tests. Separately, current Loo-Cast workspace manifests disable their own test harnesses as documented elsewhere.

The semantic objects are indexed projections, not a second editable model: edits still target the source buffer, and the “New Rust item” flow modifies only the open buffer until explicit Save ([authoring flow](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/authoring.rs#L28-L70>)). The outline and diagnostics are bounded, useful inspection infrastructure. They do not yet provide the proposed full Rust ownership model: Vapor-managed crate metadata, enforced crate/module templates across content kinds, semantic refactors across all references, field-level component inspector actions, or shared policy consumption by CLI, service, CI and IDE.

There is also a design-level downgrade to make visible. The Oct 23 plan calls conventions “dogmatic defaults with explicit escape paths” ([plan invariant](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-23-semantic-workbench.md#L16-L20>)), whereas the owner described the canonical organization as an intended Vapor-enforced invariant, with narrowly understood cases allowed to remain ordinary source rather than making every rule optional. The likely reconciliation is not “warnings everywhere” or “ban all Rust layouts”: define which crate/content classes opt into the canonical contract, then make that selected contract authoritative and give exceptions an explicit declared representation. This is an interpretation of the two sources, not an owner-approved resolution.

Historical trajectory: `Vapor-GUI/e30cdac` (Oct 23, “Build the semantic IDE workbench”) adds the multi-format semantic model and IDE slice (+6,748/−490 across 18 files). GUI commits `320541c` and `7b8ebf6` then add IDE module creation and typed module kinds. Nested `Vapor/868bbc1` moves canonical Rust module creation behind a Client service operation (+743/−161 across 20 files, including adjacent protocol/build changes); `5743065` centralizes the nine-kind vocabulary. The sequence progresses from semantic visibility, to UI authoring, to service-owned filesystem mutation. It does not yet progress to a shared enforcement policy consumed by every authoring/build path. The source tree also contains an untracked `docs/superpowers/` directory in the nested Vapor checkout; it was not opened or modified, and this review does not assume it is part of the committed design.

### Evidence and limits

Read-only source, plan, guide and Git-history inspection across Vapor-GUI and the nested Vapor repository. No source files changed. No tests/builds ran. No runtime/editor interaction was observed. Confirmed: the IDE has semantic navigation and advisory convention diagnostics; module creation is a typed service operation; file ordering/labels have source-level test cases. Not established: successful current compilation, diagnostics behavior under every Rust syntax/macro pattern, actual user-facing visual quality, whether every semantic object class is selectable in all views, or whether rules are enforced outside the IDE.
## October 25 — the semantic model is shared; adapter authority is intentionally uneven

The IDE and shared GUI core use one bounded `SemanticObject`/diagnostic shape, but that does not mean all languages have equal semantic power. The common model caps one document at 2 MiB, 4,096 objects and 64 levels ([shared bounds](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/semantic.rs#L1-L18>)). The adapters deliberately project different things:

- **Rust:** Rust Analyzer supplies workspace-resolved declarations and language features; local syntax metadata adds selected roles and child projections. This is the strongest semantic adapter, but layout convention remains warning-only as described above.
- **Vapor/Cargo TOML:** `toml_edit` provides source spans and nested tables. `ContentKind::ALL` classifies the known authored manifest filenames; `AuthoredContentManifest::parse` adds source-anchored shape/role diagnostics to the shared content model. Semantic nodes annotate selected recognized fields but do not copy literal values into the outline. This is real shared-domain integration, though it is not a general manifest editor or complete validation UI ([TOML adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/toml_semantics.rs#L1-L156>)).
- **Rhai:** a bounded hand-written token/declaration projection exposes functions, parameters and bindings. The diagnostic path calls Rhai’s compiler to report syntax/parse errors but does not evaluate scripts or expose runtime capability semantics. The source comments explicitly label the outline syntax-only ([Rhai adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/rhai_semantics.rs#L1-L22>), [parse diagnostics](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/rhai_semantics.rs#L254-L292>)). This matches the current decision to keep live scripting in the game workbench, while falling short of the broader capability-graph-aware authoring environment discussed for a future IDE.
- **XML:** `quick_xml` produces generic element and attribute-name outlines and bounded parse diagnostics. It does not apply a domain schema, and element/attribute values remain only in source text ([XML projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/xml_semantics.rs#L1-L35>)).

The adapters therefore share identity, ranges, bounds, navigation and diagnostic presentation without pretending the languages share one parser or authority model. The source confirms useful common infrastructure, plus separate and intentionally incomplete domain readers. The plan’s broader work unit to “apply the shared contract” to Vapor content/Rhai/TOML/XML is partly implemented already; treating the entire adapter tranche as missing would be inaccurate. The remaining distinction is between outline, domain validation, execution, and edit operations—not merely whether a format is listed as supported.

### Evidence and limits

Current adapter source, shared semantic contract, and IDE guide inspected read-only. No checks ran. “Rhai compiles for syntax diagnostics” means the local diagnostic function invokes `rhai::Engine::compile`; it is not proof of runtime behavior, host registration, policy validation or safe execution. XML parsing does not establish schema validity. The 2 MiB/object/depth bounds are constants in source, not a measured responsiveness guarantee.

### The IDE has a sizeable focused test suite, but its boundary is mostly pure-model behavior

The currently checked-in `vapor_ide_ui/src/tests.rs` contains 65 unit tests. They cover Cargo diagnostic path resolution and producer provenance; diagnostic deduplication, filtering and virtualized materialization; Rust symbol/layout classification; bounded local outlines; stale LSP/document/workspace result rejection; UTF-8/UTF-16 position conversion; TOML/XML/Rhai parsing and source ranges; navigation labels/order; canonical module/item scaffolding; formatting/quick-fix edit validation; and source-save revision handling ([test inventory and cases](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/tests.rs#L1)). The crate manifest does not disable its test target, unlike several Loo-Cast engine crates. This is meaningful test design—not evidence that the tests pass today, because none were run in this review.

The suite is strongest where the code is deterministic and local: strings, paths, spans, stale-result predicates, bounded projections, and edit application. It does not itself establish the cross-process Rust Analyzer lifecycle, OS-specific service launch, LSP pipe ordering under concurrent GUI updates, true filesystem watcher behavior, multi-client workspace switching, or UI layout/interaction. Some of those have adjacent service tests or source traces elsewhere, but this file is not an end-to-end acceptance suite. Also, a passing pure helper test would not prove the corresponding screen calls that helper correctly. This distinction matters because the suite's size can otherwise be misread as broad IDE verification.

### Client protocol v33 centralizes typed actions, but its transport remains one JSON-line envelope

`vapor_client_protocol` is a substantial typed boundary, not just a bag of DTOs: it re-exports action families, durable composition records, operation/catalog snapshots, typed console events, semantic diagnostics and language-server status. Requests carry a frontend origin, expected revision, request ID and typed action; accepted responses separate the request's operation ID from the snapshot's primary active operation. The service and client both reject mismatched protocol versions. This aligns with the owner-directed single Client API and makes operation origin/identity inspectable ([protocol types and version](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/message.rs#L1), [public protocol surface and frame cap](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/lib.rs#L1-L63), [service handshake and validation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L160-L205)).

The actual local transport is newline-delimited JSON over a permission-restricted local socket/named pipe. It has a 32 MiB per-frame limit; outgoing service queues also have frame and byte capacities and reject additional output when full. Client input uses a bounded queue. This limits unbounded buffering, but the accepted single-frame ceiling is still large, and high-frequency Language Server Protocol JSON-RPC traffic shares the same outer connection and frame budget as ordinary service actions ([framing](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/transport.rs#L1-L48), [local endpoint permissions](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/local_socket.rs#L1-L87), [bounded outbound queue](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L680-L742)). The protocol crate has 16 tests for action/frame round-trips and additive defaults for older snapshot/payload shapes; the transport has tests for clean EOF, malformed text, oversized input and output. Those tests were not run. The additive-default cases do **not** make cross-version peers interoperable: service and client require exact protocol-version equality (v33). No measurement establishes practical latency, memory cost, starvation behavior, or compatibility of the deployed Steam payload. This is a source architecture description plus verification gap—not a claim that the current 32 MiB bound has caused a failure ([protocol test cases](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/lib.rs#L65-L1035)).

### Process-level tests cover the service boundary on one host, not the shipped platform matrix

The service integration test target contains 13 child-process tests. It exercises fixture startup/shutdown, request/event/snapshot ordering, typed Workshop search/acquisition/review and fixture-only publish refusal, fixture rejection of workspace builds, workspace run-configuration resolution, composition-state import/persistence across service restart, and the checked-in simulator scenarios ([process tests](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/tests/process.rs#L1-L1035)). This is more than unit testing of the session reducer: the tests launch the built service process and use the real Client framing path. The test source has explicit fixture/production host configurations, but the suite is still executed only for the host on which Cargo builds/runs it; no current Windows result is available here, and Steam UGC, SteamPipe, Rust Analyzer, target cross-compilation and front-end rendering are not exercised by these fixtures. No tests were run in this research pass. Therefore earlier descriptions that called the whole system “untested” need qualification: service process semantics do have focused host-local integration coverage, while the user's Windows startup, live Workshop, and full depot flows remain distinct unverified acceptance paths.
## October 25 — `vapor_gui_core` is a useful seed, not the promised egui workbench toolkit

There is already a shared GUI crate, so the accurate diagnosis is not “every frontend is built from scratch.” `vapor_gui_core` currently provides a code editor wrapper (including syntax highlighting and source-range selection), filterable/virtualized console controls, a small titled Panel surface, vector-drawn console severity marks, shared semantic models/indexes, a workspace path tree, and Rhai semantic projection. Launcher and IDE both consume the console state/record conversion; Launcher uses the shared Panel and severity icons; IDE uses the code editor and semantic model ([public core surface](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/lib.rs>), [Panel](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/panel.rs>), [code editor](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/code_editor.rs>), [console](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/console.rs>)). Some duplication has genuinely been removed.

The toolkit boundary remains narrow and mixed-purpose. The reviewed public widget surface has no reusable split-layout/resizable-dock system, general button/toolbar/menu vocabulary, cross-product panel layout policy, application-preview harness, or component-gallery workflow. IDE layout still directly assembles `egui::TopBottomPanel`, `SidePanel`, `CentralPanel`, `ScrollArea` and resizing; the shared `Panel` is a compact card-like frame, not a layout contract. Several different concerns live side by side in `vapor_gui_core`: visual widgets, editor rendering, console interaction, semantic index data, workspace trees and a Rhai parser. This is a functional shared crate but not yet the deliberately designed “hypercharge egui” library described by the owner.

One useful measure of incompleteness is reuse asymmetry: `ConsolePanelState` is shared across Launcher and IDE, and the IDE/Launcher each own the rendering location; the public `show_records` helper has no current caller in the inspected frontend source. Meanwhile most screen-specific panel and layout decisions remain inside `vapor_launcher_ui` and `vapor_ide_ui`. That is not automatically wrong—product-specific composition belongs in those frontends—but it means the core currently standardizes selected controls and data contracts rather than visual rhythm, interaction states, navigation, panel geometry or responsive behavior. Source search found no UI-preview app or toolkit specification in the inspected Vapor-GUI docs/crates; this supports “not located in this repo slice,” not a claim that no mockup or plan exists elsewhere.

The UI host also still centralizes multiple products as `GuiMode` values, including Launcher, Studio, Chooser, Installer and IDE, with a shared `run_product` host and dark-theme initialization ([host contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/lib.rs#L12-L72>)). This is direct evidence of one GUI-host architecture with product frontends/modes; it does not establish the currently published Steam executable/entrypoint mapping or visual behavior on Windows. The code boundary is thus partly separated (`vapor_launcher_ui`, `vapor_ide_ui`) and partly umbrella-hosted (`vapor_gui`); Installer remains in the umbrella crate. Any future toolkit migration should first identify which screen responsibilities really share layout and interaction semantics, instead of turning every repeated egui call into a generic abstraction.

This current slice should be cross-read with the earlier console finding: record/history/filtering and a few widgets are shared, while command authority, full console geometry and game F2 integration remain separate. It also narrows the owner’s requested future: there is enough existing machinery to extend and review, but no evidence yet of an IDE-like live UI lab that makes rapid layout iteration cheap.

### Evidence and limits

Read-only inventory of the `Vapor-GUI` crate tree and direct call-site search. No GUI was opened, no performance or interaction behavior was measured, and no toolkit design spec was found in the searched docs/crates. The unused public `show_records` function finding is scoped to current frontend references in this checkout; it may be intended for downstream consumers. Do not infer that a custom toolkit should absorb all raw egui or that the current core has no value.

## October 25 — the Engine/Game split is a package-label boundary, not yet a source or dependency boundary

The current workspace has three Cargo members: `spacetime-engine`, `loo-cast-game`, and `loo-cast-packagepack`. The Game library is a 17-line adapter: it supplies a stable content ID/title and installs `spacetime_engine::game::LooCastGamePlugin` plus `LooCastDeveloperAdaptersPlugin` ([adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-game/src/lib.rs#L1-L16>)). The Packagepack binary calls `spacetime_engine::run(loo_cast_game::install)` ([entrypoint](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-packagepack/src/main.rs#L1-L5>)). This is a real static-link composition shape: the executable depends on both Cargo libraries. It is not yet proof that Vapor's resolved content graph generates those Cargo edges or can substitute an independently acquired Game artifact. The three current authored identities are Engine, Game and Packagepack ([declared workspace projects](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/Workspace.vapor.toml#L15-L23>), [Engine artifact](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/Engine.vapor.toml#L3-L6>), [Game artifact](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-game/Game.vapor.toml#L3-L6>)); there is no separate Vapor `Crate` identity in this workspace. Thus the modules that describe themselves as generic remain in the Engine package’s `src/game` tree rather than independently addressable Crate content. This is the precise current-state gap behind the owner's request to make reusable modules Vapor-managed Crates; it does not mean every module should be split into a crate.

The scale is material: `spacetime-engine/src/game` contains 158 Git-tracked Rust files and 20,226 source lines at `c070bf3`. This count includes comments and blanks; it is not semantic LOC, and this pass did not classify every file. The full top-level inventory, with purpose descriptions taken from the module map in source, is:

| Module | Files / source lines | Declared scope |
|---|---:|---|
| `player` | 36 / 4,147 | Local-player gameplay and presentation |
| `playground` | 23 / 2,753 | Reusable in-game test playground |
| `console_commands` | 13 / 2,227 | Loo-Cast commands over generic developer console |
| `locomotion` | 13 / 2,152 | Generic controlled-subject locomotion |
| `navigation` | 17 / 2,143 | Generic controlled-subject navigation and travel policy |
| `world` | 10 / 1,478 | Loo-Cast scenario bootstrap, authored fixtures, scenario lifetime |
| `spacecraft` | 9 / 1,165 | Reference spacecraft built from generic USF/control primitives |
| `devtools` | 8 / 733 | Loo-Cast adapters into generic developer facilities |
| `flight` | 7 / 1,028 | Flight policy, contact/safety state and derived telemetry |
| `health` | 6 / 579 | Generic damageable state, damage and death |
| `control` | 3 / 498 | Semantic and local runtime control authority |
| `orbit` | 1 / 274 | Canonical orbital mechanics shared by simulation, prediction and presentation |
| `surface` | 1 / 273 | Read-only physical-surface proximity telemetry |
| `combat` | 5 / 260 | Weapons, projectiles and manifestation-space hit detection |
| `item` | 4 / 258 | Generic item identity, metadata, actions and presentation |
| `mod.rs` | 1 / 214 | Composition root, schedule and plugin wiring |
| `inventory` | 1 / 44 | Generic local inventory-selection state |

This is not one undifferentiated gameplay block. The table gives structural scope, not a semantic disposition for each file.

Its own module map mixes ownership claims. `player`, `world`, `playground`, `spacecraft`, and `console_commands` are visibly Loo-Cast-facing or scenario/reference-specific. Yet `health`, `inventory`, `item`, `locomotion`, and `navigation` explicitly call themselves generic; `flight` calls itself policy/state/telemetry; `orbit` calls its mechanics canonical and shared. Those descriptions are evidence of intended reuse, but do not establish that each abstraction is stable, sufficiently generic, or correctly owned by Engine. Conversely, placement under `game/` does not prove a capability must remain Game-specific. The accurate conclusion is that this is a mixed semantic domain requiring module-by-module classification against real consumers, not a mechanical directory move. The source module map is at [game/mod.rs](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/mod.rs#L1-L29>).

There is a concrete extraction obstacle beyond directory placement. `spacetime-engine/src/physics/collision_query/runtime.rs` orders generic-looking Engine collision-query sets before and after `crate::game::locomotion::LocomotionSet::Prepare` ([reverse edge](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/physics/collision_query/runtime.rs#L47-L60>)). The Game composition also orders Game locomotion with Engine physics gravity and character reference-frame resolution ([composition schedule](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/mod.rs#L103-L124>)); that direction is expected for a composition root. The physics reference goes back from Engine into Game. Both modules currently share one Cargo crate, so this is not a Cargo dependency cycle, but it is a semantic reverse edge that prevents clean crate extraction until the schedule contract moves to a neutral interface or adapter. The narrow search found no other exact `crate::game`/`spacetime_engine::game` imports outside the Game subtree; that is not a full dependency proof.

The Engine root says game-specific orchestration lives under `game`, and reusable Engine domains should not depend on it except through explicit adapters ([root boundary note](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/lib.rs#L34-L41>)). The collision-query schedule dependency is not visibly identified as such an adapter. This is a documented rule contradicted by one concrete implementation edge. At the same time, the API seam itself is real: `SpacetimeEnginePlugin` installs baseline Engine facilities, and `EngineApp`/`run(install_game)` lets the selected game extend that host ([Engine host contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/lib.rs#L63-L112>)). The critique is therefore not “there is no separation”; it is that identity, composition, Cargo ownership, module ownership, and schedule dependency have advanced to different degrees.

### Historical cross-check and implication

The July 7 fresh workspace established sibling Engine/Game/Packagepack identities before they had meaningful implementations or Cargo dependencies ([bootstrap history](</home/leslieghf/.codex/.chatgpt-projects/g-p-6ab69f33d17481919fb92a0c5592210c/artifacts/loo-cast-vapor-history-timeline.md#loo-cast-chronology>)). Later, `loo-cast-game` became a distinct content identity while its implementation remained in `spacetime_engine::game`; the October 17 Packagepack binary made static linking real without moving that implementation. The latest 158-file subtree shows this is no longer a tiny temporary stub in practical scope, even though its package adapter remains tiny. The history therefore contains distinct milestones that must not be collapsed: semantic identity, executable static composition, and source ownership. Only the first two are evidenced as implemented.

This connects to the owner's definition: Engine provides reusable capability; Game composes it into a particular game; Rust is allowed in either and is not the semantic discriminator. Current code does not make that division inspectable at the Cargo/module boundary. The consequential open work is not simply “move game code”: classify existing modules as reusable Engine capability, Loo-Cast-specific policy/content, or an adapter; then express schedule contracts without Engine importing Game implementation. Cross-check those decisions against actual consumers and the content-graph plan before migration. This review leaves that classification open rather than answering it on the owner's behalf.

### Evidence and limits

Read-only inspection of the current workspace manifests, three crate roots, `game/mod.rs`, the Engine crate root, and collision-query schedule reference; Git-tracked Rust inventory at `c070bf3`. Source status was unchanged. No build, test, runtime/UI run, full per-file semantic classification, or extraction prototype was performed. The 20,226-line count is reproducible inventory, not evidence that every line is useful or that a target LOC is justified. Module descriptions and package edges show where a deeper ownership audit is necessary; they do not settle the final placement of each feature.

## October 25 — player composition and runtime developer tools are not role-separated in the binary

The ordinary Packagepack entrypoint does not choose a reduced player-only Engine/Game build. `spacetime-engine/Cargo.toml` has no `devtools` feature; its only declared features concern profiling, while the default feature set is empty ([feature list](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/Cargo.toml#L11-L16>)). `SpacetimeEnginePlugin` always installs `DeveloperToolsPlugin` and `DeveloperConsolePlugin` ([Engine plugin list](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/lib.rs#L80-L105>)). The `loo-cast-game` adapter always adds `LooCastDeveloperAdaptersPlugin` beside `LooCastGamePlugin` ([Game installation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-game/src/lib.rs#L11-L16>)). Thus the code and dependencies for Bevy Inspector, egui docking, developer visualization, script-workbench support and game-specific developer adapters are part of the same statically linked composition, not opt-in Rust features at the Cargo boundary.

The normal DeveloperTools overlay starts disabled and toggles on F3 ([default and toggle](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/tools/mod.rs#L45-L70>), [F3 handler](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/mod.rs#L135-L139>)). Separately, the editor shell installs unconditionally and its F2 handler changes `PrimaryViewPresentation` from immersive to embedded with no `DeveloperTools::enabled()` or Vapor-role check ([shell install and F2 path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/devtools/editor/shell/mod.rs#L62-L134>)). The editor includes hierarchy, semantic and ECS inspectors, gizmos, resource inspection and asset inspection; the generic DeveloperTools plugin also configures the script workbench. The checked source path contains inspect-edit and inspect-action request surfaces. This demonstrates a reachable, compiled developer-editor path in the same game executable by source structure. It does not prove a deployed release shipped the current checkout or reproduce the key path in a running game.

This is not automatically a security vulnerability: the inspected behavior is a local game process and this review did not establish a remote trust boundary. It is a clear product/role boundary question, because the user's player/composer/developer tiers are currently represented in Vapor installation state, while the gameplay binary's F2/F3 paths do not consume that state. It may be intentional to ship discoverable editing/debug tools to all players; it may instead be intended for Developer-only compositions, a launch-time role capability, or compile-time targets. The current source does not encode which policy is intended. The distinction also matters to the Engine/Game decision: shared Engine devtools may be reusable capability, while Loo-Cast focus/inspection adapters and actual gameplay editor policy are Game-specific. Moving files alone will not decide who receives the capability.

### Evidence and limits

Read-only inspection of the current Cargo feature declarations, Engine and Game plugin composition, DeveloperTools default/toggle, and editor-shell F2 handler. No build-feature matrix or deployed binary was inspected; no role was read from the running game. No source worktree was changed. Treat “available in this source-built composition” as confirmed and “present in the deployed Steam build” as unverified.

## October 25 — the checked-in default Vapor run configuration names a removed Engine binary

The workspace default still selects Cargo package `spacetime-engine`, binary `spacetime-engine` ([run table](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/Workspace.vapor.toml#L29-L44>)). But the Engine member's `Cargo.toml` declares only `[lib]` and no `[[bin]]` target ([Engine manifest](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/Cargo.toml#L1-L11>)); its `src/` root contains `lib.rs` and `reconstructible.rs`, with no `main.rs`. The actual runnable target is `loo-cast-packagepack`, whose `main.rs` statically composes Engine and Game. The current workspace's run configuration therefore points at a binary target absent from the checked-in Cargo package.

This is not merely a stale label that Vapor silently repairs. The managed `vapor run` path resolves the named profile, then constructs `cargo run --manifest-path Cargo.toml`, adding the configured `--package` and `--bin` literally ([run executor](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/run.rs#L241-L283>)). Source inspection therefore predicts Cargo target-selection failure for this default profile; no command was run to capture its exact diagnostic. `profiling`, `profiling-memory`, and `full-debug` inherit the same default selection, so changing profile or adding Tracy features does not repair the missing binary. This is distinct from Steam Packagepack launch, which resolves an installed Packagepack runtime artifact, and from the October report that Windows launched the deployed Loo-Cast composition successfully. Those facts can both hold while source `vapor run` is stale.

The history pinpoints the divergence. October 17 commit [`4551c53`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/4551c534bf5ad9debd2fc51364de93f7ad995e1b) deletes `spacetime-engine/src/main.rs`, adds `loo-cast-packagepack/src/main.rs`, and moves the executable role to Packagepack; its `Workspace.vapor.toml` diff adds the three project entries but leaves the existing default run profile untouched. October 20 adds runtime target declarations and a `full-debug` profile, while also leaving the selected package/binary unchanged. This is a commit-diff-confirmed stale configuration, not a runtime-confirmed failure. It is also an architectural question: source-run should likely use the Packagepack to exercise the actual player composition, while a separate engine-only harness—if still useful—needs a real binary/example target and explicit name. The current checked-in profiles do not encode that distinction.

### Evidence and limits

Read-only comparison of `Workspace.vapor.toml`, root workspace members, Engine and Packagepack Cargo manifests/source roots, Packagepack `main.rs`, and Vapor's managed run command construction. No build or `vapor run` command was executed. The absent `spacetime-engine` bin target is confirmed by the inspected manifest/source tree; the exact error wording and behavior of the current pinned Cargo version are not runtime-verified. Steam launch and the reported Windows launch remain separate evidence.

## October 25 — the Client protocol is the product state surface, not a thin transport DTO layer

The current `vapor_client_protocol` crate has eight Rust files and 2,650 source lines. `action.rs` is an eight-line re-export of the domain's `ClientAction` family; `composition.rs` re-exports domain composition records and adds a legacy-storage import seed; `state.rs` defines the cross-frontend snapshot and event surface; `message.rs` defines newline-delimited request/response/event frames; `semantic.rs` defines editor object references; and `language_server.rs` bounds and parses a selected subset of LSP diagnostics. `catalog.rs` supplies literal case-insensitive search, not compatibility or install policy. The crate depends on `vapor_client_domain`, `vapor_console_core`, and `vapor_telemetry`, and publicly re-exports domain actions and types. It provides a typed serialized IPC contract, but does **not** isolate wire DTOs from domain definitions: domain type evolution is wire evolution, with one shared exact version constant. That may be the deliberate “same API” strategy the owner described; it is not a stable compatibility adapter around an independently evolving domain.

The protocol carries multiple interaction kinds through one connection: Client action requests, state snapshots, operation/output events, language-server JSON-RPC messages and semantic diagnostics, plus telemetry. Client origins currently enumerate Launcher, Studio, IDE, Installer, CLI and Unknown. There is no Chooser or launched Game/Composition origin, and the request origin is a client-supplied enum rather than authenticated process identity. `RequestId` is an unconstrained string at the protocol boundary; the normal Client generates a process/time prefix plus monotone counter, but the service does not validate uniqueness or length before echoing it. The local socket ACL and app-root/state-directory endpoint scoping provide the surrounding local boundary; these protocol fields alone should not be treated as trusted attribution or authorization.

Every `ClientResponse` embeds a complete `ClientSnapshot`; the service then broadcasts another complete snapshot after the request. The snapshot includes durable state, catalog, composition preview, Superworkspace projection, Workshop, operations, role/tool readiness, profiles, release/publishing state and available actions. This is a clear state-reconciliation contract and helps a frontend recover after missed events. It also makes the ordinary request path pay for both a response snapshot and a broadcast snapshot, in addition to the separate snapshot rediscovery cost described above. Frames are capped at 32 MiB; the service allows up to eight local clients, each with an outbound queue capped at 40 MiB. Those configured limits bound serialized outbound queues at up to 320 MiB in aggregate, before accounting for session state, cloned snapshots, encoding buffers, child tools or other process memory. This is a capacity ceiling derived from constants, not measured peak usage or proof that the process reaches it.

The same state surface does not preserve static typing uniformly. `ClientSnapshot` exports `ContentKind`, but catalog/workspace/acquisition/authoring `kind` values are generally strings; `InstallationRoleSnapshot.role`, `HostSummary.mode`, and several repository kinds are strings too. `CatalogEntry` also carries both a human-readable `dependencies: Vec<String>` compatibility projection and a structured `dependency_details` vector, while `CatalogQuery` searches the display labels. This preserves display and potentially unknown values, but the protocol has no explicit typed-known/opaque-unknown wrapper for artifact kind and role; consumers repeatedly parse or compare serialized spellings. The resulting boundary can enforce action/profile and some lifecycle semantics centrally, but cannot rely on every snapshot fact being a validated domain enum. The older dependency labels were added as serde-defaulted/omitted-when-empty fields without changing version 30 (`25aeced`), so that specific additive compatibility is real; later changes to operation identity and diagnostic/origin payloads did bump the exact protocol version. This is narrower and more accurate than calling all fields untyped or all old clients compatible.

The history shows a fast-expanding contract. The shared-service extraction (`f9e8b13`, October 18) starts at protocol version 13. By October 20–23, recorded changes advance through versions 21–33, including workspace/deploy/documentation actions, bounded output and cancellation, LSP transport, per-request operation identity, and structured semantic/diagnostic events. Some commits batch multiple version increments (for example 23→25, 27→30, 31→33), so the numeric sequence is not a one-commit-per-version ledger. Both service startup and each request require exact equality; mismatches are rejected, not negotiated. For binaries delivered together in one depot this is a reasonable fail-fast contract, but it makes stale sibling executables and an old still-running service a hard incompatibility. The source's 15-second idle shutdown reduces, but does not eliminate, version skew during deployment or manual launches. No mixed-version process scenario was exercised.

This is a useful diagnostic lens for the user's “one coherent service/API” goal: that direction is materially implemented, including per-request operation identity that avoids confusing a request's operation with another active operation. Yet attribution, state reconciliation, domain/wire versioning and process lifetime remain distinct contracts. The product API is broad and increasingly cross-domain, while snapshots and operation semantics remain coupled to an exact build of all frontends. That is not automatically over-engineering or a defect; the key unanswered design question is whether the local service supports only lockstep depot siblings or independently updated clients/IDE/CLI, because the current wire contract implements the former.

### Historical cross-check and evidence limits

Source and Git history checked at Vapor `5743065` (October 23): protocol crate modules and manifests; request creation and handshake in `vapor_client`; local service handshake/request handling and queue constants; and protocol evolution commits from `f9e8b13` through `4fe3ab2`. The `CatalogEntry` history at `25aeced` specifically adds structured dependency details while retaining labels at protocol version 30; later operation identity and diagnostic/origin payload changes advance the version. Current source contains focused frame-size, malformed-frame, version-rejection, queue-budget, LSP diagnostic-bound and semantic-range tests; these were inspected but not run. No process was launched, no stale frontend/service combination was tested, and the 320 MiB queue ceiling was not profiled. The protocol tree is mapped at module/ownership level; its 2,650 lines and individual test cases have not each received line annotations.

## October 25 — camera choices exist, but control and presentation are still split across paths

The current player camera model is more deliberate than a simple global “Q/T rotates the camera” implementation. `PlayerCamera` stores the one primary camera's mode/orbit rotation/FOV; `ViewCameraProfile` on the local view target stores per-subject supported modes, orientation authority, eye geometry and third-person tuning. The reference spacecraft supports Cockpit/Chase/Orbit, characters support only first/third person. F5 cycles supported modes; `camera cockpit|chase|orbit` offers direct console selection. Third-person boom resolves scale-aware physical-metre settings through collision and portal crossings, with collision distance kept separate from persistent zoom intent. Orbit mode routes mouse movement to observer orientation; for inertial flight outside Orbit, the camera follows the craft, mouse delta instead feeds the pilot's angular-rate intent, and keyboard Q/E are actual ship roll inputs. The user's earlier complaint that Q/T altered camera state is not what this current input map says: current defaults bind Q/E to roll, F5 to camera cycle, and no T key appears in the default map. This current source does not establish what was deployed at the time of the report.

Selection is nevertheless narrow and fragmented. There is one cycle key plus a game-console command; no inspected camera-selection panel or direct per-mode binding exists. Cockpit free-look is absent for the spacecraft's `SubjectAttitude` policy: the current model offers ship-locked cockpit, horizon-stabilized chase and independently rotated orbit, but no temporary head-look/look-around state. Third-person tuning is target-owned; the primary `PlayerCamera` itself is still a singleton/global entity queried separately. The `camera` console command first checks the local profile for Orbit availability, then mutates the first `PlayerCamera`; source assumes one local subject/camera and does not prove those two queries designate the same view if multiple subjects are introduced. This is a known single-player boundary, not a reproduced multi-camera failure.

Debug freecam is a separate observer path, not a player movement mode. Its current default is disabled, exclusive of gameplay input, USF projection Follow and view-demand Frozen. It consumes the same semantic device bindings, moves at a base 20 m/s with an 8× fast modifier, and permits one live Rhai scalar transform clamped to 1e9 m/s. Movement uses the PlayerController's look sensitivity, converts metres into the current view target's scale-local units, and directly translates the primary camera transform without collision casts; this is noclip relative to the ordinary movement collision path, not a separate camera entity or arbitrary canonical-motion owner ([frame movement and speed transform](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/camera/freecam/movement.rs#L22-L109>), [canonical observer bridge](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/player/camera/freecam/observer.rs#L20-L91>)). Projection Follow can move the presentation observer while the default view-demand policy remains Frozen, so freecam does not automatically request newly visible presentation data. That deliberate separation protects gameplay-owned dense demand but means the camera may travel beyond loaded/presented geometry unless a developer changes demand policy. The one-speed-plus-boost control resembles the requested characteristic travel-speed knob, but the control is linear m/s, not a logarithmic speed-range selector. There is no persistence or dedicated compact UX in the inspected resource; console runtime variables and the developer preset are its visible controls. The resource and primary camera remain singletons rather than entries in a camera/observer registry.

The HUD is telemetry-backed, but the layout is authored in fixed screen pixels: 260-pixel wings, 125-pixel center gap, fixed top offset and 14–15-pixel text, with a 22-pixel Unicode diamond marker. The velocity marker is projected using camera-space direction and fixed ±110-pixel clamping rather than viewport/FOV projection. This yields concrete resolution/font/readability risks that source cannot settle without seeing the rendered game. Binding-aware alert labels exist; a separate contextual-help builder still spells some scroll modifiers literally and has a fixed 16-row cap, as established in the October 9 review. `PlayerInputBindings` is a runtime-only Bevy resource with console `bind`/`unbind`/`unbindall`; this path provides configurable execution but no inspected save/load route. Thus camera modes and semantic actions are not wholly absent, but “available” means source-level mode state/console operation, not a cohesive selectable, persistent and contextually taught camera UX.

### Historical cross-check and evidence limits

The focused current-source read covers the `player` crate-root wiring, camera model/input/pose/freecam, semantic binding registry and mutation model, camera console command, and HUD formatter/layout/update path. The freecam-specific implementation was introduced as v2 in October 1 `cffbab6a` and extracted into `movement`, `observer` and `policy` modules during October 6 `ab65b8e`; the latter is organization change, not a new independently validated camera product ([v2 introduction](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/cffbab6a3a16c41944e53e3409292dfd532b5e7b), [module extraction](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/ab65b8e2190a42e81f1bbae6b22a090297d8d987)). This cross-checks the October 9 `46e1eac` player/HUD/controls changes and existing source review of the user-reported camera/control issue and binding-help omissions. No deployed binary, screenshot, resolution matrix, input rebinding, camera transition or freecam session was run. The fixed-pixel observations and code paths are source-confirmed; streaming sufficiency, projection continuity, clipping, visual quality and perceived camera behavior remain unverified. This completes a focused cross-domain slice, not all 3,459 lines in the player-facing modules or the full `game` subtree.

## October 25 — Installer is a partial service facade with a second bootstrap owner

### Current product and ownership shape

`Vapor-Installer` is a separate Vapor workspace and repository, currently at `0.5.0`; its two Rust packages are a precompiled CLI shim and an eframe UI product module hosted inside Vapor-GUI. The workspace pins Rust `1.97.0` in its Vapor manifest and uses eframe `0.36.2` ([workspace](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/Workspace.vapor.toml>), [Cargo workspace](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/Cargo.toml>), [README product boundary](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/README.md#L1-L18>)). The installer UI itself is a 913-line single Rust file; the standalone CLI/parser, bridge, and entrypoint bring the repository's handwritten Rust total to 1,332 lines. This is not evidence that the implementation is necessarily too large: it identifies where most Installer behavior currently lives and which boundary is doing the work.

The Installer is not yet a facade over one service API for all operations. `InstallerApp::new` resolves an explicit app root or discovers it locally through `VaporInstallation`, then creates the GUI's own Core installation value ([root selection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L41-L85>)). Its Status, Install, Repair, and Uninstall actions call `vapor_core` directly on background threads. Role refresh and role transitions instead connect through `vapor_client::Client` to the Client service ([direct local operations](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L87-L157>), [service action path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L515-L608>)). A role change is now a service-owned background operation with an accepted operation ID; the Installer waits for that matching operation to finish and then refreshes role state. This is a genuine shared-service integration, but only for the role subdomain.

The service-backed role path is a meaningful foundation, not merely an IPC wrapper: the service registers a background operation context, promotion passes that context into Core developer-environment reconciliation, and the role receipt is persisted only after reconciliation succeeds. This action is marked non-cancellable in the service's action policy. Demotion intentionally changes the role receipt without deleting the developer tools, caches or authored source ([service dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L1307-L1365>), [background-operation policy](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L1650-L1690>), [Core promotion/demotion semantics](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/role.rs#L140-L221>)). However, the Installer discards most of the available operation stream presentation, and Core role state is still resolved again by service-side application code rather than passed from the Installer as an explicit installation identity. The boundary is therefore partially integrated, with some robust operation machinery already in place.

That service operation reservation does not cover the Installer's direct local Install/Repair/Uninstall or first-run helper jobs. The service maps `installation-role` to `InstallationTools`, but those local tasks never register a corresponding reservation with the service ([service resource mapping](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L711-L755>), [Installer local task dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L87-L184>)). Another frontend can therefore request a role reconciliation while the Installer is directly mutating installation state, or vice versa; the Installer's own busy state only gates its own window. This is a source-derived cross-process concurrency risk, not a reproduced race.

First launch adds a third execution path: setup calls Core installation locally, invokes the precompiled player's setup helper in-process, and only then asks the service to promote the selected role. The user is required to finish this flow before Play ([setup sequence](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L146-L184>), [mandatory setup screen](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L240-L300>)). That design matches the owner's direction that first launch must require setup and select a role, but it splits one user-visible transaction across Core, the embedded tool implementation, and the Client service. In particular, the Installer checks the Player receipt as one gate and the selected role snapshot/readiness as another; earlier review found those predicates do not always describe the same completion state. This is cross-referenced in [Installer role and setup state](#october-25--installer-role-and-setup-state-do-not-share-one-authority).

Play does not launch a composition through the Client service: the Installer searches beside its current executable for `vapor`, starts `vapor launch default` with the app root as cwd and `VAPOR_HOME`, suppresses all three standard streams, and closes the Installer window if process creation succeeds ([launch bridge](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L194-L225>)). This is a small direct-launch adapter, not proof that composition verification/launch succeeded; the child result is intentionally invisible to the user in this path. The service may still own later work performed by the Vapor Shell, but the Installer does not receive or display that outcome.

### What the precompiled CLI actually owns

The Installer CLI compiles the checked-in app-root tool implementation into its executable by path-including `resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools.rs`; it does not invoke a Rust script runner or require a preinstalled Rust toolchain ([bridge module](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer/src/script_bridge.rs#L1-L9>), [Installer README](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/README.md#L8-L18>)). That satisfies a real bootstrapping constraint: installation must work before the managed toolchain is available. It does not unify the capability with the Client service. The embedded implementation directly creates directories, invokes downloads/extractors, writes setup receipts and shell/Windows PATH integration, installs SteamCMD and developer tools, and removes managed paths ([shared player setup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/app_setup.rs>), [shared entrypoints](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/entrypoints.rs>)). It is a second executable owner for some app-root lifecycle semantics, even though the domain primitives and reports also exist in `vapor_core`.

The CLI help describes `--app-root`, `--dry-run`, and `--quiet`; the parser stores those values. However, the common `run_tool` path uses `--dry-run` only to print a planned operation and otherwise passes `options.app_root` and `quiet` to `script_bridge::run` ([CLI option model/parser](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer/src/cli.rs#L6-L18>), [help and route](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer/src/cli.rs#L27-L84>), [dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer/src/cli.rs#L190-L205>)). The bridge names these parameters `_app_root` and `_quiet`, discards them, and invokes no-argument functions which reparse process arguments and environment themselves ([bridge implementation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer/src/script_bridge.rs#L37-L52>)). Thus `--app-root` can still be found by the included script through `env::args`, but the advertised in-process API does not pass an explicit root as data; correctness depends on the delegated implementation reparsing ambient process state. `--quiet` is accepted then has no effect on the delegated operations. The dry-run output is descriptive rather than a structured plan generated by the operation being previewed. This is a source-confirmed interface/implementation mismatch, not a claim that every CLI invocation fails.

There are also two different meanings of setup. Core's `install_installation_for` establishes state and the canonical Superworkspace plus machine command integration; the embedded `setup_player` creates app-local player directories, obtains app-local SteamCMD, writes the root anchor and Player receipt. Core has explicit typed `UninstallOptions` for external-user-data and Superworkspace purging, with preflight protection; the Installer UI currently calls `uninstall_installation_for` with `UninstallOptions::default()` and explicitly says it preserves user data and authored source ([Core install owner](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/install.rs#L34-L64>), [Core uninstall contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/uninstall.rs#L1-L120>), [Installer's conservative call](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L130-L140>)). “Uninstall” is therefore not the requested “remove everything outside the Steam depot” operation: Core removes selected integration/state but does not delete the Steam App Instance root, leaving depot file removal to Steam. With default options, if legacy `<installation>/state` exists, Core migrates it into the OS user-data tree (merging only missing legacy files if external state already exists) before deleting the legacy copy; this is a migration, not a purge ([migration](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/installation.rs#L130-L175>), [uninstall ordering](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/uninstall.rs#L62-L101>)). The implementation also always removes legacy `rustup-home`, `cargo-home`, and `development` directories inside the installation root, even with default options; the opt-in `purge_app_external` removes the external user-data root and legacy `state` directory; the opt-in `purge_superworkspace` removes the canonical Superworkspace only after validating its top-level contents and first-party Git checkouts. Both purge flags default false ([options and execution](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/uninstall.rs#L1-L120>), [legacy app-local cleanup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/uninstall.rs#L265-L290>)).

The destructive purge guard is more qualified than “read-only preflight.” It rejects unknown/symlink Superworkspace top-level entries, checks repository origin, worktree cleanliness, submodule state, local-only branches and unpublished tags before deleting the tree. However, `ensure_git_checkout_safe` runs `git fetch --quiet --prune origin` as part of those checks ([preflight and tree validation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/uninstall.rs#L77-L160>), [repository checks and fetch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/uninstall.rs#L640-L720>)). Thus the purge can mutate each source checkout's Git metadata and requires network access before deletion; it is not an observationally read-only safety check. Its “expected origin” test only checks whether the normalized remote string ends with `GHF-Studios/<repo>` and does not pin or verify the hosting authority, so a remote on another host with that suffix can satisfy the check ([origin predicate](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/uninstall.rs#L596-L611>)). The top-level `.idea` and `.run` directories are accepted without content inspection, then removed with the whole Superworkspace; this is consistent with a full explicit purge, but must be named in a reviewable destructive-action summary ([allowed entries](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/uninstall.rs#L546-L591>)). The September 15 commit calls this change “Make uninstall purge transactional,” but the implementation is preflighted rather than atomic: it removes legacy app-local state first, then the Superworkspace, then external app state, and only afterwards machine integration. A mid-delete or integration failure can therefore leave a partially completed uninstall; machine integration being last only ensures safety-validation refusals happen before that final step. Windows PATH removal has another target mismatch: install integration selects `HostTarget::current()` (including `x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm`), while uninstall only derives a PATH entry under an MSVC build and returns without cleaning it for other Windows ABI builds ([install target choice](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/install.rs#L74-L90>), [host target mapping](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/host.rs#L53-L100>), [uninstall PATH branch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/uninstall.rs#L419-L430>)). For the supported GNU-linked Windows Vapor binary, this means the current code can leave its user-PATH entry behind. The source check also has a time-of-check/time-of-use interval between validation and recursive deletion. The two unit tests in this module cover only managed shell-profile and legacy-anchor matching, not either purge path. These are confirmed code properties; no purge was executed, and this review does not claim a demonstrated data-loss event.

### History, strengths, and systemic consequence

The current split is historically understandable. The July 18 precompiled bootstrap began as an app-root script tool; July 27 collapsed setup into shared app-root tools and moved workflows into a compiled control surface. On October 14, `0a49cee` added the GUI module, and October 20–23 commits then bound it to an explicitly selected app root, added role management, resolved the service beside target-specific binaries, made setup mandatory on first launch, tracked accepted service operation identity, and kept promotion choices available when toolchain readiness checks fail (`0a49cee`, `85d3ecf`, `c11a791`, `ccd5ecb`, `2592142`, `0a84194`, `d1b38d4`, `b3ddcf9`; [repository history](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer>)). Each change addresses a concrete user-observed failure: a separate installer entrypoint, wrong app-root context, Windows target-subdirectory service lookup, missing first-run gate, and role setup operations whose completion must be observed. The accumulated path is capable, but its boundaries grew around the failure at hand rather than from one fully shared application lifecycle API.

What is already strong and should be counted accurately: installation and teardown domain APIs are centralized in `vapor_core`; role-changing operations are sent to and tracked by the Client service; long-running UI work is dispatched off the egui frame; service lookup derives from the active executable's target-specific directory; uninstall's default preserves user data and authored source; and Core's opt-in purge performs a preflight before mutation. The current problem is **incomplete authority convergence**, not absence of all shared machinery. The service protocol can already own asynchronous, attributable operations, while the UI and CLI still execute substantial lifecycle work out of process or through a compile-time copy of the tool implementation. As the owner's goal puts it, Launcher, Studio, IDE, Installer and CLI should be different facades over the same service/API; today's Installer is the clearest counterexample to that intended product boundary.

This causes more than code duplication. The UI, CLI, service, Steam entrypoint and shell can observe different phases and failure messages for the same conceptual action; a maintenance operation bypasses service scheduling/progress/log-origin and service-instance coordination; and a successful `Command::spawn` is rendered as completion before the launched composition has reported success. These are architectural consequences visible from call ownership, not measured reports of races or user-visible failure in every current path. The right future audit questions are: what must run before the service can bootstrap itself; which post-bootstrap operations must be service-owned; how first-launch setup is represented as one durable state transition; and how the CLI remains a recoverable facade without becoming a second implementation. No implementation proposal is being made here.

### RustRover authoring and source acquisition are a third, hybrid execution mode

The same compiled tool surface also owns Superworkspace creation, four hardcoded source presets, Git clone/status, and a custom RustRover project writer. The clone path rejects `--all`, runs host `git clone --recurse-submodules`, then appends the checkout to `Superworkspace.vapor.toml`; a clone can succeed before the manifest update fails, leaving an unregistered source directory. It neither uses Registry-backed discovery nor the service's app operation scheduler ([preset/clone path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/source_workspace.rs>), [clone route](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/entrypoints.rs#L153-L173>)). This directly explains the earlier roadmap finding that source acquisition exists through two divergent paths: service/Registry for Studio and hardcoded/host-Git for Installer.

The generated RustRover project is more than Cargo detection. It recursively walks `sources/`, skips `.git`, `target`, `.vapor` and `Loo-Cast-Legacy`, identifies outer workspaces by finding a literal `[workspace]` line, writes Cargo/Rust/module/project/settings XML, installs a Rust toolchain shim, emits 17 run configurations, removes only names enumerated in a large legacy-stem list, then verifies selected file contents and `rustc`/Cargo metadata ([manifest discovery](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/rust_cargo.rs>), [generator and verification](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/rustrover.rs#L46-L130>), [configuration generation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/rustrover.rs#L276-L330>), [run configuration declarations](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/rustrover.rs#L413-L553>), [patch workflow](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/entrypoints.rs#L482-L550>)). That is substantial real developer-product behavior, but currently sits in one 796-line hand-built XML generator and its adjacent 648-line command/workflow router, not in the emerging IDE/service semantic-file model. Its project discovery, Rust convention model and Rust Analyzer model are therefore separate authorities. A Cargo run-configuration kind and writer branch are declared, but none of the 17 current run-configuration records uses it; this is source-visible dormant complexity, not a RustRover runtime defect.

This workflow deliberately mixes transports: IDE setup/source-clone/build/stage/publish commands are surfaced as interactive RustRover run configurations; a number of operational commands re-enter the app-local `vapor` CLI (and therefore its Client-service path), while tool setup and clone remain local subprocess/filesystem operations. The resulting user-visible workflow is not one service-owned operation stream from start to finish. On non-Unix targets the toolchain shim returns native Rust binary paths, but generated shell configurations still use JetBrains `ShConfigurationType` with `/usr/bin/env`; source therefore shows a Windows portability warning that requires a Windows RustRover launch to confirm. `ide_run_main` also falls back to the Linux triple if host-target detection fails rather than returning the original unsupported-host error, which can redirect a supposedly host-local IDE workflow to an invalid app binary directory ([IDE workflow setup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/entrypoints.rs#L175-L229>), [generated interpreter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/rustrover.rs#L719-L746>), [platform shim split](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/rustrover.rs#L46-L89>)). Neither warning was run on Windows.

### Bootstrap output, integrity, and filesystem safety are weaker than the service operation model

The Installer role path receives an `OperationAccepted` response, then waits up to 20 minutes for the matching operation ID. It does not display that operation's phase, progress or message fields; the UI remains on one spinner/status line while the service works. Direct Install/Repair/Uninstall run on a thread, but likewise return only one final `InstallerTaskResult` string. The embedded tool helper inherits process output instead of publishing structured output records; this does not feed the shared Console ([Installer polling](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L515-L608>), [status-only task UI](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L660-L693>), [helper process runner](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/process_io.rs#L1-L19>), [command runner](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/process_io.rs#L106-L129>)). This matters against the user's repeated request for visible, attributable setup/toolchain progress: the lower service has operation events, but the Installer path does not expose them.

The app-root tool downloads SteamCMD, Rustup, Zig and LLVM-MinGW from URLs compiled into the source. Only the LLVM-MinGW archive is checked against a compiled SHA-256; SteamCMD, the Rustup bootstrap binary and Zig rely on transport success without a local digest check. The pinned Rust channel does not make the rustup-init download itself version-pinned. This is a source-confirmed asymmetry in artifact integrity policy, not evidence that a downloaded file was compromised ([download/verification code](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/process_io.rs#L1-L56>), [tool URLs/versions](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools.rs#L10-L41>)).

There are two additional small but concrete implementation details. First, `cross_status` checks the same `libunwind.dll` path twice and can print a duplicate missing-component diagnostic ([duplicate readiness check](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/app_setup.rs#L321-L365>)). Second, filesystem containment compares a lexically normalized candidate with a canonical root but does not resolve symlinks in the candidate path; the subsequent `create_dir_all`/`File::create` operations follow existing directory symlinks. A symlink inside the app root could therefore redirect a setup write outside the lexical root. This is a source-level containment limitation, not a demonstrated exploit; the safer Core uninstall's separate canonical preflight does not cover these tool-helper setup writes ([lexical containment](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/filesystem.rs#L118-L155>), [receipt/write helpers](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/filesystem.rs#L49-L66>)).

The Windows setup path deserves direct runtime checking: PowerShell handles downloads, ZIP extraction, hashing and `SetEnvironmentVariable`, but the common child-process runner sets no Windows no-console flag or redirected structured output. Since this setup helper can be called from the GUI process, visible PowerShell console windows and unreported setup output are plausible; the source alone cannot establish whether the deployed Windows parent context suppresses them ([shared command runner](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/process_io.rs#L106-L129>), [Windows download/extract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/process_io.rs#L1-L20>), [Windows ZIP path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/process_io.rs#L68-L76>)).

### Evidence limits

The Installer UI, CLI and bridge source were read in full, as were the shared tool entrypoints, app-setup, app-root discovery, Cargo discovery, source workspace, RustRover generator, process/filesystem helpers, Core install/uninstall API, service role-dispatch path, and Core role transition semantics. Developer-environment reconciliation internals were not read end to end. The pre-existing dirty change in the UI file only reformats four expressions and does not alter behavior; it was preserved.
