No build, tests, UI launch, Steam run, Windows RustRover launch, or uninstall/purge was performed. Consequently, this section proves the exposed ownership boundaries and selected source-level mismatches; it does not establish successful Windows/Linux execution or the safety of every destructive path.
### October 25 — preserved Loo-Cast WIP is mostly duplicated, with an unmerged workbench cluster

The project contains a second Loo-Cast checkout at `b77a397` (October 8), not the authoritative October 25 checkout at `c070bf3`. Comparing all 75 changed or untracked paths byte-for-byte against current source found 66 identical files, eight different files, and one old untracked file missing from current source. The large 2,507-insertion/578-deletion number is relative to the old October 8 base, not a unique patch still awaiting integration.

The divergent cluster includes six script-workbench files and two celestial-fixture files. The untracked `script_workbench/operations.rs` is the clearest distinct proposal: it launches sibling `vapor-ide-host` (or `VAPOR_IDE_HOST`) as a one-shot JSON-lines helper, discovers content from a selected source root on a worker thread, and returns a local result to the in-game editor. The same WIP adds persisted editor-session drafts and calls that helper from the workbench workspace. The current source has neither this module nor its caller; the current workbench owns Rhai documents locally, while the Steam payload still contains the older host binary. This means the shipped host’s lack of a caller is accurate for the authoritative tree, but a preserved alternate WIP did contain a caller. That proposed path is not the current shared Client service model: it reuses a separate one-shot host and local workspace scan, so it would need explicit reconciliation with the later service/API direction before revival. The other four workbench-file diffs and two fixture-file diffs still need line-level semantic review; byte inequality alone does not establish that behavior was abandoned. The WIP and plan were not edited or executed.

The exact checkout state and comparison method are recorded in the [evidence atlas](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#current-source-inventory--refreshed-october-26-2026).

### October 25 — historical rebase runtime evidence versus the current chart boundary

The September 26 diagnostic bundle is unusually strong historical evidence because it pins the test to Loo-Cast `e14e928`, records source hashes, and preserves production and counterfactual headless runs. The production log reports two concrete defects after an origin rebase: an unchanged child-local position is reinterpreted as a shifted canonical position, and a static floor's collider AABB remains at its pre-rebase location so a query at the rebased location misses until ordinary physics refresh. The `--refresh` counterfactual updates the collider immediately and restores the query; a 100-unit threshold variant reproduces both faults, so the cause was not unique to the 256-unit threshold. The separate report of Earth surface switching at ±256m was not exercised by this diagnostic; neither its cause nor its relation to the reproduced query miss is established.

The later source response is visible in history: `93b1a2a` (September 29) adds a physics chart-rebase path, and `0e48843` (October 6) consolidates chart modules. At the October 25 snapshot, rebasing uses a scale-tagged `UsfChartDelta`, preflights conversions across relevant transform/physics/collider representations, applies scale-adjusted deltas per body/layer, and directly shifts Avian tight/enlarged AABBs while updating proxies and refitting affected trees. This is a source-supported structural response to the two narrow historical mechanisms, not a present runtime verification. No current replay was run; the Earth surface report and the later Moon-braking report remain distinct and unverified, with no demonstrated common cause.

The present backend adapter makes that distinction concrete: spatial `rebase_local_frame` preflights each direct/inherited chart representation, updates canonical origin and unparented runtime transforms, then emits `UsfOriginRebased`; the physics consumer shifts every Avian `Position`, tight/enlarged collider AABB, and registered BVH proxy without marking ordinary change detection, then refits each touched tree once. Collider chart membership is shared between the preflight and consumer and inherits from `ColliderOf` when there is no direct `UsfScaleLayer` ([canonical transaction](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/spatial/chart/rebase.rs>), [membership resolver](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/spatial/chart/membership.rs>), [Avian backend consumer](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/physics/chart_rebase.rs>), [ordering](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/spatial/mod.rs>)). This removes the specific “chart shift looks like physical collider motion” path at the source level. It still depends on the canonical rebase message reaching this backend consumer and does not establish terrain collision, general high-speed contact, or braking correctness.

### October 26 — canonical collision queries are wired into flight, but demand and provider coverage are partial

The current model separates a canonical sweep from local collider representation and from physical response. `UsfCanonicalSweep` stores semantic SI start/displacement/duration/radius. A fixed-step query frame assigns revision-scoped request IDs, records conservative candidates and resolutions, and discards stale-frame publications. `UsfSweepResolution` distinguishes Clear, Contact, and Unknown; tie ordering treats Unknown as weaker evidence than Contact or Clear, while the consumer chooses the smallest safe fraction. Candidate data remains observational; the flight movement commit is a separate authority ([public contracts](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/physics/collision_query/contract.rs>), [frame/journal](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/physics/collision_query/frame.rs>), [runtime sets](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/physics/collision_query/runtime.rs>), [module boundary](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/physics/collision_query/mod.rs>)).

The active path is specifically canonical kinematic flight. Spacecraft spawn installs a validated query demand. `prepare_flight_movement` proposes a sweep only when collision is required, canonical position exists, and desired velocity is nonzero. Fixed schedule order resets proposals before locomotion preparation, collects after preparation, invokes providers, finalizes, and makes flight motion commit wait for finalization. If a required request or resolution is missing, the motion consumer defaults to Unknown at safe fraction 0; a valid contact clips displacement and removes inward normal velocity, while an invalid contact normal or Unknown stops accepted velocity. That is fail-closed safety behavior, not a graceful fallback to locally resident Avian collision ([spacecraft demand](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/spawn.rs>), [proposal and commit](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/runtime/flight/mod.rs>), [ordered query sets](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/physics/collision_query/runtime.rs>), [locomotion scheduling](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/locomotion/mod.rs>)).

Only the voxel plugin currently registers a provider. It finds conservative body-sphere and semantic edit bounds, then sphere-traces the semantic field with ordered Add/Remove edits for at most 256 steps; Paint edits do not change this collision field. Unrepresentable/incomplete bounds or exhausted traces return Unknown, not Clear. It does not query arbitrary Avian colliders or non-voxel collision authorities. The demand's `lookahead_seconds` is validated and exposed but has no consumer anywhere in the inspected engine source; the active sweep is one proposed fixed step, so this field presently does not drive ahead-of-motion query residency through this API ([voxel candidate generation and trace](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/collision_query/mod.rs>), [bounded semantic resolver](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/collision_query/resolve.rs>), [provider registration](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/mod.rs>)).

This is a substantial source implementation, not merely a planned API, but it is not evidence that high-speed collisions work end to end: no source tests were found in either collision-query subtree, no sweep was executed here, and voxel semantic geometry is the only provider domain located. The user's Moon approach/braking report has no established causal link to this path; source proves the intended fail-closed mechanism, not the reported motion outcome. See the [current-state cross-reference](current-state-semantic-cross-reference.md#canonical-collision-sweeps-protect-kinematic-flight-with-a-voxel-only-provider).

### October 25 — Cargo output is structured, but build progress is only step-granular

The current managed workspace-build provider requests Cargo's JSON message stream for check/test/Clippy/docs/build operations. Compiler messages become structured diagnostics with severity, code, rendered text, primary/related spans and a bounded raw JSON payload; artifact/build-script events are summarized, while unknown or unstructured records remain text. The generic process reader preserves oversized output by emitting bounded chunks (normally 8 KiB; Cargo JSON allows 256 KiB per chunk/record path), and the service buffers background messages and caps client-visible operation output at 512 records with an explicit older-output-omitted notice. This is real machinery behind the user's summarized-plus-inspectable command-output direction, though the record view shows a diagnostic's first line and exposes details through fields/hover rather than establishing a complete expandable transcript or durable log store.

Progress is less granular than output: a workspace build reports a completed step only after a whole Cargo invocation returns. During a long compiler step, streamed Cargo output can change while the operation's fraction remains unchanged. This is a source-level consequence of the callback placement, not a measured UI freeze or incorrect progress display. Parser unit tests and the service's omission-bound test exist in source, but no tests or runtime were run for this audit. Evidence: [Cargo JSON parser](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/cargo_output.rs#L1), [build invocation and progress boundary](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/workspace_build.rs#L138), [bounded managed process reader](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/managed_process.rs#L1), [operation-output queue limits](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L50), [record conversion](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/console.rs#L444).

### October 25 — two public IDE repairs disagree about which RustRover files are canonical

The current CLI `ide status`/`ide repair` implementation and the shared Core maintenance implementation both target the Superworkspace's `.idea` directory, but encode opposite file contracts. `vapor_cli::ide` writes `cargoProjects.xml`, `rust.xml`, and `vapor.xml` from templates ([CLI implementation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/ide.rs#L18), [CLI dispatch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command.rs#L144)). `vapor_core::ide` instead reconciles Cargo/Rust/VCS state into JetBrains `workspace.xml` and `vcs.xml` plus generated `.run/Vapor` configurations, and explicitly classifies `cargoProjects.xml` and `rust.xml` as obsolete so repair deletes them ([Core implementation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ide.rs#L1), [maintenance integration](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/maintenance.rs#L130)).

Consequently, CLI `ide repair` can recreate the exact files that Core maintenance marks obsolete; after Core repair, CLI `ide status` can report its own expected files missing. That is a source-derived incompatible ownership contract, not a claim that a user actually ran the two commands in sequence. The CLI's IDE commands also perform filesystem reads/writes locally rather than expressing them as Client service actions, while the broad installation-maintenance path separately invokes Core. The intended RustRover integration is real in both paths, but their behavior is not one shared implementation. Relevant chronology: Core's reconciliation is present by `5679c1d` (September 6); the separate CLI implementation arrives with the October 18 facade rename `c5b7025`. No filesystem mutation or runtime check was performed.

The Core path also has an explicit platform gap: `run_configurations::build` returns an empty list under `cfg(windows)`, while the non-Windows branch generates the Vapor Installation, Client, Platform Server, Loo-Cast and registered-workspace `.run` configurations. Core still reconciles Cargo/VCS project state on Windows, so this does not mean the entire RustRover integration is absent; it means its generated Vapor command/run surface is intentionally missing there. The inspected file contains no alternate Windows generator. This matters to the user's cross-platform developer workflow, but whether a native Windows run-configuration format is intentionally deferred or accidentally omitted is not stated in the code. [Platform-gated generator](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ide/run_configurations.rs#L1-L19), [Core maintenance call site](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/ide.rs#L270-L285). No Windows RustRover run was performed.

## October 25 — Studio's Composer edits authored source graphs, not the broader acquired-content graph

The current Studio page is explicit about its input boundary: it edits a selected project manifest and describes candidates as “projects” in “these project folders.” Its candidate list comes from `catalog.sources`; Packagepack receives dedicated required Engine/Game slots, while other dependency edges are edited through the same generic source-project selector ([page framing and source input](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/composition.rs#L18), [Packagepack role slots](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/composition.rs#L83), [source-only candidate list](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/composition.rs#L204)). It previews availability and makes a Packagepack active from its authored selector; the same source-edit surface can prepare Workshop upload for the edited artifact ([preview/selection](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/composition.rs#L342), [staging](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/composition.rs#L408)). The `SourceCatalog` separately tracks source discovery and the local acquired-content catalog ([catalog state](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/catalog.rs#L14-L30)); this Composer screen consumes the former, not the latter, for its dependency choices. A secondary Catalog detail action offers `Add to composition` only for a workspace-located runtime item that also matches a registered source project; the target must be a project-backed composition in the same open workspace. It then reopens the Packagepack source graph and records the item as a pending source draft ([Catalog affordance](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/components/content_detail.rs#L350-L420), [runtime/source/workspace eligibility](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/components/content_detail.rs#L483-L530), [project-backed guard and draft routing](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/components/content_detail.rs#L533-L590)). This is a workspace-build-result-to-source-draft path, not arbitrary downloaded Workshop/Library content and not an independent pack-centric workflow.

That boundary does not match the user's clarified full Composer goal yet. Composer is meant to combine *already existing content and packs* into new packs; the pack itself is a typed manifest, while compiled content/artifacts live outside it, and only a Packagepack carries a finished runnable executable. The older roadmap records the separation as “Vapor determines semantic composition; Cargo executes Rust package/build realization,” while explicitly marking generic realization narrow ([historical Cargo boundary](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Premium%20Docs/Vapor%20Rewrite%20Progress%20And%20Roadmap.md#5--cargo-realization>)). Current Core makes that narrowness executable: reconciliation accepts a Crate root, verifies its direct Vapor-to-Cargo edges, and repairs only missing declarations with `cargo add`; it refuses conflicts because it lacks previous-realization history ([Crate-only reconciliation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cargo_reconciliation.rs#L1-L12), [scope limit](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cargo_reconciliation.rs#L128-L160), [safe repair limit](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cargo_reconciliation.rs#L236-L285)). Thus two layers are narrower than the user's model in different ways: Studio primarily authors source references (with one constrained acquired-item handoff), while the Cargo bridge validates only one Rust-backed content kind. Workspace search found no callsite for `verify_local_crate_cargo_dependencies` or its repair function outside their Core definitions/internal call and public re-export; the typed operation is not wired into the current Client service/Studio composition path. The action taxonomy reinforces the boundary: Composition graph edits and SaveComposition are Composer actions without a declared managed-Rust prerequisite; ValidateContent and PackageContent are Developer actions requiring ManagedRustToolchain ([action profiles](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/actions.rs#L413-L465)). That is coherent for manifest-only editing, but the owner's clarified Composer can perform Cargo metadata/link composition over already-built libraries; no current service action owns that operation. This finding does not imply every selection or manifest save should invoke Cargo—it identifies the missing Composer-scoped realization action and its tool prerequisite.

This is not evidence that source-project editing is wrong for the Developer workflow, nor that acquired Workshop content must become editable source. It identifies a missing bridge between Composer's product promise and distinct lifecycle projections: acquired/installable content, source projects, resolved pack graphs, and build artifacts should remain distinguishable yet selectable through compatible typed identities. The current page makes source selection concrete but does not show the generalized graph model (required versus optional policy, alternatives/cardinality, conflicts, and package-root closure) the user's latest content-kind explanation requires. Those are separately named proposals in the local Oct 24 graph-model document, not current implementation or an accepted exhaustive contract; review them before treating a schema as final. The 1,032-line page is not itself proof of bad architecture, but its single `draw_composition` method owns draft mutation, selectors, confirmation, save/discard, active selection, package preview, Workshop handoff and workspace status, making this a useful current-state hotspot for later semantic decomposition.

### Historical cross-check and evidence limits

The roadmap's early “Proven” labels describe an initial vertical slice and are explicitly narrower than production distribution; later owner direction supersedes its old `Library` content-kind vocabulary with `Crate` while keeping “Library” for locally available content. The present Composer consequently demonstrates real source-manifest editing and Packagepack selection, plus a constrained workspace-runtime-to-source-draft handoff, not the full pack-centric acquired-content composition workflow. No UI was run, no Cargo reconciliation operation was invoked, and no generated Packagepack build was examined. The source scan does not establish whether an external automation or not-yet-integrated editor can compose from acquired content.

## October 25 — Developer readiness omits one foreign target path

## Developer-ready omits part of the cross-target tool set

`DeveloperEnvironmentStatus::is_ready` requires the pinned Rust installation, Rust Analyzer, the Windows GNU Rust target and llvm-mingw linker, Tracy Profiler, and Tracy analysis. It does not include Zig or the app-local Linux cross-linker wrapper. The provider's separate `CrossToolchainStatus::inspect` checks Zig, llvm-mingw tools, the Windows runtime DLL, and the Linux wrapper, but a whole-crate source search found no production callsite for `inspect`; the actual Cargo build asks `configure_linker_env` for a foreign target only at build time ([Developer readiness fields and conjunction](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L13-L31), [provider cross-toolchain inventory](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/cross_toolchain.rs#L11-L68), [target-specific linker configuration](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/cross_toolchain.rs#L70-L93), [build-time requirement](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/workspace_build.rs#L453-L469)).

That creates a source-confirmed difference between “Developer setup ready” and “all supported release targets can be built.” On a Windows host, a Linux GNU build needs the bundled Zig linker and wrapper; the Developer role status has no field or prerequisite for them. The standalone setup script does install Zig and the wrapper, but it is a separate operation and reports its own status. The current source therefore has target-specific build checks without a unified, role-owned readiness/reconciliation model for every supported host-target pair. No Windows or cross-target build was run, so this is a code-path conclusion, not a reproduced user failure.


## October 25 — bundled recovery setup has a second, less-safe toolchain installer

The app also carries standalone Rust scripts for player/developer setup. Their shared Rust module pins its own Rust version, Zig and llvm-mingw versions, Windows GNU target, archive URLs and checksums; `setup_development_main` calls a local implementation rather than invoking `DeveloperEnvironment::reconcile` ([duplicated tool pins](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools.rs#L10-L41), [standalone entrypoints](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/entrypoints.rs#L47-L64), [fallback development workflow](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/app_setup.rs#L29-L49)). Both paths install into the app-local Rust and `tools/llvm-mingw` directories, so this is a competing provisioning owner, not merely a differently rendered status screen.

For llvm-mingw, the standalone path deletes/recreates the live directory before downloading and verifying the archive ([reset implementation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/filesystem.rs#L1-L21), [delete-before-download order](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/resources/vapor/tools/_shared/vapor_tools/app_setup.rs#L199-L225)). Core instead uses a temporary download, checksum validation, staged extraction and rollback-safe promotion. Thus the emergency path can destroy a valid previous linker before the replacement is known-good, while Core's path is intentionally transactional. Both setup routes call Player setup first, which writes a Player-ready receipt before Developer setup succeeds. This reflects the previously observed mismatch between player prerequisites and “selected setup complete.” The bundled script may remain useful when the service is unavailable; the issue is that its copy of ownership and safety policy can drift independently. The repository history supports a two-generation reading: parent commit [`b42b57b` (July 28, 2026)](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Client/commit/b42b57b) introduced the standalone app-root workflow control surface with 970 lines across setup and entrypoint files; child commit [`a10ca0e` (October 21, 2026)](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/a10ca0e) later added Core's distinct 473-line cross-target toolchain implementation, and [`92ab2b9`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/92ab2b9) refined that path. The later work did not edit the parent fallback. This is evidence of additive evolution across repository ownership boundaries; it does not establish that either implementation was intended to retire the other. No setup script or toolchain was run for this audit.

## October 25 — Windows cross-target capability and playable payload are separate contracts

Core owns a pinned `llvm-mingw` release, checks its SHA-256, bounds the download, extracts into a staging directory, validates required linker/archiver/runtime files and a UCRT/target marker, then promotes the verified bundle while retaining the prior installation for rollback ([pinned version, archives and host gate](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cross_target_toolchain.rs#L11-L58), [download, checksum and staged install](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cross_target_toolchain.rs#L59-L145), [bundle readiness contract and rollback](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cross_target_toolchain.rs#L167-L229)). Its host boundary is x86-64 Linux or x86-64 Windows; other hosts are rejected. The Developer environment treats that linker plus the Rust Windows target as required setup, alongside Rust, Rust Analyzer and both Tracy tools ([readiness conjunction](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L13-L31), [reconciliation stages](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L123-L177)).

This clarifies two superficially similar Windows errors. A managed cross-target toolchain permits a developer to build for `x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm`; it does not prove the Workshop Packagepack contains a built executable for that target. Player launch requires the latter independently. Likewise, a host unsupported by the linker installer is not a missing-target artifact error. The implementation currently couples role readiness to Windows cross-target and Tracy readiness, even if a developer's immediate task does not need those tools. This is a source-level setup-policy fact; the historic Windows reports were not re-run against this snapshot.

## October 25 — the Studio Projects surface combines manifest composition and source release work

The Projects workspace is explicitly a source-project browser. For each registered project it exposes project validation, package building, manifest opening, dependency selection, composition-root assignment, temporary package preview, Workshop metadata edits, runtime-output edits, and project unregistration ([workspace routing](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workspace.rs#L65-L101), [project rows and details](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workspace_content_panel.rs#L125-L145), [primary source/manifests/dependency actions](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workspace_content_panel.rs#L215-L293), [preview, publication metadata, runtime outputs and unregister](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/workspace_content_panel.rs#L295-L351)). The shared navigation groups Compose and Workspace together under the same “Creator Tools” heading, and applies an amber frame rather than a capability/role filter ([group declaration and area assignment](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/navigation.rs#L27-L54), [area rendering](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/app_shell.rs#L202-L226)).

This is a real integrated developer surface, but it does not yet communicate the owner’s progressive workflow boundary. Composer may edit Cargo composition manifests and link already-built libraries; source authoring/build tooling belongs to the Developer level. The panel places both categories of work in one available Creator space. Shared action profiles classify packaging as Developer, but that does not automatically make the UI progressively discoverable or hide advanced controls. The conclusion concerns product structure and presentation only; it is not evidence of a service authorization bypass. Nor does it mean every Rust-related Composer task must move to the IDE: Composer still needs Cargo metadata and composition operations without editing the constituent crates. This is the concrete current counterpart to the broader authored-source-versus-acquired-content gap in the preceding section. No UI or authorization path was run.

## October 25 — IDE Problems caps build output, but source diagnostics have no comparable aggregate bound

The IDE keeps file-source diagnostics in a `BTreeMap<PathBuf, Vec<ProblemRow>>`, tracks build diagnostics by one active operation, and caps only the build vector at 2,000 rows with an explicit omission summary ([store and cap](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/diagnostics.rs#L60-L95), [build insertion/cap](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/diagnostics.rs#L126-L157)). LSP/source rows are replaced per file and merged with matching Rust/Cargo/Vapor diagnostics by severity/code/message/span; origin priority selects the primary row while retaining linked diagnostics ([source replacement](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/diagnostics.rs#L178-L205), [correlation and origin priority](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/diagnostics.rs#L395-L455)). The raw diagnostic payload itself is truncated at 64 KiB and diagnostics are scoped to document/workspace context. That is substantial, deliberate machinery rather than an unstructured list.

The bound is asymmetric: no total source-diagnostic or file-count cap is visible in `ProblemStore`. The Problems view asks the store to count matches, then asks again for a virtualized visible range; `rows_in_filtered_range` walks all source and build rows and re-evaluates matching until it reaches the requested filtered offset ([filtered count and range scan](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/diagnostics.rs#L258-L285), [virtual range traversal](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/diagnostics.rs#L343-L383), [view use](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_ide_ui/src/console_view.rs#L1-L32)). Query normalization lowercases diagnostic fields during each match. Thus row construction is virtualized but filter/count cost remains proportional to retained diagnostics, and only one diagnostic class has a global count bound. This is a conditional large-workspace memory/CPU risk, not proof of observed IDE lag; no benchmark or large-workspace run was performed.

The IDE's 65 focused tests include ProblemStore lifecycle, merge, filtering and semantic-range selection. They support semantic correctness of those cases, not the memory/performance behavior above. The current design therefore has a sound typed merge model and bounded build history, but its scale policy is incomplete across diagnostic origins. This is another instance where the owner’s reusable-console goal needs a shared policy for retention, indexing and inspectability, not merely a shared renderer.

### Evidence and limits

Read-only inspection of `ProblemStore`, its IDE view callsites and the checked-in test module. The source cap asymmetry is confirmed; workspace-scale impact is not measured. No tests, UI, or Rust Analyzer process were run.


## October 25 — role tiers collapse to one developer bundle while action profiles describe only three capabilities

The latest implementation has two different classifications, and neither is a complete model of the other. `VaporRole` orders Player, Composer, ContentDeveloper and EcosystemDeveloper, but `requires_developer_environment()` returns one shared yes/no answer for the last three. Promotion to any of them reconciles the same `DeveloperEnvironment`: pinned Rust/Cargo with rustfmt, clippy, rust-src and rust-analyzer; the Windows `gnullvm` target; the installation-specific LLVM-MinGW linker/runtime; Tracy Profiler; and Tracy analysis tooling ([role threshold](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/role.rs#L23), [bundle status and readiness](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L13), [reconciliation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L93), [exact Rust components and target](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/toolchain.rs#L235)). Demotion changes the persisted role but deliberately leaves all installed tooling and caches in place ([demotion contract](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/role.rs#L197)). The current Developer Environment guide explicitly describes this full bundle for “Composer and higher,” so that broad install is not an undocumented accident; it is the current declared contract ([guide](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/developer-environment.md#L8)).

Action profiles slice the same domain differently. Composer-level manifest authoring is classified as Composer without a Rust prerequisite; composition `RunSource`, content validation/packaging and workspace build operations are Developer-tier with a generic managed-Rust prerequisite; Language Server start is Developer-tier with a separate Rust-Analyzer prerequisite; Tracy operations add the Tracy capability. The service checks only the declared `LocalCapability` values (`ManagedRustToolchain`, `RustAnalyzer`, `TracyProfiler`), and `WorkflowTier` explicitly describes product depth rather than installation or authorization. Neither level carries a target-specific GNU-LLVM capability, and action admission does not compare the caller's installed `VaporRole` to the profile ([workflow contract](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/workflow.rs#L1), [per-action profile](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/actions.rs#L380), [capability admission](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L61)). A further concrete mismatch is `CreateContent`: it falls through to Developer-tier classification, yet the four Pack kinds intentionally scaffold as metadata-only projects, with neither a Cargo package nor Rust source. The common service admission path does not enforce workflow tier; because this action declares no local tool capability, the capability gate returns before checking tool readiness. Thus the implementation has a real Rust-free Pack-manifest path, but it neither classifies nor gates that operation at the Composer boundary. [Action profile fallback](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/actions.rs#L448), [Pack scaffold mapping](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/source.rs#L397), [service authoring branch](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/authoring.rs#L330), [capability gate early return](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L767). This can make a role report “developer environment ready” based on the flat full bundle while individual actions know only a smaller, differently sliced set of prerequisites. The Windows target/linker are instead enforced by setup/readiness as aggregate role conditions.

The historical role model intended cumulative work scope: Composer authors the four Pack kinds from existing content, Content Developer adds Engine/Game/mod authoring, and Ecosystem Developer adds Vapor/first-party development ([Premium role model](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Premium%20Docs/Architecture/Vapor%20Role,%20Authentication%20And%20Authorization%20Model.md#L30), [product experience model](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Premium%20Docs/Experience/Vapor%20Product%20Experience%20Model.md#L100)). The owner's later clarification narrows Composer's Rust use: it is compositional Rust/Cargo work (for example, linking existing libraries or updating Cargo metadata), not authoring constituent Rust source. That sits between today's `Authoring::SaveComposition` (no managed Rust capability) and Developer-tier `PackageContent`/`ValidateContent` (managed Rust) rather than matching either exactly. It is a product-contract gap, not evidence that all Composer operations should invoke Cargo. The full role ladder's increasing workflow scope also is not represented as progressively distinct local tool sets: the current `VaporRole` setup predicate gives ContentDeveloper and EcosystemDeveloper no additional declared local capabilities beyond Composer, while the per-action `WorkflowTier` has only Player/Composer/Developer and does not map to all four installed roles.

This matters for three linked reasons. First, Composer promotion currently installs analysis/profiling and cross-compilation tools whether or not a given composition task needs them; that is consistent with the current guide, but obscures which capabilities are essential to the role versus useful bundled tools. Second, ContentDeveloper and EcosystemDeveloper are broader product levels without a corresponding capability delta in role setup; their differentiators may be workflow surfaces or remote authorization, but source does not define them as added local provisioning. Third, demotion is not a storage cleanup operation, so role change cannot reclaim the sizeable managed Rust/Tracy/cross-target footprint. None of this proves the bundle is too large or that demotion should uninstall it: the existing non-destructive policy explicitly avoids deleting caches. It identifies the exact policy seam for a future role/capability and disk-ownership decision.

The cross-check also clarifies why the user's Windows setup report cannot be reduced to “Rust target missing.” The generic action-capability model cannot express target or linker readiness, while `DeveloperEnvironmentStatus` can; setup is meant to install both the target and host-appropriate linker bundle as one role reconciliation. The old app-root Installer tool scripts separately install Rust/Cargo, Zig, LLVM-MinGW and wrappers, so the present tool inventory is still split between a service-owned capability bundle and a legacy bootstrap path. The exact duplicated ownership and first-launch postcondition defects are recorded in the [Installer role/setup trace](#october-25--installer-role-and-setup-state-do-not-share-one-authority) and [evidence atlas](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#installation-identity-role-state-setup-receipts-and-developer-tools-have-split-ownership).

### Tracy analysis support is a hard Windows gate for every non-Player role

The broad role bundle has a target-specific failure hidden inside its always-required setup path. `ManagedTracyToolset::is_installed()` requires both the profiler and `tracy-csvexport`; `install_missing()` provisions both. The CSV exporter installer returns an explicit unsupported-target error unless the host is Linux x86_64 GNU, and its source-build fallback uses ambient `tar` and `cmake` ([Tracy toolset readiness and reconciliation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/tracy.rs#L80-L120), [CSV exporter target restriction](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/tracy.rs#L150-L177)). `DeveloperEnvironment::reconcile_inner` calls that combined setup while promoting any role that requires the shared developer environment ([role reconciliation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L126-L179)); `DeveloperEnvironmentStatus::is_ready()` also requires the analysis executable ([aggregate readiness](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L13-L31)). Therefore on Windows, Composer/Content Developer/Ecosystem Developer promotion cannot complete through this path when the exporter is absent—even if Rust, Rust Analyzer, GNU target/linker and Tracy Profiler are otherwise ready. This is a source-confirmed target gate and is consistent with the reported Windows promotion failure; it was not reproduced on that machine. The design implication is narrow: optional profiling analysis must not make the entire role/toolchain unavailable on unsupported hosts, or a managed Windows artifact/build path must exist. This finding does not explain the separate historical service-start timeout without additional evidence.

**Evidence limits:** source inspection only. No role promotion, demotion, disk measurement, target build, Rust Analyzer start, Tracy launch, or Windows run was performed. The implementation guide confirms the broad policy currently; the owner's clarified Composer semantics and the older cumulative role model expose the unresolved granularity. Tool installation sizes and incremental role deltas remain unmeasured.

### Tracy report analysis is whole-capture work behind a generic operation

The service accepts `AnalyzeProfileTrace` as a background operation, but the Core analyzer runs `tracy-csvexport` with `Command::output()`, retaining its complete stdout and stderr before parsing. It then keeps every matching zone duration in per-zone vectors, sorts those vectors, and only applies the requested `top` limit after all rows have been read and aggregated. Thus `top = 50` bounds the returned report size, not CSV memory, aggregate memory, or sorting work. The operation worker receives a final `ProfileReport` result but does not stream analysis progress or incremental findings through the managed-process output path. This is a source-derived large-capture memory/observability risk, not a measured failure; no trace was analyzed during this review. It is distinct from the Windows install gate above: Linux can provision analysis and still incur whole-capture resource use, while Windows can launch the collector but cannot satisfy the combined analysis-tool readiness contract. [Whole-output capture and aggregation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/profiling.rs#L245-L370), [service background operation wrapper](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L1442-L1477), [managed output reader is bypassed by this analyzer](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/managed_process.rs#L1-L31).

## October 25 — Studio's Creator boundary is a shared yellow box, not a progressive workflow map

The current navigation does make creator work visually distinct: `NavigationArea::Creator` draws a framed amber section. But the area contains Create, Compose, Workspace and Publish in one flat group; `draw_navigation_group` uses the area only to choose color and framing, and renders every section without consulting the installed role, active workflow tier or readiness. The Play page separately exposes “Create content,” “My projects,” and a “Project tools” card unconditionally. This does satisfy the earlier request for a visibly cordoned creator area, but not the subsequently clarified Player → Composer → Developer progression: there is no Composer/Developer sub-boundary, capability-sensitive navigation, or clear explanation of how the same project moves through those levels. This is a discoverability/product-model gap, not a claim that these actions are unauthorized; current service code also does not use workflow tier as an authorization gate. This is source inspection, not a visual run. [Navigation groups and areas](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/navigation.rs#L14-L54), [area only changes styling](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/app_shell.rs#L202-L226), [Home creator shortcuts](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/home.rs#L104-L149).

## October 25 — operation queuing is Studio-local even though readiness is advertised across frontends

The service owns canonical operation reservations and explicit conflict domains. Its snapshot marks some composition actions `queueable` when a conflicting operation is active, and frontend action availability treats `enabled || queueable` as actionable ([service queueable projection](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/snapshot.rs#L215-L287), [Studio action projection](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/app.rs#L91-L101), [Launcher action projection](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_launcher_ui/src/lib.rs#L545-L558)). But the service-side operation registry rejects an actual conflicting reservation with `OperationInProgress`; it does not retain the request as a queued service operation ([reservation decision](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L711-L765)).

This is not a duplicate lifecycle runner: `vapor_core::OperationService` supplies bounded output normalization, shared phase/progress/cancellation events, and terminal-state wrapping; the Application layer adds typed operation kinds and composition identity; Client Service owns admission, resource reservations, workers and cancellation policy ([Core lifecycle runner](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/operation.rs#L1-L308), [Application operation projection](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/operation.rs#L1-L110), [service worker integration](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L1670-L1745)). That separation is coherent. The queue mismatch is specifically the cross-frontend retry/admission contract: one frontend implements an adapter queue, while the protocol advertises queueability to all.

Studio adds a frontend queue after receiving that rejection: it puts the original typed action in a local FIFO capped at 64 and retries one item after an operation reaches terminal completion. Its response handler special-cases `OperationInProgress`, then calls `start_next_service_operation` after results; if the service connection drops, it explicitly clears the waiting queue and tells the user to check the result before retrying ([conflict response handling](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/catalog.rs#L238-L270), [retry after completion](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/operations.rs#L516-L528), [bounded local queue](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/operations.rs#L28-L75), [disconnect behavior](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/catalog.rs#L337-L345)). This is useful progress toward the user's request to queue actions instead of freezing the whole UI, but the queue is owned by one Studio process, not the shared service or a durable/shared scheduler.

Launcher exposes the same `queueable` affordance as enabled, yet its response handler only logs an error and changes the status line; there is no corresponding queued-request retention or retry path. A request can therefore look enabled because it is queueable, then be rejected when it reaches a conflicting service reservation ([Launcher affordance and response handling](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_launcher_ui/src/lib.rs#L490-L518), [same availability rule](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_launcher_ui/src/lib.rs#L545-L558)). This establishes an actual cross-frontend behavior mismatch. CLI/direct service clients also do not inherit Studio's in-memory queue; concurrent conflicts are rejected at the common service boundary.

The design lineage is clear. The October 22 workflow-boundaries design calls for independent operations to proceed or queue and the plan says conflicting operations serialize, while its verification task for conflict serialization and concurrent clients remains unchecked ([design intent](/home/leslieghf/.codex/.chatgpt-projects/g-p-6ab69f33d17481919fb92a0c5592210c/artifacts/vapor-workflow-boundaries-design.md#L60), [implementation-plan review focus and remaining task](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-22-workflow-boundaries.md#L22)). Git history shows the service registry arriving in `3b692e7` (“Add workflow tiers and concurrent client operations”) on October 22, followed by Studio's `142a0f4` and `b7d457d` queue/retry changes the same day. That sequence is a service-level concurrency foundation plus a Studio-specific queue adapter, not one shared queue contract. The important asymmetry emerged because Launcher consumes the same availability projection but not the Studio adapter.

This does **not** mean every long operation should be queued. The service already permits non-conflicting work concurrently, and a request can become unsafe or stale while waiting; any shared queue must preserve operation-specific resource keys, revalidate state before execution, expose cancellation and ordering, and define what happens when its owner disconnects. The source establishes the present mismatch and the design's still-open verification item, but no concurrent runtime experiment was performed. No code/tests were run for this research entry.

## October 25 — persisted operation history can suppress a new operation after service restart

Operation identity is documented and implemented as **process-local**: `OperationId::fresh()` increments a static `AtomicU64` beginning at 1 ([identity allocator](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/operation.rs#L11-L23)). Client Service creates operation IDs with that allocator, and its local process exits after all clients disconnect and the 15-second idle grace elapses ([service operation creation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L1658-L1685), [idle lifetime](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L24-L27), [shutdown condition](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L508-L531)). A later service process therefore restarts the sequence at 1.

Studio persists up to 20 completed operation events in egui storage, restores that history during app construction, and then restores the service's durable operation-history snapshot after connection ([UI restore](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/app.rs#L144-L146), [restore on construction](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/app.rs#L190-L192), [service snapshot restore](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/app.rs#L294-L301), [history retention](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/operations.rs#L77-L84)). Before parsing or applying any incoming service lifecycle event, Studio compares its numeric ID string against every persisted history entry and returns immediately on a match ([event deduplication](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/operations.rs#L302-L316)).

This creates a deterministic collision condition, not merely a theoretical possibility: if the restarted service's operation `1` arrives while Studio retains a prior terminal operation `1`, its `OperationChanged` event is discarded as a duplicate. Snapshot reconciliation can still add/update the active-operation projection and later remove it when no longer active, so source does **not** establish that the task itself is invisible or fails. The changed-event path nevertheless cannot add the new terminal history row or apply its terminal status/message/action-specific handling; `OperationOutput` has a separate active-ID guard and may still be accepted while the snapshot marks that ID active. This is especially consequential for history and event-derived completion feedback. The identity contract needs a service/session generation or globally unique ID, or deduplication must distinguish active/reused identities from persisted historical records.

This finding links the service's intended short-lived lifecycle to Studio's durable history: each is reasonable alone, but numeric IDs are not scoped by process/session at the protocol boundary while history survives that boundary. A similar issue may affect other consumers that persist operation history; only Studio's event guard was traced here. No sequence was executed to reproduce the collision, and no code or tests were changed.

## October 25 — Studio teaches one compatible selection; the content graph cannot express pack branches

The latest owner model keeps the existing ten content kinds fixed, but gives Packs a wider purpose than a curated list of simultaneously compatible add-ons. A Pack is a typed manifest: Enginepack and Gamepack bundle a base with optional extensions; Modpack groups additions for an experience; any pack may describe mutually exclusive paths. Packagepack is the playable-selection identity and its release includes the finished executable. The owner's wording also says the Packagepack must remain editable/forkable with access to its source and constituent code, while code and compiled libraries are not physically inside Packs. Two useful readings remain possible: a separately stored source closure bound to the Packagepack identity/release, or source owned by referenced Content plus a separately versioned Packagepack manifest. The local October 24 graph design adopts the first identity-level wording, while the owner-review architecture draft adopts the second source-ownership wording; these are not yet reconciled into a precise provenance/download contract ([graph-design wording](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-24-vapor-content-graph-design.md#L5), [architecture-draft wording](vapor-ecosystem-architecture-plan-draft.md#4-fixed-content-vocabulary-and-intended-semantics)). The graph-design file is local untracked work, not a shipped contract, and current behavior must not be retroactively treated as proof of either reading.

Studio's Create screen still presents Packagepack as “one Engine and one Game,” Enginepack/Gamepack as selecting one base, and Modpack as a “compatible” add-on collection; its repeated explanatory text reinforces the same narrow model ([template cards and summaries](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/create.rs#L615-L643), [per-kind description](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/create.rs#L703-L713)). The card copy is not just terse: it describes a Pack as a selected resolved setup and implies all Modpack members coexist, rather than revealing that a manifest may declare branches from which one playable path is selected. The October 15 lifecycle plan marks “Compose Packagepacks from compatible content identities” complete ([plan status](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-15-vapor-studio-full-stack-content-lifecycle.md#L121)); that acceptance criterion was too narrow relative to the owner's later direction and should not be treated as completion of general pack composition.

The shared source contract confirms the architectural gap behind the wording. `DependencySpec` carries an identity, version requirement, and optional flag ([dependency model](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/content.rs#L124)); authored manifests also have a `conflicts` list and role-specific fields, so it would be inaccurate to say conflicts are wholly absent ([authored content fields](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/authored_manifest.rs#L74)). However, the provider-neutral `ContentCandidate` contains only a map of dependencies, and the resolver skips optional edges in the default graph rather than choosing among alternatives ([candidate model](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/catalog.rs#L8), [resolution behavior](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/resolution.rs#L422)). Conflict declarations survive packaging and are checked against already-enabled installed content during installation ([packaged conflict projection](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/packaging.rs#L643), [install-time conflict check](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content.rs#L1863)); that is useful conflict prevention, but it is not branch-aware resolution of mutually exclusive members inside a pack.

Current cardinality is hard-coded: a resolved Packagepack must contain exactly one Engine and one Game; Enginepack and Gamepack each require exactly one of their base kind; Modpack only requires at least one Mod ([root shape validation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/resolution.rs#L200)). Authored dependency relationships additionally encode fixed exclusive choice slots for Packagepack engine/game alternatives, but the resolver traverses every non-optional dependency and the resulting graph has no record of a branch choice or why another branch was omitted ([choice-slot vocabulary](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/content.rs#L194), [resolved graph traversal](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/resolution.rs#L435)). So a Packagepack may choose one Engine or Enginepack and one Game or Gamepack, but this is not the richer general alternative model described by the owner. The fixed target checks are valuable invariants for a runnable selection; the defect is promoting them into the only pack graph shape.

There is a second precise seam in authoring. Studio's source-content creation validates selected dependencies against `catalog.sources`, requires optional items also to be selected in that source graph, then mutates Cargo workspace membership for code-bearing kinds ([source-only dependency selection and Cargo membership](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L445)). It is not yet a general Composer operation over acquired Library content and prebuilt reusable artifacts; that separate limitation is traced in [the acquired-content bridge review](#october-25--studios-composer-edits-authored-source-graphs-not-the-broader-acquired-content-graph). Creation does correctly scaffold Packs as metadata-only while Rust-bearing kinds receive Cargo projects ([kind-specific scaffolding](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/source.rs#L395)); this preserves the important “packs are manifests” distinction even as the resolver and UI narrow the Pack semantics.

The code generator's current role mapping also disagrees with the flagship's actual build graph and the owner's Engine/Game/Packagepack meanings: generic templates generate Engine as a binary and Packagepack as metadata-only, while the Loo-Cast Engine manifest declares a library, `spacetime-engine` is a Cargo library, and `loo-cast-packagepack` is the binary that depends on both Engine and Game ([generator mapping](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/source.rs#L436), [Engine artifact declaration](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/Engine.vapor.toml#L1), [Engine crate kind](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/Cargo.toml#L1), [Packagepack executable graph](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-packagepack/Cargo.toml#L1)). The generator emits a placeholder Engine `main.rs`; it does not generate a Packagepack linker/entrypoint. That makes the starter/template contract unsuitable as a canonical example of “Engine supplies reusable capability; Packagepack composes prebuilt content into the launchable artifact.” It is a source-level template mismatch, not proof that every Engine in every ecosystem must expose the exact Loo-Cast Cargo shape. The precise target-specific library formats and how a Packagepack selects them remain part of the unresolved build contract.

The current evidence therefore splits into four truths: the vocabulary is centralized at the approved ten kinds; Pack-only metadata scaffolding exists; authored conflict declarations can prevent an installation collision; but Studio copy, graph resolution, and the accepted 15 October completion language still describe a simpler compatible-set model. The exact formal representation of selected branches, feature requirements, conflicts, target cardinality, and build/link edges remains an open design task in the October 24 note, not an implementation to assume. No source tree, generated content, build, test, or runtime was changed or exercised for this finding.


## October 25 — CLI is a partial service facade, not an all-service frontend

The latest CLI source corrects an overly broad reading that it is either “just a service facade” or an entirely parallel implementation. Its main player/composition and content operations connect to the local Client and send typed protocol actions. Workspace Cargo workflows and docs build/publish also enter through `WorkspaceAction`; the CLI renders returned operation records. This is an implemented shared route, not merely a future direction ([router](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command.rs#L58-L121>), [workspace tools](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command.rs#L227-L265>), [docs operations](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command.rs#L425-L463>)). The reusable connection helper starts or connects to the sibling service executable, and `launch --current-workspace` passes a workspace root to the service rather than running Cargo in the CLI process ([connection and current-workspace launch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/client_commands.rs#L62-L90>), [service client config](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/client_commands.rs#L155-L176>)).

At the same time, this is not a pure transport/presentation boundary. `client deploy local` calls Core deployment directly; `client launch` invokes the installed Entrypoint; the CLI itself owns source-path validation and session projections, local IDE repair and Git-provider operations, filesystem documentation open/path behavior, diagnostics capture, and a distinct `vapor sdk` command grammar. The dependency manifest confirms the binary directly links Core, provider, Client, protocol, console and SDK-CLI crates ([local Core deployment](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/client_commands.rs#L18-L59>), [local versus service routes](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command.rs#L144-L225>), [SDK branch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command.rs#L113-L121>), [crate dependencies](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/Cargo.toml#L8-L18>)). Source selection sharpens that distinction. `source open/close/add/remove` and registered-source queries are sent as authoring actions to the service; the CLI then stores a validated session root, current directory, nearest content context and Cargo index in `ShellState` for prompt and command behavior. This is an observed projection of service selection into session state, not evidence of a second durable CLI source registry ([service authoring calls](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/source_commands.rs#L236-L269>), [registration/query routes](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/source_commands.rs#L307-L368>), [shell projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/state.rs#L82-L157>)). This is not automatically wrong: terminal I/O, an explicit local deployment command and host-tool linking can belong to a frontend/adapter. The architectural issue is that the boundary between adapter duties and service-owned domain policy is not expressed as a complete contract, so a command-by-command audit is needed before claiming all clients share the same behavior.

The SDK subcommand makes this split concrete. It has its own parser and calls `vapor_sdk_core` directly; implemented branches include workspace status/sync/check/fmt/build/test/deploy, SDK-root package/publish, Steam status/login, and toolchain status/install. Other accepted grammar returns a visible `not_implemented` result ([SDK entry](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/lib.rs#L1-L12>), [dispatcher](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/output/mod.rs#L23-L74>), [stub contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/output/stub.rs#L1-L19>), [managed Cargo functions](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/mod.rs#L49-L81>)). The result is not simply “two shell syntaxes”: overlapping build/test workflows can be executed once as service operations and again as direct SDK Core calls. SDK-root package/publish also sits outside Client-service action identity, resource scheduling and progress records; this is distinct from the service-backed top-level `root package` and `root publish` commands. The explicit stub output is a strength—it avoids falsely presenting unimplemented grammar as completed work—but does not make the second authority surface coherent with the owner's chosen one-service model.

The structural pivot predates those command-specific additions. On October 19, `5e8474f` removed the CLI-local source and source-registry modules, cut the monolithic router from about 2,400 lines to a dispatcher, and introduced dedicated client/content/root/source command modules that issue protocol actions. The diff stat records 3,227 insertions and 3,972 deletions across 23 files; it did not erase the SDK command tree, which remained a separate direct Core adapter ([commit](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/5e8474f946970550658ff7bdf653a116799fe777)). This was a genuine boundary migration and code reduction, but the surviving SDK branch demonstrates that it was not a full “all operations through Client” conversion. The history then shows staged service convergence: October 20 routed workspace launch, docs build/publication and cleanup; October 21 added composition commands; October 22 added shared console-event rendering ([`f83ba52`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/f83ba52fcb0044c164c3ad6876848d9487a71a66), [`3e89f02`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/3e89f029c17781241de031c615332ca3309cd45c), [`c1c7d94`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/c1c7d945a51e684e73a7c273c8cf8e1073c1a438), [`d9207aa`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/d9207aa7e59cd920b409fc7ddb00eee93089f874), [`061eb7b`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/061eb7baf22139c815898196ae7a5572d1aa1aab), [`42fe658`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-CLI/commit/42fe658f4556cb2347befe290d445e1fb009a450)). This supports “partial, progressively centralized facade”; it does not prove that remaining local paths are accidental or approved as permanent. The next evidence pass should classify each command by owner (service/domain, frontend, host adapter, bootstrap/recovery) and compare that classification with Installer, Studio and Launcher.

### October 26 follow-up — root operations are service-routed; bootstrap and SDK paths remain distinct

The current CLI checkout is `a09c49c` (October 23) and clean at the October 26 inspection. A command-level trace sharpens the earlier classification: ordinary root `build` is not a CLI-local Cargo exception. It maps `CargoWorkflow::{Build, BuildRelease}` to `WorkspaceToolOperation` and sends `WorkspaceAction::RunTool` through the Client service; root `deploy` and `package` send their dedicated Workspace actions; root `publish` stages and publishes through typed Publishing actions ([root build/deploy/package/publish routing](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/root_commands.rs#L17-L194), [RunTool service route](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command.rs#L227-L265)). Thus the standard application lifecycle has materially converged on the shared service.

Two local paths have different jobs: `client deploy local` calls Core's local deployment routine before normal service-backed shell setup, and `client launch` invokes the installed Steam Entrypoint ([startup fast path](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/app.rs#L41-L55), [bootstrap and entrypoint calls](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/client_commands.rs#L22-L60)). These are plausible bootstrap/host-integration responsibilities; source alone does not establish whether every detail is the intended permanent boundary. The sharper architectural exception is `vapor sdk`: the CLI dispatches it to `vapor_sdk_cli::run`, whose workspace/release/toolchain operations call SDK Core directly, outside Client action identity and operation scheduling. This overlaps with the service-backed primary grammar rather than being only a thin alias. The current source therefore supports a specific conclusion: **the normal CLI lifecycle is service-centered, while an embedded SDK command family preserves a parallel execution surface**. Whether that family should be folded into the service or documented as a separate low-level API remains an owner decision. No command was executed; this is a source-routing trace, not runtime evidence.

### October 26 — SDK toolchain repair is advertised but unimplemented

The embedded SDK command tree exposes `toolchain repair` in its CLI model, command specification and help-facing description, but the output dispatcher implements only `status` and `install`; `Repair` falls into the generic `not_implemented` stub. The available install call is not a repair substitute: it rejects any existing expected toolchain root before invoking Rustup, even when status reports missing files. Status itself intentionally reports `PresentUnverified` after checking only the toolchain directory and `cargo`/`rustc` file presence; it does not verify the required rustfmt, Clippy, rust-src or installed target components. Thus the advertised command and the readiness model exceed the actual repair path ([SDK command model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/cli/toolchain.rs#L1-L25>), [dispatcher falls back for Repair](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/output/mod.rs#L67-L74>), [repair specification](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/spec/toolchain.rs#L29-L35>), [install rejects existing toolchain root](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/toolchain/install.rs#L19-L46>), [limited status check](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/toolchain.rs#L284-L312>)).

There is also an important host/target distinction rather than a demonstrated Windows-host defect. The October 22 fix maps the Windows GNU-LLVM Vapor executable host to Rustup's Windows MSVC host triple; the SDK's static host list follows that Rustup identity. Its own install plan nevertheless derives targets from the same Linux/MSVC list, while the shared Developer environment separately owns the GNU-LLVM target and linker. `vapor sdk toolchain install` and Developer-role provisioning are therefore not interchangeable setup routes, even though both speak of installing Vapor's toolchain ([Rustup host mapping](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/1c92bd7822949e8823ac279245135c2fadf5109c), [SDK host/target lists](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/toolchain.rs#L115-L139>), [SDK install target plan](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/toolchain/plan.rs#L20-L43>), [shared GNU target ownership](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L90-L139>)). This is a source-level route comparison, not a Windows installation or build result.

### October 26 — runtime promotion has parallel writers with different replacement guarantees

Two current Client-provider paths write declared runtime binaries and libraries to the same installation `bin/<target>` layout. `release::promotion` serves local deployment and Packagepack packaging; `release.rs::promote_release_outputs` serves the application release matrix. Both derive target-specific outputs, append `.exe` for Windows, copy Windows runtime DLLs, and stage the same named artifacts. Their replacement semantics have drifted: the application-release path preserves the prior file and attempts rollback if its staged rename fails, while `release::promotion::promote_file` deletes the prior file before the final rename, so a failure at that point can leave the destination absent. The older path also removes several retired executable names; consolidating the writer would need to retain that distinct cleanup behavior rather than just deduplicate identical lines ([application release promotion](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/release.rs#L281-L393>), [workspace/package promotion](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/release/promotion.rs#L40-L125>), [non-rollback replacement](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/release/promotion.rs#L182-L218>), [deployment and packaging callers](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/deployment.rs#L14-L53>, </home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/deployment.rs#L66-L110>)).

The history explains how both paths came to coexist: October 20's `d0cc4ba` added the workspace/package promotion module, while later `f9f129e` consolidated host build outputs in the broader release module without removing its separate promotion loop. These paths have distinct orchestration inputs, but share the installation artifact boundary; no concurrent execution or promotion failure was reproduced ([promotion-module introduction](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/d0cc4bae6bcf39a9cd10e28304b91a569ceb484c), [later release consolidation](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f9f129ee0413bf53fafc371690f5c0b8f098861b)).

## October 26 — Identity manages local account roles; ecosystem authorization is not integrated

The current Identity service is a usable Steam-anchored account and role-administration application, not merely a future authorization stub. Its role API accepts only `root` and `content-developer`; it resolves both supplied SteamID64 and GitHub login to the same existing profile, then requires that profile to be enabled and to have both linked accounts. API grants/revokes accept a server-local admin token or a valid root dashboard session; the browser form path requires the root session. A root profile receives `content-developer` as an effective role even if only the root role is stored. Each grant/revoke mutation and its audit event share one SQLite transaction; the audit listing returns at most 50 recent records without exposing internal profile IDs ([role administration handlers](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/admin_handlers.rs#L88-L323), [role persistence and effective-role model](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/profiles.rs#L75-L165), [service API and dashboard contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/README.md#L88-L146>)). These are meaningful safeguards and should remain distinct from downstream authorization.

The last-active-root invariant has a source-visible concurrency window: `revoke_role` reads the active-role and active-root counts before opening the write transaction, then updates a selected root row without rechecking the aggregate inside that transaction. Two overlapping revocations of different root profiles could each observe multiple active roots and then both revoke one. SQLite may serialize their writes, but serialization alone does not repeat the policy check. This is an inferred race from statement ordering, not a reproduced database failure; the existing focused test proves only that one sequential attempt to revoke a sole root is rejected ([guard and transaction order](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/profiles.rs#L125-L164), [sequential invariant test](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/profiles.rs#L749-L767)).

The intended cross-service boundary is newer and still unimplemented. The accepted design says Registry owns content identity/catalog/release records, Identity authorizes people and roles, and Steam transports/enforces Workshop distribution. The separate authorization contract proposes audience-bound session introspection; its initial consumers are Docs and Diagnostics, with publishing later. Current Identity routes contain no introspection endpoint, and a production-source search of Client, Registry, Docs and Diagnostics found no Identity consumer. Registry still owns only provider/repository/ecosystem topology. These documents therefore describe a destination, not a working publish authorization path ([accepted server boundary](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/server-domain-boundaries.md#L33-L64>), [introspection proposal](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/docs/cross-service-authorization-contract.md#L31-L110>), [Identity route table](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Platform-Server/Vapor-Identity-Server/src/main.rs#L80-L110)).

Identity's `root`/`content-developer` facts are also not the Installer's local Player/Composer/Developer setup tiers.
