The Client source has no production Identity client, so the reported Windows local-role promotion problem cannot be attributed to this server's role-grant route from available evidence. The desired remote account authority and local tool provisioning are separate systems today, without the linking contract needed to make them one user-visible capability. Historically, July 23–24 builds Identity quickly from Axum/SQLite/provider-verification scaffolding into Steam/GitHub-linked profiles, sessions, role grant/revoke and audit views; the July 25 cross-service contract then proposes consumers; September adds Registry as a different topology service; October 22 documents the accepted Workshop authority split. Identity's own current HEAD remains `6110547` (October 22, metadata only), and its worktree is clean. This review is source/doc/commit evidence only; no endpoint, concurrency test, deployment or live VPS state was exercised.

### October 26 — composition state persists selection and resolution, not installation status

The October 18 Client extraction (`f9e8b13`) introduced a service-owned `studio-state.json` store alongside the new Composition domain model. Current persistence has two schema levels: outer `ClientStateDocument` version 2 and `CompositionDocument` version 1. On first creation only, the service imports the legacy eframe `profiles`, active profile ID/index, workspace root, drafts, operation history and recovery backup. A legacy profile's selected content ID becomes a Packagepack reference without an exact version or resolved graph. Its per-composition workspace is preserved separately from the active authoring workspace; malformed profile data is retained in `recovery_backup` ([legacy decoder](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/composition.rs#L141-L202>), [one-time seed import](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/legacy_import.rs#L10-L58>)).

An existing `studio-state.json` is authoritative: outer schema 1 is promoted to the current version and saved, current-version state is loaded, and unsupported versions or invalid JSON return an error without consulting the eframe seed. If the file is absent, the service imports the seed and immediately writes the new state. Save uses a PID-specific create-new temporary file, flushes it, renames it into place, and syncs the containing directory on Unix; an included test asserts a blocked temporary path preserves the previous bytes ([load/schema handling](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/persistence.rs#L25-L68>), [replacement](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/persistence.rs#L72-L109>), [failure test](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/persistence.rs#L190-L219>)). Source and test-definition observations only; the test was not run.

Before saving and after loading, the service resets each composition's runtime `installation` field to `Unknown`, but retains selected root, resolved graph/provenance, launch settings and active ID. If the saved active ID no longer exists, it selects the first composition ([runtime projection and normalization](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/persistence.rs#L112-L130>)). That is a coherent split between durable selection/resolution and re-observed install state. It does not settle the product-model tension: owner direction says Packagepack itself is the playable selection and “composition” is informal shorthand, while the implementation persists a collection of Composition records and an active ID around those Packagepack roots. Whether that remaining record should exist only as user selection/settings state is unresolved; the storage mechanism alone does not answer it. No real user-data migration or startup behavior was exercised.

### October 26 — Studio creates a playable selection through two durable mutations

Studio's `create_composition_from_content` first sends `CompositionAction::Create`, which creates and activates an empty record, then calls `assign_composition_root`, which sends a separate `SetRoot` carrying exact content identity and optional workspace root. Only after the second response does Studio preview the selection. If that second step fails, the function returns `false` but does not remove the already-created, now-active empty composition. This is a real partial-success seam across two service requests; the source does not establish that users have hit it ([Studio action sequence](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/compositions.rs#L180-L207>), [root binding and failure return](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/compositions.rs#L218-L284>)).

The service already has an atomic `CreateFromContent` action. It verifies that the selected catalog item still exists at the exact version, is an available, conflict-free Packagepack, and offers the create-composition action before mutating durable state; its focused service test checks successful creation and rejection of non-Packagepack content. But that action carries only name, content ID and version—it has no workspace association ([action shape and domain transition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/composition.rs#L236-L264>), [service validation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/composition.rs#L311-L360>), [service tests](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L4539-L4609>)). Studio therefore cannot simply substitute that action without losing the source-workspace binding. A complete fix belongs in the shared action contract: include the optional workspace binding and preserve service-side availability/conflict validation, then let the UI make one durable mutation. No test or runtime action ran in this audit.

The history shows the seam forming rather than resolving: October 19 `9501276` introduced Studio's two-step helper while removing the earlier “recent Workshop acquisitions” route ([commit](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/950127675595812a0c47380a423a72c14e33c4f1)); October 21 `8765f62` added atomic `CreateFromContent` to the shared domain/service and backend tests, but its payload omitted workspace and the Studio helper remained unchanged ([commit](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/8765f621c4adab75a705e6eaec49954f2013687f)). This is a confirmed cross-frontend contract gap, not evidence that all composition selection is broken.

### October 26 — Play can acquire/install/repair before launching while reporting `Running`

On service startup, the default Packagepack selector from the installed App manifest is only used to fill the untouched `id = "default"`, `name = "Default"`, empty-root placeholder; the resulting root and human-readable name are saved. A custom composition or renamed placeholder is left alone. The service then loads the durable active ID and refreshes catalog/workspace views, but it does not verify each persisted composition's installed state at startup ([startup seed and state selection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L566-L632>), [placeholder-only seed](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L2128-L2168>)).

That leaves `installation = Unknown` after each restart. The service snapshot nevertheless makes Launch available whenever the active composition has a root and is not specifically `OutOfDate`; `Unknown` and `NotInstalled` do not disable Play ([launch action availability](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/snapshot.rs#L125-L180>), [launch queueability](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/snapshot.rs#L241-L268>)). The launch worker sets its initial phase to `Running`, then calls `run_installed_composition_with_context`. That application routine installs a missing graph, or repairs it when an expected graph exists; `install_composition` first calls `acquire_root_seed_closure`, which downloads/imports root-seeded Steam Workshop items before installation ([operation phase and worker](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/composition.rs#L102-L130>), [phase mapping](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/composition.rs#L420-L430>), [launch-time install/repair](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/content.rs#L792-L860>), [install and Workshop seed acquisition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/content.rs#L532-L601>)). The install/acquire calls do not receive the operation context, so their progress is not represented as Acquiring/Installing phases here; only the subsequently launched process is wired to report output. This is an execution-state and reporting mismatch: pressing Play can perform distribution/install work under a `Running` label.

The service's fixture test explicitly encodes the `Unknown` rule: once a root Packagepack is selected while installation remains `Unknown`, Launch is enabled; an `OutOfDate` state disables it. This proves the action-policy branch is intentional in the tested projection, but not whether implicit acquisition on Play is intended product policy. The test was not run, and the fixture launch does not exercise Steam or real provider installation ([fixture readiness assertions](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L4716-L4865>)).

Completion has a second lifecycle distinction: the application returns the installed graph even when starting the executable yields a `launch_error`. The service applies that graph and records installation state before converting the launch error into a failed operation; if the durable save succeeds, the newly installed/resolved state is retained despite Play failing. This makes install-before-launch a persistent side effect rather than an all-or-nothing launch transaction. It is source-defined behavior, not a reproduced failure ([result projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/composition.rs#L744-L860>), [save-before-operation-failure handling](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/composition.rs#L150-L212>), [application result carrying both graph and launch error](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/content.rs#L792-L860>)).

### October 26 — Studio's command palette is a second, manually gated action surface

The palette is more than navigation: it searches local catalog entries, compositions and unregistered workspace candidates, can launch a Workshop search, and directly invokes several workspace operations. But its built-in `Play` entry is `Navigate(Home)`; it only opens the Home page even though its keywords promise to “launch current composition.” That label is not a launch command ([entry table](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/command_palette.rs#L42-L47>), [dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/command_palette.rs#L411-L445>)).

Availability is separately reconstructed inside the palette from broad UI flags: all workspace operations require `!self.operation.running`, and several navigation/search actions have their own hardcoded checks. The shared protocol already transports service `AvailableAction` records with enabled state, reason and a `queueable` bit ([palette gate](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/command_palette.rs#L186-L209>), [available-action contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/state.rs#L27-L47>), [service queueability projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/snapshot.rs#L217-L277>)). Therefore the palette can disagree with current service readiness and independently prevent actions during an unrelated operation; it does not surface the service's specific reason. The source supports duplicated admission policy, not a claim that every palette action is currently broken or rejected.

History shows why the boundary split persisted: October 17 `86ac1eb` added the searchable palette in `app_shell.rs`; October 19 `d169e48` routed Studio workflows through the shared Client and changed the palette's local operation enum to Studio's wrapper, but retained the palette's hardcoded action list and gating ([initial palette](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/86ac1ebe3981e23eb4c87e0c70e8c7fdd4795f64), [service routing](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor-Studio/commit/d169e4859c14496ad3295ef9aa2c3bcc8aa13cef)). This is a semantic integration gap: frontends already receive service readiness metadata, but this command surface still owns a second eligibility model. No UI/runtime interaction was performed.

### October 26 — Workspace discovery is asynchronous but only coarsely interruptible

Opening a workspace canonicalizes and persists the selected directory, resets cached views if its root changed, schedules Library refresh, then schedules workspace-content discovery. In production those scans are background operations; the request handler does not synchronously walk the workspace tree. Discovery reports two phases: registered-source discovery, then unregistered-project scanning. The underlying scan calls receive no operation context, so cancellation is observed only between them; there is no per-directory progress or interrupt check within either call ([workspace open and view reset](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L953-L1020>), [async discovery operation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/catalog.rs#L21-L65>), [phase boundaries and scans](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/catalog.rs#L320-L390>), [async Library refresh](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/catalog.rs#L119-L170>)).

This source shape can explain coarse or apparently stalled progress during a large scan, but it does **not** establish why the reported Studio view remained at “100%, 3/3”: the service path inspected reports two discovery phases, and no GUI/client session was run to identify which operation produced that exact display. If “composition check” means `composition.verify`, the current service calls `verify_installation` without operation progress reporting ([verify dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/composition.rs#L573-L582>)); Studio only displays a progress bar when the service supplies progress, and removes terminal composition operations from its active list ([snapshot progress mapping](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/operations.rs#L135-L153>), [terminal-event handling](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/operations.rs#L342-L413>)). So the exact 100%/3-of-3 active display is not explained by the current `composition.verify` source path either; a stale/different build or another operation remains possible. Treat the UI symptom as reported, and the coarse/non-interruptible scan as confirmed implementation, without claiming either is the reproduced cause.

This is not proof that automatic setup-on-Play violates the intended player journey. The owner has separately required first-launch Vapor tool setup before Play, and has described explicit composition install/download flows; those decisions do not unambiguously settle whether a selected-but-uninstalled Packagepack should auto-acquire when Play is pressed. The operation's eventual result is checked and launch failure propagates, but no UI, Steam download, install or game process was run. The source establishes the hidden lifecycle coupling and phase shape, not a reproduced hang or mislaunch.



## October 25 — Cargo tool identity is shared; build outputs are not

The source shows a meaningful split between **toolchain environment** and **build cache ownership**. Provider builds and SDK builds both use Core's `RustToolchainCommandEnvironment`; that contract pins the Rust/Cargo executable environment and explicitly leaves discovery/cache ownership to the caller ([Core command environment](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/toolchain.rs#L38-L82>), [service provider adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/managed_cargo.rs#L20-L77>), [SDK adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/cargo.rs#L22-L75>)). This is real shared machinery, so it would be inaccurate to say every entrypoint independently chooses rustc or rebuilds the Rust environment contract.

Their target directories remain independent: service workspace operations write under the installation root's `output/dev|release/<project>`; SDK workspace operations write below `ManagedToolchain.user_data_root/output/dev/<workspace-id>`; Core's run/development path writes below `user_data_root/development/<project>/target` ([provider](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/workspace_build.rs#L443-L457>), [SDK](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/cargo.rs#L22-L30>), [Core run/development](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/development.rs#L421-L469>)). The suffix identity differs too: Cargo project name in the service/Core paths versus normalized workspace identity in SDK. Thus same-source workflows may hold separate dependency/build artifacts, and the Service's release profile is not colocated with SDK/Core development output. The cleanup implementation confirms the split. The October 20 `4a95c71` pass explicitly added a Workspace Clean that removes only service-managed `installation-root/output/dev/<project>`; the API checks names and handles symlinks safely, while preserving release outputs. The Core `DevelopmentOperation::Clean` is separate and removes the `user_data_root/development/<project>/target` tree; SDK's workspace command model defines no Clean variant ([service cleanup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/workspace_build.rs#L230-L295>), [service cleanup dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/workspace.rs#L830-L847>), [Core cleanup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/development.rs#L429-L447>), [SDK workspace variants](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/mod.rs#L16-L33>), [cache-cleanup commit](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/4a95c71627ce4e14d5979ddc686a0fd584a8e0ec)). The safe removal helper is a strength, but neither operation represents the full multi-root cache inventory or one user-facing cleanup scope. Historically, this is not because Vapor ignored the problem: October 20 first centralized the Rust subprocess environment (`ef611da`), then consolidated host build outputs (`f9f129e`), then added a cancellation-aware, symlink-safe development-cache clean (`4a95c71`) ([environment refactor](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/ef611daafe8647a731a64cd7db10d3c1e2552557), [host-output change](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f9f129ee0413bf53fafc371690f5c0b8f098861b), [cleanup change](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/4a95c71627ce4e14d5979ddc686a0fd584a8e0ec)). The code did reduce duplicated tool environment setup and created a bounded cleanup action. Its scope stopped at the service provider's workspace output tree, while pre-existing Core run output and the parallel SDK command retained separate roots. This is a case of partial consolidation with a measurable boundary left open, not an absence of any cache-management work. The repository has not shown one profile registry mapping each operation to an owned cache, shared reuse compatibility, size/last-use telemetry, and cleanup policy. This substantiates the user's request for Vapor-managed build profiles as a real design gap; it does not quantify this host's disk usage or establish that any one root is currently large. No cache deletion, build, or disk measurement was performed.


The application-release path is a distinct and heavier operation than a Steam upload. The service's staging task may call `build_application_release` first, which selects Cargo projects declaring binaries and runs six commands—fmt, check, test, Clippy, docs and release build—for every selected project/runtime-target pair. Cross-target tests compile with `--no-run`; host-target tests execute. `fmt --all -- --check` is target-independent but is nevertheless repeated once per runtime target. The progress counter advances only after each Cargo subprocess exits, although output lines are streamed while it runs, so progress is coarse during any one long step. Checks write into the `dev` target root and release builds into `release`; after all matrix jobs, binaries and declared libraries are promoted one file at a time into `bin/<target>`. This is a valid target-matrix gate, but it explains why release staging can do far more work than the phrase “publish” suggests and why a single long command can appear stalled between progress ticks. The promotion is atomic per file, not transactional across the whole matrix: a later missing artifact or copy error can leave earlier files already replaced. These are code-derived workload and failure-boundary findings, not measured duration or a reproduced partial install. [Matrix, step selection and progress](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/release.rs#L80-L133>), [Cargo target directories and per-step arguments](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/release.rs#L143-L239>), [sequential output promotion](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/release.rs#L281-L368>), [service task that optionally builds before staging](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/publishing.rs#L226-L315>).

## October 25 — Workspace selection has two persisted authorities and unequal validation

The repository now names the root distinctions explicitly. `App.vapor.toml` with `[root]` identifies an installed runtime App; `Workspace.vapor.toml` identifies a source-bearing workspace; `Superworkspace.vapor.toml` identifies a local checkout container. `VaporInstallation::discover` resolves from `VAPOR_HOME` or the installed executable path and explicitly has no authored-Workspace fallback ([installation contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/installation.rs#L47-L110>), [Workspace recognition](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/workspace.rs#L1-L18>), [Superworkspace role](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/superworkspace.rs#L1-L22>)). This supports the owner's correction: a Steam App root should not be required to contain `Workspace.vapor.toml`.

The current selection implementation nevertheless has two persistent roots. Core's Installation state file `sources.toml` stores the configured Superworkspace, known source roots and an active source. Core CLI resolution prefers an explicit path, then the most-specific known source containing CWD, then that Core active source ([source state](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/source.rs#L25-L79>), [resolution precedence](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/source.rs#L119-L139>), [known-root/CWD selection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/source.rs#L252-L280>)). Separately, the shared service persists `authoring_workspace_root` in `ClientPersistentState` and restores it as `bootstrap.workspace_root` ([state field](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/state.rs#L6-L27>), [service restore](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L588-L607>)). `Workspace Open` updates the service value but does not update Core's active source; `AuthoringAction::OpenSource` updates Core's source state but its result handler does not set the service workspace root ([Workspace Open](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L953-L1002>), [OpenSource dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/authoring.rs#L185-L213>)). These are separate persistent selection paths, not one source registry projected through multiple frontends.

The root checks are also asymmetric, but the caller matters. `remember_source` loads and validates `VaporWorkspace`; the direct Core `open_source` API checks only that a path canonicalizes to a directory outside the Installation before recording it as active, despite its doc comment saying “Validate” ([remember](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/source.rs#L141-L178>), [open](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/source.rs#L180-L217>)). The service `Workspace Open` action likewise checks canonicalization and directory-ness, not the Workspace marker. These direct APIs can therefore persist an arbitrary directory as authoring context. The ordinary CLI `source open` path is narrower: it runs provider source-root validation before sending `OpenSource`, and its shell state accepts only Root/Workspace entities ([CLI prevalidation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/command/source_commands.rs#L236-L245>), [shell-state gate](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_cli/src/state.rs#L123-L148>)). This distinction locates the risk at the direct service/Core API boundary; it is not evidence that normal CLI source opening accepts arbitrary directories. The source-workspace creation route initializes a workspace before invoking `open_source`, so this finding is not evidence that the creation flow itself creates an invalid root ([create route](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/authoring.rs#L567-L607>)).

This boundary formed in stages. Core's source registry and permissive `open_source` were introduced in the September 6 `5679c1d` change; the separate stricter `remember_source` operation arrived October 16 in `aef5d98`. The shared service extraction on October 18 (`f9e8b13`) introduced durable `authoring_workspace_root` as its own state field. On October 22, `8259961` added a narrowly targeted repair: clear a persisted authoring path only when `App.vapor.toml` exists and `Workspace.vapor.toml` does not. That change documents and tests one App-as-source failure mode, but it does not unify the two selection records or validate every source-open route. The corrected marker concepts and the remaining split must both be preserved in future documentation: the Steam folder is not a workspace, and source-workspace selection is not yet one authoritative state machine. No Windows Installer run or multi-frontend state round-trip was performed for this review.


## October 25 — SDK absorption centralized code, not every workspace operation

The 14 October `0e5789bfe8d7590d401f33f7617ae75a6a2f023c` change moved the SDK core into the shared Vapor repository (+3,278 / −29 lines over 49 files), including direct workspace Cargo orchestration, toolchain management, Steam and first-party root packaging/publishing. This is a genuine code-consolidation milestone. It does not mean the graphical SDK or all user workflows were complete, nor that the new Client service owned every operation. On 19 October, `5e8474f946970550658ff7bdf653a116799fe777` moved the main CLI workflow families through the shared Client, but the `vapor sdk` grammar remained embedded as a second command dispatcher.

At this checkout the split is specific: ordinary `vapor build/check/fmt/test` sends typed Client actions; `vapor sdk workspace build/check/fmt/test/sync/deploy` calls `vapor_sdk_core` inside the CLI process. The service also calls the same SDK-Core root publication function, so `vapor_sdk_core` is neither dead nor wholly outside the service. Direct CLI execution skips the service's operation reservation, origin tracking and console event stream, even when it invokes shared Rust functions. The typed SDK grammar has further content authoring/packaging commands, but those branches emit an explicit `not_implemented` result; do not generalize that status to Workspace Cargo or first-party root publication ([SDK direct dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/output/mod.rs#L23-L74>), [stub branch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/output/stub.rs#L1-L19>), [service root publishing reuses SDK Core](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/publishing.rs#L48-L120>)).

`workspace sync` is the most consequential surviving legacy generator. It walks upward from CWD (or starts at `--workspace`) for `Workspace.vapor.toml`, derives a workspace ID from `[workspace].organization` and `.name`, reads the listed `projects[].path`, and creates the generated Cargo workspace/package manifests plus seeded `src/lib.rs` files ([identity search](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/identity.rs#L20-L84>), [project-path resolution](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/manage.rs#L100-L174>), [sync writes](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_sdk_core/src/workspace/manage.rs#L54-L98>)). The path is joined to the workspace root and used for both manifest reads and generated writes without rejecting absolute/parent components or canonicalizing containment. Because the sync path creates a missing `src` tree and managed files, a crafted project path can cause an explicit sync invocation to create files outside the declared workspace. The command guard defaults to no confirmation for Workspace Sync; it confirms deploy instead ([guard policy](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-CLI/crates/vapor_sdk_cli/src/safety.rs#L150-L209>)). This is a conditional source-level write-boundary risk, not an exploit reproduction or evidence of a reported incident. The Client provider's Workspace project parser separately rejects absolute and parent components ([relative-path validator and callers](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/workspace.rs#L540-L653>)); this is only lexical containment, not canonical symlink containment. The mismatch confirms that two authoring engines enforce different contracts.

The apparent documentation contradiction around “sync” is also a naming collision, not evidence that either page is wrong: SDK `workspace sync` generates Cargo structure, while Shell `source sync` is a deliberately non-operative provider-sync hook. The docs name the latter as a no-op correctly, but the same bare word makes a cross-surface reader likely to miss the implemented workspace generator. The intended single local service is therefore a partially delivered boundary, not a false claim across the board. Main CLI workflows and GUI surfaces mostly use the service; some lower-level operations remain direct frontend adapters; shared root publication logic is consumed both by service and SDK CLI; and the legacy workspace generator still owns a separate manifest-driven write/build surface. The correct migration question is operation-specific: which code is reusable domain machinery, which side effects must be serialized/reported by the service, and which shell commands should remain explicit recovery adapters? No CLI command was executed, no files were written by `workspace sync`, and no build/test was run for this finding.


## October 25 — authored content and runtime artifacts are co-staged; Pack edges do not generate Cargo links

The generic `content package` implementation copies the complete authored artifact root into a new staged package, with only `.git`, `target`, and `output` excluded; it then stages the declared binaries and libraries for the selected runtime targets and writes the deployed manifest ([copy/stage/write](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/packaging.rs#L275-L303>), [exclusion list](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content.rs#L2451-L2453>)). Workshop publication invokes this package path for each selected artifact before passing the directory to SteamCMD ([package-to-upload path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/workshop.rs#L534-L565>)). Therefore the present release payload contains the source tree as well as compiled runtime outputs. The inspected pipeline does not attach a Git revision or establish that the included binaries were produced from that exact copied source. This may support source recovery, but it couples source and target payload size/update cadence; the owner's later GitHub source/separate-release idea was posed as an option, not finalized. No real uploaded Workshop payload was downloaded or inspected in this pass.

The docs also blur the distinction between a Pack's Vapor manifest and its registered source project. The current book says Packagepack is “metadata, not a Rust crate,” but both the example and flagship workspace register a Packagepack project whose Cargo crate has the launch binary; the example directory additionally has a `src/lib.rs`. That arrangement is compatible with the owner's direction if the manifest is the Pack and the source project realizes its link root, but the book and generic template do not state or produce that two-part contract. The date sequence rules out treating the wording as merely an untouched July stub: Loo-Cast introduced the executable Packagepack on October 17 (`4551c53`), the full metadata-only claim was committed October 20 (`a194167`), and the example Cargo root followed October 21 (`c157496`). The docs were refreshed after the first implementation but missed its changed realization model.

The current examples also keep two graphs manually aligned. The Wheel Salvage Packagepack manifest selects the terminal Engine, the Game, and a mod ([manifest](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Examples/content/hello-world-packagepack/Packagepack.vapor.toml#L3-L21>)); the Cargo Packagepack crate separately names the Game, Engine, and Mod crates in its linker dependency graph ([Cargo graph](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Examples/content/hello-world-packagepack/Cargo.toml#L1-L17>)). Loo-Cast's Packagepack binary likewise directly depends on the Engine and Game crates ([Cargo graph](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/loo-cast-packagepack/Cargo.toml#L1-L14>)). The Vapor resolver validates a selected manifest graph and packaging stages outputs already built for each discovered artifact; the inspected path does not translate an arbitrary resolved Pack graph into Cargo dependencies or statically link independently acquired compiled libraries. This is a source-confirmed boundary of the examined path, not proof that no other build mechanism exists elsewhere; it matches the broader gap between manifest composition and the current source-workspace Composer.


## October 25 — the Playground “Creative Menu” is a game inventory, not a content authoring surface

The Loo-Cast `PlaygroundUiPlugin` composes a fixed creative inventory menu, hotbar and HUD within the game implementation. The menu pages registered `ItemCatalog` rows (45 items/page) into a 590-pixel panel with 58-pixel fixed slots, and cursor/hotbar interactions edit the player's runtime hotbar rather than any Vapor content graph ([plugin boundary](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/ui/mod.rs#L1-L25>), [layout](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/ui/creative_menu/layout/mod.rs#L5-L74>), [catalog](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/ui/creative_menu/catalog/mod.rs#L5-L76>), [hotbar operations](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/ui/creative_menu/hotbar/mod.rs#L1-L55>)). Toggling it closed clears the held item and releases the modal focus claim; the help panel then only reports how to close it, not how to select/swap items ([toggle path](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/input.rs#L51-L88>), [context-help early return](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/playground/ui/hud/context_actions.rs#L37-L67>)). This is not a Workshop/Library browser, source editor or Composer workflow. The overloaded word “creative” names an in-game sandbox tool, whereas Vapor Composer is a separate product role. The fixed dimensions and help omissions are source observations; no runtime fit/usability conclusion is claimed.

## October 25 — the ten-kind vocabulary loses semantic resolution at the Client catalog boundary

Vapor's shared content module defines the owner's fixed ten-kind vocabulary as a Rust enum, with canonical manifest names and spellings ([kind enum and names](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/content.rs#L30-L122>)). The provider-facing local catalog then weakens that value to `String`: `CatalogContent.kind` is documented as canonical, but its type cannot enforce that claim. Catalog merge groups observations by exact ID/version and flags kind disagreements, yet has no typed kind invariant at its own boundary ([catalog model and merge](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/catalog.rs#L45-L63>), [merge conflict checks](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/catalog.rs#L108-L180>)). The protocol repeats the string and separately derives a four-value `CatalogItemRole`: Packagepack, Crate, the other eight recognized kinds collapsed to RuntimeContent, and unknown values to Other ([wire entry and broad role](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/state.rs#L446-L486>)). That role is useful for coarse lifecycle presentation, but it is not a substitute for the ten-kind semantic identity the owner wants shared across acquisition, composition and authoring.

The conversion is operational, not merely cosmetic. Service projection reparses the string to assign the broad role and reparses parent and child kinds when deciding whether source content can be added to a composition ([projection and kind parsing](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/catalog.rs#L498-L621>)). Meanwhile, the local Library discovery function deliberately emits only Cache and Installed locations; source-workspace projects live on a separate discovery path despite `CatalogLocationKind::Workspace` existing in the shared domain model ([acquired catalog discovery](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/catalog.rs#L6-L74>)). This split partly matches the product distinction between acquired player content and editable source, but it means the local catalog merge cannot itself reconcile one identity across source, acquired and installed states. The service later projects them together only through separate workspace/catalog machinery.

The source-authoring provider retains a richer source-side model than the Client catalog: `ContentArtifact` carries the typed `ContentKind`, source paths, version, declared binary/library outputs, per-target runtime payloads, presentation, dependency/conflict references and Workshop policy; `ContentCatalog` pairs these artifact records with the resolver candidate set and can select the latest satisfying version ([provider artifact and selection model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/model.rs#L14-L105>), [target payload and authored references](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/model.rs#L158-L207>)). Studio does not edit this object directly. It receives separate projections for the dependency graph, Workshop policy, and runtime output declarations; each projection carries the exact manifest text as a stale-write token ([source editor snapshots](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/model.rs#L209-L260>)). Their save paths validate that snapshot against the current file, parse/edit the TOML document, acquire a per-manifest lock, replace through a temporary/backup path, then reopen and validate the result, restoring the backup on validation failure ([graph save](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L1309-L1440>), [shared manifest replacement](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L1548-L1611>), [runtime and Workshop editors](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L1468-L1519>), [Workshop editor](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L1631-L1715>)). This is a meaningful guarded authoring foundation, not an absence of structure. The trade-off is whole-manifest optimistic concurrency: any successful edit invalidates other open projections of that manifest, so independently editing graph, Workshop, and runtime panels requires refresh/reload rather than field-level merge. The three DTOs also serialize kind as `String`, so the stronger provider `ContentArtifact.kind` contract is weakened again at the service/Studio edit surface.

The lineage reveals a deliberate trade-off rather than a simple accidental omission. The October 18 shared-service extraction (`f9e8b13`) introduced `CatalogLocationKind::{Workspace, Cache, Installed}` and an application catalog that merged all three by exact content identity; even in that first shared version, however, `CatalogContent.kind` was already a string. The October 22 workflow-tier change (`3b692e7`) renamed that API to `discover_local_content_catalog`, removed Workspace entries and documented authored source as a separate discovery surface ([initial catalog model](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/f9e8b13), [source/acquired split](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/3b692e7)). The change makes a meaningful UX distinction—Library is for acquired content, source projects belong in authoring—but implements the distinction by splitting projections rather than preserving one typed identity with distinct location/workflow views. So the current fragmentation is partly the result of a reasonable product boundary implemented at the wrong semantic layer, not evidence that source and player Library should be presented identically.

**Assessment:** a canonical vocabulary exists, but its invariants stop before the main Client catalog and protocol. Broad UI roles are layered on as another classification, and source discovery is a parallel projection rather than another provider observation in one identity model. This concretely reinforces the owner's concern about duplicated/conflated semantics and the need for one typed core with distinct workflow projections. It does not establish that the catalog currently displays an incorrect kind or caused the reported filter failure; no UI, Workshop query or cross-platform workflow was exercised. No implementation change is proposed by this audit.

## October 25 — source-manifest editors are typed views over one optimistic snapshot

The provider has a substantially more deliberate authoring boundary than a raw TOML text editor. A discovered `ContentArtifact` keeps the typed `ContentKind`, exact source paths, optional version, binary/library declarations, target-specific runtime payloads, presentation, dependency/conflict references and Workshop policy; `ContentCatalog` associates those source artifacts with resolver candidates and selects latest versions satisfying a declared requirement ([artifact/catalog model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/model.rs#L14-L105>), [target payload and reference model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/model.rs#L158-L207>)). Studio receives three narrower snapshots for graph links, Workshop policy and runtime outputs, each carrying the complete original manifest string as its optimistic-concurrency token ([source editor snapshot types](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/model.rs#L209-L260>)).

The save operations re-read and compare that whole source, validate the requested typed projection against the local catalog or field policy, edit with `toml_edit`, and use a per-manifest create-new lock plus temporary/backup replacement; after writing they reopen the artifact and restore the backup if the new manifest cannot be validated ([graph validation and write](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L1309-L1440>), [shared replacement transaction](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L1548-L1611>), [runtime output editor](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L1468-L1519>), [Workshop policy editor](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L1631-L1715>)). This is real structure and guarded authoring machinery, not a mere TOML text box. Its ownership trade-off is whole-file optimistic concurrency: a save in one projection makes another open projection of that same manifest stale, so the second must reload rather than merge field-level changes. The authoring DTOs also expose `kind` as `String`, weakening the typed value that `ContentArtifact` already holds before it reaches the service/Studio boundary. These are source-derived semantics; no editor interaction, concurrent-save race, or rollback fault was exercised.

The history dates this boundary to the service migration rather than to the later IDE workbench: [`d7e21dc3`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/d7e21dc332a8b8874541eeb5ca0a4fffeeb655d0) added the provider authoring module and model in one 3,148-line change; [`a10ca0e6`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Vapor/commit/a10ca0e6) changed only a small follow-up in these two files. So structured graph/metadata editing was already part of the shared-service extraction. It should not be described as a feature that first appeared in the newer IDE semantic workbench, whose role is editor/navigation rather than authority for these manifest writes.

## October 25 — the voxel plan cap truncates results after some demand paths finish enumerating

The current demand planner has distinct controls that are easy to mistake for one hard work limit. `ReconstructibleFrameBudget` paces synchronous units using per-class estimates, but admits the first unit of each class and cannot preempt work once admitted ([budget policy](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/reconstructible.rs#L76-L153)). Voxel residency invokes the entire `refresh_demand_plan` operation as one Planning unit ([call site](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/streaming/demand/systems.rs#L35-L55)). The desired chunk budget is capped at 65,536 and is used to stop the moving non-view predictive tube ([budget formula](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/streaming/demand/plan/mod.rs#L84-L120), [tube cap](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/streaming/demand/plan/tube.rs#L63-L204)).

The stationary and view-backed paths do not receive that cap. `collect_all_region_leaves` loops through every cell in the region extent; `collect_culled_region` recursively visits nodes and prunes by view/surface predicates, but has no maximum-work argument. `demanded_chunk_addresses_with_motion` calls those paths, builds a merged map, sorts it, and truncates to the desired count only afterward ([region enumeration](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/streaming/demand/plan/regions.rs#L19-L130), [dispatch and final truncate](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/streaming/demand/plan/tube.rs#L219-L310)). Region spans check per-axis integer extents, but not total volume or work ([extent construction](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/region/mod.rs#L14-L40)). A very broad but coordinate-representable stationary/view demand can therefore exceed both the nominal set cap and the frame allowance before later chunk-generation throttling takes effect. This is a **source-derived missing practical work-bound risk**, not an observed hang; the finite integer extent bound still permits enormous volumes, and no runtime profile was performed.

Generation itself is more tightly bounded: the batch planner separately limits chunks by `load_budget_per_frame`, `max_batches` and per-batch limits, with latency-sensitive roles placed in single-item batches ([generation scheduler](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/voxel/streaming/generation/batching/mod.rs#L29-L99)). This later limit protects materialization throughput; it does not bound the earlier region walk, allocation or sorting. The current design still has useful moving-tube selection, view/surface culling, prioritized work, and a cooperative pacer. The mismatch is specifically between those controls and synchronous enumeration. The plan module has no focused test for a maximum enumeration count; its nearby region test checks only the surface-shell predicate. No test was run.

The history shows the direction was not simply “add a larger cap.” `cb094c1` (October 2) introduced cooperative pacing across reconstructible work classes. `f588206` (October 8) removed unconditional whole-body demand and unused shell planning; `eb6814f` later that day added expanded voxel intent and contact-aware region/tube selection. This review does not claim those changes caused a runtime hitch or were wrong: the cleanup reduced unnecessary whole-body work, but the latest source still does not apply its result cap during every enumeration path. See [the spatial-demand chronology](loo-cast-vapor-history-timeline.md#october-25--the-desired-set-is-capped-after-uncapped-region-enumeration).

## October 25 — the spacecraft is a complete reference loop, not a vehicle lifecycle

The current `SpacecraftPlugin` composes a useful end-to-end fixture: wait for the player's detailed celestial chart and collision readiness; create a semantic ship, one authority partition and one logical manifestation; transfer local control to that manifestation; fly with the shared locomotion/flight/navigation facilities; detect and resolve a physical landing; board from a nearby landed ship; and prove a walkable disembark pose before returning control to the player. The visible ship is a disposable child presentation. Its orbit telemetry is derived from canonical relative position/velocity and the selected gravity source; it does not author or propagate the ship's orbit ([plugin schedule](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/mod.rs#L98-L124>), [fixture spawn and readiness gate](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/spawn.rs#L17-L104>), [ship realization](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/spawn.rs#L106-L227>), [derived orbit state](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/orbit.rs#L52-L126>)). This is substantial integration evidence: the player is not the ship, constituency is not control, the semantic subject is not its local physical realization, and collision readiness gates the initial control handoff.

Landing requires the controlled ship to be at its detailed scale, in the spacecraft-flight regime, landing-capable, below its preferred contact speed and not separating upward; an Avian hull cast must hit a walkable surface in the active physics chart. Acceptance synchronizes local and semantic position, stops canonical and projected velocity, marks surface contact, inhibits motion and requests both propulsion systems off. Takeoff clears contact/inhibition, restores the spacecraft regime, enables actuation and applies a fixed 5 m/s upward velocity ([landing predicate and shape cast](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/landing.rs#L26-L127>), [land/takeoff state changes](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/landing.rs#L129-L235>)). Entry uses a 12-metre cross-scale reach check and only considers landed ships. Exit is stronger than teleporting to a seat offset: it shape-casts the player's hull beside the ship, filters the ship/player/excluded entities, checks the ground-normal threshold, then updates the player's canonical position and chart before requesting the return transfer ([entry](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/boarding/entry.rs#L1-L130>), [pose proof](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/boarding/pose.rs#L1-L60>), [exit sequence](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/boarding/exit.rs#L1-L167>)). The current visibility projection follows semantic constituency, not the control marker, which prevents a lingering hidden-player state after a successful transfer ([visibility derivation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/spacecraft/boarding/visibility.rs#L1-L35>)).

The same source sets a strict scope ceiling. Startup refuses to create a second spacecraft manifestation and the landing action requires one controlled ship; orbit telemetry can derive samples for every manifestation. The reference hull/camera/profile/flight and travel settings are authored directly in Rust. No inspected spacecraft content definition, fleet, seats/occupants collection, save identity or recoverable vehicle lifecycle exists. Boarding and disembark mutate player visibility, demand, collision components and constituency before the queued transfer is resolved. In the built-in path, their guards establish the resolver's local-controller, semantic-target and affinity preconditions; this is not evidence of an ordinary failed transfer, but there is no spacecraft rollback if a future caller or mutation invalidates one. The separate control/USF section documents that accepted control still precedes chart admission, so the overall sequence is not one atomic “boarded and interaction-ready” transaction.

The lineage explains why this is a reference loop. September 22 constituency/control commits ([`71867eb`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/71867eb)) establish person→ship relationships and a generic local-control request model, but initially do not provide lifecycle semantics. September 29 adds canonical collision-query request wiring ([`1d868d8`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/1d868d8)); September 30 reworks landing/disembark shape casts and defers the chart change to the control handoff ([`4768d04`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/4768d04), [`879e197`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/879e197)). The October 7 visibility/terrain repair ([`25af9d1`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/25af9d1)) makes embarked visibility derive from semantic constituency. October 9's broad flight/player tranche changes the surrounding motion contract, but its last direct spacecraft edits in [`46e1eac`](https://github.com/GHF-Studios/Loo-Cast/commit/46e1eac) comprise only three changed lines across the spacecraft module and spawn file. Later control/spatial work continues to alter its surrounding contracts without turning the craft into content-authored vehicles. This sequence is a progression from graph vocabulary, through physical queries, to a runnable fixture—not evidence of a general vehicle API. The owner-reported high-speed Moon braking/collision failures remain separate historical runtime evidence; this source inspection did not reproduce them or establish that the current reference ship closes them.

## October 25 — Earth arrival search is sophisticated relative to the current spherical field

The player bootstrap's `resolve_good_spawn` searches eight fixed arc-distance rings from 0 to 160 km, with twelve samples per nonzero ring. It estimates surface normals and four-point roughness using a probe radius clamped to 75–500 m based on the controlled hull; selects an ideal candidate at ≤18° slope, otherwise a fallback at ≤32°, otherwise the lowest score among any candidates; and rejects sampled points whose SDF is outside a 0.25 m surface-boundary tolerance. The implementation is deterministic for a given authored hint and field because candidate order is fixed and equal scores preserve the earlier candidate.

This is a real bounded spawn-selection algorithm, but the live field is constructed as a sphere. On that field the derived normals are radial and local roughness is zero, so the slope/roughness policy cannot demonstrate its intended discrimination across varied terrain. The source comments mention rocky terrain and cave voids, but no such field is supplied by this fixture. After candidate selection, hull support plus a fixed 0.75 m character gap or 25 m ship gap is applied radially. The bootstrap immediately writes the semantic body position and chart transform, then queues a separate coverage-gated transition. Therefore the transition is coverage-aware, but its gate does not precede the initial semantic placement; source evidence alone neither proves a collision fault nor demonstrates collision-ready placement. The distinction is important given the historical Moon braking and surface-collision reports, which were not replayed in this pass. See [the current worldgen/fixture cross-check](vapor-ecosystem-evidence-atlas.md#7a-worldgen-means-deterministic-construction-inputs-today-not-procedural-worlds), [spawn resolver](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/world/fixture/spawn.rs), and [bootstrap transaction](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Loo-Cast/spacetime-engine/src/game/world/fixture/player/mod.rs).


## October 25 — role setup is one all-tools transaction, not a progressive capability plan

A closer pass over the actual setup operation sharpens the earlier role/action analysis. `VaporRole::requires_developer_environment()` is a boolean shared by Composer, Content Developer and Ecosystem Developer. Promotion calls one `DeveloperEnvironment::reconcile()`, which installs pinned Rust components, the Windows GNU target, the host-specific LLVM-MinGW bundle, and Tracy profiler plus analysis tools before persisting the role ([role promotion](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/role.rs#L145), [shared reconciliation](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L111)). The installer describes this exact policy to users: Composer “prepares Rust, Cargo, Windows build support, and Tracy” ([role description](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Installer/crates/vapor_installer_ui/src/lib.rs#L501)).

But `DeveloperEnvironmentStatus::is_ready()` aggregates those six independent pieces into one boolean, while operation admission checks only the capabilities named by each action profile. The Composer build-and-launch profile requires Managed Rust; Language Server start requires Rust Analyzer; Open Profiler requires Tracy. No action profile requests Windows GNU support. Also, cross-target linker installation returns `UnsupportedHost` outside x86_64 Linux/Windows, while Tracy analysis has its own platform restrictions. Therefore role promotion can fail because of a feature unrelated to that user's immediate task, and a role snapshot cannot distinguish “Rust is ready, Tracy analysis unsupported” from “the whole developer environment is unavailable” when discovery itself errors. This is a confirmed mismatch between role provisioning and per-operation capability ownership, not a reproduced platform incident.

The coupling is wider than promotion: Core maintenance diagnoses a developer installation as unhealthy unless the same aggregate bundle is ready, and broad repair invokes the same full reconciliation. A missing optional or host-unsupported component can therefore make a healthy-for-the-current-task installation appear unhealthy and make generic repair fail ([maintenance health rule](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/maintenance.rs#L52), [maintenance repair](/home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/maintenance.rs#L187)).

This does **not** imply that role promotion should silently become partial or that demotion should delete tools. The current policy explicitly installs the full bundle and preserves it on demotion. It means the intended Player → Composer → Developer ladder is not yet translated into a capability plan: required, optional, host-specific, and independently useful tools are bundled into one promotion and maintenance transaction, although the service already models narrower capabilities. Exact code references and historical caveats remain in [the role/action analysis](#october-25--role-tiers-collapse-to-one-developer-bundle-while-action-profiles-describe-only-three-capabilities).

## October 25 — Studio's composition panel lets unrelated authoring dirt block player operations

The shared service makes Install, Update, Repair, Verify, and Launch operations against one composition resource, with the composition's associated workspace optional. Install/update/repair workers pass that workspace only when present; installed Launch likewise accepts the optional workspace for context ([service action snapshot](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/snapshot.rs#L145-L278>), [operation dispatch](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/composition.rs#L534-L616>), [application install API](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/content.rs#L534-L546>)). Studio's composition details panel then adds a broader frontend-only gate: every primary action except Play/Verify on a non-workspace root requires the global workspace editor to be clean, and `install_selected`, `update_selected`, `repair_selected_installation`, and `preview_selected_composition` independently call `require_saved_workspace` ([panel gate](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/pages/compositions_installation_panel.rs#L195-L246>), [lifecycle handlers](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/composition_lifecycle.rs#L96-L165>), [global dirty-state rule](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/workspace_ops.rs#L383-L407>)). Because `has_unsaved_workspace_edits()` spans every open editor document and authoring draft, editing an unrelated source project can disable installing or updating a separately selected acquired composition. The service's queueability is also consulted for actions with IDs, but local dirty-state blocking is applied afterward and cannot be overridden by a queueable resource reservation. This is a source-confirmed boundary mismatch between the Player lifecycle and global Developer editing state; no UI interaction was run. The gate may be necessary when a composition is actually built from its associated source, but the same policy is currently applied without that relation being required. Preserve source-root safety while separating unrelated player actions from unrelated dirty editors.

## October 25 — the service simulator proves typed process flows, not concurrent frontend behavior

Vapor Client includes a valuable isolation boundary: `simulate` launches a fixture-mode `Client` over stdio, and the production local-service entrypoint rejects fixture mode ([simulator bootstrap and mode](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/simulator.rs#L16-L54>), [production service rejection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/server.rs#L54-L59>)). Scenario actions are typed protocol values; expectations can check response/error, terminal operation action/status/message, active selection, catalog projection and workspace counts ([scenario schema](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/scenario.rs#L1-L34>)). The process integration test invokes all five named checked-in scenarios through a child service process, while separate process tests cover selected Workshop and workspace round trips ([scenario process test](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/tests/process.rs#L840-L852>)). This is stronger than a pure mock and is useful evidence for typed request/response and fixture isolation.

The scenario runner itself awaits every accepted asynchronous operation to a terminal event before moving to the next step ([serial step loop and terminal wait](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/simulator.rs#L42-L112>), [terminal wait implementation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/simulator.rs#L252-L294>)). Its expectation schema cannot express intermediate progress/output sequences or send an independent action while an earlier operation is running. So these checked-in scenarios do not verify queueing, conflict handling across simultaneous frontends, operation-origin attribution or streaming-console behavior. That is a limit of this scenario facility, not proof that the service lacks separate unit/process tests for every such property; the inspected process suite has specific round trips and a service-restart persistence test, but no named simultaneous-client test was found in its function inventory. On early scenario failure, the child client is dropped and its `Drop` implementation sends Disconnect then kills/reaps any still-running child ([client cleanup](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client/src/process.rs#L553-L562>)); no simulator-specific lingering child is implied. No simulator or tests were run in this audit.


## October 25 — managed-tool infrastructure is a Tracy-shaped adapter, not yet a lifecycle manager

Core defines a reusable request identity—tool name/version, executable names, required host capabilities—and derives an install path partitioned by tool, version, target triple and capability key. It also offers executable discovery and a GitHub-release downloader that distinguishes a genuinely missing asset from HTTP/integrity failures. This is a useful seed, but the current consumer search finds `ManagedToolRequest` and its release helper used only by Tracy; `find_executable_on_path` has no other production caller. So “managed tools” currently names shared path/download primitives, not a general install/repair/update/remove contract ([request and path identity](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/managed_tool.rs#L20-L103>), [release download and verification](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/managed_tool.rs#L111-L246>)).

The download path has meaningful safeguards: exact release tag and asset selection, mandatory SHA-256 metadata, digest verification before promotion, executable permissions on Unix, and a distinct “missing” result so providers can choose a fallback only for absence. But the expected digest comes from the live GitHub release API rather than an independently pinned value; the response and asset are buffered wholly in memory without a size bound; and replacement removes an existing destination before renaming the verified temporary file. A filesystem failure during promotion can therefore lose the previous copy. These are source-level resilience/integrity limits, not evidence of an observed bad download. The parallel cross-target linker provisioner has a stronger shape: a source-pinned checksum, streaming size limit and staged replacement; the tool paths do not yet share that assurance level ([managed download](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/managed_tool.rs#L118-L246>), [cross-target linker contract](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/cross_target_toolchain.rs#L1-L114>)).

Tracy is explicitly pinned to `0.14.0` and a source commit. Its profiler first attempts a Vapor release artifact; only a missing artifact permits Linux x86_64 GNU to build from the pinned upstream archive. That fallback fetches the commit-addressed archive into memory and does not verify a separately pinned archive checksum or cap its size. Tracy CSV export is a second, separately implemented Linux-only source build; if missing on Windows it errors. Readiness requires both the profiler and CSV exporter, and developer-role reconciliation always attempts the Tracy tools after Rust, Rust Analyzer and the Windows GNU linker. Thus the Windows toolchain promotion path is incomplete whenever CSV export is absent, even if the profiler itself is installed; the source does not establish whether the current release happens to contain all needed assets ([Tracy requirement and install behavior](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/tracy.rs#L90-L167>), [host-specific acquisition/fallback](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/tracy.rs#L332-L444>), [source fallback staging](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/tracy.rs#L462-L590>), [developer readiness/reconciliation](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L23-L31>), [developer setup sequence](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/developer_environment.rs#L105-L177>)).

The history shows incremental ownership improvements rather than a completed general facility. On September 29, `2da87f8` added the managed-tool and Tracy implementations as a 989-line tranche. On October 15, `2b20ad9` removed unused Tracy origin/provenance fields. On October 21, `92ab2b9` routed Tracy's background subprocesses through the shared quiet-process helper, addressing Windows console behavior. That is a real process-launch convergence; it did not unify artifact identity, integrity policy, staged replacement or platform availability. The docs describe Tracy as part of required developer setup, but do not establish a cross-platform analysis-tool contract ([developer environment guide](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/docs/developer-environment.md#L1-L30>)). No build, install, test, or runtime verification was performed for this source audit.


## October 25 correction — fixed choice groups are used by authoring, not by generic resolution

A prior cross-reference sentence said the `dependency_choice_group` helpers had no consumers beyond tests and re-exports. That was incorrect. `validate_source_relationship_cardinality` consumes them when checking selected children in source-authoring flows; for Packagepack it requires exactly one Engine/Enginepack choice and one Game/Gamepack choice. The correct gap is boundary-specific: authoring validates these fixed slots, but the provider-neutral resolved graph does not preserve an explicit choice group or selected branch. Its selector resolves all required edges independently, skips optional edges, and validates the resulting flattened graph later. The Core adapter only maps local catalog records to that shared resolver, then optionally adds kind/graph validation or a Packagepack projection ([authoring cardinality check](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/authoring.rs#L2189-L2235>), [generic resolution](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_content/src/resolution.rs#L312-L463>), [Core local adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/resolution.rs#L15-L135>)).

This correction narrows rather than removes the design mismatch. The source-authoring UI can validate a pair of fixed role slots; it does not establish that installed/catalog resolution can choose among general alternatives or represent intentionally incompatible paths inside a Pack. This is consistent with the October 24 local proposal and the owner's direction, but the proposal remains uncommitted and is not implementation evidence. No tests or builds were run for this audit correction.

## October 25 — Studio embeds a telemetry console, but Tracy launch still depends on a live session

`vapor_devtools::DevtoolsApp` is a real embedded Studio page, not an unused crate: Studio owns it, routes Client telemetry/session/profile-analysis messages into it, renders it in Diagnostics, and translates its queued actions back into typed Client actions ([Studio ownership and rendering](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/app.rs#L80>), [message adapter](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/catalog.rs#L350-L376>), [Diagnostics and profiler actions](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-Studio/crates/vapor_studio_ui/src/app_shell.rs#L449-L487>)). The panel explicitly explains that a telemetry session is created by `vapor launch --current-workspace --profiling`, and that Steam launch options do not create one. Its Open Tracy button simply submits `DeveloperAction::OpenProfiler`; the service rejects fixture sessions and otherwise asks the host provider to open the managed profiler ([panel header and guidance](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_devtools/src/app.rs#L112-L146>), [service action](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session.rs#L1499-L1514>)). Thus “no active run” is a session-lifecycle limitation, not evidence that the button launches a capture itself; source inspection does not establish the precise message shown in the reported runtime case.

The diagnostics panel has useful foundations: resizable trace/inspector panels, a 1,200-record bounded log history, filtering, and bounded metric/snapshot histories. Its embedded console is separately rendered in a fixed maximum 180-pixel region and iterates all filtered retained records each frame rather than using the shared console panel's visible-row virtualization ([retention limits](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_devtools/src/model.rs#L8-L10>), [console rendering](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_devtools/src/app.rs#L263-L313>), [shared panel's visible-row renderer](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor-GUI/crates/vapor_gui_core/src/console.rs#L305-L380>)). This makes Devtools a concrete counterexample to treating console sharing as complete: it reuses record types and styles but maintains a separate panel and rendering path. No runtime session, large-log profile, or visual review was performed.
## October 26 — authored Workspace snapshots flatten dependencies before they reach the service protocol

The provider's source `ContentArtifact` retains typed `ContentKind` and structured dependency/conflict records; the source-editor projections also carry guarded manifest snapshots. The application boundary then creates `SourceContent` with `kind: String` and `dependencies: Vec<String>`, formatting each edge as only `relationship · id` ([provider artifact model](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_provider/src/content/model.rs#L14-L105>), [application projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/workspace.rs#L10-L21>), [flattening](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/workspace.rs#L158-L185>)). The service copies those values into `WorkspaceSourceProject`, whose protocol shape preserves both as strings ([wire DTO](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/state.rs#L411-L423>), [service projection](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_service/src/session/catalog.rs#L397-L414>)). The summary edge drops at least optionality, version requirement, Workshop identity and reason. By contrast, the separate local catalog protocol carries `CatalogDependency` with those fields ([catalog edge](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_domain/src/catalog.rs#L66-L79>), [catalog wire fields](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_protocol/src/state.rs#L454-L460>)).

This is a concrete split in the shared semantic surface: the authoring-workspace snapshot is currently adequate for source identity checks and display summaries, but cannot serve as a complete dependency graph for later resolution, compatibility, or lifecycle decisions. It is not evidence that the resolver itself has lost these fields; the loss occurs in this application/service projection. The same boundary also makes content-kind identity a free-form string where the provider has a canonical enum. The owner’s clarified model says Packs are typed selection manifests and content owns the reusable implementation and its compiled library/runtime artifact; Packagepack is the root playable selection and may carry its final executable. That is a design direction, not proof that current provider, catalog and Workspace DTOs implement one shared Pack/content graph. The October 18 shared Client extraction (`f9e8b13`) introduced the application source projection; the October 19 service move (`d7e21dc`) added the protocol snapshot and service mapping. Those commits centralized the route while retaining a lossy projection. No UI, wire round-trip, resolver, or runtime behavior was exercised in this review.

One adjacent ambient dependency remains: most application workspace operations take the selected application executable and derive `InstallationPaths` from it, but `remember_workspace` instead rediscovers the installation from inherited `VAPOR_HOME` or the process executable ([explicit path construction](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/workspace.rs#L150-L157>), [implicit exception](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_client_application/src/workspace.rs#L368-L374>), [discovery precedence](</home/leslieghf/Vapor/Vapor-Client/Vapor/crates/vapor_core/src/installation.rs#L87-L114>)). This is a consistency risk when callers operate on a non-default installation, not a reproduced wrong-installation write.
## October 26 — flight has three cooperating safety models, but no end-to-end braking proof

Current flight behavior is not one collision or travel system.
